wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.name: The US 2 pullout by the maintenance yard
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.notes: This is the roadhead and, realistically, the accommodation. The pullout sits roughly seven miles east of Stevens Pass at the east tunnel end. The route walks west along the highway shoulder for a few hundred yards, crosses the Nason Creek bridge and drops onto an old logging spur that parallels the creek to the railway grade; parties then follow the tracks a short way before scrambling up the bank at about 2,700 ft and climbing steep timber to snowline around 3,700 ft. A variation stays on the spur, crosses Henry Creek, takes the right fork and then the left to the bottom of a clearcut at about 4,200 ft, climbs the clearcut directly south and traverses east into the trees to gain the north ridge. TWO CAUTIONS THAT ARE NOT ABOUT CLIMBING. The highway shoulder walk is on a fast, busy road with poor sightlines and is more dangerous than anything above it, and the railway line is active — treat both as hazards to be got off quickly rather than as part of the walk. Winter parking here is genuinely tight and the shoulder is where the ploughs put the snow, so an early arrival is worth more than an early start.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.water: Nason Creek runs alongside and under the highway bridge the route crosses, and it needs treating. There is no potable supply. THERE IS NO WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN ITSELF once you leave the creek and the lower spur — the north ridge and the clearcut above carry nothing, so in summer everything is carried from here, and in winter the answer is melting snow.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.permit: None. This is not designated wilderness, there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no lottery anywhere on this peak. Highway shoulder parking needs no forest pass, which is worth knowing because the trailheads a few miles either side of it do. There is no fee and no registration. Note that the WSDOT rest area further along the highway is a rest area and not a campground, and overnight camping there is not what it is for.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.capacity: Shoulder parking and a pullout by the road turnoff for the maintenance station, with room for about three vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground, no fee site, no table and no toilet. In winter the plough berm decides how much of it exists on any given morning.

wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.name: The clearcut benches on the north ridge, around 4,200 feet
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.notes: Included as a contingency and as an honest negative. There is no reason to sleep on Arrowhead: the whole outing is six miles and three thousand feet and a fit party is up and down in seven or eight hours, so the only situation where this ground matters is a winter party that has broken trail through deep new snow, run out of daylight low down, and would rather bivouac than descend a steep wooded slope in the dark. Under those conditions the flat around the top of the clearcut at roughly 4,200 ft is the obvious place, being out of the timber and out of the terrain trap of the creek drainages. What you get is a snow camp with no shelter and no water; what you avoid is a night descent. In summer this same ground is slash and regrowth and there is nothing to recommend it. THE ROUTE IS CHOSEN FOR ITS AVALANCHE CHARACTER and is described as steep but safe by that measure, which is exactly the sort of judgement that changes with the year's snowpack — assess it rather than inheriting it.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.water: None whatsoever. Henry Creek on the lower spur is the last water on the way up and it is a long way below. In winter this is a snow camp and you melt; in summer you carry, and the amount you would have to carry is the argument against being here at all.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.permit: None — non-wilderness national forest and old logging ground, no permit, no quota, no fee. Fires are a poor idea in a clearcut full of dry slash and are prohibited under the summer restrictions that run most years on this side of the pass. Some of the lower spur network crosses a mix of ownership, so read the signs at the junctions rather than assuming everything is public.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.capacity: No established site of any kind. Under deep snow the clearcut and the flat bench above it give as much room as a party wants; in bare conditions there is very little usable flat ground and it is all slash, stumps and brush. Recorded to say plainly that nobody camps on this mountain, rather than to invent a site for it.

wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.name: Tumwater Canyon campgrounds on US 2
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.notes: The nearest developed drive-in camping to Arrowhead that is not already recorded in a neighbouring zone file, deliberately chosen over the Lake Wenatchee corridor camps for that reason. It is a drive of half an hour or so west along the highway to the pullout, which suits a party that wants a proper night with water and a table before a dawn start. The catch is the season: these canyon campgrounds run roughly late spring to early autumn, which is precisely the half of the year when Arrowhead is at its worst. FOR THE WINTER ASCENT, WHICH IS THE ONE MOST PARTIES WANT, THESE ARE CLOSED and the answer is a night in the vehicle at the pullout or a very early drive from town. Note also that the December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this district and a closure order covering them runs into 2027, and that a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026; neither touches the highway itself, but both change what is open either side of it, so check before relying on a specific campground.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.water: Piped potable water at the developed sites during the operating season, plus the river alongside. This is the one place where water is not a problem, and it is the sensible place to fill everything before driving up to the pullout.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.permit: A per-night fee at the developed campgrounds, with some sites reservable in advance and the rest first come, first served. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply through the summer in the canyon and are commonly total bans by late season — this is one of the driest and most fire-prone stretches of highway in the state.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.capacity: Small developed forest campgrounds strung along the highway in the canyon between Leavenworth and the Chiwaukum front, taking modest vehicles and a moderate number of parties. Sites are a mix of first come and reservable, and they fill on summer weekends with Leavenworth traffic that has nothing to do with the mountains.

wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.name: The lower spur and Henry Creek flat
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.notes: Recorded chiefly as the water point rather than as a camp, because knowing where Henry Creek is matters more on this mountain than knowing where you could pitch. The spur climbs east-southeast off the highway after the Nason Creek bridge, crosses the creek, and then forks twice — right at the first junction by an unnamed creek, left at the second — before reaching the bottom of the clearcut at about 4,200 ft. In winter the fork-finding is the navigational crux of the day and it is done under snow with the road cuts filled in, which is why parties who have been up before make much better time than parties who have not. As sleeping ground it is a poor substitute for the pullout, being no warmer, no flatter and a mile further from the car, and its one genuine use is for a party arriving in the small hours who would rather walk a mile and sleep than sit on the highway shoulder. Bring an axe for the steep timber above regardless of season; the slope from the railway grade to snowline is unrelenting.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.water: Henry Creek at the crossing, and Nason Creek below — both need treating and both run all year. This is the last water on the route and the only water on it, and its position at the very bottom of the climb is the whole water story of this peak: everything above is dry, so this is where you fill.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.permit: None. No wilderness, no permit, no quota. The spur network crosses mixed ownership in places, including railway and utility corridors, so read the signage at junctions and do not assume a road is open ground just because it is drivable-looking. No fee, no registration.
wa_arrowhead_mountain_south_route.capacity: Rough ground on the old logging road network in the first mile, where the spur crosses Henry Creek. Room for a tent or two on the road grade itself. Nothing established, nothing signed, and no reason to be here except timing.

wa_austera_peak.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
wa_austera_peak.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
wa_austera_peak.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
wa_austera_peak.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
wa_austera_peak.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

wa_austera_peak.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
wa_austera_peak.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
wa_austera_peak.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
wa_austera_peak.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
wa_austera_peak.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

wa_austera_peak.name: Eldorado Basin camp
wa_austera_peak.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
wa_austera_peak.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
wa_austera_peak.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
wa_austera_peak.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

wa_austera_peak.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
wa_austera_peak.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
wa_austera_peak.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
wa_austera_peak.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
wa_austera_peak.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

wa_austera_peak.name: Klawatti Col camp
wa_austera_peak.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_austera_peak.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_austera_peak.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_austera_peak.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_austera_peak.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_austera_peak.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_austera_peak.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_austera_peak.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_austera_peak.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come
