Around nine hours from the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side; the American approach over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River is far longer, on the order of seventeen miles, but is the one that keeps the permit straightforward. Expect mosquitoes.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.water: Running water at the camp, fed by semi-permanent snowfields just above; those patches are described as holding meltwater well into the later part of the season.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, Bear Mountain cross-country zone: maximum party of six and six permits per night. This zone cannot be reserved in advance — it is walk-up only, from the Wilderness Information Center. Cross-country camping is restricted to durable ground.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.capacity: No published tent count. The binding number is the permit: six people per party, six parties a night in the zone.

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Artist Point and the Heather Meadows road end
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: The obvious place to sleep is, plainly, the one place you cannot. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Silver Fir Campground
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: The closest developed campground to the Heather Meadows end of the highway, roughly fourteen miles east of Glacier on the west side of the road just after the river crossing, and about eight miles below the Heather Meadows lots. This is the practical answer for a party that drives up the night before a scramble on Table Mountain, Mount Herman or Mount Ann and wants to be at the trailhead early without sleeping in a day-use car park. It is emphatically staging rather than plan: you are three thousand feet below the objectives and the drive up in the morning takes twenty minutes. Because there are no reservations it is a gamble on a Friday evening in July and August, and the fallback is the campground further down the valley. It stays open later into the autumn than the road to Artist Point does, which matters for anyone climbing these peaks in October.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: Piped water at the campground during the operating season, and the river alongside. Confirm the water is turned on if you are arriving at the shoulders of the season.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: A campground fee is charged per night and paid on site; this is a fee campground rather than a pass site, so a recreation pass does not cover the overnight. Fires are allowed in the provided rings unless a county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry August is common. Standard national forest food-storage sense applies — black bears work this valley.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: About twenty sites in forest beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and drinking water in season; first come, first served, and it fills on summer weekends

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Douglas Fir Campground
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. This is a busy, family-friendly circuit and the sites go early on a summer weekend, so arrive with a plan for finding all four taken.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: The lakes, and they are reliable all season. There is no potable water anywhere on the circuit, so treat everything.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit is required or issued. Recreation pass on the vehicle at whichever of the four trailheads you start from. CAMPING IS RESTRICTED TO THE MARKED SITES — the meadows here are heather over thin soil and the designation exists because they were being destroyed. No campfires at all, carry-in stoves only. Party size twelve. Food must go in a bear-resistant canister or be hung at least ten feet up and four feet out from the trunk and branches; there is no hardware provided.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Bearpaw Lake
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: The base for Bearpaw Mountain and the only camping anywhere near its own line. Canyon Creek Road leaves the Mount Baker Highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north for a long, slow fourteen miles or so of alternating tarmac and serious potholes before a signed spur climbs right to the lake trailhead; the last couple of miles are single lane with brush closing in that will mark a car. From the trailhead it is roughly a mile to the lake, short but steep. The peak's easiest line is a class three scramble from the southwest, following the timbered ridge east of the lake, with a direct variation onto the steeper part of the ridge that gives a narrow and locally exposed scramble. ROAD ACCESS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK AND NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: Canyon Creek Road has been closed at around mile four by a landslide carrying large timber and debris, with more downed trees below the block, which cuts off the lake spur and the road end entirely. When that closure is in force there is no alternative approach to this peak, only a very long road walk. Snow lies on this ground into July in most years.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: The lake, at camp. Treat it. This is the only water on the peak's own approach and there is nothing on the ridge above.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE any designated wilderness — this ground sits west of the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary, so there is no self-issue permit and no wilderness party limit here, and the twelve-person rule and blanket fire ban that govern the Heather Meadows half of this zone do not automatically apply. What does apply is a recreation pass at the trailhead, and whatever county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry summer is usually a total one. Pack out everything including human waste; there is no toilet.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: A few rough informal sites at a small lake in the trees; low use, no facilities, no toilet and nothing built

wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.name: Excelsior ridge camps and the high spring, Canyon Creek Road end
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the established high camping on the Canyon Creek road system, at the far end of the same road that serves Bearpaw, and it is listed with the caveat that IT IS NOT ON BEARPAW'S OWN ROUTE. Bearpaw is the prominent summit standing to the west, seen across the drainage from the pass and the ridge, and reaching it from here means dropping and re-climbing rather than walking a connecting line. Its value is as the answer to what a party does when the day goes wrong or when they want two objectives out of one long, slow drive: legal, watered, established camping at the road end of a road most people will only want to drive once. The trail leaves the road end, meets a junction in less than a mile with the Canyon Ridge trail going left, reaches the small lakes just beyond and then climbs through forest and into open meadow towards the pass. The same landslide closure that gates the Bearpaw spur gates this trailhead as well; the alternative is to walk up from the highway instead, which is a far bigger day. Meadows here are at their best in July and August and again for autumn colour in September and October.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.water: A spring about half a mile short of Excelsior Pass is the best and most dependable water in this high country and is the reason the camps are where they are. The lakes lower down at the trailhead end are shallow and warm late in the season. Treat everything, and fill at the spring rather than counting on anything on the crest.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.permit: The ridge camps sit inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, which the High Divide trail enters at the pass — so from there on it is party size twelve, no campfires of any kind, carry-in stoves only, camp on durable ground and pack out all waste including human waste. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead and there is a self-issue register. The ground below the pass around the lakes is outside the wilderness and less strictly governed, but the burn bans still apply.
wa_bearpaw_mountain_scramble.capacity: Scattered informal sites on the ridge running south from Excelsior Peak and along the High Divide, plus a cluster near the spring; a handful of small parties, spread out, with no built sites and no toilet

wa_beckey_davis.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_beckey_davis.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_beckey_davis.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_beckey_davis.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_beckey_davis.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_beckey_davis.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_beckey_davis.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_beckey_davis.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_beckey_davis.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_beckey_davis.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_beckey_davis.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_beckey_davis.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_beckey_davis.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_beckey_davis.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_beckey_davis.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_beckey_davis.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_beckey_davis.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_beckey_davis.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_beckey_davis.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_beckey_davis.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_beckey_davis.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_beckey_davis.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_beckey_davis.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_beckey_davis.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_beckey_davis.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_beckey_davis.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_beckey_davis.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_beckey_davis.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_beckey_davis.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_beckey_davis.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_beckey_tate.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_beckey_tate.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_beckey_tate.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_beckey_tate.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_beckey_tate.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_beckey_tate.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_beckey_tate.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_beckey_tate.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_beckey_tate.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_beckey_tate.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_beckey_tate.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_beckey_tate.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_beckey_tate.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_beckey_tate.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_beckey_tate.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_beckey_tate.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_beckey_tate.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_beckey_tate.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_beckey_tate.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_beckey_tate.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_beckey_tate.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_beckey_tate.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_beckey_tate.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_beckey_tate.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_beckey_tate.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_beckey_tate.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_beckey_tate.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_beckey_tate.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_beckey_tate.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_beckey_tate.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_bedal_peak_standard.name: Bedal Basin, below the north side of Bedal Peak
wa_bedal_peak_standard.notes: The high camp for BEDAL PEAK, sitting directly under its steep north side and its cliffs, and the only sensible place to sleep for a party attempting the peak rather than just visiting the basin. Getting here is about two and a half miles from the road end at around 2,800 ft, climbing steadily through old forest and across avalanche tracks, and the trail deteriorates as it goes — it receives very little maintenance, is thickly overgrown in the avalanche chutes by midsummer, and effectively gives out about a mile and a half in, after which the way is up the rocky creek bed and through thin forest into the basin. Expect brush, wet feet and route-finding rather than a walk. The basin holds the remains of a pioneer cabin among the boulders, which makes a useful landmark for orienting the last of the approach. The peak above needs route-finding and, on most lines, real climbing rather than scrambling, so the short approach should not be read as a short day. The spur road itself is the other constraint: two steep, rough miles where high clearance is genuinely wanted rather than merely advised. Bedal Campground sits a mile down the main loop road from the junction and is the drive-in fallback for a party that arrives too late to start up the spur, and it is already recorded in the earlier upper-loop file. Snow lies in the basin into July.
wa_bedal_peak_standard.water: Bedal Creek and its meltwater feeders run through the basin and are reliable through the climbing season, thinning late in a hot August. The creek is crossed twice on the way up and both crossings are straightforward by midsummer but pushy in snowmelt.
wa_bedal_peak_standard.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS, which begins about half a mile up the trail — free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the road end, no reservation and no quota, and a twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass to leave a vehicle. Fires are legal in principle at this elevation but inappropriate in a small meadow basin with limited dead wood, and summer restrictions usually prohibit them outright; carry a stove.
wa_bedal_peak_standard.capacity: A meadow basin with room for several small parties on durable ground near the boulders, though flat spots are fewer than the open look of the place suggests. It is quiet — this trail sees very little traffic and you can have the basin to yourself on a summer weekend.

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Lower Anderson Lake
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM AS OF 2026: an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four, well below the road end, and that failure has closed the trailhead and the Sno-Park with no quick fix. When it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. From camp the summit is a short ascent to the southeast, and it is possible to reach the top without crossing glaciers at all, which is what makes this a scramble for a competent party rather than a rope-up. Immediately north the ground falls away past post-glacial moraine to the saddle above the green lake below the glacier, and that is the line onward for anyone continuing east or north across the range. It is a fully exposed shelf with nothing to shelter behind and the weather here comes across from Baker with no warning. The season is roughly mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse is a long snow slope, later and the water is gone.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier melt near camp through most of the season, and tarns in the moraine below. Late in a dry summer expect to be melting snow. Treat anything you find, and do not count on liquid water in early season when the whole shelf is still covered.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: This camp sits on the boundary country between the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness and North Cascades National Park, and which one it falls in decides whether you need a permit at all. Ask specifically when you plan the trip: the Forest Service side needs no overnight permit, while the park side needs a backcountry permit written for the correct cross-country zone. No campfires on either side of the line. Camp on snow, rock or gravel and never on the heather, keep well back from water, and pack out all waste — on snow and glacier that means blue bags carried out.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: Open ground for a couple of small parties on gravel, rock and heather about half a mile northeast of the summit; informal, with nothing built and no toilet

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward Berdeen, or for the long line north over the divide toward Hagan and Blum. What sets it apart from every other high site here is that it has water at six thousand feet, which nothing on the connecting ridges does. It is alpine meadow, so the heather is the thing to protect and the tent goes on rock. Snow covers this basin well into July and the lakes can still be part frozen at the start of the season. There is no shelter, no cell coverage, and no quick way down from here in any direction.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: The lakes, dependable and right at camp — the best water this high anywhere on the massif. Treat it.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required for an overnight, collected in person at the wilderness information center. No campfires. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste in a blue bag from snow and glacier ground. The party limit in a park cross-country zone is small — confirm the number when you collect the permit rather than assuming a Forest Service twelve.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: Room for a small party or two on alpine meadow and heather benches beside the upper pair of lakes; established by use rather than designation, with no facilities

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Berdeen Lake benches
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: The camp for Berdeen Peak and the substance of the Bacon Creek side of this zone. The documented approach starts at the Bacon Creek road end at valley-bottom elevation, scrambles up Porkbelly Ridge, crosses the east side of the peak around 6,400 ft and drops to camp above the lake — a very big first day with four thousand feet of gain, much of it trackless. The lake sits in a deep cirque a little over a mile east of Hagan Mountain and drains east over an enormous waterfall into a tributary of Bacon Creek, which is the geography that settles the argument about which road it belongs to: it faces Bacon Creek, not Baker Lake. It can be reached from the Blum Lakes over the divide to the northwest, but that is a traverse variation for a party already committed to a long trip, not an approach. From camp Berdeen Peak's east ridge is the way up, and the ground south and west continues onto the Bacon massif. Season is roughly mid-July into September, held back at the front by snow on the ridge and at the back by short days on a route with no trail.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: The lake and its inlet streams, fed off the glaciers above and reliable all season. Treat it. This is the first dependable water since the valley bottom, over four thousand feet below.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required for any overnight and written for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp — a different thing to ask for, and it must be collected in person at the wilderness information center, which is a long way round on the far side of the range from the Anderson Creek trailheads. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and never in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste. A bear canister is the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from; they can usually be borrowed at the permit office.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: A handful of tent-sized spots on benches above the lake shore; the basin is large but the flat, durable ground is limited, and this is a cross-country zone with a small party cap rather than an established campground

wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMPING ON THIS APPROACH and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brush with better travel once the ridge crest establishes itself, and no benches, clearings or water worth the name in four thousand feet. THE ROAD IS THE FIRST PROBLEM: it carries very large potholes over long stretches, a bridge on the main road beyond one of the side creeks has been out, and the spurs off it are variously blocked by missing bridges, washouts and downed timber, so how far a vehicle gets is a live question that changes year to year and adds miles at the bottom when it goes against you. A party that runs out of daylight on the ridge flattens a spot among the trees and moves at first light; that is the realistic use of this camp, not a plan. The same road end is the start for the Diobsud Creek side of Bacon Peak, which is climbed on a longer line past Salvation Peak with a glacier saddle camp around 6,250 ft — a spring and early summer objective needing snow travel gear, and a different proposition entirely from the summer scramble off the Anderson Creek road.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.water: The creek near the road end, treated. Above it there is nothing dependable until the lake basin high on the ridge, so fill everything before you start climbing.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.permit: The road end and the lower part of the ridge are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, where a night in a pullout is generally tolerated and no permit is issued. The ground higher up crosses into North Cascades National Park, so if you sleep anywhere above the lower ridge you need a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone. The boundary is not marked on the ground on this ridge, so ask at the permit office where it falls before planning a bivy rather than deciding on the hill. No campfires above the road, and total burn bans are common on this side through a dry August.
wa_berdeen_peak_scramble.capacity: Rough parking at the road end and whatever flat ground you can find in the timber; one party, found rather than chosen. There is no camp here, and that is worth saying plainly.

wa_beyond_redlining.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_beyond_redlining.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_beyond_redlining.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_beyond_redlining.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_beyond_redlining.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_beyond_redlining.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_beyond_redlining.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_beyond_redlining.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_beyond_redlining.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_beyond_redlining.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_beyond_redlining.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_beyond_redlining.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_beyond_redlining.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_beyond_redlining.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_beyond_redlining.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_beyond_redlining.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_beyond_redlining.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_beyond_redlining.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_beyond_redlining.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_beyond_redlining.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_beyond_redlining.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_beyond_redlining.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_beyond_redlining.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_beyond_redlining.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.name: Copper Glance Lake
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
wa_big_craggy_peak_scramble.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

wa_big_four_mountain_northwest_ridge.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
wa_big_four_mountain_northwest_ridge.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
wa_big_four_mountain_northwest_ridge.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
wa_big_four_mountain_northwest_ridge.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
wa_big_four_mountain_northwest_ridge.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.

wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
