wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
wa_buckhorn_marmot_pass.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.name: Boston Basin high camp
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.notes: The comfortable planned camp, roughly 6,300 to 6,400 ft on a sandy flat below a permanent snowfield, about three to four hours from the road. Everything on this route beyond it is committing, because the way onto the Boston Glacier goes over Sharkfin Col and that involves a rappel or a steep downclimb on poor rock that many parties describe as harder than the face itself. Coming back to this camp means reversing it. A lower camp at about 5,300 ft with its own composting toilet is the alternative if the upper sites are full.
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.water: Meltwater creeks and the permanent snowfield behind camp, reliable through the season
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required. Boston Basin is one of the small number of zones that accepts advance reservations, and composting toilets serve both the upper and lower camp areas.
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.capacity: Hardened sites; the zone allows six parties per night and up to twelve people per party

wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.name: Boston Glacier bivy
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.notes: A planned but fully exposed glacier bivy used to shorten summit day, on one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48. You are camping on a crevassed surface, so probe the platform and its surroundings before dropping the rope, and mark the perimeter. There is no shelter, no running water and no ground: everything is melted, and wind or a change in weather has nowhere to be dodged. The serious point is that it sits past Sharkfin Col — retreat from here means reclimbing that col, so committing to this bivy commits you to the route in a way that camping in Boston Basin does not.
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.permit: The glacier is its own cross-country zone on the park permit system, capped at six people per party and six parties per night; human waste on snow and glacier terrain has to be packed out in a blue bag
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.capacity: Whatever platform you cut; the Boston Glacier cross-country zone allows six parties per night, six people per party

wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.name: Sahale–Boston col bivy
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.notes: A tiny, spectacular perch on the col between Sahale and Boston, used by parties linking this face with other climbs in the basin or descending over Sahale Arm. It is an emergency-sized site, not a camp: there is room for one small tent, and cornices overhang the Davenport side, so probe out from the sleeping platform before settling in and do not wander in the dark. Wind exposure is total.
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.capacity: One small two-person tent's worth of flat ground

wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.notes: Around 7,600 ft at the end of the Sahale Arm trail, about six miles and 4,000 ft from Cascade Pass trailhead. It is the standard base for the southwest side of Buckner: from camp you drop east onto Sahale's southeast ridge, scramble down easy ground to a snow finger, and cross into Horseshoe Basin before starting up. Marine fog rolling through the camp overnight is common and can leave you with no view of the objective until morning.
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.water: Streams of glacier runoff beside the camp; filter it. Late in a dry season the flow can be some distance down the moraine
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required and is picked up in person at the Marblemount ranger station; the site is in heavy demand and reservations go through the park's lottery and booking system
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.capacity: A small number of built tent pads, each inside a low dry-stone wall — the walls exist because nothing shelters this ridge from wind. It is one of the most sought-after sites in the park

wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.name: Upper Horseshoe Basin bivy
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.notes: A cross-country alternative used by parties who would rather not depend on a Sahale Glacier Camp permit: descend into the upper basin and sleep on whatever ground you reach. The basin is a mix of clean granite slabs, snow patches and loose rock, and the lower basin is the awkward part to travel. It puts you at the foot of the southwest slopes, but it is genuinely primitive and the slabs that look flat rarely are.
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.water: Snowmelt in the basin; a matter of what is running when you arrive rather than a fixed source
wa_buckner_mountain_southwest_face.capacity: Informal — a party or two levelling a spot on slabs or snow, with no facilities of any kind

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Village
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Lake
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Leroy Basin
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Ice Lakes
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_buckskin_mountain_southwest_slopes.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_bulls_tooth_standard.name: Chiwaukum Chain Lakes
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Bulls Tooth and the only place a party should plan to sleep for the standard scramble. From the upper lake the route works around the shore to the base of a northwest-facing couloir filled with big white talus, climbs that to the ridge, and finishes on the summit block; the top section is reversed as a short, exposed Class 3 downclimb with no rappel, so no rack is needed; a short rope is optional for confidence. The rappels some parties describe belong to the lower, fang-shaped tower nearby, not this summit. Reaching the basin from the Icicle side is about two and a half miles and two thousand feet of climbing off the Icicle Creek trail on the Chain Lakes trail, which itself is roughly five miles and nineteen hundred feet from the junction — a full day with an overnight load. That trail was destroyed by a landslide a couple of miles south of Lake Josephine and has never been rebuilt to its old standard: it is passable on foot, it is not recommended for stock, and it is slow and vague where the slide crossed. From the west the basin is reached over Frosty Pass instead. Snow lingers in these basins into July in a normal year and the couloir holds it longer, which suits a party carrying an axe and hurts one that is not.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.water: Excellent and the reason this is the camp. All three lakes hold water through the season, the inlet streams run well into late summer, and the basin is the last dependable supply before the scramble. Everything above the lakes is dry once the snow has gone, so fill completely here for summit day. Treat it; the shoreline sees steady if light use.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register and covers both day and overnight use; there is no quota, no reservation and no lottery on this side of the wilderness, which is the opposite of the Enchantments permit zone a few miles south. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the Icicle Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this wilderness, which includes every lake in this basin — carry a stove. Party size is capped, camp on existing bare ground and keep well back from the lakeshores.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.capacity: Numerous informal sites spread around the three lakes, on benches and in the timber edges. There is room for several parties and you will rarely be competing for ground — the walk in is long enough from either end that this basin stays quiet even in high summer.

wa_bulls_tooth_standard.name: Doelle Lakes
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.notes: About one and eight tenths miles from the Chain Lakes over a gap that takes some six hundred feet of climbing, this basin sits at nearly the same height as the upper Chain Lake and is the more scenic option and it looks straight across at Bulls Tooth, which is the highest thing in view from here. It is the natural camp for a party that is traversing rather than going in and out — the usual line runs Icicle Creek to the Chain Lakes, over to Doelle, out past Bulls Tooth to Frosty Pass and down Wildhorse Creek to Whitepine, and this basin is the middle of it. As a base for the scramble alone it is slightly further from the couloir than the Chain Lakes are, so parties climbing the peak and returning the same way usually stay lower. The meadows here are exposed and hold weather; there is very little shelter and nights are cold well into August at this height. The connecting ground between here and the Chain Lakes is open enough to be simple in clear weather and genuinely confusing in cloud.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.water: Both lakes, reliable through the climbing season, plus snowmelt in the talus early. This is the other dependable supply in the group and the one to use if the Chain Lakes basin is occupied.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the trailhead register, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass at the Icicle Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 5,000 feet, and at this elevation the ground is thin subalpine meadow that scars for years, so pitch on bare gravel or existing sites and use a stove.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.capacity: Flat camping in alpine meadow threaded with talus, with room for several parties spread out. Genuinely lightly used — most people who reach the Chain Lakes stop there.

wa_bulls_tooth_standard.name: Frosty Pass and the Wildhorse Creek headwaters
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.notes: This is the pivot of the western approach to Bulls Tooth and the last camp before the peak from that side. The Frosty and Wildhorse Creek trail runs about eleven miles and thirty-five hundred feet from the Whitepine side to the pass, where it meets the Icicle Ridge trail; from the pass the high country opens out east and north toward Lake Grace, Snowgrass Mountain, the Doelle Lakes and Bulls Tooth itself. THE TRAIL IS NOT MAINTAINED BEYOND THE PASS, so the ground linking this camp to the peak is route-finding on open high country rather than trail walking, and it is the part of the trip most likely to go wrong in poor visibility. Lake Grace lies off to the side and is the better camp of the two if you want water you can count on and shelter from the wind, at the cost of some distance. Parties doing the full traverse come over this pass in either direction, and it works as well for a party who has climbed the peak from the Chain Lakes and is walking out west as it does for one coming in. Season is roughly mid-July through early October; the north-facing approach slopes hold snow late and the pass is a cold, exposed place to be caught out.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.water: Snowmelt and small streams in the headwater meadows below the pass on the Wildhorse side, dependable into midsummer and thinning badly by late season. The pass itself carries nothing you can rely on. This is the last water on the western approach before the high ground, and the Icicle Ridge trail east of here is notoriously dry, so fill in the meadows rather than at the crest.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the White Pine trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet — this camp is above that line and there is very little to burn regardless. Camp on the existing bare sites; the meadow here is fragile and heavily walked.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.capacity: Established ground at and just below the pass for a couple of parties, with more scattered spots in the meadows on the Wildhorse side. A crossroads rather than a destination, so expect the occasional through party in July and August and nobody at all in September.

wa_bulls_tooth_standard.name: Whitepine Creek valley camps and the Wildhorse junction ford
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.notes: These exist to break the walk, and on an approach this long that matters more than it sounds. It is roughly three miles of easy valley trail from the road end to the Wildhorse Creek junction, and then six and a half miles of climbing to Frosty Pass — a poor single day with a loaded pack after the drive out from the west side. THE CRUX OF THE WHOLE APPROACH IS THE WHITEPINE CREEK FORD, a few hundred yards short of the Wildhorse junction near the ruins of the old bridge. Early in the season with snowmelt running it is a serious crossing and it is the thing that turns parties round; by late July or August it is usually a boots-on wade with a stick. Camping short of it and crossing in the morning, when the flow is at its lowest and you are fresh, is the standard tactic and the right one. Coming out, most parties walk straight through. The valley is forested and pleasant and the walking is fast, which is the argument for the Whitepine approach over the Icicle one whenever the Icicle road or the French Creek bridge is out.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.water: Whitepine Creek runs alongside for the whole of this stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous part of the approach, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Frosty Pass and everything above it is a different story.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the White Pine trailhead register. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below 5,000 feet in existing rings outside a burn ban, but this is dry east-side timber and the district runs restrictions through most of the summer, so plan on a stove.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the first few miles of the Whitepine Creek trail, most taking one or two tents, each with its own bit of creek. Nothing developed and no toilets.

wa_bulls_tooth_standard.name: White Pine road end trailhead
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.notes: The staging point for the western approach and the shorter drive from anywhere on US 2. The road leaves the highway west of Leavenworth and runs about four miles of gravel to the trailhead at roughly 2,800 feet. Sleeping here rather than pushing into the valley in the dark is worth doing, because the ford above wants daylight and a party that arrives at it tired in the evening will camp short of it anyway. THE ROAD IS THE PART TO CHECK. The December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this whole district and a closure order covering the damaged ones runs into 2027; the Icicle road on the other side of the range carries multiple landslides limiting vehicles to the end of the road, and a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026, shutting more than sixty trails in these two districts. Confirm the White Pine road and the Whitepine and Wildhorse trails are open before committing to the drive, and have the Icicle side as a fallback rather than an assumption, because in some seasons it has been the worse of the two.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.water: Whitepine Creek is at hand and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill everything here before starting, since the good water lasts only as far as the valley and the high country above Frosty Pass has almost none.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is taken from the register here rather than arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Fire restrictions on this dry east slope are close to permanent through the summer and commonly ban all open flame including in rings.
wa_bulls_tooth_standard.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the end of the road with room for a modest number of vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground here, no facilities and no fee site — this is a roadhead, recorded because a party arriving late from the west side needs somewhere to be.

wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_burgundy_spire_north_face.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
