wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_cadet_peak_scramble.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_cadet_peak_scramble.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_cadet_peak_scramble.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_cadet_peak_scramble.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_cadet_peak_scramble.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Nada Lake
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_cannon_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Nada Lake
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: Entiat Meadows
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.name: Entiat Meadows
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.name: Carne Basin
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.notes: The only camp on the route itself: about 2.9 miles up, where the trail leaves the forest and levels into a small cirque near 6,100 ft. Nearly every party climbs Carne car-to-car and never needs it, but it suits anyone who wants the larches at dawn and dusk or the summit at first light. From the basin the top is a little over a mile and roughly a thousand feet further, past the Old Gib junction and up to the south-ridge saddle.
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.water: A small stream runs through the basin and is the first water since the fork low on the trail; treat it. Nothing above the basin can be relied on once the snow is gone.
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.permit: The basin sits below the point on the south ridge where the trail enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness; fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk, since the summit is inside it. Carry a stove and use the existing bare sites.
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.capacity: Several established sites spread around the cirque, enough for a few small parties.

wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. The free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_carne_mountain_trail_route.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
