wa_classic_route_3.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

wa_classic_route_3.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
wa_classic_route_3.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
wa_classic_route_3.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
wa_classic_route_3.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
wa_classic_route_3.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

wa_classic_route_3.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_classic_route_3.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
wa_classic_route_3.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
wa_classic_route_3.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
wa_classic_route_3.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

wa_classic_route_3.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
wa_classic_route_3.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.
wa_classic_route_3.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
wa_classic_route_3.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter

wa_classic_route_3.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
wa_classic_route_3.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. It has been closed through 2026 for a rehabilitation project, so confirm its status before planning around it. When running it is low, forested and warm, which makes it a reasonable shoulder-season option when the higher campgrounds are shut.
wa_classic_route_3.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
wa_classic_route_3.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.

wa_clean_break.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_clean_break.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_clean_break.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_clean_break.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_clean_break.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_clean_break.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_clean_break.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_clean_break.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_clean_break.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_clean_break.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_clean_break.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_clean_break.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_clean_break.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_clean_break.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_clean_break.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_clean_break.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_clean_break.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_clean_break.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_clean_break.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_clean_break.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_clean_break.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_clean_break.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_clean_break.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_clean_break.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_clean_break.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_clean_break.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_clean_break.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_clean_break.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_clean_break.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_clean_break.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Village
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Lake
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Leroy Basin
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Ice Lakes
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.name: Colchuck Lake
wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.notes: The base camp for the route, about 4-4.5 mi and 2,200 ft from the Stuart Lake trailhead. Parties heading for the couloir generally camp toward the far, south end of the lake so they are already at the moraine in the morning; a large flat boulder there is a well-used pitch. In cold conditions, camping back in the trees off the shore is warmer and far more sheltered than the open lakeside. Typical starts from camp run between about 3 and 5 a.m., which puts you at the base of the couloir in the couple of hours before the sun reaches it.
wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.water: The lake, which is often still part-frozen in the season this route is in condition.
wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October and must be obtained in advance through Recreation.gov, with the advance lottery running mid-February to 1 March. Group size is capped at eight, campfires are prohibited, dogs are not allowed anywhere in the permit area, and there is no dispersed camping between FR 7601 and Icicle Creek. Day use needs only a free self-issued wilderness permit. Because the quota season starts on 15 May, an early-spring ascent — when this couloir is normally in its best condition — falls outside the overnight permit requirement.
wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.capacity: Numerous sites strung along the shoreline and more clustered at the north end. Under the overnight quota the Colchuck zone issues a small number of permits a day, group permits included, so the camp is never as crowded as the day-hiker traffic suggests.

wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.name: Crag View, Squak Glacier
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.notes: This is the camp for Sherman Peak's Squak Glacier route and it is the site the Mount Baker file does not cover, since everything written there is on the Easton or the Coleman. It sits about 3.5 miles and 3,300 ft above Schriebers Meadow: the Park Butte trail past Sulphur Creek and the meadows, then a climbers' path leaving the trail around 4,600 ft and running up onto the moraine. From here the route makes a rising traverse of the Squak toward Sherman's south ridge, roughly 3,600 ft to the summit. The Squak is an early-season objective and the reason is specific — a bergschrund opens across the line as the season goes on and can shut the route down entirely by late summer, so a July plan is a different proposition from a May one. The lower part of the approach is outside the wilderness and carries snowmobile traffic into early July. Forest Road 13 off Road 12 is gravel and holds snow late; check it before a long drive.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.water: No potable water at the trailhead or anywhere on the route. Melt channels run near the moraine edge in early summer and are gone or unreliable by August, so plan on melting snow and carry the fuel for it.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit, but camping below 6,000 ft on this route is prohibited, which is the practical reason Crag View exists where it does. A recreation pass is required to park at the Park Butte trailhead. Party size is capped at 12 once you enter the wilderness, campfires are prohibited, and there is no toilet anywhere on the route — carry blue bags, which are handed out free at the ranger offices in Sedro-Woolley and at Glacier. Nothing may be buried in snow or dropped into a crevasse or moat.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.capacity: The established climbers' camp on the Squak, with room for several parties on gravel benches and snow platforms at the toe of the glacier; quieter than the Easton side even on a summer weekend

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.name: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.notes: Parties who want Sherman's summit day short move above Crag View and camp on the Sulphur moraine at the glacier's edge around 7,000 ft, or push on to the flatter ground below the rock prow closer to 7,600 ft. The gain is real, since it takes a good chunk out of the traverse to the south ridge and puts you at the base of the steep snow with the night's freeze still holding. The cost is a fully exposed camp on a volcano's south flank, where wind is the usual reason parties come back down to Crag View, and you are already on glacier and roped to get here. Camping this high also means committing to melt water, which drives fuel weight up. Where exactly the platforms are usable moves year to year with the crevasse pattern, so arrive with daylight to scout rather than in the dark.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.water: None. Melt snow. Anything running here in early summer is a bonus and will not be there later in the year.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness rules as at Crag View — no permit to camp, recreation pass at the Park Butte trailhead, 12-person party limit, no campfires, all waste packed out in blue bags.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.capacity: Dug snow platforms and moraine gravel for one or two parties along the right-hand edge of the glacier, with a second bench under a rock prow several hundred feet higher; no established sites and no shelter

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.name: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.notes: Colfax's three north-side ice lines — the Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano — all start off the Coleman somewhere near 8,000 ft, and this is the staging ground for a party that does not want to cover the whole approach from the Hogsback on climb morning. The important thing about it is where you do not put the tent: ice and rock come off the Colfax seracs onto this part of the glacier with some regularity, so the usable camping is out on the flats well clear of the fall line, never tucked in against the toe of the face because it looks sheltered. Many parties skip this camp entirely and climb these routes in a long day from the trailhead or from the Hogsback, which is a reasonable answer to the same hazard. These are cold-season routes, roughly late October into May, and the ice changes character completely across that window. Access is the current constraint rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road washed out in the December 2025 floods and has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, open to walkers and bikes at the contractors' discretion with repairs anticipated through 2026 — confirm the road before planning to carry a heavy load.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.water: None to rely on. Melt snow. Surface runoff sometimes appears on the rock of the buttes in a hot spell and should not be planned around.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight permit; camping is dispersed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge. Party limit 12, no campfires, no toilets on the route, waste packed out in blue bags available free from the ranger offices. Registering a climb is voluntary and worth doing.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.capacity: Dug platforms for a party or two on the flats out from the foot of the faces; no established site and nothing to shelter behind

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.name: Cougar Divide meadow camps
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.notes: This is the north-side approach to Hadley Peak and it has nothing to do with the Black Buttes or the Coleman — a party here is on the far side of the mountain from the Heliotrope Ridge climbers. Cougar Divide is an unofficial, unmaintained path along the ridge crest, reached from Wells Creek Road, whose first several miles are badly potholed to the Nooksack bridge and then improve. From the meadows at the head of the divide the ground opens onto Chowder Ridge, and the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley. The gate opening in July combined with mosquitoes that are genuinely bad here until midsummer pushes the sensible window to mid-August through early October, which is also when the talus is clear and the route is straightforward walking with the odd second-class step.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.name: Skyline Divide crest camps
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.notes: The other approach to Hadley Peak, from the west along the divide and over Chowder Ridge. The road in has been the problem for years rather than the trail: flood damage at around mile three has left the trailhead inaccessible to vehicles for extended periods with no firm repair date, and the trail has been listed as closed on that account, so this is the first thing to confirm and not an afterthought. When it goes, the crest is easy walking with big views and the last three quarters of a mile up to Chowder Ridge is talus with one steeper step before you top out west of the Hadley Glacier. Camping on the open crest means taking whatever weather arrives off the mountain, and the exposure is the reason parties often drop into the basin instead.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.water: None at the trailhead and none along the trail after early summer, when the snow patches below the crest are gone. Carry everything or plan the trip around a lingering snowfield you have confirmed is still there.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead. No campfires anywhere, party size capped at 12, all waste packed out. There is no permit or quota for camping, but the meadows are heavily used and heavily damaged, so camp on bare ground.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.capacity: Several exposed sites along the open crest of the divide once the trail tops out; popular and visible, with no screening from wind or weather

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.

wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
wa_colfax_peak_cosley_houston.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain.
