wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.name: Skyline Divide crest camps
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.notes: The other approach to Hadley Peak, from the west along the divide and over Chowder Ridge. The road in has been the problem for years rather than the trail: flood damage at around mile three has left the trailhead inaccessible to vehicles for extended periods with no firm repair date, and the trail has been listed as closed on that account, so this is the first thing to confirm and not an afterthought. When it goes, the crest is easy walking with big views and the last three quarters of a mile up to Chowder Ridge is talus with one steeper step before you top out west of the Hadley Glacier. Camping on the open crest means taking whatever weather arrives off the mountain, and the exposure is the reason parties often drop into the basin instead.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.water: None at the trailhead and none along the trail after early summer, when the snow patches below the crest are gone. Carry everything or plan the trip around a lingering snowfield you have confirmed is still there.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead. No campfires anywhere, party size capped at 12, all waste packed out. There is no permit or quota for camping, but the meadows are heavily used and heavily damaged, so camp on bare ground.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.capacity: Several exposed sites along the open crest of the divide once the trail tops out; popular and visible, with no screening from wind or weather

wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.water: The most reliable water on the Hadley approach — the creek runs from snowmelt above the basin and holds up later than anything on the ridge crests. Treat it. This is the reason to camp here rather than higher.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
wa_colfax_peak_polish_route.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Diablo Lake
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.notes: The practical staging ground for the whole west end of the corridor: directly under Colonial Peak and a short drive from the Pyramid Lake and Thunder Creek trailheads. Because it lies west of the usual winter gate at the Ross Dam trailhead, a handful of walk-in sites normally stay reachable through winter with no services and no fee — though a gate moved down to Newhalem would cut that off. Treat serviced opening and closing dates as approximate; they shift with snow and staffing. Arriving late on a summer Friday without a reservation is a poor plan.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.water: Potable tap water during the serviced season; no supply in winter, when Thunder Arm and the creek are the only sources and need treating
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway

wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.
wa_colonial_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Dispersed; a few flat spots at the lakes and a hidden pocket among the trees, enough for one or two parties

wa_columbia_peak_scramble.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_columbia_peak_scramble.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_columbia_peak_scramble.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_columbia_peak_scramble.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_columbia_peak_scramble.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_columbia_peak_scramble.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_complete_south_buttress.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
wa_complete_south_buttress.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
wa_complete_south_buttress.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
wa_complete_south_buttress.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
wa_complete_south_buttress.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

wa_complete_south_buttress.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
wa_complete_south_buttress.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
wa_complete_south_buttress.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
wa_complete_south_buttress.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_complete_south_buttress.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_complete_south_buttress.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
wa_complete_south_buttress.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
wa_complete_south_buttress.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
wa_complete_south_buttress.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
wa_complete_south_buttress.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_complete_south_buttress.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
wa_complete_south_buttress.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
wa_complete_south_buttress.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
wa_complete_south_buttress.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
wa_complete_south_buttress.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

wa_complete_south_buttress.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_complete_south_buttress.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
wa_complete_south_buttress.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
wa_complete_south_buttress.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

wa_complete_south_buttress.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
wa_complete_south_buttress.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
wa_complete_south_buttress.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
wa_complete_south_buttress.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
wa_complete_south_buttress.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Clear Creek Campground
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Squire Creek Pass
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass

wa_concord_tower_north_face.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_concord_tower_north_face.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_concord_tower_north_face.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_concord_tower_north_face.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_concord_tower_north_face.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_concord_tower_north_face.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_concord_tower_north_face.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_concord_tower_north_face.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_concord_tower_north_face.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_concord_tower_north_face.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_concord_tower_north_face.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Holden Village
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Holden Lake
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Leroy Basin
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Ice Lakes
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_copper_peak_south_route.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Wing Lake
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Lewis Lake
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
wa_corteo_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Diablo Lake
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: The practical staging ground for the whole west end of the corridor: directly under Colonial Peak and a short drive from the Pyramid Lake and Thunder Creek trailheads. Because it lies west of the usual winter gate at the Ross Dam trailhead, a handful of walk-in sites normally stay reachable through winter with no services and no fee — though a gate moved down to Newhalem would cut that off. Treat serviced opening and closing dates as approximate; they shift with snow and staffing. Arriving late on a summer Friday without a reservation is a poor plan.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.water: Potable tap water during the serviced season; no supply in winter, when Thunder Arm and the creek are the only sources and need treating
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit.
