wa_doorway_flake.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
wa_doorway_flake.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
wa_doorway_flake.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
wa_doorway_flake.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

wa_doorway_flake.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
wa_doorway_flake.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
wa_doorway_flake.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
wa_doorway_flake.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

wa_doorway_flake.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
wa_doorway_flake.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
wa_doorway_flake.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need

wa_doorway_flake.name: Squire Creek Pass
wa_doorway_flake.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
wa_doorway_flake.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
wa_doorway_flake.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
wa_doorway_flake.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass

wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.name: Eldorado Basin camp
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.name: Klawatti Col camp
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_dorado_needle_east_ridge.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_dot_mountain_scramble.name: Copper Glance Lake
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
wa_dot_mountain_scramble.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.name: Colchuck Lake
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.notes: The planned base camp for the route, roughly two and a quarter hours from the trailhead. Camp as close to the south end as you can — everything you save there is time you are not walking in the dark, because the moraine above the lake still adds about a thousand feet before the first pitch. The permit difficulty is why a great many parties simply climb the route in a single push from the car instead.
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.permit: An overnight permit for the lake's zone in the quota'd wilderness permit area is required from mid-May through October and is one of the harder ones to draw; outside that window permits are free and unlimited
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.capacity: Established sites along the west shore and around the south end; busy and competitive on summer weekends

wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.name: First large flat ledge low on the ridge
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.notes: An emergency bivy, not a camp. It is the first genuinely flat spot after the initial pitches and is normally used as a break and gear-sorting stance, but it is somewhere to stop if a party is benighted low on the ridge. There is no water, no shelter and no easy way off from here, so treat it as a place to survive a night rather than a planned stage.
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.capacity: One ledge, big enough for a party of two to sit out a night

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Holden Village
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Holden Lake
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Leroy Basin
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Ice Lakes
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_e_se_face.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_e_se_face.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_e_se_face.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_e_se_face.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_e_se_face.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_e_se_face.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_e_se_face.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_e_se_face.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_e_se_face.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_e_se_face.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_e_se_face.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_e_se_face.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_e_se_face.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_e_se_face.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_e_se_face.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_e_se_face.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_e_se_face.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_e_se_face.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_e_se_face.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_e_se_face.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_e_se_face.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_e_se_face.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_e_se_face.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_e_se_face.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_e_se_face.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_e_se_face.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_e_se_face.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_e_se_face.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_e_se_face.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_e_se_face.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Barclay Lake
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: The traverse of Mount Index's three peaks is the one objective in this zone that is genuinely an overnight rather than a long day, and this is where parties sleep. The line links South, Middle and North Peaks along a crest of loose ridges and gullies with rappels between them, and the recorded practice is a flat spot right on the crest between the two Middle Peak summits with snow nearby, which solves the water problem in early season. Parties who have done it in a push describe going light and treating the bivouac as an emergency plan that they were glad to have and glad not to need — take minimal gear rather than a full camp, because everything you carry has to come over some genuinely poor rock. Approach is the Lake Serene trail as for everything else on the mountain. The rock on Index is famously rotten and the descent options off the ridge are limited, so committing to a bivouac here means committing to finishing the traverse; do not plan it as a place to sit out bad weather.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: Snow on the crest into early summer, and nothing at all once it goes. On a dry traverse you carry water for the whole ridge or you drop off it.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: One small party. A flat patch on the ridge crest between the two Middle Peak summits — a stance, not a site.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Money Creek Campground
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Beckler River Campground
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.

wa_eagle_rock_scramble.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. It sits about eleven miles up the Index-Galena Road from US 2 at roughly 1,200 ft on the North Fork Skykomish, which put it within twenty minutes of the Lake Serene trailhead and made it the obvious base for Mount Index. Flooding washed out the Index-Galena Road near mileposts 10 and 14, the road is gated closed through that section with permanent repairs estimated in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the county has said environmental review and permitting may take several years. The campground is inaccessible and closed as a result, and the neighbouring campground further up the same road is closed with it. Confirm the road status before counting on it; if the gate is still shut, the working substitutes for an Index-area night are Money Creek down the highway or a dispersed pullout on the Beckler system. Nothing on the Reiter Road side fills the gap — the lower Reiter Foothills road corridor is state land signed day use only with no camping and a Discover Pass required, which is the approach used for Mount Persis, so plan Persis as a day out from the valley.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
wa_eagle_rock_scramble.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.water: Bean Creek runs through the basin and is the reason the camp is here, but it is a small east-side creek and by late August only one of the several channels may still be running. The dependable fill is lower down, where the trail crosses Bean Creek at the split with the Earl Peak branch — top off there rather than assuming the basin will provide, and assume nothing at all above the basin, because the climb to Earl Pass and the whole southwest ridge are dry.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A stand of trees at the edge of the meadow holds four or more multi-tent sites, and there are scattered singles beyond it; two or three parties fit comfortably and it fills on summer weekends. No toilet of any kind.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Beverly Turnpike camps at the Fourth Creek junction
