wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: The best all-round camp on the Beverly Creek side, ringed by the peaks it serves — Iron Peak stands to the southwest, Teanaway Peak to the northwest, and the Bean and Earl ridges close it in to the southeast. It sits two and seven tenths miles up the Beverly Turnpike trail from the Beverly Creek trailhead. For Iron Peak it is the east-side option, which matters because the standard approach from the road end is entirely waterless: a party wanting to sleep out before the scramble is far better off here beside the creek than dry-camped on the saddle. It also links Earl Peak to Iron Peak over two days without returning to the car, and it is the staging point for the Fourth Creek crossing north to Ingalls Creek, which involves fording Ingalls Creek and is genuinely dangerous during June runoff. Ground is forested and level, insects are moderate, and the camp is low enough to be warm at night well into September.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.water: Beverly Creek runs briskly right beside the camp and is the most reliable water anywhere in this group of peaks. That reliability ends abruptly at the junction: the sites up on the saddle where the Fourth Creek and Hardscrabble trails meet are dry, and there is nothing on the climb to Iron Peak's saddle from this side. A small running source sits roughly four tenths of a mile down the Hardscrabble side of that saddle, off-trail, and is worth knowing about if you have committed to the high ground and misjudged.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery. Northwest Forest Pass at the Beverly Creek trailhead. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness slip from the trailhead box covers travel where the trails cross the boundary north of here. No campfires above 5,000 feet, and expect a valley-wide burn ban from midsummer; this is dry, brittle east-side timber that has already carried one large fire.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A cluster of good sites near the creek holding four or five tents, spread over enough ground that two parties are not on top of each other

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Iron Peak saddle dry camp
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: A perch rather than a campsite, and included because Iron Peak's standard approach offers nothing else. The trailhead sits on the North Fork Teanaway Road roughly half a mile above the De Roux campground turn and a mile and a half short of the road end, at about 3,800 feet. The trail climbs a rib at a steady moderate grade with no flat ground and no water until it reaches the saddle, from which the scramble turns west up the ridge to the summit, and most parties continue on to Mount Teanaway from the same saddle. Almost nobody sleeps here and almost nobody needs to — this is a half-day objective for a fit party — but a group that has started late, or one linking Iron Peak with the Beverly Creek peaks over the divide, has this saddle as the only level ground on the route. It is windy, exposed and cold after dark even in August. If there is any choice at all, the creekside camps at the Fourth Creek junction on the other side of the divide are a far better place to spend a night.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.water: None. This is the defining fact about the route and the camp both. The Iron Peak trail passes a steep unnamed creek in the first eighth of a mile from the trailhead and then turns away from it for good; you can hear water in the gullies on either side for half the climb and cannot reach any of it. Carry everything you intend to drink and cook with from the road, and plan on more than feels necessary, because this is a south-facing, sun-hammered hillside.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: No permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Iron Peak trailhead. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation and there is nothing here to burn in any case. Pitch on gravel or bare ground; the saddle carries thin meadow that does not recover.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: A few flat spots at and just below the saddle between Iron Peak and Mount Teanaway; one or two small tents, no shelter, and nothing resembling an established site

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is PROHIBITED anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

wa_east_face.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_east_face.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_east_face.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_east_face.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_east_face.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_east_face.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_east_face.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_east_face.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_east_face.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_east_face.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_east_face.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_east_face.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_east_face.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_east_face.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_east_face.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_east_face.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_east_face.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_east_face.name: Cub Lake
wa_east_face.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_east_face.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_east_face.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_east_face.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_east_face.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_east_face.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_east_face.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_east_face.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_east_face.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_east_face.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_east_face.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_east_face.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_east_face.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_east_face.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_east_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_east_face.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_east_face_2.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_east_face_2.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_east_face_2.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_east_face_2.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_east_face_2.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_east_face_2.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_east_face_2.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_east_face_2.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_east_face_2.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_east_face_2.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_east_face_2.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_east_face_2.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_east_face_2.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_east_face_2.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_east_face_2.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_east_face_2.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_east_face_2.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_east_face_2.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_east_face_2.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_east_face_2.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_east_face_2.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_east_face_2.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_east_face_2.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_east_face_2.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_east_face_2.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_east_face_2.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_east_face_2.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_east_face_2.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_east_face_2.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_east_face_2.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_east_face_3.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_east_face_3.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_east_face_3.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_east_face_3.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_east_face_3.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_east_face_3.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_east_face_3.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_east_face_3.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_east_face_3.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_east_face_3.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_east_face_3.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_east_face_3.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_east_face_3.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_east_face_3.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_east_face_3.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_east_face_6.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_east_face_6.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_east_face_6.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_east_face_6.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_east_face_6.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_east_face_6.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_east_face_6.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_east_face_6.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_east_face_6.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_east_face_6.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_east_face_6.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_east_face_6.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_east_face_6.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_east_face_6.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_east_face_6.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_east_face_6.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_east_face_6.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_east_face_6.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_east_face_6.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_east_face_6.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_east_face_6.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_east_face_6.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_east_face_6.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_east_face_6.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_east_face_6.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_east_face_6.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_east_face_6.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_east_face_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_east_face_6.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_east_mcmillan_spire_west_ridge.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_east_ridge_2.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
wa_east_ridge_2.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
wa_east_ridge_2.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
wa_east_ridge_2.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
wa_east_ridge_2.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

wa_east_ridge_2.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
wa_east_ridge_2.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
wa_east_ridge_2.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
wa_east_ridge_2.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
wa_east_ridge_2.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

wa_east_ridge_2.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
wa_east_ridge_2.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
wa_east_ridge_2.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
wa_east_ridge_2.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
wa_east_ridge_2.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

wa_east_ridge_2.name: Slide Lake
wa_east_ridge_2.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
wa_east_ridge_2.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
wa_east_ridge_2.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
wa_east_ridge_2.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.

wa_east_ridge_2.name: Enjar Lake and Hamar Lake
wa_east_ridge_2.notes: The working camps on the western side of Snowking Mountain, reached by continuing past Slide Lake for roughly four hours of increasingly rough going. Either lake serves; parties pick whichever the light allows. From here Snowking is climbed on its west and northwest ground rather than by the east ridge and glacier line used from Cyclone Lake, which is the practical reason the two approaches are worth keeping apart. No elevations are recorded because no confident figures were found for either lake. This side is quieter than the Kindy Ridge side and correspondingly less travelled, so route-finding is on you and the boot path is intermittent to absent. Best from July into September, and expect wet brush on the way through regardless.
wa_east_ridge_2.water: Both lakes, dependable through the season. These are the last reliable water on the western approach before the ice.
wa_east_ridge_2.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit taken at the Slide Lake register. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Slide Lake trailhead. Camp back from the water, stoves only, pack out human waste.
wa_east_ridge_2.capacity: Unimproved lakeside spots for a party or two at either lake. No toilet, nothing established.

wa_east_ridge_3.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_east_ridge_3.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_east_ridge_3.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_east_ridge_3.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_east_ridge_3.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_east_ridge_3.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_east_ridge_3.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_east_ridge_3.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_east_ridge_3.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_east_ridge_3.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_east_ridge_3.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_east_ridge_3.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_east_ridge_3.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_east_ridge_3.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_east_ridge_3.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_east_ridge_3.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_east_ridge_3.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_east_ridge_3.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_east_ridge_3.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_east_ridge_3.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_east_ridge_3.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_east_ridge_3.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_east_ridge_3.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_east_ridge_3.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_east_ridge_3.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_east_ridge_3.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_east_ridge_3.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_east_ridge_3.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_east_ridge_3.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_east_ridge_3.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_east_ridge_4.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_east_ridge_4.notes: The base camp for the whole Southern Pickets and the one this route is built around: parties sleep here, climb, and come back to it, so plan two nights rather than moving camp. It sits about 400 ft below the 6,200 ft saddle the approach crosses, with flowers, running water and a full view of the range. The approach to it is roughly 7 miles and 6,000 ft of gain with no water at all on the last 3,500 ft, so fill up at the 1,600 ft crossing on Goodell Creek. From camp, the East Ridge is reached across heather and slabs and then the Terror Glacier below Inspiration's south side, which is low-angle but genuinely crevassed — rope up and carry rescue gear even though it is a short crossing.
wa_east_ridge_4.water: Streams run through the basin off the snowfields above and are dependable in a normal season, though heavy with glacial silt — filter and treat. In a heavy snow year the flow can be buried and parties have had to hunt a few hundred feet below camp for water coming off an outcrop
wa_east_ridge_4.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone. Terror Basin is not one of the six zones that take advance reservations, so the permit is walk-up. Pitch on gravel, rock or snow — camping in meadows or within 100 ft of water is not allowed
wa_east_ridge_4.capacity: Several tent spots on gravel and rock in the basin flats, plus a bivy platform sized for two; the Terror Basin cross-country zone is capped at six parties a night and six people per party

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends
