wa_east_ridge_6.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_east_ridge_6.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_east_ridge_6.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_east_ridge_6.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_east_ridge_6.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_east_ridge_6.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_east_ridge_8.name: Snow Lake Camp
wa_east_ridge_8.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
wa_east_ridge_8.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
wa_east_ridge_8.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
wa_east_ridge_8.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

wa_east_ridge_8.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
wa_east_ridge_8.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
wa_east_ridge_8.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
wa_east_ridge_8.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
wa_east_ridge_8.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

wa_east_ridge_8.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
wa_east_ridge_8.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
wa_east_ridge_8.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
wa_east_ridge_8.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
wa_east_ridge_8.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

wa_east_ridge_8.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_east_ridge_8.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
wa_east_ridge_8.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
wa_east_ridge_8.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
wa_east_ridge_8.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

wa_east_ridge_8.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
wa_east_ridge_8.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.
wa_east_ridge_8.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
wa_east_ridge_8.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter

wa_east_ridge_8.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
wa_east_ridge_8.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. It has been closed through 2026 for a rehabilitation project, so confirm its status before planning around it. When running it is low, forested and warm, which makes it a reasonable shoulder-season option when the higher campgrounds are shut.
wa_east_ridge_8.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
wa_east_ridge_8.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.

wa_east_slope.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
wa_east_slope.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
wa_east_slope.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
wa_east_slope.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
wa_east_slope.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

wa_east_slope.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
wa_east_slope.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
wa_east_slope.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
wa_east_slope.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
wa_east_slope.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

wa_east_slope.name: Tricouni Camp, Thunder Creek trail
wa_east_slope.notes: Despite sharing the peak's name this camp is about a mile and a half further up the valley than the point where climbers leave the trail, so it is a fallback rather than a first choice. It is worth knowing about when McAllister is booked out on the night you need, since a short extra walk each way costs less than losing the trip. The forest here is more open than at McAllister. Nothing about it shortens the climb.
wa_east_slope.water: Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek nearby, reliable through the climbing season
wa_east_slope.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit system and fees as McAllister — designated site, part reservable and part held for walk-up at Marblemount.
wa_east_slope.capacity: Small designated hiker camp, a few sites

wa_east_slope.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
wa_east_slope.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
wa_east_slope.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
wa_east_slope.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
wa_east_slope.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

wa_east_slope.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
wa_east_slope.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
wa_east_slope.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
wa_east_slope.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
wa_east_slope.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

wa_east_slope.name: Klawatti Col camp, Eldorado ice-cap traverse approach
wa_east_slope.notes: This is the multi-day route in, from the Eldorado side across the ice, and it is NOT how most parties reach these two peaks — it is recorded so the option is visible, not recommended as a shortcut. It is a genuinely different undertaking: full glacier travel with crevasse rescue capability, several nights on snow, and a committing exit. Camps are on rock islands surrounded by ice, so they are windy and there is no shelter. Choose it because you want the traverse.
wa_east_slope.water: Meltwater and snow across the ice cap; essentially always available in season but usually means melting
wa_east_slope.permit: A DIFFERENT approach means a different permit. Parties coming across the ice cap from Eldorado start in a zone that does accept advance reservations, but the zone boundaries out here are not obvious on the ground and a traverse can cross more than one. Sort the whole itinerary night by night with Marblemount, since a reservation for one zone is not a permit for the next.
wa_east_slope.capacity: Rock islands in the ice with room for a few tents; party size capped by the zone permit

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_east_wilmans_spire.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_east_wilmans_spire.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_east_wilmans_spire.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_east_wilmans_spire.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_east_wilmans_spire.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
wa_east_wilmans_spire.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_east_wilmans_spire.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_east_wilmans_spire.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_east_wilmans_spire.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_east_wilmans_spire.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_east_wilmans_spire.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_easy_getaway.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
wa_easy_getaway.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
wa_easy_getaway.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
wa_easy_getaway.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
wa_easy_getaway.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

wa_easy_getaway.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
wa_easy_getaway.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
wa_easy_getaway.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
wa_easy_getaway.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_easy_getaway.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_easy_getaway.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
wa_easy_getaway.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
wa_easy_getaway.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
wa_easy_getaway.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
wa_easy_getaway.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_easy_getaway.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
wa_easy_getaway.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
wa_easy_getaway.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
wa_easy_getaway.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
wa_easy_getaway.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

wa_easy_getaway.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_easy_getaway.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
wa_easy_getaway.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
wa_easy_getaway.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

wa_easy_getaway.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
wa_easy_getaway.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
wa_easy_getaway.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
wa_easy_getaway.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
wa_easy_getaway.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.name: Eldorado Creek Basin
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.notes: The usual first camp, about three miles and 3,300 ft from the car and the first flat, pretty ground after the long climb through timber and the boulder field. Camp on durable surfaces only — snow, rock or bare ground — and stay a hundred feet back from water; the meadow here is exactly what the rule is protecting. A comfortable planned camp, and the natural choice for parties who reach it late in the day.
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.water: Eldorado Creek and snowmelt through the basin, reliable
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.permit: A national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, reservable in advance and picked up at the ranger station in Marblemount
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Open camping on rock and gravel benches — no built pads; the zone allows six parties a night, twelve people to a party

wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.name: Roush Creek Basin
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.notes: A higher alternative to the basin below, reached by climbing to the rocky ridge near 6,100 ft and dropping a few hundred feet down the far side. That drop has to be re-gained on the way out, which is the main argument against it, but it puts you closer to the glacier toe with water still running. A planned camp, not a bivy.
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.water: Reliable running water in the basin
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.permit: Same national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Open camping on the rib and in the basin, between roughly 6,100 and 6,400 ft

wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.name: Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier saddle high camp
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.notes: The best-positioned planned camp, on the broad flat apron where the glaciers meet, with the East Ridge and the summit knife-edge laid out in front of you. It is entirely exposed — no trees, no shelter, and weather arrives with nothing in the way. Both the Eldorado and the Inspiration carry real crevasse hazard that gets worse as the day warms, so you rope up before you reach camp and again when you leave it.
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.water: Snowmelt only — bring a stove, there is nothing running at this height
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.permit: Same national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone. A composting toilet serves this camp; if you sleep away from it, human waste must go into blue bags and come out with you
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Flat glacier apron and rock beside it, roughly 7,500-7,800 ft; the zone limit of six parties a night applies

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Eldorado Basin camp
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Klawatti Col camp
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come
