Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: Eldorado Basin camp
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: Klawatti Col camp
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first three and a half miles are relentless forest switchbacks with nothing to drink. Stopping here makes the second day the good one. Note that the climbers' line for Elephant Butte does not continue to the lookout at all — it leaves this trail at an unmarked junction somewhere around four thousand three hundred to four thousand four hundred feet and turns north up the ridge crest west of the creek. No elevation is recorded for the camp because no confident figure was found. Both this camp and the trail it sits on have been closed by fire for most of the last three years; confirm before planning around it.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.water: Sourdough Creek runs at the camp and is the first water on the whole climb from Diablo — the lower trail has essentially none. Early in the season the crossing can be bridged by snow, which is worth treating with care rather than walking onto.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, collected at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing process. This is a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night rather than open ground, so a walk-up can be refused. A BEAR CANISTER IS REQUIRED here through the main season; the park lends them free at the permit desk. No fires. Pets are not allowed at the camp.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.capacity: A few tent spots only, with a hard limit of FOUR people on the site. That is the smallest party cap of anything on this approach and it rules the camp out for a larger group entirely.

wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.name: Pierce Mountain Camp
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.notes: About a mile east of the lookout, on the seldom-used trail that runs out along the ridge toward Ross Lake. Its value to this peak is as the other way in: a party can reach the same ridge system from the Ross Dam trailhead further east on Highway 20, going the long way around Sourdough Mountain, and that is exactly what a recent traverse did when the Sourdough trail was closed by fire. It is brushy and overgrown low down and adds distance, so nobody chooses it while the direct trail is open. The lookout itself is closed to the public and is not somewhere to sleep. No elevation is recorded because the figures found for it were not confirmable.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.water: The tarns beside the camp, and they are the only dependable supply on that whole upper stretch. They are shallow standing pools, so treat what you take.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. A bear canister is required here through the main season, as at Sourdough Camp. No fires.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.capacity: Small designated camp set among tarns, with the same limit of FOUR people. Assigned by night on the permit.

wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went for the summit from there. It is still a long way: from the ridge high point the ground drops something like fifteen hundred feet before you regain that and another thousand to the top, and a full trip is closer to twenty miles and ten thousand feet of gain and loss over two nights. Several strong parties have reached the ridge in a single push and turned round because the butte was still too far. The north-east side of the crest is very steep, so stay on it or just south-west of it. Snow-free is roughly late July into September, which is unhelpfully the same window in which the water disappears.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.water: Small tarns and snowmelt ponds scattered over the ridge — plentiful in late June, and the single best reason to come early. THEY DO DRY. By August in a warm year parties report water on the ridge becoming a real problem, and which pools survive latest is not documented anywhere reliable. Late in the season carry enough to camp dry.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. There is NO Stetattle Ridge zone — the ridge falls between the Sourdough zone and the Elephant Butte zone, and your permit has to name the one you will actually sleep in. Both allow a party of six and six parties a night. Neither is reservable in advance: they are walk-up zones, issued in person, with a share of the allocation held for same-day and next-day pickup. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow pockets that make the ridge look inviting, and not within a hundred feet of a tarn. NO FIRES in a cross-country zone. Waste in a cathole, or carried out on snow and bare rock. A canister is not formally required in these two zones, but the ridge is open ground with nothing to hang from, so bring one anyway.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.capacity: Dispersed cross-country ground rather than sites. Small grassy pockets and gravel benches recur the length of the ridge, easily enough for the zone's limit of six parties, and no two accounts stop in the same place.

wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in the corridor reachable in winter — a late-March overnight on continuous snow is a known way to do the ridge, with the caveat that spring sun softens the slopes badly by mid-morning. For a summer ascent of the butte it is a detour, since the climbers' line leaves the trail well below the lookout and never comes here. It also carries the same warning as everything else: the trail, both designated camps, and the Sourdough and Elephant Butte zones have all been closed by an active fire in the drainage, on top of an earlier fire that shut the trail for two and a half years before it briefly reopened. Check the closure status first; it is the single thing most likely to end this trip.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.water: Melted snow in the cold months, which is when this site makes sense. In summer there is nothing at the summit and the tarns further along the ridge are the supply.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Sourdough cross-country zone: six people per party, six parties a night, walk-up only. The lookout building is closed and camping is not permitted at it, so the site is the open ground near the top rather than the structure. Same durable-surface, no-fire and no-meadow rules as the rest of the zone.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.capacity: Open ground near the summit, a small party at a time. In winter and spring it is a snow camp with no defined pitch at all.

wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at walking-to-scrambling ground. The EAST ridge is a different proposition entirely and has been described by a party crossing it on a long Picket traverse as among the hardest ground of that whole trip, needing roped downclimbs and rappels — so do not read the easy summit as an easy mountain from every side. The named benches near the pass east of the butte belong to the traverse route rather than to this approach, and a party coming from Stetattle Ridge will not pass them. NO ELEVATION IS RECORDED: no account that slept on this shoulder coming from Stetattle Ridge stated one, and the figures published for the traverse-side benches describe different ground.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.water: Snowmelt and small pools, entirely seasonal. There is no dependable source and nothing to plan on. Fill on the ridge before committing to the descent toward the butte.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Elephant Butte cross-country zone: six people maximum, six parties a night, walk-up only from Marblemount. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail and out of sight of both, which up here is automatic. Durable surfaces only, no fires, waste packed out above treeline.
wa_elephant_butte_standard_route.capacity: No established site and no name. Parties travelling the crest report finding flat ground on the shoulder and on the benches near the pass east of the peak, tight enough that three tents felt crowded. Treat it as somewhere you stop, not somewhere you book.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: Spider-Formidable Col
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: Drop Creek high camp
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. It starts at the South Fork Cascade River trailhead, which is little more than a bend in the Cascade River Road around mile 17 to 18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, well below the road end at Cascade Pass. The first mile is maintained, then the trail deteriorates into ups, downs and overgrown nettle sections; past the Middle Fork turnoff you cross Drop Creek on a log and turn up into its valley on a climbers' path. That path fades after a few hundred vertical feet, but the forest above about 4,000 feet is open and the bushwhacking is unusually easy for this part of the range, with one short slide alder thicket below 4,600 feet. The camp is the obvious flat ground at around 7,100 feet with water, and from it the ground steepens to class 3 with a permanent snowfield near 7,400 feet and one narrow chasm crossing that is worth protecting. The whole approach avoids glacier travel entirely, which is why it has become the late-season choice, and recent trail work has made it the most pleasant it has been in years. Reckon on roughly twenty-five miles and eight thousand feet for the round trip.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: Running water beside the camp for most of the season, fed by the snowfield above, and a second reliable source lower down around 5,600 feet before the steep meadow climb. Late in a dry summer take the lower water seriously, because the high source is a snowfield that is shrinking.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is the usual requirement for the vehicle at Forest Service trailheads on this road, unlike the park trailhead at the end of it, so check before leaving the car. No fires at this elevation.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for a party or two, on heather and rock. Unimproved, no toilet, no windbreaks.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: South Fork Cascade River valley camps
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: The fallback first night on the Drop Creek approach to Formidable, for a party that starts late or is not confident of reaching the high camp in one push. It exists because the valley section is slower than its mileage suggests once the maintained tread runs out, with overgrown stretches and repeated small gains and losses. Camping here costs you the high camp's position and its view, and it means carrying the whole climb the next day, so most parties push through; it is recorded because the alternative to knowing it is there is a headlamp bushwhack up Drop Creek. No elevation is given because no confident figure was found for the usual sites.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: The South Fork and Drop Creek itself, running all season. Water is never the problem down here; the log crossing in high water can be.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Forest Service trailhead. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but it is damp valley forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: Rough forest sites along the valley trail and near the Drop Creek crossing, party-sized only. Nothing established.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: Le Conte Pass
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

wa_elephant_head_standard.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
wa_elephant_head_standard.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
wa_elephant_head_standard.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
wa_elephant_head_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
wa_elephant_head_standard.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

wa_ellation.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
wa_ellation.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
wa_ellation.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
wa_ellation.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
wa_ellation.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

wa_ellation.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
wa_ellation.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
wa_ellation.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
wa_ellation.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
wa_ellation.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

wa_ellation.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
wa_ellation.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
wa_ellation.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
wa_ellation.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
wa_ellation.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

wa_ellation.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
wa_ellation.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
wa_ellation.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
wa_ellation.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
wa_ellation.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

wa_ellation.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
wa_ellation.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.
wa_ellation.water: The river and its tributaries are everywhere and never fail, but the North Fork is heavily glacier-fed and runs opaque with rock flour. Filter from a clear side stream rather than the main channel where you can.
wa_ellation.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
wa_ellation.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

wa_ellen_pea.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_ellen_pea.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_ellen_pea.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_ellen_pea.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_ellen_pea.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_ellen_pea.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_ellen_pea.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_ellen_pea.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_ellen_pea.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_ellen_pea.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_ellen_pea.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_ellen_pea.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_ellen_pea.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_ellen_pea.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_ellen_pea.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_ellen_pea.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_ellen_pea.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_ellen_pea.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_ellen_pea.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_ellen_pea.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_ellen_pea.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_ellen_pea.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_ellen_pea.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_ellen_pea.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_ellen_pea.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_ellen_pea.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_ellen_pea.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_ellen_pea.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_ellen_pea.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_ellen_pea.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Entiat Meadows
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in.
