That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Entiat Meadows
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.water: Bean Creek runs through the basin and is the reason the camp is here, but it is a small east-side creek and by late August only one of the several channels may still be running. The dependable fill is lower down, where the trail crosses Bean Creek at the split with the Earl Peak branch — top off there rather than assuming the basin will provide, and assume nothing at all above the basin, because the climb to Earl Pass and the whole southwest ridge are dry.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.capacity: A stand of trees at the edge of the meadow holds four or more multi-tent sites, and there are scattered singles beyond it; two or three parties fit comfortably and it fills on summer weekends. No toilet of any kind.

wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.name: Beverly Turnpike camps at the Fourth Creek junction
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.notes: The best all-round camp on the Beverly Creek side, ringed by the peaks it serves — Iron Peak stands to the southwest, Teanaway Peak to the northwest, and the Bean and Earl ridges close it in to the southeast. It sits two and seven tenths miles up the Beverly Turnpike trail from the Beverly Creek trailhead. For Iron Peak it is the east-side option, which matters because the standard approach from the road end is entirely waterless: a party wanting to sleep out before the scramble is far better off here beside the creek than dry-camped on the saddle. It also links Earl Peak to Iron Peak over two days without returning to the car, and it is the staging point for the Fourth Creek crossing north to Ingalls Creek, which involves fording Ingalls Creek and is genuinely dangerous during June runoff. Ground is forested and level, insects are moderate, and the camp is low enough to be warm at night well into September.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.water: Beverly Creek runs briskly right beside the camp and is the most reliable water anywhere in this group of peaks. That reliability ends abruptly at the junction: the sites up on the saddle where the Fourth Creek and Hardscrabble trails meet are dry, and there is nothing on the climb to Iron Peak's saddle from this side. A small running source sits roughly four tenths of a mile down the Hardscrabble side of that saddle, off-trail, and is worth knowing about if you have committed to the high ground and misjudged.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery. Northwest Forest Pass at the Beverly Creek trailhead. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness slip from the trailhead box covers travel where the trails cross the boundary north of here. No campfires above 5,000 feet, and expect a valley-wide burn ban from midsummer; this is dry, brittle east-side timber that has already carried one large fire.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.capacity: A cluster of good sites near the creek holding four or five tents, spread over enough ground that two parties are not on top of each other

wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group

wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.name: Iron Peak saddle dry camp
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.notes: A perch rather than a campsite, and included because Iron Peak's standard approach offers nothing else. The trailhead sits on the North Fork Teanaway Road roughly half a mile above the De Roux campground turn and a mile and a half short of the road end, at about 3,800 feet. The trail climbs a rib at a steady moderate grade with no flat ground and no water until it reaches the saddle, from which the scramble turns west up the ridge to the summit, and most parties continue on to Mount Teanaway from the same saddle. Almost nobody sleeps here and almost nobody needs to — this is a half-day objective for a fit party — but a group that has started late, or one linking Iron Peak with the Beverly Creek peaks over the divide, has this saddle as the only level ground on the route. It is windy, exposed and cold after dark even in August. If there is any choice at all, the creekside camps at the Fourth Creek junction on the other side of the divide are a far better place to spend a night.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.water: None. This is the defining fact about the route and the camp both. The Iron Peak trail passes a steep unnamed creek in the first eighth of a mile from the trailhead and then turns away from it for good; you can hear water in the gullies on either side for half the climb and cannot reach any of it. Carry everything you intend to drink and cook with from the road, and plan on more than feels necessary, because this is a south-facing, sun-hammered hillside.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.permit: No permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Iron Peak trailhead. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation and there is nothing here to burn in any case. Pitch on gravel or bare ground; the saddle carries thin meadow that does not recover.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.capacity: A few flat spots at and just below the saddle between Iron Peak and Mount Teanaway; one or two small tents, no shelter, and nothing resembling an established site

wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is PROHIBITED anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
wa_esmeralda_peaks_scramble.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Entiat Meadows
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_first_amendment.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_first_amendment.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_first_amendment.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_first_amendment.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_first_amendment.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_first_amendment.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_first_amendment.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_first_amendment.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_first_amendment.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_first_amendment.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_first_amendment.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_first_amendment.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_first_amendment.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_first_amendment.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_first_amendment.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_first_amendment.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_first_amendment.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_first_amendment.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_first_amendment.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_first_amendment.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_first_amendment.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_first_amendment.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_first_amendment.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_first_amendment.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_first_amendment.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_first_amendment.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_first_amendment.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_first_amendment.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_first_amendment.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_first_amendment.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_fish_whistle.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
wa_fish_whistle.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_fish_whistle.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_fish_whistle.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_fish_whistle.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_fish_whistle.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_fish_whistle.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_fish_whistle.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_fish_whistle.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_fish_whistle.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_fish_whistle.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_fish_whistle.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_fish_whistle.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_fish_whistle.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_fish_whistle.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_fish_whistle.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_fish_whistle.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_fish_whistle.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_fish_whistle.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_fish_whistle.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_fish_whistle.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_fish_whistle.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_fish_whistle.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_fish_whistle.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_fish_whistle.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_fish_whistle.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_fish_whistle.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_fish_whistle.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_fish_whistle.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_fish_whistle.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.name: Clear Creek Campground
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.name: Squire Creek Pass
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass

wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
