wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Glacier Gap
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.name: Mackinaw Shelter
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.notes: PLANNED low camp and the last reliable flat ground with running water before the trail steepens. Roughly five miles in, in forest. Most parties either sleep here on night one of a three-day trip or top off water here, because there is nothing dependable between here and White Pass — that stretch is 2,000 ft of switchbacks.
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.water: North Fork Sauk River at camp
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.capacity: several parties; established riverside sites around the old shelter

wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.name: White Pass
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.notes: PLANNED camp at the effective end of maintained trail, where the climbers' path toward Glacier Gap begins. Open meadow with good sites but no dependable water once the snow is gone, so treat it as a place you may have to carry into. Camp on durable ground — these meadows are heavily used.
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.water: seasonal snowmelt and seeps; can be dry late in the year
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.capacity: several parties in the meadow sites at the PCT junction

wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.name: Glacier Gap
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.notes: PLANNED high camp and the standard staging point for the Cool Glacier and the cleaver. Plenty of established gravel sites with rock walls already built, which exist because the gap funnels wind — it is known for wind and for storms rolling through after dark, so use the walls and pitch low. Some sites are dry camps; the seep below camp is the dependable one and it is the last water on the route. The last mile and a half in is loose scree and boulders.
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.water: a running seep just below camp, plus snowmelt; two sources within a few minutes' walk in most seasons
wa_glacier_peak_disappointment_peak_clea.capacity: many sites, several with stacked rock windbreaks

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes: PLANNED high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes: EMERGENCY only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Glacier Gap
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.name: Boulder Basin
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a forested ridge with a full pack. It is about ten miles from the road end, and the road itself has a long history of washouts, so confirm where the trailhead actually is before you plan the day.
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.water: Waterfalls and snowmelt streams run through the basin; dependable into late summer but shrinking as the season goes on. Filter it
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.permit: No backcountry permit is required for overnight use in this wilderness
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.capacity: Several established sites on heather and rock benches at treeline, spread through the basin between roughly 5,500 and 6,000 ft

wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard camp.
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.capacity: A small forested site or two just north of the trail junction

wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.notes: The lowest planned stop, about 5.5 miles in and still widely used. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Useful as a first night for parties splitting the approach, or as a retreat in bad weather, but it is a long way and a lot of gain below the glacier.

wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.name: Last stream crossing, top of the forest
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.notes: Listed for the water rather than for the camping, and the water is the point. The trail climbs steeply from the trailhead through about a dozen switchbacks in the first mile and stays in deep forest for two and a half, crossing several small creeks on the way; the highest of them sits right where the trees thin into heather and huckleberry. Above this line the mountain gives you nothing. Parties heading to the benches or the crest should stop here, top up, and accept carrying the weight for the last stretch. Late in a dry summer even these crossings run thin, so do not assume the lower ones are still flowing on the way down. Elevation is not stated because the exact crossing shifts with the season and the snowpack; navigate to it by the transition out of the timber, not by an altimeter reading.
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.water: THIS IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN, at roughly mile 2.7 where the final creeks cross the tread. Treat it. Everything on the ridge above is dry, so fill every container here whether or not you intend to camp
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary the trail crosses around mile 2. No overnight permit is required and none is issued. Twelve-person party limit. Campfires are not permitted on this trail, so carry a stove. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid here. Black bears work this slope in huckleberry season and food must be secured overnight
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: One or two tents on rough ground beside the trail where the timber gives out; there is no established site and the slope is steep, so flat spots are few

wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.name: Open benches on the broad ridge
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.notes: The best camping on the mountain if you are willing to haul water, and the natural base for the south ridge scramble. A series of level shelves on a broad, open ridge above treeline, past a viewpoint knob near 5,200 ft, with Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit filling the skyline and the Border Peaks and the Pickets beyond. From here the maintained trail continues to its end on the shoulder and the scramble to the summits goes on from there, so a camp at the benches leaves a short and pleasant summit morning. The slope faces south and melts early, so this is usually accessible from late June, sometimes earlier; the trade is that it bakes and stays dry all summer. It is fully exposed to wind and to weather rolling in from the west with nothing to duck behind. Excellent huckleberries in early autumn, and bears know it.
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.water: NONE. Everything must be carried up from the last crossing in the forest. Snow patches linger into July in shaded pockets and can be melted early in the season, but by August the whole crest is dry
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead. No campfires. Camp on bare ground, gravel or an existing flat rather than in the heather, and store food securely against bears
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: Two or three small tents spread across the benches, kept apart so the heather is not trampled into one bare patch

wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.name: Ridge crest at the end of the maintained trail
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.notes: The highest ground with anything like a flat pitch, where the maintained trail ends on Goat Mountain's shoulder and the route becomes a steep boot path up grass and heather to the false summit and the west peak. The crest carries on upward from here toward 5,600 ft and above, and the east peak, which is the higher of the two, is a further meadow scramble along the ridge with no trail. Camping here shortens summit day to almost nothing, which is the only argument for it: it is stony, cramped and completely exposed, and it is the driest spot on a dry mountain. Snow can lie across the upper slope into July and the grass traverse above is genuinely slippery when wet, so this is a fair-weather choice. Sunrise and sunset from the crest are the reason people put up with all of it.
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.water: NONE, and the nearest is the forest crossings far below. In early season there are snow patches on the north side of the crest to melt; from midsummer there is nothing at all
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. This is national forest rather than national park — the park boundary lies well east beyond Hannegan Pass — so no park backcountry permit applies
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: One or two tents on the shoulder where the tread runs out; small, stony and windy

wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.name: Basin below the east peak
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.notes: The one camp on Goat Mountain that solves the water problem, in the basin lying east and below the higher east peak, seen from the overlook near the top of the maintained trail. It has ample flat terrain and running water, which nothing on the ridge does. The cost is that reaching it means leaving the trail entirely and dropping off the crest on trackless ground, which is more commitment than most parties want for a scramble that can be done in a day from the benches — so it is chosen mainly by people camping two nights, going for the east summit as well as the west, or arriving too late in the season for the crest to hold snow. Approach it from the end of the maintained trail rather than trying to contour in low. No elevation is given because the usable ground spreads across the basin floor rather than sitting at one identifiable spot.
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.water: Present, which makes this basin unique here — snowmelt streams and pools that last well into the season, unlike anything on the crest. Treat it, and check that it is still running before relying on it in a dry late summer
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. Camp on durable ground away from the water and secure food overnight
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.capacity: Two or three tents with room to spread out; the most generous ground on the mountain

wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
wa_golden_horn_north_face.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
wa_golden_horn_north_face.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: Granite Pass
wa_golden_horn_north_face.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: Snowy Lakes basin
wa_golden_horn_north_face.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.

wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
wa_golden_horn_north_face.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
wa_golden_horn_north_face.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.

wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.name: North Fork Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT junction
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.notes: This sits right at the junction where the PCT leaves Bridge Creek for the North Fork, roughly ten miles in from the SR 20 trailhead, so it is the natural first-night stop for a party that started late. It is a long way below the climb, which means a very big second day to reach the glacier bivies. Its value is logistical rather than tactical — it shortens the drive-day push without needing a cross-country zone permit. Being a valley-bottom camp in forest, expect bugs through midsummer.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.water: Reliable year round — Bridge Creek and the North Fork run beside the camp
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round; reserve the specific camp on Recreation.gov or take a walk-up from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee applies.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.capacity: Small designated hiker camp with a handful of numbered sites; the site is reserved by name on the permit

wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.name: Walker Park Camp
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.notes: Roughly two miles up the North Fork trail from the junction, this is the first camp that meaningfully shortens the walk to the Goode Glacier drainage. The tread to here is still ordinary maintained trail, so it is an easy target even arriving in the dark. Parties usually treat it as a place to shed weight rather than a base, since the climb is still hours of rough ground above. No elevation is recorded — the valley section stays well under 4,000 ft, but no confident figure was sourced.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.water: Reliable — sits on the North Fork of Bridge Creek
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.permit: Designated-camp permit, booked by camp name; same NPS fee structure as any Bridge Creek camp, and it must be carried for the night you actually sleep there.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.capacity: Small designated camp, a couple of parties at most

wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.name: Grizzly Creek Camp
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.notes: About four miles up the North Fork trail, this is the last designated camp before the country turns unpleasant, and the practical decision point for the whole approach. Beyond it the tread gets brushy and faint — stinging nettles are a recurring complaint and long trousers are worth carrying regardless of the heat — and the North Fork has to be forded or crossed on a log, with difficulty that swings hard with snowmelt. A party arriving late, or facing high water, is usually better off sleeping here than committing to the bushwhack and the crossing in poor light.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.water: Reliable — Grizzly Creek and the North Fork are both at hand
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.permit: Designated-camp permit reserved by name through Recreation.gov or issued walk-up at Marblemount; per-person and reservation fees apply.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.capacity: Larger than the other North Fork camps and open to stock parties, so you may be sharing it

wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.name: Fireweed Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.notes: A Bridge Creek corridor camp on the PCT well short of the North Fork junction, near the Twisp Pass trail area. It is only useful to a Goode party as an overflow choice when the North Fork camps are booked out, which happens in peak season because so few sites serve this valley. Camping here adds miles to an already long approach day. Treat it as a fallback rather than a plan.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.permit: Designated-camp permit, same Recreation.gov / Marblemount walk-up system and the same per-person and reservation fees.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.capacity: Designated camp with hiker and stock use

wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.name: Goode Glacier approach bivy, timbered knoll
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.notes: Reached by leaving the North Fork trail after Grizzly Creek, fording the creek and grinding up timber and scree beside the drainage off the Goode Glacier, this is the classic first bivy under the buttress. Reports differ on whether it is the better choice: it sits noticeably west of the line of travel, so some parties consider the extra push to higher ground worth doing. Sparse timber gives a little shelter, which matters more here than the small elevation saving. Human waste goes in a cathole or is packed out above treeline, and there is no toilet.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.water: Meltwater from the Goode Glacier drainage nearby, but flow is seasonal and can be a walk away or thin late in the year
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.permit: Inside the Goode CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE, not a designated camp — the permit is issued for the zone, party size is capped at six, no campfires, and camping is only allowed on durable ground such as snow, rock or bare earth.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small tents on a timbered knoll

wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.name: Upper bivy in the rock bands east of the buttress toe
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.notes: Sitting in the rock bands just east of where the Northeast Buttress meets the ground, this puts you at the base with a few hundred feet already banked for summit day, which is the argument for grinding past the lower knoll. The exact elevation is reported inconsistently — figures in the 5,400 to 5,600 ft range all refer to broadly the same shelf system, so navigate to the terrain rather than to a number. It is exposed and rocky, so a poor choice in unsettled weather compared with the timbered ground lower down. Confirm you have water before committing to it late in the summer.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.water: Running meltwater has been found at or near these sites, but it is snow-fed and not dependable once the drainage dries out later in the season
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.permit: Goode cross-country zone permit, six-person maximum, no fires, durable surfaces only; zone camping must also keep clear of designated camps and trails by the park's stated distances.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge.capacity: Tight — commonly described as just enough flat ground for a party of about four
