wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.name: Crag View, Squak Glacier
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.notes: This is the camp for Sherman Peak's Squak Glacier route and it is the site the Mount Baker file does not cover, since everything written there is on the Easton or the Coleman. It sits about 3.5 miles and 3,300 ft above Schriebers Meadow: the Park Butte trail past Sulphur Creek and the meadows, then a climbers' path leaving the trail around 4,600 ft and running up onto the moraine. From here the route makes a rising traverse of the Squak toward Sherman's south ridge, roughly 3,600 ft to the summit. The Squak is an early-season objective and the reason is specific — a bergschrund opens across the line as the season goes on and can shut the route down entirely by late summer, so a July plan is a different proposition from a May one. The lower part of the approach is outside the wilderness and carries snowmobile traffic into early July. Forest Road 13 off Road 12 is gravel and holds snow late; check it before a long drive.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.water: No potable water at the trailhead or anywhere on the route. Melt channels run near the moraine edge in early summer and are gone or unreliable by August, so plan on melting snow and carry the fuel for it.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit, but camping below 6,000 ft on this route is prohibited, which is the practical reason Crag View exists where it does. A recreation pass is required to park at the Park Butte trailhead. Party size is capped at 12 once you enter the wilderness, campfires are prohibited, and there is no toilet anywhere on the route — carry blue bags, which are handed out free at the ranger offices in Sedro-Woolley and at Glacier. Nothing may be buried in snow or dropped into a crevasse or moat.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.capacity: The established climbers' camp on the Squak, with room for several parties on gravel benches and snow platforms at the toe of the glacier; quieter than the Easton side even on a summer weekend

wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.name: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.notes: Parties who want Sherman's summit day short move above Crag View and camp on the Sulphur moraine at the glacier's edge around 7,000 ft, or push on to the flatter ground below the rock prow closer to 7,600 ft. The gain is real, since it takes a good chunk out of the traverse to the south ridge and puts you at the base of the steep snow with the night's freeze still holding. The cost is a fully exposed camp on a volcano's south flank, where wind is the usual reason parties come back down to Crag View, and you are already on glacier and roped to get here. Camping this high also means committing to melt water, which drives fuel weight up. Where exactly the platforms are usable moves year to year with the crevasse pattern, so arrive with daylight to scout rather than in the dark.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.water: None. Melt snow. Anything running here in early summer is a bonus and will not be there later in the year.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness rules as at Crag View — no permit to camp, recreation pass at the Park Butte trailhead, 12-person party limit, no campfires, all waste packed out in blue bags.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.capacity: Dug snow platforms and moraine gravel for one or two parties along the right-hand edge of the glacier, with a second bench under a rock prow several hundred feet higher; no established sites and no shelter

wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.name: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.notes: Colfax's three north-side ice lines — the Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano — all start off the Coleman somewhere near 8,000 ft, and this is the staging ground for a party that does not want to cover the whole approach from the Hogsback on climb morning. The important thing about it is where you do not put the tent: ice and rock come off the Colfax seracs onto this part of the glacier with some regularity, so the usable camping is out on the flats well clear of the fall line, never tucked in against the toe of the face because it looks sheltered. Many parties skip this camp entirely and climb these routes in a long day from the trailhead or from the Hogsback, which is a reasonable answer to the same hazard. These are cold-season routes, roughly late October into May, and the ice changes character completely across that window. Access is the current constraint rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road washed out in the December 2025 floods and has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, open to walkers and bikes at the contractors' discretion with repairs anticipated through 2026 — confirm the road before planning to carry a heavy load.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.water: None to rely on. Melt snow. Surface runoff sometimes appears on the rock of the buttes in a hot spell and should not be planned around.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight permit; camping is dispersed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge. Party limit 12, no campfires, no toilets on the route, waste packed out in blue bags available free from the ranger offices. Registering a climb is voluntary and worth doing.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.capacity: Dug platforms for a party or two on the flats out from the foot of the faces; no established site and nothing to shelter behind

wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.name: Cougar Divide meadow camps
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.notes: This is the north-side approach to Hadley Peak and it has nothing to do with the Black Buttes or the Coleman — a party here is on the far side of the mountain from the Heliotrope Ridge climbers. Cougar Divide is an unofficial, unmaintained path along the ridge crest, reached from Wells Creek Road, whose first several miles are badly potholed to the Nooksack bridge and then improve. From the meadows at the head of the divide the ground opens onto Chowder Ridge, and the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley. The gate opening in July combined with mosquitoes that are genuinely bad here until midsummer pushes the sensible window to mid-August through early October, which is also when the talus is clear and the route is straightforward walking with the odd second-class step.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.name: Skyline Divide crest camps
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.notes: The other approach to Hadley Peak, from the west along the divide and over Chowder Ridge. The road in has been the problem for years rather than the trail: flood damage at around mile three has left the trailhead inaccessible to vehicles for extended periods with no firm repair date, and the trail has been listed as closed on that account, so this is the first thing to confirm and not an afterthought. When it goes, the crest is easy walking with big views and the last three quarters of a mile up to Chowder Ridge is talus with one steeper step before you top out west of the Hadley Glacier. Camping on the open crest means taking whatever weather arrives off the mountain, and the exposure is the reason parties often drop into the basin instead.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.water: None at the trailhead and none along the trail after early summer, when the snow patches below the crest are gone. Carry everything or plan the trip around a lingering snowfield you have confirmed is still there.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead. No campfires anywhere, party size capped at 12, all waste packed out. There is no permit or quota for camping, but the meadows are heavily used and heavily damaged, so camp on bare ground.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.capacity: Several exposed sites along the open crest of the divide once the trail tops out; popular and visible, with no screening from wind or weather

wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.water: The most reliable water on the Hadley approach — the creek runs from snowmelt above the basin and holds up later than anything on the ridge crests. Treat it. This is the reason to camp here rather than higher.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

Party size is capped at 12 once you enter the wilderness, campfires are prohibited, and there is no toilet anywhere on the route — carry blue bags, which are handed out free at the ranger offices in Sedro-Woolley and at Glacier. Nothing may be buried in snow or dropped into a crevasse or moat.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.capacity: The established climbers' camp on the Squak, with room for several parties on gravel benches and snow platforms at the toe of the glacier; quieter than the Easton side even on a summer weekend

wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.name: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.notes: Parties who want Sherman's summit day short move above Crag View and camp on the Sulphur moraine at the glacier's edge around 7,000 ft, or push on to the flatter ground below the rock prow closer to 7,600 ft. The gain is real, since it takes a good chunk out of the traverse to the south ridge and puts you at the base of the steep snow with the night's freeze still holding. The cost is a fully exposed camp on a volcano's south flank, where wind is the usual reason parties come back down to Crag View, and you are already on glacier and roped to get here. Camping this high also means committing to melt water, which drives fuel weight up. Where exactly the platforms are usable moves year to year with the crevasse pattern, so arrive with daylight to scout rather than in the dark.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.water: None. Melt snow. Anything running here in early summer is a bonus and will not be there later in the year.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness rules as at Crag View — no permit to camp, recreation pass at the Park Butte trailhead, 12-person party limit, no campfires, all waste packed out in blue bags.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.capacity: Dug snow platforms and moraine gravel for one or two parties along the right-hand edge of the glacier, with a second bench under a rock prow several hundred feet higher; no established sites and no shelter

wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.name: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.notes: Colfax's three north-side ice lines — the Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano — all start off the Coleman somewhere near 8,000 ft, and this is the staging ground for a party that does not want to cover the whole approach from the Hogsback on climb morning. The important thing about it is where you do not put the tent: ice and rock come off the Colfax seracs onto this part of the glacier with some regularity, so the usable camping is out on the flats well clear of the fall line, never tucked in against the toe of the face because it looks sheltered. Many parties skip this camp entirely and climb these routes in a long day from the trailhead or from the Hogsback, which is a reasonable answer to the same hazard. These are cold-season routes, roughly late October into May, and the ice changes character completely across that window. Access is the current constraint rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road washed out in the December 2025 floods and has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, open to walkers and bikes at the contractors' discretion with repairs anticipated through 2026 — confirm the road before planning to carry a heavy load.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.water: None to rely on. Melt snow. Surface runoff sometimes appears on the rock of the buttes in a hot spell and should not be planned around.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight permit; camping is dispersed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge. Party limit 12, no campfires, no toilets on the route, waste packed out in blue bags available free from the ranger offices. Registering a climb is voluntary and worth doing.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.capacity: Dug platforms for a party or two on the flats out from the foot of the faces; no established site and nothing to shelter behind

wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.name: Cougar Divide meadow camps
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.notes: This is the north-side approach to Hadley Peak and it has nothing to do with the Black Buttes or the Coleman — a party here is on the far side of the mountain from the Heliotrope Ridge climbers. Cougar Divide is an unofficial, unmaintained path along the ridge crest, reached from Wells Creek Road, whose first several miles are badly potholed to the Nooksack bridge and then improve. From the meadows at the head of the divide the ground opens onto Chowder Ridge, and the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley. The gate opening in July combined with mosquitoes that are genuinely bad here until midsummer pushes the sensible window to mid-August through early October, which is also when the talus is clear and the route is straightforward walking with the odd second-class step.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.name: Skyline Divide crest camps
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.notes: The other approach to Hadley Peak, from the west along the divide and over Chowder Ridge. The road in has been the problem for years rather than the trail: flood damage at around mile three has left the trailhead inaccessible to vehicles for extended periods with no firm repair date, and the trail has been listed as closed on that account, so this is the first thing to confirm and not an afterthought. When it goes, the crest is easy walking with big views and the last three quarters of a mile up to Chowder Ridge is talus with one steeper step before you top out west of the Hadley Glacier. Camping on the open crest means taking whatever weather arrives off the mountain, and the exposure is the reason parties often drop into the basin instead.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.water: None at the trailhead and none along the trail after early summer, when the snow patches below the crest are gone. Carry everything or plan the trip around a lingering snowfield you have confirmed is still there.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead. No campfires anywhere, party size capped at 12, all waste packed out. There is no permit or quota for camping, but the meadows are heavily used and heavily damaged, so camp on bare ground.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.capacity: Several exposed sites along the open crest of the divide once the trail tops out; popular and visible, with no screening from wind or weather

wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.water: The most reliable water on the Hadley approach — the creek runs from snowmelt above the basin and holds up later than anything on the ridge crests. Treat it. This is the reason to camp here rather than higher.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Lower Blum Lake
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Middle Blum Lake
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: South Hagan bench
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, said plainly rather than recommending a place that does not exist. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
wa_hagan_mountain_south.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
wa_hagan_mountain_south.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires
wa_hagan_mountain_south.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Glacier Gap
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_honeymoon_route.name: Royal Lake
wa_honeymoon_route.notes: This is the front door to the whole Needles group and the default answer for anyone climbing Deception, Clark, Johnson, Walkinshaw, The Incisor or Sundial. It sits about seven miles and two and a half thousand feet from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, up the Dungeness and then the Royal Creek fork, which is walkable with a heavy pack in an afternoon. The honest trade is this: Royal Lake is comfortable, has real designated tent pads and is where the permit system actually issues sites, but it leaves you an extra mile and roughly five hundred to a thousand feet of loose boot path below the upper basin every single climbing morning. On a Needles day that difference is real, because the rock above the basin is dirty and slow and you want to be off it before the afternoon. Parties that only want one peak, or that have anyone who would rather not sleep at six thousand feet on gravel, are right to stay here. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a normal year and the mosquitoes at the lake are notorious through midsummer, which is another argument for going higher. Book the moment the reservation window opens; this is one of the hardest permits on the peninsula to get on a weekend.
wa_honeymoon_route.water: The lake and the outlet creek run all season. Filter or treat; this is a heavily used basin and the shoreline is fragile.
wa_honeymoon_route.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Royal Basin is one of the park's named quota areas. Essentially the whole quota is reservable in advance through the federal recreation booking system, with the summer block released in a single mid-April drop for the mid-May through mid-October season; there is no same-day walk-up window, so a party that turns up without a permit has no legal camp. Expect a flat per-permit reservation charge plus a per-adult, per-night fee, with under-sixteens free and an annual wilderness pass available if you camp here often. Dates outside the online season are arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, and loaners are sometimes available on a first-come basis when you collect the permit. Every camp along Royal Creek and up through the meadows and the basin sits inside the same reservation, so there is no legal way to sneak a night lower down without one.
wa_honeymoon_route.capacity: Ten designated sites, and only two of them will take more than a single tent. One separate group site holds roughly seven to twelve people and has to be booked as a group site. That is the entire overnight capacity of the lake basin, which is why permits go so fast.
