wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.name: Basin Creek Camp
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.notes: The closest designated camp to the Horseshoe Basin trail junction, which sits at about 3,600 ft on the valley trail, so it is the practical base for anything up in the cirque. It has a separate cooking area, a bear box and its own privy. Capacity is tiny — three sites — so a party of four fills most of it and a weekend permit is not something to count on. From here the basin trail climbs roughly 1,300 ft in about 1.5 miles to the Black Warrior Mine and the waterfall headwall below Ripsaw Ridge and Buckner's north side.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.water: Reliable — Basin Creek runs beside the camp all season
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.permit: NPS backcountry permit required (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA); designated camp reserved by site on Recreation.gov, with roughly 40% of inventory held for walk-up the day before at Marblemount or Golden West in Stehekin. Per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.

wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.name: Cottonwood Camp
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.notes: The eastern gateway to the basin, at the end of what used to be the upper Stehekin Valley road. It has a privy, fire rings, picnic table and bear boxes, though the boxes are set well back from the cooking area. ACCESS IS THE THING TO PLAN AROUND: the road washed out for the last time in 2003 and the Stehekin shuttle now turns around at High Bridge, so reaching Cottonwood from the boat means an extra day of walking the old roadbed rather than the bus ride older descriptions assume. Check the current shuttle schedule before committing — upper-valley service has varied year to year.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.water: Reliable — creek water a short walk below the camp
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp, same Recreation.gov reservation and walk-up system as the rest of the complex.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Several sites, including one that takes a larger group and a few small secluded ones

wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.name: Pelton Basin Camp
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.notes: A set of hand-built rock-walled tent platforms at the toe of the glacier, at the top of Sahale Arm. It is high, exposed and above the last dependable water, so late-season parties should plan to melt snow or carry up from lower on the arm. For the Horseshoe Basin peaks it is a high camp rather than a basin camp — it serves approaches that cross Sahale Arm and drop toward Doubtful Lake and the head of the basin, and it puts you on the right side of the divide for Buckner's north aspect. Reported elevation varies slightly between sources.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.water: Unreliable — snowmelt and glacier runoff only, and the seasonal trickles commonly dry up by late summer
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; one of the most contested designated camps in the park. Realistically needs the early-access lottery or the general on-sale window in late April.

wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.name: Doubtful Lake Camp
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.notes: Doubtful Lake lies in a cirque below Sahale Arm, reached by a spur that drops off the arm trail. It is the natural middle camp on the Sahale Arm variation of the approach, breaking up a long crossing between Cascade Pass and the head of Horseshoe Basin. Water is the one thing never in question here, which matters if the alternative is Sahale Glacier Camp late in the season. The spur loses meaningful elevation off the arm, so factor the reclimb into the next day.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus its inlet and outlet streams
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camping at the lake, reserved or walked up like the other Cascade Pass-area sites.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.capacity: A small designated camp at the lake, site count not published. Treat it as a handful of spots rather than a place a large party can count on.

wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.name: Buckner cross-country zone bivy
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.notes: The option for climbers who want to sleep on the route rather than at a valley camp — high bivies on moraine, slab or snow under Buckner's north side and the Ripsaw Ridge peaks. Zone rules are strict and worth reading before you go: camp at least a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight, and only on snow, rock or bare ground. No meadow camping, nothing within 100 ft of water, no fires. Because the permit is walk-up only, a trip built around a zone bivy is one you cannot lock in ahead of time — carry a fallback.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.water: Conditions-dependent — snowmelt and seasonal streams in the upper basin, dependable early, thin or gone by late season
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.permit: NPS cross-country zone permit required, WALK-UP ONLY. Buckner is not among the zones that take advance reservations, so it cannot be booked on Recreation.gov and must be picked up in person, generally no more than a day ahead.
wa_hurry_up_peak_south_ridge.capacity: 6 people per party, 6 parties per night in the zone

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.water: The river and its tributaries are everywhere and never fail, but the North Fork is heavily glacier-fed and runs opaque with rock flour. Filter from a clear side stream rather than the main channel where you can.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
wa_icy_peak_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.name: Boundary Camp
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: Nada Lake
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.

wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline

That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.name: Nada Lake
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps

Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.name: Nada Lake
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_scramble.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
