wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
wa_inner_constance_northwest_buttress.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

wa_inner_constance_standard.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
wa_inner_constance_standard.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
wa_inner_constance_standard.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
wa_inner_constance_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
wa_inner_constance_standard.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

wa_inner_constance_standard.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
wa_inner_constance_standard.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
wa_inner_constance_standard.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
wa_inner_constance_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
wa_inner_constance_standard.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

wa_inner_constance_standard.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
wa_inner_constance_standard.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.
wa_inner_constance_standard.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
wa_inner_constance_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
wa_inner_constance_standard.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

wa_inner_constance_standard.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
wa_inner_constance_standard.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
wa_inner_constance_standard.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
wa_inner_constance_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
wa_inner_constance_standard.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

wa_inner_constance_standard.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
wa_inner_constance_standard.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
wa_inner_constance_standard.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
wa_inner_constance_standard.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
wa_inner_constance_standard.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

wa_inner_constance_standard.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
wa_inner_constance_standard.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
wa_inner_constance_standard.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
wa_inner_constance_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
wa_inner_constance_standard.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

wa_inspiration_peak_west_ridge.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_inspiration_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the standard base camp for the whole Southern Pickets and a genuinely comfortable one — a small flat gravelly basin with flowers, running water and a full view of the range, sitting about 400 ft below the notch in the ridge above it. It is a planned camp, not a bivy: parties sleep here, climb the peak, and come back to it. Getting to it is the hard part, roughly 7 miles and 5,700 ft of gain with a steep, chossy 400 ft descent off the notch to finish, so plan on arriving late and staying two nights rather than trying to move camp. Park rules bite here because the ground is meadow: pitch on gravel, rock or snow, never on vegetation, and stay 100 ft from the streams. There is no water at all on the last 3,500 ft of the approach, so fill up low.
wa_inspiration_peak_west_ridge.water: Running streams through the basin fed by the snowfields above, reliable through the season but heavy with glacial silt — filter and treat it
wa_inspiration_peak_west_ridge.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone. It is not one of the zones that takes advance reservations, so the permit is picked up in person.
wa_inspiration_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Several tent sites on bare ground in the rocky meadows plus a two-person bivy platform; the zone allows six parties a night, six people per party

wa_inspiration_traverse.name: Eldorado Creek basin
wa_inspiration_traverse.notes: Open basin above the boulder field; a lower camp for parties splitting the approach.

wa_inspiration_traverse.name: Inspiration Glacier high camp
wa_inspiration_traverse.notes: Rock outcrops at the edge of the Inspiration Glacier below Eldorado's East Ridge. The standard base for Eldorado and the start of the traverse.

wa_inspiration_traverse.name: Klawatti col
wa_inspiration_traverse.notes: Rock tent sites on the col below the south side of Klawatti Peak with running water and big views; well placed for Klawatti, Austera and Primus.

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.water: Bean Creek runs through the basin and is the reason the camp is here, but it is a small east-side creek and by late August only one of the several channels may still be running. The dependable fill is lower down, where the trail crosses Bean Creek at the split with the Earl Peak branch — top off there rather than assuming the basin will provide, and assume nothing at all above the basin, because the climb to Earl Pass and the whole southwest ridge are dry.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.capacity: A stand of trees at the edge of the meadow holds four or more multi-tent sites, and there are scattered singles beyond it; two or three parties fit comfortably and it fills on summer weekends. No toilet of any kind.

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.name: Beverly Turnpike camps at the Fourth Creek junction
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.notes: The best all-round camp on the Beverly Creek side, ringed by the peaks it serves — Iron Peak stands to the southwest, Teanaway Peak to the northwest, and the Bean and Earl ridges close it in to the southeast. It sits two and seven tenths miles up the Beverly Turnpike trail from the Beverly Creek trailhead. For Iron Peak it is the east-side option, which matters because the standard approach from the road end is entirely waterless: a party wanting to sleep out before the scramble is far better off here beside the creek than dry-camped on the saddle. It also links Earl Peak to Iron Peak over two days without returning to the car, and it is the staging point for the Fourth Creek crossing north to Ingalls Creek, which involves fording Ingalls Creek and is genuinely dangerous during June runoff. Ground is forested and level, insects are moderate, and the camp is low enough to be warm at night well into September.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.water: Beverly Creek runs briskly right beside the camp and is the most reliable water anywhere in this group of peaks. That reliability ends abruptly at the junction: the sites up on the saddle where the Fourth Creek and Hardscrabble trails meet are dry, and there is nothing on the climb to Iron Peak's saddle from this side. A small running source sits roughly four tenths of a mile down the Hardscrabble side of that saddle, off-trail, and is worth knowing about if you have committed to the high ground and misjudged.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery. Northwest Forest Pass at the Beverly Creek trailhead. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness slip from the trailhead box covers travel where the trails cross the boundary north of here. No campfires above 5,000 feet, and expect a valley-wide burn ban from midsummer; this is dry, brittle east-side timber that has already carried one large fire.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.capacity: A cluster of good sites near the creek holding four or five tents, spread over enough ground that two parties are not on top of each other

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.name: Iron Peak saddle dry camp
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.notes: A perch rather than a campsite, and included because Iron Peak's standard approach offers nothing else. The trailhead sits on the North Fork Teanaway Road roughly half a mile above the De Roux campground turn and a mile and a half short of the road end, at about 3,800 feet. The trail climbs a rib at a steady moderate grade with no flat ground and no water until it reaches the saddle, from which the scramble turns west up the ridge to the summit, and most parties continue on to Mount Teanaway from the same saddle. Almost nobody sleeps here and almost nobody needs to — this is a half-day objective for a fit party — but a group that has started late, or one linking Iron Peak with the Beverly Creek peaks over the divide, has this saddle as the only level ground on the route. It is windy, exposed and cold after dark even in August. If there is any choice at all, the creekside camps at the Fourth Creek junction on the other side of the divide are a far better place to spend a night.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.water: None. This is the defining fact about the route and the camp both. The Iron Peak trail passes a steep unnamed creek in the first eighth of a mile from the trailhead and then turns away from it for good; you can hear water in the gullies on either side for half the climb and cannot reach any of it. Carry everything you intend to drink and cook with from the road, and plan on more than feels necessary, because this is a south-facing, sun-hammered hillside.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.permit: No permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Iron Peak trailhead. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation and there is nothing here to burn in any case. Pitch on gravel or bare ground; the saddle carries thin meadow that does not recover.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.capacity: A few flat spots at and just below the saddle between Iron Peak and Mount Teanaway; one or two small tents, no shelter, and nothing resembling an established site

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is PROHIBITED anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

wa_ives_peak_r1.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
wa_ives_peak_r1.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
wa_ives_peak_r1.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
wa_ives_peak_r1.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
wa_ives_peak_r1.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

wa_ives_peak_r1.name: Goat Lake basin
wa_ives_peak_r1.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
wa_ives_peak_r1.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
wa_ives_peak_r1.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
wa_ives_peak_r1.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

wa_ives_peak_r1.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
wa_ives_peak_r1.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
wa_ives_peak_r1.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
wa_ives_peak_r1.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
wa_ives_peak_r1.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

wa_ives_peak_r1.name: Chambers Lake Campground
wa_ives_peak_r1.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
wa_ives_peak_r1.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
wa_ives_peak_r1.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
wa_ives_peak_r1.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

wa_ives_peak_r1.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
wa_ives_peak_r1.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.
wa_ives_peak_r1.water: The South Fork Tieton and its tributaries throughout, and the lake itself higher up; abundant by the standards of the range's east side but still to be treated
wa_ives_peak_r1.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
wa_ives_peak_r1.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites

wa_j_tnar.name: Barclay Lake
wa_j_tnar.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_j_tnar.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_j_tnar.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_j_tnar.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_j_tnar.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_j_tnar.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_j_tnar.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_j_tnar.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_j_tnar.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
wa_j_tnar.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
wa_j_tnar.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

wa_j_tnar.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_j_tnar.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
wa_j_tnar.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
wa_j_tnar.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

wa_j_tnar.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
wa_j_tnar.notes: The traverse of Mount Index's three peaks is the one objective in this zone that is genuinely an overnight rather than a long day, and this is where parties sleep. The line links South, Middle and North Peaks along a crest of loose ridges and gullies with rappels between them, and the recorded practice is a flat spot right on the crest between the two Middle Peak summits with snow nearby, which solves the water problem in early season. Parties who have done it in a push describe going light and treating the bivouac as an emergency plan that they were glad to have and glad not to need — take minimal gear rather than a full camp, because everything you carry has to come over some genuinely poor rock. Approach is the Lake Serene trail as for everything else on the mountain. The rock on Index is famously rotten and the descent options off the ridge are limited, so committing to a bivouac here means committing to finishing the traverse; do not plan it as a place to sit out bad weather.
wa_j_tnar.water: Snow on the crest into early summer, and nothing at all once it goes. On a dry traverse you carry water for the whole ridge or you drop off it.
wa_j_tnar.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: One small party. A flat patch on the ridge crest between the two Middle Peak summits — a stance, not a site.

wa_j_tnar.name: Money Creek Campground
wa_j_tnar.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
wa_j_tnar.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
wa_j_tnar.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

wa_j_tnar.name: Beckler River Campground
wa_j_tnar.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.
wa_j_tnar.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
wa_j_tnar.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.

wa_j_tnar.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
wa_j_tnar.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. It sits about eleven miles up the Index-Galena Road from US 2 at roughly 1,200 ft on the North Fork Skykomish, which put it within twenty minutes of the Lake Serene trailhead and made it the obvious base for Mount Index. Flooding washed out the Index-Galena Road near mileposts 10 and 14, the road is gated closed through that section with permanent repairs estimated in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the county has said environmental review and permitting may take several years. The campground is inaccessible and closed as a result, and the neighbouring campground further up the same road is closed with it. Confirm the road status before counting on it; if the gate is still shut, the working substitutes for an Index-area night are Money Creek down the highway or a dispersed pullout on the Beckler system. Nothing on the Reiter Road side fills the gap — the lower Reiter Foothills road corridor is state land signed day use only with no camping and a Discover Pass required, which is the approach used for Mount Persis, so plan Persis as a day out from the valley.
wa_j_tnar.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
wa_j_tnar.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
wa_j_tnar.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.

wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Diablo Lake
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.notes: The practical staging ground for the whole west end of the corridor: directly under Colonial Peak and a short drive from the Pyramid Lake and Thunder Creek trailheads. Because it lies west of the usual winter gate at the Ross Dam trailhead, a handful of walk-in sites normally stay reachable through winter with no services and no fee — though a gate moved down to Newhalem would cut that off. Treat serviced opening and closing dates as approximate; they shift with snow and staffing. Arriving late on a summer Friday without a reservation is a poor plan.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.water: Potable tap water during the serviced season; no supply in winter, when Thunder Arm and the creek are the only sources and need treating
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway

wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley.
