It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.
wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge.capacity: Dispersed; a few flat spots at the lakes and a hidden pocket among the trees, enough for one or two parties

The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier.capacity: Dispersed; a few flat spots at the lakes and a hidden pocket among the trees, enough for one or two parties

wa_jack_mountain_south_face.name: Crater Creek Meadows bench
wa_jack_mountain_south_face.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard staging point for the south face, on a heather bench above Crater Creek northwest of point 7001. Reached in roughly eight hours and eleven miles from the car, after the Jerry Glacier traverse and the drop into Crater Creek Basin. Parties choose it over Jerry Lakes specifically because it shortens the summit day onto the face. Terrain gives moderate wind shelter. Permit status is not confirmed for this basin — check the zone before you go.
wa_jack_mountain_south_face.water: Crater Creek, about 200 ft below camp
wa_jack_mountain_south_face.capacity: small — comfortable for a party of two

wa_jack_mountain_south_face.name: Jerry Lakes basin
wa_jack_mountain_south_face.notes: PLANNED camp, a grassy boulder-strewn bowl with several separate sites; the best of them sits by the small lake between the two large ones. Snow-free by mid-August. It is the more pleasant camp of the two and the obvious stop if you arrive late, but it leaves a longer traverse to the face on summit day. Open bowl, so afternoon wind. Fire-scarred forest on the approach into the basin. Check the zone for permits.

wa_jack_mountain_south_face.name: Jerry Lakes Peak south saddle
wa_jack_mountain_south_face.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — on record only as an unplanned night out, sat through in a bivy sack and an emergency blanket with little wind protection and a cold, sleepless result. Worth knowing exists if a party is caught on the ridge between the lakes and the Crater Mountain saddle, and worth planning not to use.

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Diablo Lake
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.notes: The practical staging ground for the whole west end of the corridor: directly under Colonial Peak and a short drive from the Pyramid Lake and Thunder Creek trailheads. Because it lies west of the usual winter gate at the Ross Dam trailhead, a handful of walk-in sites normally stay reachable through winter with no services and no fee — though a gate moved down to Newhalem would cut that off. Treat serviced opening and closing dates as approximate; they shift with snow and staffing. Arriving late on a summer Friday without a reservation is a poor plan.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.water: Potable tap water during the serviced season; no supply in winter, when Thunder Arm and the creek are the only sources and need treating
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.name: Pelton Basin
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.name: Buttress bivy at the heather-to-rock transition
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.notes: This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, and it is what makes the route a two-day climb for most parties — it typically takes eight to twelve hours of climbing from the base of the buttress to reach it, with two to three hours of glacier and summit snow above. It sits where the steep heather and rock give way to the snow and glacier, so it is the last flat, watered ground before the upper mountain. It is also the point of no easy return: the ground below is 4,000 ft of steep brush, heather and rock above the valley, and retreating down it in the dark is far worse than sitting out the night. Wind is the main comfort variable; some nights are dead calm and warm, some are not.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.water: Running water or snowmelt seeps are usually available here through summer; it dries out in a hot, low-snow year, so carry the capacity to melt or to go dry
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.permit: Overnight camping anywhere in the park backcountry needs a National Park Service permit; the peak falls in the Johannesburg cross-country zone, capped at six people per party and six parties per night
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.capacity: Small ledges and heather platforms; enough for a party of two, not a tent camp

wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.name: Chopped platforms on the upper glacier
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.notes: An improvised, secondary option above the standard bivy for parties who ran out of daylight higher up. Summer sun cupping means real work with an axe to get a flat platform, and it is fully exposed to wind and to crevasse hazard, so probe and anchor. Treat this as an emergency bivy rather than a plan.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.capacity: Whatever you cut — one or two bodies

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_kaleetan_peak_south_ridge.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Wing Lake
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Lewis Lake
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

wa_katsuk_peak_gully.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_kendall_peak_standard.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_kendall_peak_standard.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_kendall_peak_standard.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Wing Lake
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Lewis Lake
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

wa_king_kong_gorillas_direct_direct.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
wa_king_kong_gorillas_direct_direct.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
