wa_koala_krack.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_koala_krack.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_koala_krack.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_koala_krack.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_koala_krack.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_koala_krack.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_koala_krack.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_koala_krack.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_koala_krack.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_koala_krack.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_koala_krack.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_koala_krack.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_koala_krack.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_koala_krack.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_koala_krack.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_koala_krack.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_koala_krack.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_koala_krack.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_koala_krack.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_koala_krack.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_koala_krack.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_koala_krack.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_koala_krack.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_koala_krack.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_koala_krack.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_koala_krack.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_koala_krack.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_koala_krack.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_koala_krack.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_koala_krack.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_kololo_peaks_standard.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a DAY OBJECTIVE with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

wa_kololo_peaks_standard.name: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.notes: The climbing camp for KOLOLO PEAKS, and the reason Kololo is a three-day trip rather than a weekend scramble. It sits in the stark rock-and-snow basin on the edge of what remains of the White Chuck Glacier, reached from the North Fork Sauk road end by twelve or thirteen miles of walking — the long river approach, then the steep switchbacking climb to White Pass, then east on the crest trail and out along the Foam Basin path toward Foam Pass. Eight hours from the road to camp is a normal rather than a slow time for a party carrying overnight gear. From here the peaks themselves are straightforward, a walk on glacier remnant and snow followed by easy scrambling on rubbly volcanic rock, and moving from one summit to the next is simple. The glacier is the thing to understand: it has retreated further and faster than almost anything in the range and much of what maps show as ice is now bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds, with the surviving ice thin, hard and holed by open crevasses late in the season. That means crampons rather than a snow plod by September, and it means route descriptions written twenty years ago describe a surface that is gone. Lower camps on the same approach sit at the river bench, at White Pass and at the gap above this basin. Exposed ground with no shelter, confusing in fog, and a long way from help.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.water: Meltwater streams and ponds through the basin, running all through the climbing season and often silty. Late in a hot summer the flow drops to a trickle off the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time. Everybody camped here drinks it, so site the toilet well away from it.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.permit: GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit collected at the North Fork Sauk trailhead box, twelve-person party limit. No fires: this is bare rock, pumice and snow above treeline with nothing to burn and nothing that recovers. Human waste is carried out or buried properly well away from the meltwater. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.capacity: Open bare-ground bivouac sites scattered through the basin, with room for several parties and no crowding — this is a big, empty place. Rock-walled windbreaks left by previous parties are the nearest thing to a built site.

wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_kyes_peak_glaciated_scramble.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_kyes_peak_northeast_ridge.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The main basecamp for LA BOHN PEAK, which stands directly at the head of this valley, and the first night of the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. Drive the Foss River road off Highway 2 a short way east of Skykomish and turn into the Necklace Valley trailhead about four miles up. The trail is famously two-faced: the first five miles along the East Fork Foss gain only about 600 ft through regenerated second growth and go quickly, then the trail crosses the river and climbs roughly 2,400 ft in the next three miles to break out at Jade Lake around 4,600 ft. Emerald is a quarter mile further, Opal about 4,790 ft above that, with Ilswoot, Locket, Jewel and Cloudy scattered on either side. A weathered memorial cabin sits in the meadow just above Emerald; it is a landmark and a piece of the valley's mining history, not a shelter to plan on. From Opal or Emerald the route to La Bohn Gap climbs east under the cliffs, so Jade is fractionally further from the gap but Emerald and Opal put you closest to the day's work. Two honest caveats. The Foss River road has been under construction with weekday delays of about half an hour through the summer, and damage higher on the road has at times cut off the upper end, so allow slack and check before committing to a dawn start. And this valley is very popular for its own sake — a midweek trip is far more pleasant than a Saturday, and the steep middle section is genuinely unpleasant under a heavy climbing pack in the heat.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: All four lakes, plus the creek linking them. Reliable the whole season.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size limited to twelve including stock. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the range, which puts every lake in the valley under a fire ban — carry a stove and do not build rings.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Sites are spread across four separate lake basins rather than concentrated, so the valley absorbs a lot of parties — several groups at Jade, several more around Emerald and Opal, and quieter singles at Ilswoot, Locket and Jewel off to the sides. On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The high camp for LA BOHN PEAK and the launching point for the west route on MOUNT HINMAN, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: The La Bohn tarns and the Chain Lakes below the gap on the south side, plus lingering snowmelt into midsummer. Late in a dry season the smaller tarns can drop and turn silty; check rather than assume.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, picked up at whichever trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. Campfires prohibited outright — everything here is well above the 4,000 ft fire-ban line and there is no wood to burn anyway. Camp on rock or bare gravel, not on the heather, which takes decades to recover at this elevation.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: A handful of small, exposed pitches on granite benches and heather shelves between the tarns — realistically two or three tents in the good spots, more if you are willing to sleep on rock. There is no sheltered ground.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Tank Lakes basin
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: A high alternative to the Necklace lakes, reached off-trail from the south end of Opal Lake and sitting at roughly 5,800 ft in a bench of slabs and tarns ringed by ridges. It is not on the direct line to LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN and adds work rather than saving it, so take it when you want a spectacular camp and a rest day rather than the fastest summit. It matters here for two reasons. First, it is the obvious second night for a party linking Necklace Valley with the high country toward Dutch Miller Gap on foot. Second, when the Necklace lakes are full on a weekend, this is where the space is. The travel from Opal is cross-country over slabs and heather with some routefinding, and it holds snow well into July, which makes it either easier or harder depending on what you are carrying. The exposure is the caveat: nothing up here breaks the wind, the basin is a poor place to sit out a storm, and getting back down to the valley in cloud demands attention.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: The tarns themselves and snowmelt. The basin holds snow late, which helps, but by September the smaller pools can be stagnant — take from the larger ones or from running melt.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. No campfires, and no scope for one — this is bare granite and heather. Pitch on rock or gravel only.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: A scatter of small hardened spots on slab and gravel among the tarns. Two or three parties before it feels crowded, and there is nothing resembling a sheltered group site.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Big Heart Lake, with Copper and Little Heart below
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The west-side base for BALD EAGLE PEAK, which sits on the divide between the two Foss forks and can be climbed from either. The trail leaves a spur off the Foss River road and climbs a staircase of lakes: Trout at about 1.6 miles, Malachite and Copper at around 3,965 ft near four miles, Little Heart at five and a half, and Big Heart at 4,418 ft after roughly seven to eight miles and some four thousand feet of gain. Beyond Big Heart, rough boot paths and a little bushwhacking lead on to Angeline at about 4,613 ft, Azurite, Otter and Chetwoot for parties who want solitude. For Bald Eagle the useful detail is that the standard west approach leaves the trail low, near Trout Lake, fords the river just downstream of the pool below the lake and takes to the forest for the northwest ridge — so a night at Copper or Little Heart is a comfortable staging camp, while Big Heart is a long way past the turn-off and is a destination rather than a basecamp. Two road caveats that matter more than usual. The Foss River road has run weekday construction delays of roughly half an hour through the summer season. And the spur road to this trailhead has been impassable to vehicles, damaged and blocked by downed trees, adding about two and a half miles of road walking each way — enough to turn a comfortable first day into a long one. Confirm the road before you plan the mileage.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Every lake on the chain. Plentiful and reliable through the season.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED AT EVERY LAKE ON THIS TRAIL regardless of elevation, and within half a mile of Trout, Malachite, Copper, Little Heart and Big Heart you must camp at an established site rather than pitching where you like. Take both rules seriously here; this is one of the most heavily used valleys on the Highway 2 side and the ground shows it.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Copper Lake and Little Heart hold a good number of established sites and take the bulk of the traffic. Big Heart has a few sites at its northern edge close to the water and a few more perched above the lake — enough for several parties, but it is the destination for most people on this trail and it fills.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Bald Eagle Lake cirque
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: A rough, off-trail bivouac at about 4,547 ft for BALD EAGLE PEAK, tucked in the cirque on the north flank of the ridge midway between Bald Eagle and its neighbour Silver Eagle to the southwest. Bald Eagle sits squarely between the West Fork and East Fork of the Foss, and although the mountain looks intimidating on a map its standard lines are no harder than class 3 to 4 and are mostly a matter of picking the right rib. The lake is worth knowing about precisely because both trailhead approaches are long: the west approach fords the West Fork low, near Trout Lake, and climbs the northwest ridge, while the ridge system directly above the Foss River road on the east side gives another line from around 1,600 ft. Either way the mountain is a big day from the car, and a night in the cirque splits it. Be honest with yourself about what this is — there is no trail to it, no site, and no shelter. It suits a small, self-sufficient party in settled weather and is a poor idea in anything else. Late July through September is the window; earlier the approach slopes hold snow and the brush is soaked.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: The lake. Take it from the inlet side if the outlet is stagnant late in the season.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever Foss River trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. No campfires — above the 4,000 ft ban line, and the ground here is far too fragile to take one. Camp on rock or gravel and leave nothing behind; this basin sees almost no traffic and should stay that way.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Nothing established. One or two parties on rough ground beside the lake, chosen on the day. Treat it as a bivouac, not a campsite.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The base for MOUNT DANIEL and the eastern option for MOUNT HINMAN, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. THE CRITICAL 2026 CAVEAT: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: THIS IS THE MOST RESTRICTED CAMP IN THE ZONE AND THE RULES ARE THE POINT. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp ONLY on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.

wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. For MOUNT DANIEL it is the family-friendly alternative to Peggy's Pond and it is honest to say what that costs: camping here rather than at the pond adds roughly two thousand feet to summit day and puts the whole approach to the southeast ridge in front of you before the climbing starts. It earns its place for three reasons — it is the fallback when Peggy's Pond is full, which it often is; it is the sensible choice for a party larger than the pond's reduced limit allows; and it is by far the better place to sit out weather, being sheltered, wooded and low. The valley floor around Fish Lake and Tucquala Lake below the trailhead also holds dispersed and developed camping if you arrive late and want to walk in fresh. Two caveats. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.water: The lakes and the Cle Elum River flowing through them. Reliable all season.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. Camp at the established sites and keep back from the shoreline — a 200 ft setback applies at listed lakes on this side of the range. Check the current campfire order before lighting anything; at this elevation a fire may be legal when the district is not under a seasonal ban, but the sites nearest the water are heavily worn and a stove is the better choice regardless.
wa_la_bohn_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Plenty. Established sites and a privy along the shores of both lakes, spread out enough that even a busy weekend does not feel packed. This is the one place in the zone where a large party can settle without a problem.

wa_labor_pains.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_labor_pains.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_labor_pains.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_labor_pains.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_labor_pains.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_labor_pains.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_labor_pains.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_labor_pains.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_labor_pains.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_labor_pains.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_labor_pains.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_labor_pains.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_labor_pains.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_labor_pains.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_labor_pains.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Copper Glance Lake
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

wa_lane_peak_r1.name: Snow Lake Camp
wa_lane_peak_r1.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
wa_lane_peak_r1.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
wa_lane_peak_r1.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
wa_lane_peak_r1.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

wa_lane_peak_r1.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
wa_lane_peak_r1.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
wa_lane_peak_r1.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
wa_lane_peak_r1.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
wa_lane_peak_r1.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

wa_lane_peak_r1.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
wa_lane_peak_r1.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
wa_lane_peak_r1.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
wa_lane_peak_r1.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
wa_lane_peak_r1.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

wa_lane_peak_r1.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_lane_peak_r1.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
wa_lane_peak_r1.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
wa_lane_peak_r1.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
wa_lane_peak_r1.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

wa_lane_peak_r1.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
wa_lane_peak_r1.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.
wa_lane_peak_r1.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
wa_lane_peak_r1.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter

wa_lane_peak_r1.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
wa_lane_peak_r1.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. It has been closed through 2026 for a rehabilitation project, so confirm its status before planning around it. When running it is low, forested and warm, which makes it a reasonable shoulder-season option when the higher campgrounds are shut.
wa_lane_peak_r1.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
wa_lane_peak_r1.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.
