wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Skyline Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Trap Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Skyline Lake

The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time.
