wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Trap Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.notes: This is the established high camp for Lincoln and the one nearly every ascent uses. It sits on the ridge overlooking the Wallace Creek basin, right at the last stand of trees, with the Black Buttes and the summit block in view above. Reaching it means walking the road to about the seventh switchback, picking up the old track that leads toward Rankin Creek, scrambling into the basin, passing east Rankin Lake, then climbing mellow snow north to the saddle near 5,480 ft and east up the basin below Seward to the ridge. From here the X Couloir on the southwest face and the north ridge are both single-push summit days, and both are long, steep, exposed snow and ice, which is why the camp is high. The peak is in condition in spring, when fresh snow has mostly stopped falling but nights are still cold enough to hold the snow, ice and rock together; by high summer the face becomes loose and dangerous. Expect the trees to be buried and the ground to be snow. Nothing here is sheltered from weather coming off Baker.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.water: Running water is unreliable at this height. In spring, when the peak is in condition, you melt snow, which is what nearly every party does. Later in the year expect to carry from the tarns at the saddle below
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary you cross on the way up into the basin. No overnight wilderness permit is required and none is issued for this area. Party size is capped at twelve. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass covers parking at the road end. This is national forest, not national park, so no park backcountry permit applies and none can be obtained for it. Stoves rather than fires, and pack out everything including waste on snow
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Two or three tents on the last flat ground beside the highest trees; more parties than that and people are pitching on open snow

wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.name: East Rankin Lake
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.notes: The lower of the two natural stopping places on the approach, in the Rankin Creek basin below the saddle. It is the sensible camp for a party that started late, that is walking extra road miles because of the washout, or that wants an easier carry on day one and a longer summit day on day two. From here the route continues north on easy-angled snow to the small saddle and then east into the upper basin, so nothing is wasted. The cost is close to a thousand feet of climbing left over for summit morning on a route where the difficulties start high. In spring the lake is a flat white plain and easy to camp on; later in the season the basin brushes up and the ground around the water is soggy.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.water: The lake, once it has melted out. In the spring climbing season it is frozen and buried, so plan on melting snow
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass for the vehicle at the road end. No campfires above treeline; use a stove. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and keep off the heather when it is out
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Two or three tents around the lake basin on snow or, late in the year, on gravel and heather away from the shore

wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.notes: The small saddle north of the Rankin basin, with a pair of tarns beside it, sitting between east Rankin Lake and the climb east into the upper basin below Seward. It is a stopgap rather than a destination: only a few hundred feet above the lake and still well short of the ridge camp, so it is chosen mostly by parties caught by weather or darkness on the way up. It is a windy notch, which is worth knowing before you commit to it in a storm. The one thing it does well is mark the point where the approach turns from valley travel to open alpine snow, so it is a useful place to re-assess conditions before carrying a heavy load higher.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.water: Two small tarns sit right at the saddle. They are usually still under snow through the spring climbing season, so treat them as a summer source and otherwise melt snow
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the road end. Stove only
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.capacity: One or two tents on the flats beside the small lakes; informal ground with no established site

wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.notes: Sleeping at the vehicle the night before is the normal way to start this climb, because the approach is long and parties want to be walking in the dark. The switchbacks above the road's lower section give rough pullouts around 2,650 to 3,420 ft depending on how far the surface lets you drive; past the first switchback the brush closes in and the potholes get serious, and a small car will not make it far. With the road currently barriered at milepost 7 the practical bivouac is wherever the closure puts you, and the Rankin Creek switchbacks are then a long walk or bike ride away — a bicycle to the closure point is worth considering. No elevation is given here because the usable spot depends entirely on how far up the road is open in a given season, which changes.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.water: Creeks cross and run down the road in spring, and Rankin Creek is nearby. Treat anything you take
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the wilderness boundary at this elevation. Dispersed roadside camping, no permit, no reservation. Check the current fire restrictions before lighting anything and expect fires to be banned outright in dry spells; a stove is the safe assumption. Pack out all rubbish
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Roadside pullouts at the lower switchbacks take a couple of vehicles each; there are no built sites, no tables and no toilets

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: This is the established high camp for Lincoln and the one nearly every ascent uses. It sits on the ridge overlooking the Wallace Creek basin, right at the last stand of trees, with the Black Buttes and the summit block in view above. Reaching it means walking the road to about the seventh switchback, picking up the old track that leads toward Rankin Creek, scrambling into the basin, passing east Rankin Lake, then climbing mellow snow north to the saddle near 5,480 ft and east up the basin below Seward to the ridge. From here the X Couloir on the southwest face and the north ridge are both single-push summit days, and both are long, steep, exposed snow and ice, which is why the camp is high. The peak is in condition in spring, when fresh snow has mostly stopped falling but nights are still cold enough to hold the snow, ice and rock together; by high summer the face becomes loose and dangerous. Expect the trees to be buried and the ground to be snow. Nothing here is sheltered from weather coming off Baker.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.water: Running water is unreliable at this height. In spring, when the peak is in condition, you melt snow, which is what nearly every party does. Later in the year expect to carry from the tarns at the saddle below
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary you cross on the way up into the basin. No overnight wilderness permit is required and none is issued for this area. Party size is capped at twelve. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass covers parking at the road end. This is national forest, not national park, so no park backcountry permit applies and none can be obtained for it. Stoves rather than fires, and pack out everything including waste on snow
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.capacity: Two or three tents on the last flat ground beside the highest trees; more parties than that and people are pitching on open snow

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: East Rankin Lake
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: The lower of the two natural stopping places on the approach, in the Rankin Creek basin below the saddle. It is the sensible camp for a party that started late, that is walking extra road miles because of the washout, or that wants an easier carry on day one and a longer summit day on day two. From here the route continues north on easy-angled snow to the small saddle and then east into the upper basin, so nothing is wasted. The cost is close to a thousand feet of climbing left over for summit morning on a route where the difficulties start high. In spring the lake is a flat white plain and easy to camp on; later in the season the basin brushes up and the ground around the water is soggy.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.water: The lake, once it has melted out. In the spring climbing season it is frozen and buried, so plan on melting snow
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass for the vehicle at the road end. No campfires above treeline; use a stove. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and keep off the heather when it is out
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.capacity: Two or three tents around the lake basin on snow or, late in the year, on gravel and heather away from the shore

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: The small saddle north of the Rankin basin, with a pair of tarns beside it, sitting between east Rankin Lake and the climb east into the upper basin below Seward. It is a stopgap rather than a destination: only a few hundred feet above the lake and still well short of the ridge camp, so it is chosen mostly by parties caught by weather or darkness on the way up. It is a windy notch, which is worth knowing before you commit to it in a storm. The one thing it does well is mark the point where the approach turns from valley travel to open alpine snow, so it is a useful place to re-assess conditions before carrying a heavy load higher.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.water: Two small tarns sit right at the saddle. They are usually still under snow through the spring climbing season, so treat them as a summer source and otherwise melt snow
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the road end. Stove only
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.capacity: One or two tents on the flats beside the small lakes; informal ground with no established site

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: Sleeping at the vehicle the night before is the normal way to start this climb, because the approach is long and parties want to be walking in the dark. The switchbacks above the road's lower section give rough pullouts around 2,650 to 3,420 ft depending on how far the surface lets you drive; past the first switchback the brush closes in and the potholes get serious, and a small car will not make it far. With the road currently barriered at milepost 7 the practical bivouac is wherever the closure puts you, and the Rankin Creek switchbacks are then a long walk or bike ride away — a bicycle to the closure point is worth considering. No elevation is given here because the usable spot depends entirely on how far up the road is open in a given season, which changes.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.water: Creeks cross and run down the road in spring, and Rankin Creek is nearby. Treat anything you take
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the wilderness boundary at this elevation. Dispersed roadside camping, no permit, no reservation. Check the current fire restrictions before lighting anything and expect fires to be banned outright in dry spells; a stove is the safe assumption. Pack out all rubbish
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.capacity: Roadside pullouts at the lower switchbacks take a couple of vehicles each; there are no built sites, no tables and no toilets

wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_little_annapurna_south_slopes.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_west_route.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_little_sister_north_face.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
wa_little_sister_north_face.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
