wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.name: Summerland Camp
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.name: Meany Crest
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.name: Silver Springs Campground
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.notes: The practical roadhead base for a Little Tahoma trip, on the White River about a mile outside the park's White River entrance and a short drive from the Fryingpan Creek trailhead. Its usefulness is timing: the park's own drive-in campground on this side is the highest in the park and normally the last to open, typically not until late June, so for an early-season attempt on Little Tahoma this is often the nearest bed available. It is low, forested and comfortable, with real water and real toilets, and worth nothing at all for acclimatisation. Book it if you want an unhurried night before the approach without spending a wilderness permit on it.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.water: Drinking water on site during the operating season, with flush and vault toilets. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed Forest Service campground outside the park boundary, reservable through the federal booking system. It sits outside the national park, which means it is not subject to the park entrance fee or to any timed-entry reservation the park may be operating for its corridors; you pay and queue for those the following morning on the way in. This covers the campground only, and has nothing to do with either the wilderness permit or the climbing fee, both of which you still need.
wa_little_tahoma_cowlitz_ingraham_glacie.capacity: Around 55 individual drive-in sites plus one group site taking roughly 20 to 50 people; tents and RVs, no hookups

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.name: Silver Springs Campground
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.notes: The practical roadhead base for a Little Tahoma trip, on the White River about a mile outside the park's White River entrance and a short drive from the Fryingpan Creek trailhead. Its usefulness is timing: the park's own drive-in campground on this side is the highest in the park and normally the last to open, typically not until late June, so for an early-season attempt on Little Tahoma this is often the nearest bed available. It is low, forested and comfortable, with real water and real toilets, and worth nothing at all for acclimatisation. Book it if you want an unhurried night before the approach without spending a wilderness permit on it.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.water: Drinking water on site during the operating season, with flush and vault toilets. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed Forest Service campground outside the park boundary, reservable through the federal booking system. It sits outside the national park, which means it is not subject to the park entrance fee or to any timed-entry reservation the park may be operating for its corridors; you pay and queue for those the following morning on the way in. This covers the campground only, and has nothing to do with either the wilderness permit or the climbing fee, both of which you still need.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.capacity: Around 55 individual drive-in sites plus one group site taking roughly 20 to 50 people; tents and RVs, no hookups

wa_live_free_or_die.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_live_free_or_die.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_live_free_or_die.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_live_free_or_die.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_live_free_or_die.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_live_free_or_die.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_live_free_or_die.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_live_free_or_die.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_live_free_or_die.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_live_free_or_die.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_live_free_or_die.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_live_free_or_die.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_live_free_or_die.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_live_free_or_die.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_live_free_or_die.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: Spider-Formidable Col
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: Drop Creek high camp
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. It starts at the South Fork Cascade River trailhead, which is little more than a bend in the Cascade River Road around mile 17 to 18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, well below the road end at Cascade Pass. The first mile is maintained, then the trail deteriorates into ups, downs and overgrown nettle sections; past the Middle Fork turnoff you cross Drop Creek on a log and turn up into its valley on a climbers' path. That path fades after a few hundred vertical feet, but the forest above about 4,000 feet is open and the bushwhacking is unusually easy for this part of the range, with one short slide alder thicket below 4,600 feet. The camp is the obvious flat ground at around 7,100 feet with water, and from it the ground steepens to class 3 with a permanent snowfield near 7,400 feet and one narrow chasm crossing that is worth protecting. The whole approach avoids glacier travel entirely, which is why it has become the late-season choice, and recent trail work has made it the most pleasant it has been in years. Reckon on roughly twenty-five miles and eight thousand feet for the round trip.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: Running water beside the camp for most of the season, fed by the snowfield above, and a second reliable source lower down around 5,600 feet before the steep meadow climb. Late in a dry summer take the lower water seriously, because the high source is a snowfield that is shrinking.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is the usual requirement for the vehicle at Forest Service trailheads on this road, unlike the park trailhead at the end of it, so check before leaving the car. No fires at this elevation.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for a party or two, on heather and rock. Unimproved, no toilet, no windbreaks.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: South Fork Cascade River valley camps
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: The fallback first night on the Drop Creek approach to Formidable, for a party that starts late or is not confident of reaching the high camp in one push. It exists because the valley section is slower than its mileage suggests once the maintained tread runs out, with overgrown stretches and repeated small gains and losses. Camping here costs you the high camp's position and its view, and it means carrying the whole climb the next day, so most parties push through; it is recorded because the alternative to knowing it is there is a headlamp bushwhack up Drop Creek. No elevation is given because no confident figure was found for the usual sites.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: The South Fork and Drop Creek itself, running all season. Water is never the problem down here; the log crossing in high water can be.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Forest Service trailhead. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but it is damp valley forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: Rough forest sites along the valley trail and near the Drop Creek crossing, party-sized only. Nothing established.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: Le Conte Pass
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Four Point Lake — the Chewuch-side base for Remmel Mountain
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: The base for REMMEL MOUNTAIN, an 8,685 ft pile of granite carrying an old lookout site and one of the great viewpoints of the wilderness. The line in is the Chewuch trail from the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop — a long, gentle valley walk of easy miles past Chewuch Falls with dispersed camping most of the way, to a signed junction at about thirteen miles for the Four Point Lake and Coleman Ridge trail. That trail FORDS THE CHEWUCH RIVER almost immediately and it is the crux of the approach: early in the season with snowmelt running it is genuinely difficult and there is not always a log. Past the ford the grade steepens sharply and about two miles of climbing reaches the lake at 6,850 ft, with a spur into the basin. From camp the summit goes on open ground by way of the Coleman Ridge side, and it is a scramble rather than a climb. Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Glacier Gap
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.

wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_luahna_peak_east_slopes.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties
