When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_luahna_peak_southwest_slope_southeast.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_luna_glacier.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_luna_glacier.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_luna_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_luna_glacier.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_luna_glacier.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_luna_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_luna_glacier.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_luna_glacier.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_luna_glacier.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_luna_glacier.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_luna_glacier.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_luna_glacier.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_luna_glacier.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_luna_glacier.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_luna_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_luna_glacier.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_luna_glacier.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_luna_glacier.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_luna_glacier.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_luna_glacier.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_luna_glacier.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_luna_glacier.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_luna_glacier.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_luna_glacier.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_luna_glacier.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_luna_glacier.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_luna_glacier.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_luna_glacier.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_luna_glacier.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_luna_glacier.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_luna_glacier.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_luna_glacier.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_luna_glacier.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_luna_glacier.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_luna_glacier.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Luna Camp (Big Beaver Trail)
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.notes: The signed camp about 8 miles up the Big Beaver Trail from the boat landing, in old-growth cedar and only modestly above lake level. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it earns its place because the water-taxi timetable often puts you on the trail late. From here it is another 1.5 miles north to the easy-to-miss boot path that leaves the trail just above the Access Creek confluence, so sleeping here sets you up to start the bushwhack fresh rather than at dusk.
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.water: Big Beaver Creek, right there and reliable
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for every overnight in the park complex, picked up from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount; Luna Camp is a designated site, not cross-country ground
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites; your permit itinerary names the camp and the night

wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.notes: The open basin at the top of the Access Creek approach, roughly 1,700 ft above Luna Camp and the standard base for the peak. Getting here is the hard part: valley-bottom devil's club, a crossing to the north bank, then a swap back to the south side near 3,700-3,800 ft where cairns and a faint path use talus benches to duck the worst slide alder. Reports put the bushwhack alone at around three hours on the way out. From camp the climb goes up talus gullies southwest to a gap in the ridge, south of Point 6,730 on heather benches, then across the basin at about 6,600 ft to Luna Col at 7,200 ft — some 4,000 ft of gain, all of it above the last dependable water, so tank up before leaving.
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.water: Access Creek at the head of the drainage; reliable, but it is the last water until lingering snowmelt higher up
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. Cross-country camping is only allowed on durable surfaces — snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadows, and never within 100 ft of water
wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.capacity: Open basin ground; parties describe it as pleasant camping for a small group rather than a set of established sites

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_lundin_peak_south_face_left.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_magic_mountain_north_face.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_magic_mountain_north_face.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_magic_mountain_north_face.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_magic_mountain_north_face.name: Pelton Basin
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_magic_mountain_north_face.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

wa_magic_mountain_north_face.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_magic_mountain_north_face.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
wa_magic_mountain_west_ridge.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Holden Village
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Holden Lake
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Leroy Basin
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Ice Lakes
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_martin_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_marvin_s_ear.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
wa_marvin_s_ear.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_marvin_s_ear.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_marvin_s_ear.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_marvin_s_ear.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_marvin_s_ear.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_marvin_s_ear.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_marvin_s_ear.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_marvin_s_ear.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_marvin_s_ear.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_marvin_s_ear.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_marvin_s_ear.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_marvin_s_ear.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_marvin_s_ear.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_marvin_s_ear.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_marvin_s_ear.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_marvin_s_ear.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_marvin_s_ear.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_marvin_s_ear.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_marvin_s_ear.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_marvin_s_ear.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_marvin_s_ear.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_marvin_s_ear.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_marvin_s_ear.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_marvin_s_ear.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_marvin_s_ear.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_marvin_s_ear.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_marvin_s_ear.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_marvin_s_ear.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_marvin_s_ear.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_massie_peak_west_route.name: Massie Lake basin
wa_massie_peak_west_route.notes: This is the climbing camp for Massie Peak and effectively the only one, because everything above it is dry and everything below it is a long way down. From the Trinity trailhead the Buck Creek trail runs a mile and a half to the junction, the Chiwawa River trail carries on up the valley and crosses the river on a bridge, and about three miles along it the Massie Lake trail turns off and climbs roughly two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake. THAT LAST STRETCH IS THE DIFFICULTY AND IT IS NOT A TRAIL IN ANY USEFUL SENSE. It is an unsigned and unmaintained old sheep driveway, steep, brushy and lost altogether in places, and the standard complaint about this lake is the amount of bushwhacking involved in reaching it. Expect to lose the line more than once and to be pushing through vegetation on the steepest part of the day. From camp the west route on Massie Peak goes on open slopes above the basin and is a scramble rather than a climb. The reward for the thrash is genuine solitude and good fishing; the register-level traffic here is a fraction of what the Buck Creek Pass side sees. Season is roughly mid-July into early October, later than a lake this height would suggest because the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.water: The lake, and it is dependable all season. This is the last certain water on the climb and the reason to camp here rather than higher: the slopes and benches above the basin run on snowmelt only and are dry by August in an ordinary year. Fill completely before going up. Treat it, though the shoreline sees very little use.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the Trinity trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book in advance. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at Trinity. Camp back from the shoreline and on existing bare ground; this is a small basin and it marks easily. Carry a stove — summer fire restrictions on this dry east side are routine and often total.
