wa_massie_peak_west_route.capacity: Informal ground around the lake for one or two parties. There is nothing developed, nothing signed and no toilet, and the basin is small — but it is also so little visited that competition for space is not a realistic worry.

wa_massie_peak_west_route.name: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
wa_massie_peak_west_route.notes: These are the first-night camps for a party that has driven a long way, or the last-night camps for one walking out, and on this approach both cases are common. The river bridge where the Buck Creek trail crosses is the usual spot and is the obvious place to stop, being flat, sheltered and on good water. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the Massie Lake turn is unsigned and the driveway above it is steep and vague — that is ground you want to meet in the morning with fresh legs and a full day, not at dusk. The valley walking below is gentle and fast, so a party that gets away from the road in the afternoon can be here comfortably. THE ROAD CLOSURE CHANGES THE ARITHMETIC ENTIRELY. With the Chiwawa River road shut above Atkinson Flat, Trinity is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns the walk to these camps into a long day on its own or a bike shuttle, and turns the trip as a whole from two nights into three or four.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.water: The Chiwawa River is alongside for this whole stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is where the approach is generous with water, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Massie Lake is the steep, hot, brushy part and there is nothing dependable on it.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit from the Trinity trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below the high country in existing rings outside a burn ban, but the Chiwawa valley is dry and bans are the norm from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the timber along the valley floor, including good ground where the trail crosses the river on the bridge. One or two parties each, nothing developed, and rarely anyone else there.

wa_massie_peak_west_route.name: Trinity trailhead roadhead
wa_massie_peak_west_route.notes: The staging point, and it is recorded because the drive is the part of this trip that most often goes wrong. In a normal year the Chiwawa River road runs about twenty-two miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, with the last stretch rough gravel genuinely unsuited to low clearance, and arriving at the end of it late and tired is how parties end up starting the walk in badly. From the roadhead a short section of closed road leads onto the Buck Creek trail, and the junction where the Chiwawa River trail branches right for Massie is a mile and a half in. THE ROAD IS SHUT ABOVE ATKINSON FLAT under a storm-damage order running into 2027, with the 2026 fire closure sitting over the same corridor on top of it, and while that stands there is no legal way to drive to this roadhead at all. When the road is open again, expect it to remain the fragile part of any plan here: it has been damaged repeatedly, it carries no through traffic to justify quick repair, and the trailhead is far enough up it that a single washout removes the whole approach.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.water: The Chiwawa River is close by and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap anywhere at this end of the road. Fill everything here, since the valley trail above is good for water and the climb to the lake is not.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is taken from the register here — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit including stock. Fire restrictions bite hard on this side from midsummer and commonly ban all open flame including in existing rings.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.capacity: A gravel parking area at the end of the public road with room to sleep in a vehicle. It is a roadhead, not a campground — no fee site, no tables, no toilet you should count on. The developed campgrounds strung along the Chiwawa River road below it are the proper drive-in option and are recorded in the Entiat and Holden file rather than repeated here.

wa_massie_peak_west_route.name: The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
wa_massie_peak_west_route.notes: Recorded honestly: Massie Peak is a day objective from the lake and there is no practical reason to sleep higher. The scramble from the basin is short enough that the only argument for going up is to be on the crest at first light, and the cost is carrying water two thousand feet and sleeping exposed with nothing to shelter behind. The one situation where these benches genuinely earn their place is the traverse northwest on the old sheepherder's line toward Pass No Pass and the Buck Creek Pass country, which runs two and a half to three miles on faint stock and game tracks that come and go, and which a party will not finish in the same day they climb the peak. If you are doing that, sleeping high on the way out makes sense. If you are climbing Massie and walking back down the driveway, it does not. Either way, do not plan on finding water and do not plan on finding a flat, cleared spot.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. By August there is usually nothing at all above the lake, and a party sleeping up here is carrying every drop from the basin below. This is the single most common way to get the trip wrong.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at Trinity. No fires this high — carry a stove. The ground is thin subalpine turf that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
wa_massie_peak_west_route.capacity: None established. There is open ground on the benches and in the meadows above the lake where a small party could put down a tent, but nothing has been built, nothing is marked, and nobody camps here as a matter of course. That is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a site.

wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_mcclellan_peak_southwest_scramble.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.name: West Fork Agnes Creek — the bivy under Agnes Mountain
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the working bivy zone for AGNES MOUNTAIN and it needs to be described honestly: THE TRAIL HAS ALL BUT VANISHED. What is marked on maps as the West Fork Agnes Creek trail is now a rough bushwhack up the drainage, last given any real maintenance a decade or more ago, and it leads nowhere except to the base of the mountain. Round trip from High Bridge is around seventeen miles of walking on top of the boat and the shuttle. The recommended line on the peak itself takes the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak first and then traverses to Agnes's south ridge, with short technical sections up to about 5.6 — so this is a climb rather than a scramble, on a peak that is seldom done precisely because the approach is so poor relative to its modest height. Navigation skill is not optional. Season is roughly July into September; earlier the creek is high and the brush is worse, later the days are too short for the mileage. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved ground and finding its own way up a drainage with no tread, this is the wrong objective.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.water: The West Fork itself for as long as you are beside it, which is most of the way. Above it, snowmelt only and only early in the season. There is no reason to be short of water low down and every reason to carry it once you leave the creek.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required for any overnight, and off-trail nights are handled as cross-country camping rather than as a named site — say what ground you intend to use when you arrange it rather than booking a camp that does not exist. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.

wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.name: Company Creek and Hilgard Pass — the lower-valley approach to Flora Mountain
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.notes: FLORA MOUNTAIN is the peak in this zone that does not start at High Bridge, and sending a party up the valley for it wastes a day. The Company Creek road leaves the Stehekin road about five and a half miles from the landing — the shuttle will drop you — and the trail from it climbs steeply, fords Company Creek at around five miles, and then follows Hilgard Creek to Hilgard Pass at 6,700 ft. THE FORD IS THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: it is a real crossing and in a high-water year it is the reason parties turn back, so check the level with a ranger before you commit to the day. Flora is one of the hundred highest summits in the state at a little over 8,300 ft and its southwest side is a talus and boulder hop rather than a climb, so once you are in position the summit is not the work. It can also be taken from a camp in the Bird Creek drainage on the Devore Creek side, which is the more commonly described base and is covered elsewhere; the Company Creek line is the one that starts from the lower valley road and it suits a party already camped at Harlequin. The views on the way up over Tupshin and Devore are the best part of the walk. July into early October, and the larch colour late in that window is worth planning around.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.water: Company Creek and then Hilgard Creek for most of the climb, which is generous by the standards of these approaches. The pass itself and the ground above it are dry once the snow has gone, so fill in the basin before going up for the summit.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.permit: The trail leaves the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area about two miles up and enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, so the rules change under your feet. A North Cascades backcountry permit covers the recreation area portion and any park camps; the wilderness above is national forest ground with a free self-issued permit and no quota. Work out which side of the line you intend to sleep on before booking anything. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass considerations apply on the forest side. Store food properly throughout; fires are inappropriate at the pass and restrictions are usual lower down by midsummer.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble.capacity: Dispersed. There is workable ground in the upper Hilgard Creek basin and around the pass, room for a party or two, with nothing developed and no facilities. The lower valley has scattered spots along the trail.

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_west_ridge.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_west_ridge.notes: The planned camp for this route and effectively the only one — a flat gravelly basin roughly 400 ft below and north of the 6,200 to 6,350 ft notch that the approach crosses. Comfortable ground, water at hand, and a direct view of the Pickets. From here it is a long traverse over benches and slabs to the Terror Glacier and the gully to the col, so most parties treat it as a two-night camp and climb from it rather than moving up. The descent off the notch into the basin is the crux of getting here: loose and steep late season, a firm snow finger with a short steep headwall early. Camp on gravel or rock, not the heather, and keep 100 ft back from the water.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_west_ridge.water: Streams running through the basin flats from the snowfields above; dependable but silty, so filter and treat
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_west_ridge.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone; it is a walk-up zone rather than one of the reservable ones
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_west_ridge.capacity: Multiple tent sites on bare ground in the rocky meadows, plus a bivy platform sized for two side by side with gear; the zone is capped at six parties per night and six people per party

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Barclay Lake
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: The traverse of Mount Index's three peaks is the one objective in this zone that is genuinely an overnight rather than a long day, and this is where parties sleep. The line links South, Middle and North Peaks along a crest of loose ridges and gullies with rappels between them, and the recorded practice is a flat spot right on the crest between the two Middle Peak summits with snow nearby, which solves the water problem in early season. Parties who have done it in a push describe going light and treating the bivouac as an emergency plan that they were glad to have and glad not to need — take minimal gear rather than a full camp, because everything you carry has to come over some genuinely poor rock. Approach is the Lake Serene trail as for everything else on the mountain. The rock on Index is famously rotten and the descent options off the ridge are limited, so committing to a bivouac here means committing to finishing the traverse; do not plan it as a place to sit out bad weather.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: Snow on the crest into early summer, and nothing at all once it goes. On a dry traverse you carry water for the whole ridge or you drop off it.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: One small party. A flat patch on the ridge crest between the two Middle Peak summits — a stance, not a site.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Money Creek Campground
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Beckler River Campground
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.

wa_merchant_peak_south_route.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. It sits about eleven miles up the Index-Galena Road from US 2 at roughly 1,200 ft on the North Fork Skykomish, which put it within twenty minutes of the Lake Serene trailhead and made it the obvious base for Mount Index. Flooding washed out the Index-Galena Road near mileposts 10 and 14, the road is gated closed through that section with permanent repairs estimated in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the county has said environmental review and permitting may take several years. The campground is inaccessible and closed as a result, and the neighbouring campground further up the same road is closed with it. Confirm the road status before counting on it; if the gate is still shut, the working substitutes for an Index-area night are Money Creek down the highway or a dispersed pullout on the Beckler system. Nothing on the Reiter Road side fills the gap — the lower Reiter Foothills road corridor is state land signed day use only with no camping and a Discover Pass required, which is the approach used for Mount Persis, so plan Persis as a day out from the valley.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
wa_merchant_peak_south_route.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Wing Lake
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Lewis Lake
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
wa_mesahchie_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.name: Pelton Basin
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
wa_mix_up_peak_east_face.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_mojo_rising.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_mojo_rising.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_mojo_rising.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_mojo_rising.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_mojo_rising.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_mojo_rising.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_mojo_rising.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_mojo_rising.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_mojo_rising.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_mojo_rising.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_mojo_rising.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_mojo_rising.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_mojo_rising.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_mojo_rising.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_mojo_rising.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
