wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_monte_cristo_peak_scramble.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Copper Glance Lake
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: Lunch Counter
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.notes: The standard high camp for the South Climb and effectively the only sheltered ground on the route, a wide rubble bench under Suksdorf Ridge about four miles and 3,700 ft above Cold Springs. Its height is given anywhere from roughly 9,200 to 9,400 ft because the bench is long and people camp at both ends rather than at one spot. The rock walls left by earlier parties are the whole reason to camp here — wind funnels across the bench and an unprotected tent takes a beating — so plan on repairing a wall rather than finding a perfect one. The summit ridge east of here forms the Yakama Nation boundary; the South Climb stays on Forest Service ground, but do not descend or traverse east off the standard line.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.water: Snowmelt only, and seasonal. Running meltwater usually appears at the upper end of the bench through early and mid summer, but it is not dependable — in a thin snow year or by late season the bench can be dry, so carry a stove and fuel to melt snow.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — this camp is above the 7,000 ft threshold that triggers it between May 1 and Sept 30. Bought through recreation.gov, valid for a single climbing trip; carry it and leave a copy in the windshield. Parking at the South Climb trailhead needs a recreation pass, and the climbing pass parking stub satisfies that within Mt. Adams Wilderness in season. Outside that window or below 7,000 ft, a free self-issued wilderness permit is what applies. Human waste must be packed out in the supplied bags.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.capacity: Large — dozens of parties on summer weekends, spread across a broad bench; scores of pre-built rock windbreaks, though the best-sheltered ones fill first

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: Morrison Creek Campground
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.notes: The fallback camp when the upper road defeats a vehicle or when Cold Springs is full, about three miles below the South Climb trailhead on the same road. The 2012 Cascade Creek fire burned through here, so shade is patchy and there is standing dead timber to consider when choosing a tent spot in wind. Camping here means driving or walking the last steep section to the trailhead in the morning, which costs about an hour but keeps the option open when the road is rough.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.water: Morrison Creek runs beside the camp but is seasonal and can be low or dry by late summer; treat what you take and do not count on it in August or September.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.permit: No climbing pass needed at this elevation — it sits well below the 7,000 ft line. A free self-issued wilderness permit covers travel into Mt. Adams Wilderness from here, and a recreation pass applies at the trailheads above.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites, several strung along the creek

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the Killen Creek trailhead. Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.notes: Parties attacking the Adams Glacier sometimes move above High Camp onto the moraines below the icefall to shorten summit day, with usable ground reported roughly between 7,100 and 7,700 ft depending on which rib and how the moraine has changed. Exact spots shift year to year as the glacier retreats and the moraine slumps, so treat any elevation given for it as approximate and be prepared to camp lower. It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform

wa_mount_adams_south_climb.name: The Lunch Counter
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.notes: The standard high camp, a broad rubble-and-snow bench up the South Spur above the Crescent Glacier; its height is given anywhere from about 9,000 to 9,400 ft depending which shelf you stop on. Wind is the defining problem — pitch inside an existing rock wall and expect to rebuild part of it. Being above treeline it is a bad place to be caught in a thunderstorm, which on Adams typically builds in the afternoon. Summit day from here is commonly 4-5 hours up.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.water: Unreliable. When nights stay above freezing there is meltwater at the foot of the snowfield between Suksdorf Ridge and the Mazama Glacier, but it is occasional even in midsummer and gone once the snow pulls back. Plan on melting snow or carrying up what you need.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.permit: A Mt. Adams Climbing Pass is required from 1 May to 30 September for anyone 16 or older going above 7,000 ft, whether or not they intend to summit; it is bought on Recreation.gov and must be carried on you and shown in the vehicle windscreen. From October through April a self-issued wilderness permit replaces it. Human waste must be packed out in carry-out bags (free at the Mt. Adams Ranger District) because decomposition above 7,000 ft is too slow to keep up. Group size limit is 12; no campfires.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.capacity: Large and informal — a spread of bare bench with dozens of stone windbreaks that climbers have built and rebuilt over the years. Room for many parties, and on summer weekends there are many.

wa_mount_adams_south_climb.name: Morrison Creek drainage
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.notes: Lower option below the Crescent Glacier, used by parties who would rather not sleep in the crowds and wind at the Lunch Counter. It costs you elevation on summit day. Morrison Creek Campground further down the road is also used by parties arriving late who do not want to drive the rough final miles of FR 8040 in the dark.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.water: Morrison Creek is the last dependable running water on the approach and a common place to top off.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.permit: Below 7,000 ft only a free self-issued wilderness permit is needed, so a camp here sits outside the climbing-pass requirement.
