wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the Killen Creek trailhead. Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards

wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.notes: Parties attacking the Adams Glacier sometimes move above High Camp onto the moraines below the icefall to shorten summit day, with usable ground reported roughly between 7,100 and 7,700 ft depending on which rib and how the moraine has changed. Exact spots shift year to year as the glacier retreats and the moraine slumps, so treat any elevation given for it as approximate and be prepared to camp lower. It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform

wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.name: Honeymoon Meadows
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.notes: PLANNED camp and the last big established site on the West Fork, roughly eight trail-miles past the ranger station. Dry ground at the far end of the meadows once the snow goes. Getting here involves at least one calf- to knee-deep ford of the West Fork depending on melt, so arrive with time to deal with a high river rather than in the dark.
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays

wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.name: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.notes: PLANNED alternative about 0.7 mile and 700 ft above Honeymoon Meadows, below Anderson Pass. Sheltered and in trees, which is its value in weather — but parties routinely walk past it without finding it under snow, so do not commit to it as your only plan on a late arrival. It is still below the pass, so it leaves the whole climbers' path and moraine for the next day.
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays

wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one worth reaching — open slopes above Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, roughly a mile past the pass up the climbers' path and moraine, and preferred by parties specifically to avoid sleeping in the forest at or below the pass. Budget 7-9 hours from the road closure to here. This is the last water on the route: the snow finger to Flypaper Pass and everything on the Eel above it has none, so fill here or plan to melt. Exposed to wind, with no built shelter.
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.water: the tarn when melted out; often still frozen in spring, so melt snow
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.capacity: a few tents on open ground near the tarn

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Deer Lake
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Heart Lake
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Cat Basin
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Appleton Pass
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
wa_mount_angeles_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
wa_mount_angeles_standard.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Artist Point and the Heather Meadows road end
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: The obvious place to sleep is, plainly, the one place you cannot. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Silver Fir Campground
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: The closest developed campground to the Heather Meadows end of the highway, roughly fourteen miles east of Glacier on the west side of the road just after the river crossing, and about eight miles below the Heather Meadows lots. This is the practical answer for a party that drives up the night before a scramble on Table Mountain, Mount Herman or Mount Ann and wants to be at the trailhead early without sleeping in a day-use car park. It is emphatically staging rather than plan: you are three thousand feet below the objectives and the drive up in the morning takes twenty minutes. Because there are no reservations it is a gamble on a Friday evening in July and August, and the fallback is the campground further down the valley. It stays open later into the autumn than the road to Artist Point does, which matters for anyone climbing these peaks in October.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: Piped water at the campground during the operating season, and the river alongside. Confirm the water is turned on if you are arriving at the shoulders of the season.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: A campground fee is charged per night and paid on site; this is a fee campground rather than a pass site, so a recreation pass does not cover the overnight. Fires are allowed in the provided rings unless a county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry August is common. Standard national forest food-storage sense applies — black bears work this valley.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: About twenty sites in forest beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and drinking water in season; first come, first served, and it fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Douglas Fir Campground
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. This is a busy, family-friendly circuit and the sites go early on a summer weekend, so arrive with a plan for finding all four taken.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: The lakes, and they are reliable all season. There is no potable water anywhere on the circuit, so treat everything.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit is required or issued. Recreation pass on the vehicle at whichever of the four trailheads you start from. CAMPING IS RESTRICTED TO THE MARKED SITES — the meadows here are heather over thin soil and the designation exists because they were being destroyed. No campfires at all, carry-in stoves only. Party size twelve. Food must go in a bear-resistant canister or be hung at least ten feet up and four feet out from the trunk and branches; there is no hardware provided.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Bearpaw Lake
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: The base for Bearpaw Mountain and the only camping anywhere near its own line. Canyon Creek Road leaves the Mount Baker Highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north for a long, slow fourteen miles or so of alternating tarmac and serious potholes before a signed spur climbs right to the lake trailhead; the last couple of miles are single lane with brush closing in that will mark a car. From the trailhead it is roughly a mile to the lake, short but steep. The peak's easiest line is a class three scramble from the southwest, following the timbered ridge east of the lake, with a direct variation onto the steeper part of the ridge that gives a narrow and locally exposed scramble. ROAD ACCESS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK AND NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: Canyon Creek Road has been closed at around mile four by a landslide carrying large timber and debris, with more downed trees below the block, which cuts off the lake spur and the road end entirely. When that closure is in force there is no alternative approach to this peak, only a very long road walk. Snow lies on this ground into July in most years.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: The lake, at camp. Treat it. This is the only water on the peak's own approach and there is nothing on the ridge above.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE any designated wilderness — this ground sits west of the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary, so there is no self-issue permit and no wilderness party limit here, and the twelve-person rule and blanket fire ban that govern the Heather Meadows half of this zone do not automatically apply. What does apply is a recreation pass at the trailhead, and whatever county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry summer is usually a total one. Pack out everything including human waste; there is no toilet.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: A few rough informal sites at a small lake in the trees; low use, no facilities, no toilet and nothing built

wa_mount_ann_scramble.name: Excelsior ridge camps and the high spring, Canyon Creek Road end
wa_mount_ann_scramble.notes: This is the established high camping on the Canyon Creek road system, at the far end of the same road that serves Bearpaw, and it is listed with the caveat that IT IS NOT ON BEARPAW'S OWN ROUTE. Bearpaw is the prominent summit standing to the west, seen across the drainage from the pass and the ridge, and reaching it from here means dropping and re-climbing rather than walking a connecting line. Its value is as the answer to what a party does when the day goes wrong or when they want two objectives out of one long, slow drive: legal, watered, established camping at the road end of a road most people will only want to drive once. The trail leaves the road end, meets a junction in less than a mile with the Canyon Ridge trail going left, reaches the small lakes just beyond and then climbs through forest and into open meadow towards the pass. The same landslide closure that gates the Bearpaw spur gates this trailhead as well; the alternative is to walk up from the highway instead, which is a far bigger day. Meadows here are at their best in July and August and again for autumn colour in September and October.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.water: A spring about half a mile short of Excelsior Pass is the best and most dependable water in this high country and is the reason the camps are where they are. The lakes lower down at the trailhead end are shallow and warm late in the season. Treat everything, and fill at the spring rather than counting on anything on the crest.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.permit: The ridge camps sit inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, which the High Divide trail enters at the pass — so from there on it is party size twelve, no campfires of any kind, carry-in stoves only, camp on durable ground and pack out all waste including human waste. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead and there is a self-issue register. The ground below the pass around the lakes is outside the wilderness and less strictly governed, but the burn bans still apply.
wa_mount_ann_scramble.capacity: Scattered informal sites on the ridge running south from Excelsior Peak and along the High Divide, plus a cluster near the spring; a handful of small parties, spread out, with no built sites and no toilet

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Deer Lake
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Heart Lake
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Cat Basin
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Appleton Pass
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
wa_mount_appleton_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
wa_mount_appleton_standard.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Wing Lake
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Lewis Lake
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

wa_mount_arriva_scramble.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: Numerous flat gravel and snow platforms along the moraine crest; the busiest camp on the north side and it fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: Pushing camp onto the glacier below the Black Buttes cuts a real chunk out of summit day and puts you above most of the weather that sits on the moraine. It costs you a fully exposed camp on snow, so platforms need walls, and everything about the site depends on that year's crevasse pattern — what was a flat bench one August can be broken up the next. Parties are already roped and on glacier travel terrain to reach it, which rules it out for anyone wanting a simple carry. Wind is the usual reason people retreat from here to the Hogsback.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: None you can rely on — this is a melt-snow camp, so budget fuel accordingly. Occasional surface runoff appears on the rock of the Black Buttes in hot spells but should not be planned around.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: The saddle between Colfax Peak and the main summit is occasionally used as a very high bivy by strong parties shortening summit day, and more often as an emergency stop by parties caught out by weather or a slow descent. It is fully exposed to wind and to whatever the mountain is doing, with no shelter of any kind, and the Roman Wall above it is not somewhere to be improvising in a storm. Treat it as a contingency rather than a plan unless the forecast is settled and your party is fast. It is also the last place on the route with any option other than continuing up or going down.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: None. Melt snow, or carry everything from lower on the route.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: One or two small parties at most; an exposed high point rather than a campsite

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: The standard Easton Glacier high camp, reached by following the Railroad Grade moraine up from Schriebers Meadow and Morovitz Meadow. The basin gives real wind protection, which is why it is preferred over the more scenic but more exposed ground on the moraine crest itself. The gravel road in is snowbound into June in most years and is rough enough to be worth checking before a long drive. There have been seasons with no toilet facilities anywhere on the mountain, with blue bags issued free at the Sedro-Woolley ranger office, so carry a pack-out system.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: Contested and season-dependent. Some parties find runoff at the north end of the camp and on the rocky ground above it; others arrive to find nothing exposed at all and must melt snow. Plan for melting and treat running water as a bonus.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — the approach runs through the Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and the upper moraine into Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit. A recreation pass is required to park at the Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead. Registering your climb at a ranger station is voluntary but sensible.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: The main climbers' camp on the south side, in a sheltered sandy basin at the crest of the moraine; multiple tent sites, busy in July and August

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: Railroad Grade and Morovitz Meadow camps
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: These lower sites suit parties arriving in the evening, anyone wanting shelter from wind, and low-snow years when the higher ground has no water at all. They are meadow and subalpine terrain, so camp on durable surfaces and off the vegetation, which is slow to recover here. Summit day from this elevation is long, and most parties treat these as a first night before moving camp up rather than as a base for the climb. In heavy snow years the alternative runs the other way and people camp as high as 6,800 ft because that is where flat snow is.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: Generally reliable — meadow streams and melt channels run here later into the season than they do at the top of the moraine, which is much of the reason to camp low
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and Mount Baker Wilderness). No overnight permit; recreation pass required to park at Schriebers Meadow.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: Scattered sites in the trees behind the eastern moraine and on the ridge east of the Railroad Grade, roughly 5,500 to 5,800 ft; smaller and quieter than Sandy Camp

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.name: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.notes: North Ridge parties generally carry from the Hogsback out onto the Coleman and bivy somewhere around 6,800 to 7,000 ft to shorten the approach to the base of the ridge, which itself rises around 4,000 ft to the summit. Where exactly that camp sits is decided by crevasse conditions on the day rather than by any fixed location, so it is worth arriving with daylight left to scout. The camp is on glacier, exposed, and above the point where you can retreat without roping up. The same Glacier Creek Road closure that affects the Coleman-Deming applies to this whole approach, so confirm road access first.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.water: None reliable. Melt snow, and carry enough fuel for a party that will also be melting for the climb.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required to camp. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.capacity: Dug snow platforms for one or two parties; no established site, and the usable spot moves year to year

wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.

It costs you a fully exposed camp on snow, so platforms need walls, and everything about the site depends on that year's crevasse pattern — what was a flat bench one August can be broken up the next. Parties are already roped and on glacier travel terrain to reach it, which rules it out for anyone wanting a simple carry. Wind is the usual reason people retreat from here to the Hogsback.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.water: None you can rely on — this is a melt-snow camp, so budget fuel accordingly. Occasional surface runoff appears on the rock of the Black Buttes in hot spells but should not be planned around.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.notes: The saddle between Colfax Peak and the main summit is occasionally used as a very high bivy by strong parties shortening summit day, and more often as an emergency stop by parties caught out by weather or a slow descent. It is fully exposed to wind and to whatever the mountain is doing, with no shelter of any kind, and the Roman Wall above it is not somewhere to be improvising in a storm. Treat it as a contingency rather than a plan unless the forecast is settled and your party is fast. It is also the last place on the route with any option other than continuing up or going down.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.water: None. Melt snow, or carry everything from lower on the route.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.capacity: One or two small parties at most; an exposed high point rather than a campsite

wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.name: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.notes: The standard Easton Glacier high camp, reached by following the Railroad Grade moraine up from Schriebers Meadow and Morovitz Meadow. The basin gives real wind protection, which is why it is preferred over the more scenic but more exposed ground on the moraine crest itself. The gravel road in is snowbound into June in most years and is rough enough to be worth checking before a long drive. There have been seasons with no toilet facilities anywhere on the mountain, with blue bags issued free at the Sedro-Woolley ranger office, so carry a pack-out system.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.water: Contested and season-dependent. Some parties find runoff at the north end of the camp and on the rocky ground above it; others arrive to find nothing exposed at all and must melt snow. Plan for melting and treat running water as a bonus.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — the approach runs through the Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and the upper moraine into Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit. A recreation pass is required to park at the Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead. Registering your climb at a ranger station is voluntary but sensible.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.capacity: The main climbers' camp on the south side, in a sheltered sandy basin at the crest of the moraine; multiple tent sites, busy in July and August

wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.name: Railroad Grade and Morovitz Meadow camps
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.notes: These lower sites suit parties arriving in the evening, anyone wanting shelter from wind, and low-snow years when the higher ground has no water at all. They are meadow and subalpine terrain, so camp on durable surfaces and off the vegetation, which is slow to recover here. Summit day from this elevation is long, and most parties treat these as a first night before moving camp up rather than as a base for the climb. In heavy snow years the alternative runs the other way and people camp as high as 6,800 ft because that is where flat snow is.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.water: Generally reliable — meadow streams and melt channels run here later into the season than they do at the top of the moraine, which is much of the reason to camp low
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and Mount Baker Wilderness). No overnight permit; recreation pass required to park at Schriebers Meadow.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.capacity: Scattered sites in the trees behind the eastern moraine and on the ridge east of the Railroad Grade, roughly 5,500 to 5,800 ft; smaller and quieter than Sandy Camp

wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.name: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.notes: North Ridge parties generally carry from the Hogsback out onto the Coleman and bivy somewhere around 6,800 to 7,000 ft to shorten the approach to the base of the ridge, which itself rises around 4,000 ft to the summit. Where exactly that camp sits is decided by crevasse conditions on the day rather than by any fixed location, so it is worth arriving with daylight left to scout. The camp is on glacier, exposed, and above the point where you can retreat without roping up. The same Glacier Creek Road closure that affects the Coleman-Deming applies to this whole approach, so confirm road access first.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.water: None reliable. Melt snow, and carry enough fuel for a party that will also be melting for the climb.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required to camp. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.capacity: Dug snow platforms for one or two parties; no established site, and the usable spot moves year to year

wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.name: Hogsback
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.notes: Shared with the Coleman-Deming route and reached by branching off Trail 677 at the old Kulshan Cabin site and climbing the moraine crest. There are no trees at this elevation, so food has to go in a bear canister or Ursack — the nearest suitable trees for hanging are lower, at Harrison Camp. Human waste goes out in blue bags; burial is not permitted on snow, rock or alpine ground. From here the North Ridge parts company with Coleman-Deming: rope up, cross the Coleman climbers' right below the Colfax icefall, and gain the ridge on the glacier's true right.
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.water: Meltwater streams run at camp — this is the last running water, and there is none once you are on the Coleman. Treat it; nothing here is potable as found. Flow swings hard with the sun, so a channel that is a step across at dawn can be a torrent by mid-afternoon.
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.permit: No quota or overnight permit; a valid Recreation Pass must be displayed at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (a Washington Sno-Park permit for winter parking on Glacier Creek Road). Mount Baker Wilderness rules apply: parties of 12 or fewer, no campfires of any kind, self-contained stoves only.
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.capacity: Sites are scattered along roughly 200 ft of moraine crest between 6,000 and 6,200 ft, so exactly where you end up depends on water and on who got there first. It is a busy camp — several parties most summer weekends.

wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.capacity: Numerous flat gravel and snow platforms along the moraine crest; the busiest camp on the north side and it fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, SR 20
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the western door to Azurite and Ballard, and the drive alone puts it a long way from anywhere — roughly thirty-three miles east of Marblemount and sixteen west of Rainy Pass, with no services in either direction. Parties commonly sleep in the lot before starting, and the low elevation means it is warm and buggy in early summer when the peaks above are still white. The trail from here runs about six miles up Canyon Creek before the Mill Creek trail branches right at around two thousand eight hundred feet, a third of a mile past the trail's own crossing of Mill Creek. The whole point of understanding this trailhead is the arithmetic that follows: the pass is around six thousand seven hundred feet and the car is at nineteen hundred, so this is a genuine multi-day trip with more than four thousand seven hundred feet of gain before any climbing starts. Access depends entirely on the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts this stretch of highway from late November or early December until somewhere between mid April and early May, occasionally much later after a damaging winter.
wa_mount_ballard_south.water: No potable water at the trailhead. Canyon Creek is close by and needs filtering.
wa_mount_ballard_south.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. This is national forest and there is no quota or reservation of any kind. A separate trail from this same lot runs north into the Pasayten Wilderness, which does carry a free self-issue permit from the kiosk, so read the board and take one only if your route actually crosses that boundary.
wa_mount_ballard_south.capacity: A large parking area just east of milepost 141, roughly a third of the way between Newhalem and Rainy Pass. Rarely busy, because almost nobody uses the trail these peaks need.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Mill Creek valley and the old Azurite Mine
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the honest middle of the western approach and the reason parties allow three days rather than two. The Mill Creek trail has had almost no use since the mine closed and it shows — long sections are faint, missing outright, or buried in slide alder, and the walking is slow, wet and scratchy in a way the mileage does not convey. The mine site itself is the natural first camp, open enough to dry gear and the last obvious flat ground before the climb. Beyond it the trail continues about three miles, and a party can either leave it near five thousand six hundred feet and climb the west slopes of Azurite directly, or carry on another mile and a half to Azurite Pass. Which of those you pick decides where the second night goes. Nobody should treat this valley as a trail walk; treat it as a bushwhack that occasionally has tread.
wa_mount_ballard_south.water: Mill Creek runs alongside for most of the way and is the reliable supply on this side. Fill before leaving it for the climb toward the pass.
wa_mount_ballard_south.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land — no permit, no quota, no reservation.
