Fires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in force, but forest-wide bans are routine from mid summer and the valley is dry, so plan on a stove. The mine workings are old industrial ground: leave the structures, timbers and hardware alone and do not go into any opening.
wa_mount_ballard_south.capacity: Unimproved. There is flat ground in the timber along the creek and open ground at the abandoned mine workings about five miles up from the trail junction, roughly eleven miles from the car. Room for a party or two in several places; nothing is built and nothing is maintained.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Azurite Pass
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the hinge of the whole zone and the only camp that serves both summits well. Azurite Peak rises directly north of the pass and Mount Ballard stands about two miles further north again along the same ridge, so a party camped here can take Azurite by its south ridge and south-west gully and then continue to Ballard, or split the two across a pair of days. Both approaches converge on this spot, which is why it is worth carrying water and a tent this high rather than trying either peak from the valley. Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.
wa_mount_ballard_south.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
wa_mount_ballard_south.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
wa_mount_ballard_south.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: These are the staging camps for the eastern approach and the comfortable answer to the night before. From Winthrop the drive runs west on SR 20 and then up the Lost River Road through Mazama to the end of the pavement, continuing a mile and a half or so on the gravel of the Harts Pass road. The West Fork Methow trailhead sits close by at around two thousand seven hundred feet, at a wooden fence just off a short spur. Being low and in timber, they are usable well before and after the high country is in condition, and they are far enough down the road that none of the Harts Pass driving difficulties apply. They also make a sensible base for a party that wants a look at the trail before committing to it, which on this side is worth doing — the West Fork Methow tread is badly overgrown and in poor repair, and the brush on the banks of the upper creeks is dense enough that the trail effectively disappears.
wa_mount_ballard_south.water: The river is right there. Treat these as basic sites and assume you will filter rather than find a working spigot.
wa_mount_ballard_south.permit: No permit and no reservation, just a nightly fee paid on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a campsite, only to park at a trailhead. These are outside any wilderness, so none of the Pasayten self-issue paperwork applies.
wa_mount_ballard_south.capacity: Two small forested Forest Service campgrounds a short distance apart along the West Fork Methow, roughly eight to nine miles up the road from Mazama. Both are first come, first served only — there is no way to reserve and you must arrive in person to claim and pay for a site. Each is modest, so a summer weekend is a gamble.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the natural first night on the eastern approach to Azurite Pass and it breaks a walk that is otherwise too long to enjoy. From the trailhead near two thousand seven hundred feet the trail follows the West Fork Methow past Trout Creek and Brush Creek toward Jet Creek, and the camp sits partway along at about four thousand three hundred and fifty feet. Two warnings are worth taking seriously. The lower trail is overgrown and faint in places, though the tread improves as it climbs. And the brush on the banks of Jet Creek becomes extremely dense with no clear path through it at all, which is the section that costs parties hours and tempers. From here it is a sustained climb of well over two thousand feet to Azurite Pass and the peaks beyond, so leave early. Anyone weighing the two approaches should know they are about the same length and about equally neglected — pick by which side of the mountains you are driving from, not by hoping one has a better trail.
wa_mount_ballard_south.water: Creek water close at hand, reliable through the season. This is the last comfortable water before the long climb to the pass, so fill completely here.
wa_mount_ballard_south.permit: None. Dispersed national forest camping — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the West Fork Methow trailhead. Fires only in an existing ring and only outside a burn ban, which by August usually means not at all.
wa_mount_ballard_south.capacity: An unimproved valley camp partway up the eastern approach, past the Trout Creek and Brush Creek junctions. Space for a party or two on flat ground in the timber. Nothing is maintained.

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Graves Creek Campground — drive-in staging for the East Fork Quinault
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: This is the only realistic drive-in base on the Quinault side and the natural place to sleep the night before starting up the East Fork toward Anderson Pass and Anderson's Thumb. Vault toilets, fire grates, tables and bear lockers, and nothing else. Reach it from the North Shore Road only — the South Shore Road has a washout roughly eight miles up from the highway, and a phone will still try to route you that way and add several miles of driving for nothing. The last six miles are narrow gravel and RVs and trailers are banned regardless of what the road is doing on the day. Treat the road status as a live question rather than a settled one: this stretch has been closed to vehicles by erosion before, and when it is, both the campground and the trailhead become a two-mile walk or ride. Sleeping here costs you nothing in approach distance, which matters when the first day out is thirteen miles to Enchanted Valley.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: None piped — there is no potable water at all, so arrive with everything you need or filter from the Quinault beside the campground
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed for a night here, and no reservation is possible. The moment you walk past the trailhead you need an Olympic wilderness permit booked on the federal recreation site: eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over, plus a six dollar non-refundable booking fee, or a forty-five dollar annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. A bear canister is required in every wilderness camp area in this park, and they are loaned free to permit holders at the wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: About 30 first-come, first-served sites, open year round and rarely full outside high summer weekends; no reservations are taken

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Dodger Point Camp — the southern gateway to the Bailey Range
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: Dodger Point is 13.5 miles from the old Whiskey Bend trailhead by way of the Long Ridge trail, which leaves the Elwha at Michael's Cabin and crosses the river on a suspension bridge. With the road walk added it is about nineteen miles and well over ten thousand feet of gain to the lookout, so this is a serious approach in its own right. It is the way in to MOUNT DANA and MOUNT WILDER, the southern end of the Bailey Range, and the connecting ridge toward Ludden Peak and on to Ferry Basin, MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER. That connection is not a trail: it involves a faint path off the ridge, a steep gully of loose rock and a section where you climb a tangle of roots and branches to regain the crest. Cream Lake below Ferry Basin is infamous for mosquitoes and for steep alder-choked gullies that swallow time, so budget generously and go in a dry spell if you can. The lookout is the best viewpoint in the valley and the camp is worth a night on its own merits.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: THE WEAK POINT. There is no water between the Elwha crossing near Michael's Cabin and the tarns just below Dodger Point — a long climb. Fill everything at the river, and expect the tarns to be low or gone by late season.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. The camp itself books normally, but any night spent off-trail on the Bailey ridge beyond it is a cross-country zone and must be arranged by telephone with the wilderness information centre. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: A handful of established sites near the old lookout, on an exposed ridge crest; small, and seldom busy

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Enchanted Valley and Anderson Pass — the approach to Anderson's Thumb
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: The East Fork Quinault runs about thirteen miles from Graves Creek to the Enchanted Valley chalet, with staged camps at Pony Bridge around three miles, O'Neil Creek around six and a half and Pyrites Creek around nine, all of which are useful for breaking the walk in. This is the approach to ANDERSON'S THUMB, the pinnacle on the Anderson massif, reached by continuing from the valley up to Anderson Pass at 4,480 ft and then onto the glacier remnant and the rock above. Camping at the pass rather than in the valley saves you several miles and roughly two thousand feet on climbing day and puts you in quiet country; camping in the valley gets you a flatter, warmer night and a spectacular setting at the cost of a very long summit day and a great deal of company. Bears are habituated and confident here, so the canister rule is enforced rather than advisory, and food left out is food lost. The same pass is reached from the Dosewallips on the east side, which is the shorter approach to the Anderson massif if that road is open — worth checking before committing to the Quinault side.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.water: Reliable everywhere — the East Fork Quinault runs the length of the valley and small streams cross the trail up toward the pass
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and the EAST FORK QUINAULT RIVER IS A QUOTA AREA — reserve on the federal recreation site rather than turning up hopeful. Summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and reservations for it release on 15 April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for adults, six dollar booking fee. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY AND STRICTLY REQUIRED HERE: this valley was closed to camping over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Canisters are loaned free at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.capacity: A large valley camping area at the chalet meadow that can hold well over a hundred people on a summer weekend, plus a much smaller and quieter camp up near Anderson Pass

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Glacier Gap
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Scatter Lake basin
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Libby Lake
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: Lower Blum Lake
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: Middle Blum Lake
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: South Hagan bench
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each

wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, said plainly rather than recommending a place that does not exist. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: Lower Blum Lake
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: Middle Blum Lake
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: South Hagan bench
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each

wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, said plainly rather than recommending a place that does not exist. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: THE GROUND THAT PUTS MOUNT BUCKINDY IN RANGE. Buckindy's standard route is a class 4 scramble on the north slopes, with glaciers on the north and east flanks, and the parties who climb it are camping either in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or at the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages. Coming in from road 1570 this is a second or third night out, well beyond the Cyclone Lake ground. There is a second way in from the south, over Green Mountain and the Horse Lake saddle from the Suiattle side, with camps on the divide and in the basins on the way, but that country has its own long road problems and is not the approach this zone is built around. Nothing here is a site in any developed sense: it is remote, lightly visited ground where the answer to where you sleep is wherever the light runs out, and a party should carry the fuel to melt snow and the tolerance for a dry, windy night.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.water: Snowmelt and small basin streams, generally running through midsummer and thinning badly after that. There is ice on Buckindy's north and east flanks, so late in the season the water that is left is glacier outflow rather than clean snowmelt.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on durable ground, pack out human waste, no fires. There is no quota and no reservation anywhere in this zone, so the constraint on a trip here is the approach rather than the paperwork.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.capacity: One or two parties on snow, moraine or heather at the passes and in the basins beneath them. Nothing built, no toilet.

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Slide Lake
