wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Royal Lake
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: This is the front door to the whole Needles group and the default answer for anyone climbing Deception, Clark, Johnson, Walkinshaw, The Incisor or Sundial. It sits about seven miles and two and a half thousand feet from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, up the Dungeness and then the Royal Creek fork, which is walkable with a heavy pack in an afternoon. The honest trade is this: Royal Lake is comfortable, has real designated tent pads and is where the permit system actually issues sites, but it leaves you an extra mile and roughly five hundred to a thousand feet of loose boot path below the upper basin every single climbing morning. On a Needles day that difference is real, because the rock above the basin is dirty and slow and you want to be off it before the afternoon. Parties that only want one peak, or that have anyone who would rather not sleep at six thousand feet on gravel, are right to stay here. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a normal year and the mosquitoes at the lake are notorious through midsummer, which is another argument for going higher. Book the moment the reservation window opens; this is one of the hardest permits on the peninsula to get on a weekend.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: The lake and the outlet creek run all season. Filter or treat; this is a heavily used basin and the shoreline is fragile.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Royal Basin is one of the park's named quota areas. Essentially the whole quota is reservable in advance through the federal recreation booking system, with the summer block released in a single mid-April drop for the mid-May through mid-October season; there is no same-day walk-up window, so a party that turns up without a permit has no legal camp. Expect a flat per-permit reservation charge plus a per-adult, per-night fee, with under-sixteens free and an annual wilderness pass available if you camp here often. Dates outside the online season are arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, and loaners are sometimes available on a first-come basis when you collect the permit. Every camp along Royal Creek and up through the meadows and the basin sits inside the same reservation, so there is no legal way to sneak a night lower down without one.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: Ten designated sites, and only two of them will take more than a single tent. One separate group site holds roughly seven to twelve people and has to be booked as a group site. That is the entire overnight capacity of the lake basin, which is why permits go so fast.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Upper Royal Basin
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: This is the climbers' camp, three quarters of a mile to a mile above the lake on an unmaintained way trail that gains around five hundred to a thousand feet. It puts you at the foot of the west wall of the basin, which is the east side of The Needles, and it is the difference between a reasonable day and a very long one on Deception, Clark, Johnson, The Incisor and Sundial. It is also the working base for Mystery, which is reached over the divide out of the head of the basin, and for Fricaba, which is a comparatively easy scramble from here and a common warm-up or bad-weather substitute. What you pay for the position: exposed camping on gravel with no trees, weather that arrives with no warning, colder nights, and a fiddly load carry up the boot path in the evening. What you get: fewer people, far fewer mosquitoes, and a start that puts you on the loose ground above the basin while it is still frozen together rather than after the sun has been on it for two hours. Snow covers the upper basin well into July most years, which is often an advantage for the approach gullies and a nuisance for finding bare ground to pitch on. If the basin is still largely snow-covered, camp on a gravel bar that has melted out rather than on snow over vegetation.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: Tarns and snowmelt streams through the basin. Late in a dry summer the upper tarns can drop and go stagnant, so check the inlet streams rather than dipping from still water, and be prepared to carry from lower in the basin in September.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Same Olympic National Park quota permit as Royal Lake, booked as the upper basin rather than the lake. All the same conditions apply: advance reservation only, mid-April release for the summer season, per-permit and per-person-per-night charges, and mandatory hard-sided bear canisters. Because there are no constructed sites, the leave-no-trace rules here are enforced in earnest: no camping on vegetation or meadow, no fires, and the park expects you to be on durable surface only. Anyone found camped on the heather is the reason this basin nearly lost overnight use.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: No numbered sites at all. Camping is permitted only on bare ground, gravel bars and rock, so the practical capacity is a handful of parties spread across the gravel beside the tarns. Two of the larger gravel bars near the upper tarn are the usual choice for a group.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Camp Handy
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: A low, sheltered, permit-free camp about three miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, and the most useful fallback in the whole zone. It does not serve The Needles: Royal Basin branches off well below it and Camp Handy is on the wrong fork. What it does is give you a legal, free, roofed place to sleep when the Royal Basin quota is gone, when you arrive too late to start the Royal Creek climb, or when the weather is bad enough that a night in the trees beats a night on gravel at five and a half thousand feet. It is also the natural first night for anyone approaching Fricaba the long way, by Boulder Shelter and Constance Pass. At barely three thousand feet in old growth it is warm, wet and buggy in early summer, and it commits you to a very big day if you try to use it as a climbing base for anything on the divide. Treat it as staging, not as a base camp.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: The Dungeness river runs right past the camp all year. Reliable.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Outside the national park. This is Olympic National Forest, inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so there is no park wilderness permit, no quota and no nightly fee. You do need a valid recreation parking pass on the vehicle at the Upper Dungeness trailhead. Bear canisters are not legally required on forest land here but food does need protecting, and if any part of your trip crosses into the park you will be carrying one anyway.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: An open three-sided shelter with log benches plus several tent sites scattered through the riverside meadow. Comfortably takes a few parties, and rarely full outside a summer weekend. No privy.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Boulder Shelter
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. This is the crossroads camp for the eastern half of the zone: from here the trail climbs to Home Lake and Constance Pass, which is the alternative and much less crowded way at Fricaba. It is permit-free, which matters a great deal in a zone where the good camps are rationed months in advance. It is not a Needles camp and no amount of enthusiasm makes it one. Also worth knowing before you plan around it: the stretch above here toward Home Lake is far more primitive than the trail below, with brush, blowdown and at least one crossing that will get you wet, so budget more time than the mileage suggests. The shelter is genuinely useful in bad weather, which is not something most of the alpine options in this zone can offer.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary is crossed on the way to Home Lake, and from that point an Olympic National Park wilderness permit and a bear canister are required, so if you intend to sleep beyond here get the permit before you leave the road.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Home Lake
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: Just over nine miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, a little over five thousand three hundred feet, and only a few hundred feet below Constance Pass. This is the second door to Fricaba, and the reason it is in this list at all: if the Royal Basin quota is unobtainable, Fricaba can still be climbed from this side without competing for a rationed permit. It is a genuinely long walk in, with the primitive brushy section above Boulder Shelter to negotiate, so it costs you most of a day. It gives you a quiet alpine lake with real water and real shelter from wind, at a height that leaves a sensible summit day. It does nothing at all for The Needles or the Royal Basin peaks, which sit over a major divide from here. Snow holds around the lake and the pass into July. Parties combining Fricaba with Mount Constance frequently use this camp, which is worth remembering when you are guessing at how busy it will be.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: The lake, immediately at camp. Reliable through the season.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Inside Olympic National Park, so an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required, but Home Lake is NOT one of the quota areas. Reserve through the federal recreation booking system with the usual per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee; because it carries no quota, availability is generally straightforward even in midsummer, which is precisely why it is worth knowing about. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, as they are throughout park wilderness.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Cedar Lake
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. Be clear-eyed about the cost: it is a long, remote walk in, well over ten miles, on a trail with a missing river bridge that pushes everyone onto the Slab Camp approach, and it is a completely different road and trailhead from Royal Basin. Almost nobody climbs Baldy or Gray Wolf Ridge from here, because both are done car to car in a long day from the steep Maynard Burn way trail on the Dungeness side, with no camp involved and no permit needed. Cedar Lake earns its place for the party doing the full ridge traverse, or wanting the Gray Wolf approach to Walkinshaw, or simply wanting solitude in a zone where the popular basin is rationed. If you only want to stand on Baldy and Gray Wolf Ridge, do not come here.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Cameron Basin
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Dose Meadows
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Deer Lake
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Heart Lake
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Cat Basin
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Appleton Pass
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

wa_mount_carrie_se_route.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
wa_mount_carrie_se_route.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_carrie_standard.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_carrie_standard.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_mount_carrie_standard.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_mount_carrie_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_mount_carrie_standard.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come
