wa_mount_daniel_daniel_glacier.capacity: Several larger sites right around the water and quieter ones further out; it is popular enough that on a busy evening the last free site takes finding. Early in July the constraint is snow rather than competition — parties have found the pond only part-thawed with just a few dry tent pads.

wa_mount_daniel_daniel_glacier.name: East summit bivouac
wa_mount_daniel_daniel_glacier.notes: A flat spot roughly 200 ft below the east summit, a little above the traverse toward the middle and west summits, reached by taking the Hyas Creek drainage and a snow couloir below the east peak. A deliberate choice rather than a forced night out — the party went past Peggys Pond specifically to escape the insects, and found none at that height. It only works while the drainage and couloir hold snow, so it is a spring and early-summer option; other parties have slept on the summit itself the same night.
wa_mount_daniel_daniel_glacier.water: Snowmelt only — this is a snow-season site.
wa_mount_daniel_daniel_glacier.capacity: One party. There is room for a small tent at best, and the party who used it slept out without one.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: The main basecamp for LA BOHN PEAK, which stands directly at the head of this valley, and the first night of the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. Drive the Foss River road off Highway 2 a short way east of Skykomish and turn into the Necklace Valley trailhead about four miles up. The trail is famously two-faced: the first five miles along the East Fork Foss gain only about 600 ft through regenerated second growth and go quickly, then the trail crosses the river and climbs roughly 2,400 ft in the next three miles to break out at Jade Lake around 4,600 ft. Emerald is a quarter mile further, Opal about 4,790 ft above that, with Ilswoot, Locket, Jewel and Cloudy scattered on either side. A weathered memorial cabin sits in the meadow just above Emerald; it is a landmark and a piece of the valley's mining history, not a shelter to plan on. From Opal or Emerald the route to La Bohn Gap climbs east under the cliffs, so Jade is fractionally further from the gap but Emerald and Opal put you closest to the day's work. Two honest caveats. The Foss River road has been under construction with weekday delays of about half an hour through the summer, and damage higher on the road has at times cut off the upper end, so allow slack and check before committing to a dawn start. And this valley is very popular for its own sake — a midweek trip is far more pleasant than a Saturday, and the steep middle section is genuinely unpleasant under a heavy climbing pack in the heat.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: All four lakes, plus the creek linking them. Reliable the whole season.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size limited to twelve including stock. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the range, which puts every lake in the valley under a fire ban — carry a stove and do not build rings.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: Sites are spread across four separate lake basins rather than concentrated, so the valley absorbs a lot of parties — several groups at Jade, several more around Emerald and Opal, and quieter singles at Ilswoot, Locket and Jewel off to the sides. On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: The high camp for LA BOHN PEAK and the launching point for the west route on MOUNT HINMAN, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: The La Bohn tarns and the Chain Lakes below the gap on the south side, plus lingering snowmelt into midsummer. Late in a dry season the smaller tarns can drop and turn silty; check rather than assume.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, picked up at whichever trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. Campfires prohibited outright — everything here is well above the 4,000 ft fire-ban line and there is no wood to burn anyway. Camp on rock or bare gravel, not on the heather, which takes decades to recover at this elevation.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: A handful of small, exposed pitches on granite benches and heather shelves between the tarns — realistically two or three tents in the good spots, more if you are willing to sleep on rock. There is no sheltered ground.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Tank Lakes basin
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: A high alternative to the Necklace lakes, reached off-trail from the south end of Opal Lake and sitting at roughly 5,800 ft in a bench of slabs and tarns ringed by ridges. It is not on the direct line to LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN and adds work rather than saving it, so take it when you want a spectacular camp and a rest day rather than the fastest summit. It matters here for two reasons. First, it is the obvious second night for a party linking Necklace Valley with the high country toward Dutch Miller Gap on foot. Second, when the Necklace lakes are full on a weekend, this is where the space is. The travel from Opal is cross-country over slabs and heather with some routefinding, and it holds snow well into July, which makes it either easier or harder depending on what you are carrying. The exposure is the caveat: nothing up here breaks the wind, the basin is a poor place to sit out a storm, and getting back down to the valley in cloud demands attention.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: The tarns themselves and snowmelt. The basin holds snow late, which helps, but by September the smaller pools can be stagnant — take from the larger ones or from running melt.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. No campfires, and no scope for one — this is bare granite and heather. Pitch on rock or gravel only.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: A scatter of small hardened spots on slab and gravel among the tarns. Two or three parties before it feels crowded, and there is nothing resembling a sheltered group site.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Big Heart Lake, with Copper and Little Heart below
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: The west-side base for BALD EAGLE PEAK, which sits on the divide between the two Foss forks and can be climbed from either. The trail leaves a spur off the Foss River road and climbs a staircase of lakes: Trout at about 1.6 miles, Malachite and Copper at around 3,965 ft near four miles, Little Heart at five and a half, and Big Heart at 4,418 ft after roughly seven to eight miles and some four thousand feet of gain. Beyond Big Heart, rough boot paths and a little bushwhacking lead on to Angeline at about 4,613 ft, Azurite, Otter and Chetwoot for parties who want solitude. For Bald Eagle the useful detail is that the standard west approach leaves the trail low, near Trout Lake, fords the river just downstream of the pool below the lake and takes to the forest for the northwest ridge — so a night at Copper or Little Heart is a comfortable staging camp, while Big Heart is a long way past the turn-off and is a destination rather than a basecamp. Two road caveats that matter more than usual. The Foss River road has run weekday construction delays of roughly half an hour through the summer season. And the spur road to this trailhead has been impassable to vehicles, damaged and blocked by downed trees, adding about two and a half miles of road walking each way — enough to turn a comfortable first day into a long one. Confirm the road before you plan the mileage.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: Every lake on the chain. Plentiful and reliable through the season.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED AT EVERY LAKE ON THIS TRAIL regardless of elevation, and within half a mile of Trout, Malachite, Copper, Little Heart and Big Heart you must camp at an established site rather than pitching where you like. Take both rules seriously here; this is one of the most heavily used valleys on the Highway 2 side and the ground shows it.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: Copper Lake and Little Heart hold a good number of established sites and take the bulk of the traffic. Big Heart has a few sites at its northern edge close to the water and a few more perched above the lake — enough for several parties, but it is the destination for most people on this trail and it fills.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Bald Eagle Lake cirque
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: A rough, off-trail bivouac at about 4,547 ft for BALD EAGLE PEAK, tucked in the cirque on the north flank of the ridge midway between Bald Eagle and its neighbour Silver Eagle to the southwest. Bald Eagle sits squarely between the West Fork and East Fork of the Foss, and although the mountain looks intimidating on a map its standard lines are no harder than class 3 to 4 and are mostly a matter of picking the right rib. The lake is worth knowing about precisely because both trailhead approaches are long: the west approach fords the West Fork low, near Trout Lake, and climbs the northwest ridge, while the ridge system directly above the Foss River road on the east side gives another line from around 1,600 ft. Either way the mountain is a big day from the car, and a night in the cirque splits it. Be honest with yourself about what this is — there is no trail to it, no site, and no shelter. It suits a small, self-sufficient party in settled weather and is a poor idea in anything else. Late July through September is the window; earlier the approach slopes hold snow and the brush is soaked.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: The lake. Take it from the inlet side if the outlet is stagnant late in the season.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever Foss River trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. No campfires — above the 4,000 ft ban line, and the ground here is far too fragile to take one. Camp on rock or gravel and leave nothing behind; this basin sees almost no traffic and should stay that way.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: Nothing established. One or two parties on rough ground beside the lake, chosen on the day. Treat it as a bivouac, not a campsite.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: The base for MOUNT DANIEL and the eastern option for MOUNT HINMAN, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. THE CRITICAL 2026 CAVEAT: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: THIS IS THE MOST RESTRICTED CAMP IN THE ZONE AND THE RULES ARE THE POINT. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp ONLY on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. For MOUNT DANIEL it is the family-friendly alternative to Peggy's Pond and it is honest to say what that costs: camping here rather than at the pond adds roughly two thousand feet to summit day and puts the whole approach to the southeast ridge in front of you before the climbing starts. It earns its place for three reasons — it is the fallback when Peggy's Pond is full, which it often is; it is the sensible choice for a party larger than the pond's reduced limit allows; and it is by far the better place to sit out weather, being sheltered, wooded and low. The valley floor around Fish Lake and Tucquala Lake below the trailhead also holds dispersed and developed camping if you arrive late and want to walk in fresh. Two caveats. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.water: The lakes and the Cle Elum River flowing through them. Reliable all season.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. Camp at the established sites and keep back from the shoreline — a 200 ft setback applies at listed lakes on this side of the range. Check the current campfire order before lighting anything; at this elevation a fire may be legal when the district is not under a seasonal ban, but the sites nearest the water are heavily worn and a stove is the better choice regardless.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.capacity: Plenty. Established sites and a privy along the shores of both lakes, spread out enough that even a busy weekend does not feel packed. This is the one place in the zone where a large party can settle without a problem.

wa_mount_deception_standard.name: Royal Creek
wa_mount_deception_standard.notes: Forested sites low in the valley, well short of the basin. An approach camp for a party arriving late rather than a base for the climb: the summit is a long way above, past Royal Lake and the upper basin.
wa_mount_deception_standard.water: Royal Creek, immediately beside the sites.
wa_mount_deception_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight stay year-round and reserved through Recreation.gov; you may only camp in the area named on your permit. Bear canisters are required in every wilderness camp in the park. This is the one Royal camp where campfires are allowed — it is the only division in the basin not designated no-fire, because it sits below the park's 3,500 ft campfire limit.
wa_mount_deception_standard.capacity: Permitted for groups of up to twelve.

wa_mount_deception_standard.name: Lower Royal Meadow
wa_mount_deception_standard.notes: Subalpine sites beside the creek a short way below Royal Lake — a useful fallback when the lake itself is booked out, at the cost of a little height on summit day.
wa_mount_deception_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, camp only in the area named on it, bear canisters required. No campfires.
wa_mount_deception_standard.capacity: Permitted for groups of up to six.

wa_mount_deception_standard.name: Royal Lake
wa_mount_deception_standard.notes: The common base camp, about seven miles in, with a seasonal ranger camp up-valley. Reckon on roughly five hours from Shelter Rock to the summit — but note that published descriptions place Shelter Rock both above and below the lake, so work out which you are looking at before you time anything off it.
wa_mount_deception_standard.water: Royal Lake and Royal Creek. Filter, boil or treat everything. Neither has been reported failing through the season.
wa_mount_deception_standard.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, and this is a quota area — reserve on Recreation.gov, which opens in mid-April for the mid-May to mid-October season. There are no longer any self-issue paper permits at the trailhead. Camping in designated sites only, bear canisters required, and no campfires anywhere in Royal Basin. Parties of seven or more must use the designated group site at the lake; affiliated groups may not combine past twelve people and must camp at least a mile apart. The trail is closed to stock at the park boundary. There are composting toilets at the lake. Parking at the Upper Dungeness trailhead, which is national forest, needs a Northwest Forest Pass.
wa_mount_deception_standard.capacity: Site counts disagree sharply: it is described both as ten sites, of which only two hold more than a single tent, and as taking eight parties. What is certain is the permit: a group of six, with one separate group site for parties of seven to twelve.

wa_mount_deception_standard.name: Upper Royal Basin
wa_mount_deception_standard.notes: The climbers' camp, a mile and about 500 ft above Royal Lake, and the point the summit day is usually measured from. A maze of tarns, moraines, heather, snowfields and house-sized boulders; the flattest ground is on the gravel bars beside the tarn. Some ask that parties not camp right at Imperial Tarn. The basin is given as 5,600 ft and its tarns nearer 5,700, so the figure here is approximate. Early July is the usual compromise on timing: the route wants snow still covering its loose rock, while the camps want to have melted out. Do not confuse this with Deception Basin, which appears in the same permit system but serves the alternative route on the far side of the peak.
wa_mount_deception_standard.water: Tarns, creeks and snowmelt throughout the basin. Nothing published suggests any of it dries up.
wa_mount_deception_standard.permit: A park wilderness permit is still required, but this is not a designated-site camp: pitch on bare ground or gravel. Because Recreation.gov lists only the designated camps, an upper-basin or cross-country booking is made by telephoning the Wilderness Information Center instead. No campfires.
wa_mount_deception_standard.capacity: No reliable current figure. An older figure has the basin taking around a dozen people in up to four groups, after a period of overuse led the park to tighten numbers — that is more than a decade old, so ask rather than assume.

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_mount_despair_east_route.name: Thornton Pass benches
wa_mount_despair_east_route.notes: PLANNED camp and effectively the only base for this route: flat rock-and-heather benches on the ridge crest just south of the pass. Parties take most of a day to reach it — around seven and a half hours of brush and cliff-band navigation from the trailhead — and then run the whole climb as an enormous out-and-back from here. It is a crest site, so wind is the trade for the flat ground. Water is the real constraint: fill at Thornton Creek low on the approach, because by late summer the snow patches near the benches can be gone. Summit day commonly ends after dark, and finding these benches again in the dark is the crux of the return; the published alternative is a cold night out on the talus, which is an outcome to plan against rather than a site.
wa_mount_despair_east_route.water: lingering snow patches only — no reliable stream at camp
wa_mount_despair_east_route.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
wa_mount_despair_east_route.capacity: a few tents on separate benches

wa_mount_despair_east_route.name: Upper Despair Lake
wa_mount_despair_east_route.notes: NOT a documented camp — reports use it as a rest and water stop on the long traverse to the peak, and no established sites are described there. It is the last reliable water before the cliff band below the southeast face, and worth knowing about as an EMERGENCY stopping point if a party is benighted on the traverse rather than as a planned camp. Snow patches and steep chutes linger around the Despair Lakes into early summer.
wa_mount_despair_east_route.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

wa_mount_duckabush_standard.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
wa_mount_duckabush_standard.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Lena Lake designated sites
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Upper Lena Lake
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Lake of the Angels
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Deer Lake
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Heart Lake
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Cat Basin
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Appleton Pass
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

wa_mount_fairchild_standard.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
wa_mount_fairchild_standard.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp.
