The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend

wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.notes: A 1935 lookout on the 6,521 ft summit, kept standing by volunteers from a local hiking club rather than by the agency, and genuinely open for anyone to sleep in on a first-come basis. It is 1.7 miles and about 1,300 ft above the Twin Lakes trailhead, which makes it one of the easiest real summits in the range to reach and a fine advance camp for a light party heading on to Mount Larrabee, though it sits off the direct High Pass line and most climbers heading for American Border Peak carry on past the junction rather than up. Treat the building as borrowed. It survives on people sweeping it out, closing the shutters properly, packing out their rubbish and leaving it drier than they found it; a run of poor behaviour is exactly why the winter season was closed. Always carry a tent or bivy, because it may well be occupied when you arrive and there is only room for two on the bunks. There are patches of ground outside the building flat enough to sleep on. The trail crosses steep, exposed snow slopes that linger into July and sometimes August, and an ice axe is the right call before the traverse is bare.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.water: None at the summit. Carry everything up from Twin Lakes, or melt snow early in the season.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.permit: Free, no reservations, no fee, and no way to book it. Locked from November through May, reopening when conditions allow, and off limits as a shelter in winter beyond stepping inside with the shutters left as they are. Wilderness rules apply on the trail and at the summit: no fires at all, party size twelve, no toilet, so pack out everything including human waste.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.capacity: Two bunks inside and floor space for a couple more at a squeeze; twelve is the legal party limit but the building comfortably holds far fewer

wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.name: High Pass camp
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower

wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.notes: The standard camp for the southeast ridge of Tomyhoi Peak, and the reason Tomyhoi is a comfortable overnight rather than a very long day. From the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft the trail climbs towards Gold Run Pass, forks left onto the meadows trail and reaches the scatter of tarns at roughly 5,580 ft in about four miles. From camp the route drops northwest over a hump to a col near 6,266 ft and follows the ridge over benches and a small glacier remnant to the false summit and the class 3 summit block. This is one of the most heavily impacted alpine basins in the district and the rules exist because the meadow was being destroyed; a single careless night on heather leaves a scar that lasts years. Mountain goats frequent the basin, are habituated, and will come to camp for the salt in urine, so pee on rock well away from the tents. Snow covers the basin into July and the tarns can still be part frozen at the start of the season.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.water: The tarns themselves. They are shallow, warm late in the season and shared with a great many campers, so filter and draw well away from where people wash.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.permit: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail EXCEPT at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.capacity: Perhaps eight to ten small sites among the tarns, all of them well used; expect company, and expect to take whichever pad is left rather than the one you wanted

wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.name: Tomyhoi Lake
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.notes: Worth knowing about mostly so you do not plan a climb around it. Despite the name, Tomyhoi Lake is not the camp for Tomyhoi Peak: the trail from the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead climbs to Gold Run Pass and then loses roughly 1,500 ft over two miles down the far side to the lake at about 3,727 ft, while the peak's southeast ridge starts from the tarns high above. Camping here and climbing the peak means regaining everything you gave away. It is a good option for a party that wants a low, sheltered, uncrowded night in the trees when the meadows are snowed under or the tarns are full, and it is the natural bail if weather closes the high ground. The last stretch of trail down to the lake is brushy and easy to lose, and the north side of Gold Run Pass is steep, exposed and holds snow into late summer, so carry an axe and traction if you are dropping in early in the season.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.permit: No camping within one mile of Gold Run Pass, which rules out the whole upper part of the descent; the lake itself is far enough down to be legal. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, recreation pass on the vehicle, no fires, party size twelve, pack out waste.
wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.capacity: A handful of rough forested sites at the lake; quiet, and rarely full

wa_mount_lawson_standard.name: Sixteen Mile Camp — the base directly under Mount Lawson
wa_mount_lawson_standard.notes: This is the camp for MOUNT LAWSON and effectively the only one. The peak rises about 3,800 ft above the river in a mile and a third, straight out of the drainage the camp sits in, and the climb is a class 2 slog on steep forest and open slope rather than anything technical — the work is the approach, not the summit. The camp is roughly twelve miles up the valley from the North Fork trailhead, past Wolf Bar, Halfway House, Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter, and the walk is gentle until the last few miles where the valley narrows and the trail climbs and drops across steep sidehill. THE FORDS ARE THE WHOLE PLANNING PROBLEM. There are three of them — Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and the North Fork itself right at this camp — and the river crossing here is regularly impassable during snowmelt or after heavy rain. Parties have been turned around at it having walked twelve miles. Go in late summer when the river is low, carry poles, and treat a high river as a trip-ending condition rather than something to force. Reach the trailhead by the North Shore Road; the South Shore Road has been washed out and a phone will still try to send you that way.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.water: Reliable. The North Fork Quinault runs at the camp, which is also the reason the camp exists and the reason it can be unreachable; treat everything.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The North Fork Quinault is not a quota area, so this is one of the easier permits in the park, but nothing here is held back as a same-day walk-up and camps this far in do not always surface in an online search — telephone the wilderness information centre if it will not show. An approved animal-resistant food container is mandatory throughout the park wilderness and free loaners are handed out with permits. This camp sits below the 3,500 ft fire line, so fires are legal in the established rings when no seasonal ban is running, and bans are usual by midsummer.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.capacity: Four established sites on the river flat, and it is rarely contested — almost everyone walking this valley is bound for Low Divide and passes straight through

wa_mount_lawson_standard.name: Elip Creek and the lower North Fork Quinault camps
wa_mount_lawson_standard.notes: These break the walk to Sixteen Mile rather than serving any summit directly, and that matters more than it sounds: the drive to the North Fork trailhead is long, most parties arrive in the afternoon, and twelve miles with a climbing pack on the same day is an unpleasant way to start. Wolf Bar at about two and a half miles is the late-arrival camp, Elip Creek at roughly six and a half is the natural halfway stop, and Trapper Shelter a mile and a half further is the last of them before the valley steepens. Grades are easy to Trapper and then the trail begins working up and down high above the river. Two of the three fords are below Sixteen Mile, so a night here also lets you look at the water level before committing to the upper valley. Deep old-growth forest, heavy shade, mosquitoes in early summer and no views whatsoever — this is shelter and mileage, nothing more.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.water: Reliable at all of them — the river or the named side creek. The lower valley is rainforest and water is never the constraint here.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance; not a quota area and usually obtainable at short notice. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. All of these sit well below the fire line so established rings are legal outside a burn ban.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.capacity: Elip Creek has four sites, Wolf Bar five and Halfway House two. Trapper Shelter above them holds two small spots and is best treated as day or emergency use only rather than a planned night.

wa_mount_lawson_standard.name: Pyrites Creek — where the Chimney Peak approach leaves the trail
wa_mount_lawson_standard.notes: This is the camp for CHIMNEY PEAK, and the reason it rather than the chalet meadow is that the approach leaves the East Fork Quinault trail at about nine miles, which is where this camp sits. Push on to the chalet and you have walked four miles past your own turning and given yourself them back again in the morning. The peak stands immediately north above the valley with its southeast face rising something like 4,800 ft in less than a mile, streaming waterfalls into the valley below — spectacular from the trail and completely useless as a line of ascent. The climb goes round to the southwest ridge and is class 3 scrambling once you are on it, with the first ascent not made until 1941, which says something about how the ground below it behaves. Expect a long, steep, largely trackless day out of the valley floor. June through September is the workable window. The walk in from Graves Creek is thirteen miles to the chalet with staged camps at Pony Bridge and O'Neil Creek before this one, so most parties take two easy days in rather than one hard one.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.water: Reliable — the East Fork Quinault and the creek the camp is named for both run all season
wa_mount_lawson_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and THE EAST FORK QUINAULT IS A QUOTA AREA. It has been run under a nightly cap of thirty permits or roughly two hundred people since 2024, so this is a booking to make the day reservations open rather than a fortnight out. The summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and releases in one drop in mid-April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over plus a six dollar booking fee, or an annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY REQUIRED IN THIS VALLEY and enforced rather than advised — the Enchanted Valley was closed over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Free loaners at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness offices.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.capacity: A modest forested riverside camp with a handful of sites, quieter than the valley above it because most parties push the extra four miles to the chalet meadow

wa_mount_lawson_standard.name: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
wa_mount_lawson_standard.notes: THE camp for both MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN, which stand less than a mile apart on either side of a small unnamed glacier directly above the basin. Both are scrambles rather than climbs — La Crosse at 6,417 ft goes at class 2 and was first climbed in 1928, White Mountain at 6,378 ft is class 2 as well — so from a camp here the two together are a single long day rather than an expedition. Lake LaCrosse sits at about 4,800 ft, roughly 400 ft higher and a mile and a half further than Marmot Lake, with Hart Lake in between; Marmot is covered in the Staircase file and is a perfectly good camp, but it is further from these two summits and it is the wrong side of the shelf. THE APPROACH IS THE ENTIRE DIFFICULTY AND THERE ARE THREE OF THEM, none short. From the Dosewallips you go up the West Fork and over LaCrosse Pass. From the East Fork Quinault you go through Enchanted Valley and over Anderson Pass. From the Duckabush you come up the river and over O'Neil Pass. Every one of those is two days in for most parties carrying gear, which is why these summits see so little traffic. July through September; the basin holds snow late and the passes either side of it later still.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.water: Reliable — both lakes hold through the season and the outlet creeks run into autumn. This is the last dependable water before anything you climb from here; the slopes and the unnamed glacier between the two summits carry no running source once the snow has gone.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. This basin is not itself one of the named quota areas, but the East Fork Quinault approach to it is, so which trailhead you walk in from changes what you have to book — check the whole itinerary rather than just the camp. An animal-resistant food container is required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the parkwide 3,500 ft line. Elk work this basin heavily and bears are regular visitors.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.capacity: A small number of sites spread between the two lakes, in and above open subalpine basin. Neither holds a crowd and the meadow ground is fragile, so use the established pads rather than making new ones.

wa_mount_lawson_standard.name: O'Neil Pass and the upper Duckabush shelf
wa_mount_lawson_standard.notes: A high, exposed alternative to the lake basin for a party that wants to be moving early on WHITE MOUNTAIN or that is traversing rather than going in and back. The pass sits at roughly 4,900 ft on the long shelf that carries the trail in a slow horseshoe between the Duckabush head and the East Fork Quinault, and Chimney Peak and the Anderson massif are both in view from it — which is the honest reason most people stop here rather than any advantage on climbing day. The trade is bad: it saves very little on either summit and it costs you shelter, water and any chance of a comfortable night. There is nothing to hide behind and the weather arrives off the Quinault with no warning. Treat it as a tactical stop on a longer route rather than a base. Snow lies on the north side of the shelf into midsummer and the meadow ground either side of the trail is soft enough to hold a footprint for years, so stay on rock or bare tread.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal runnels only, and the pass itself dries out as the summer goes on. Fill at Lake LaCrosse or down in the basin before coming up; this is ground you carry water to.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. Which booking you need depends on the approach — the Duckabush side is not a quota area, the East Fork Quinault is. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. No fires at this elevation. If the ground you intend to use is not an established site, say so when you book and expect to be routed to a cross-country zone permit arranged by telephone rather than online.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.capacity: Informal rather than developed — a small amount of workable ground on the shelf near the pass, room for a party or two, with no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_lawson_standard.name: Honeymoon Meadows and Camp Siberia — the West Fork Dosewallips side of LaCrosse Pass
wa_mount_lawson_standard.notes: This is the eastern way to LaCrosse Basin and the one to use when the East Fork Quinault quota is gone. From the road end the trail runs up to Dose Forks at about 7.6 miles, Big Timber at 10.3, Diamond Meadow at 12.7 and Honeymoon Meadows at 15, with the LaCrosse Pass trail branching a little before that and Camp Siberia at around 16 near Anderson Pass. From Honeymoon Meadows the pass trail climbs roughly 2,000 ft in a couple of miles, the first 1,500 in forest before it breaks into open meadow, and drops the other side toward the LaCrosse Basin lakes — so MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN are two days in from here rather than one. THE ROAD IS THE CATCH AND IT HAS BEEN FOR TWO DECADES. The Dosewallips road washed out well below the old trailhead and has never been rebuilt, so the walk starts with several miles of abandoned road before any trail begins, and every mileage quoted above is measured from the old road end rather than from where you will actually park. Bicycles help on that stretch. Add the road walk to every figure before deciding this is the short way.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.water: Reliable at all of them — the West Fork Dosewallips runs beside the trail the whole way and the meadows carry side streams into the autumn
wa_mount_lawson_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The Dosewallips side is not a quota area and these camps are usually available at short notice, which is a real advantage over the Quinault approach to the same country. Animal-resistant food container required. Honeymoon Meadows sits near the fire line and Camp Siberia above it, so assume no fires at either.
wa_mount_lawson_standard.capacity: Honeymoon Meadows is an open riverside meadow camp with several sites and is the pleasant one; Camp Siberia near Anderson Pass is smaller, higher and colder, with a few spots and an old shelter frame. Diamond Meadow and Big Timber lower down break the walk further.

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
wa_mount_lincoln_harniss_chute.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

wa_mount_lincoln_standard.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
wa_mount_lincoln_standard.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Moraine camp above the pass
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Fremont Glacier saddle
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: The highest option, on outcrops at the glacier's edge around 8,000 ft, about two miles past Park Creek Pass. It makes for the shortest summit day but commits you to a fully exposed alpine camp, and getting there is a long day in its own right from the valley.
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.water: Running water reported nearby in season
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.permit: Inside the park and inside a cross-country zone, so it must be on the permit like every other night
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.capacity: A party or two on rock outcrops; no shelter of any kind

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Valley camps on the walk in
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Neve Camp
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
wa_mount_logan_r1.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
wa_mount_logan_r1.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
wa_mount_logan_r1.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Junction Camp
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
wa_mount_logan_r1.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
wa_mount_logan_r1.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
wa_mount_logan_r1.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Skagit Queen Camp
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
wa_mount_logan_r1.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
wa_mount_logan_r1.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
wa_mount_logan_r1.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
wa_mount_logan_r1.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
wa_mount_logan_r1.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
wa_mount_logan_r1.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Fremont Glacier moraine high camp
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: Reached by leaving the trail in the flat sandy meadows a short distance north of Park Creek Pass and climbing several hundred feet into old moraine, this is the high camp for the Fremont Glacier side of Mount Logan and the only realistic way to get above the pass legally. The ground is flat, sandy and sheltered, which matters on a rib this exposed. Parties also report usable bivy ground higher, near where the climbers' route meets the glacier around eight thousand feet, though water up there is entirely a function of what snow is left. Which option is better is genuinely conditions-dependent and worth asking at the permit desk the morning you pick up.
wa_mount_logan_r1.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff, and it is seasonal. Sources near the first stream crossings north of the pass are more dependable; higher moraine camps can go dry late in a hot summer, so carry capacity to melt or haul.
wa_mount_logan_r1.permit: Requires a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE permit from Marblemount, not a designated-camp permit. Fires prohibited outright. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows or within 100 ft of water. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, and out of sight of both. Waste in a cathole, or carried out in a blue bag above treeline or on glaciers.
wa_mount_logan_r1.capacity: Cross-country zone camping rather than a designated site, so no fixed site count. Most zones cap a party at six. One permit covers the party.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
wa_mount_logan_r1.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
wa_mount_logan_r1.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
wa_mount_logan_r1.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.
