wa_mount_logan_r2.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
wa_mount_logan_r2.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

wa_mount_logan_r2.name: Fremont Glacier moraine high camp
wa_mount_logan_r2.notes: Reached by leaving the trail in the flat sandy meadows a short distance north of Park Creek Pass and climbing several hundred feet into old moraine, this is the high camp for the Fremont Glacier side of Mount Logan and the only realistic way to get above the pass legally. The ground is flat, sandy and sheltered, which matters on a rib this exposed. Parties also report usable bivy ground higher, near where the climbers' route meets the glacier around eight thousand feet, though water up there is entirely a function of what snow is left. Which option is better is genuinely conditions-dependent and worth asking at the permit desk the morning you pick up.
wa_mount_logan_r2.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff, and it is seasonal. Sources near the first stream crossings north of the pass are more dependable; higher moraine camps can go dry late in a hot summer, so carry capacity to melt or haul.
wa_mount_logan_r2.permit: Requires a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE permit from Marblemount, not a designated-camp permit. Fires prohibited outright. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows or within 100 ft of water. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, and out of sight of both. Waste in a cathole, or carried out in a blue bag above treeline or on glaciers.
wa_mount_logan_r2.capacity: Cross-country zone camping rather than a designated site, so no fixed site count. Most zones cap a party at six. One permit covers the party.

wa_mount_logan_r2.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
wa_mount_logan_r2.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
wa_mount_logan_r2.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
wa_mount_logan_r2.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
wa_mount_logan_r2.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_mount_lyall_south_route.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

wa_mount_lyall_south_route.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

wa_mount_lyall_south_route.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

wa_mount_lyall_south_route.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

wa_mount_lyall_south_route.name: West Fork Agnes Creek — the bivy under Agnes Mountain
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.notes: This is the working bivy zone for AGNES MOUNTAIN and it needs to be described honestly: THE TRAIL HAS ALL BUT VANISHED. What is marked on maps as the West Fork Agnes Creek trail is now a rough bushwhack up the drainage, last given any real maintenance a decade or more ago, and it leads nowhere except to the base of the mountain. Round trip from High Bridge is around seventeen miles of walking on top of the boat and the shuttle. The recommended line on the peak itself takes the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak first and then traverses to Agnes's south ridge, with short technical sections up to about 5.6 — so this is a climb rather than a scramble, on a peak that is seldom done precisely because the approach is so poor relative to its modest height. Navigation skill is not optional. Season is roughly July into September; earlier the creek is high and the brush is worse, later the days are too short for the mileage. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved ground and finding its own way up a drainage with no tread, this is the wrong objective.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.water: The West Fork itself for as long as you are beside it, which is most of the way. Above it, snowmelt only and only early in the season. There is no reason to be short of water low down and every reason to carry it once you leave the creek.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required for any overnight, and off-trail nights are handled as cross-country camping rather than as a named site — say what ground you intend to use when you arrange it rather than booking a camp that does not exist. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.

wa_mount_lyall_south_route.name: Company Creek and Hilgard Pass — the lower-valley approach to Flora Mountain
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.notes: FLORA MOUNTAIN is the peak in this zone that does not start at High Bridge, and sending a party up the valley for it wastes a day. The Company Creek road leaves the Stehekin road about five and a half miles from the landing — the shuttle will drop you — and the trail from it climbs steeply, fords Company Creek at around five miles, and then follows Hilgard Creek to Hilgard Pass at 6,700 ft. THE FORD IS THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: it is a real crossing and in a high-water year it is the reason parties turn back, so check the level with a ranger before you commit to the day. Flora is one of the hundred highest summits in the state at a little over 8,300 ft and its southwest side is a talus and boulder hop rather than a climb, so once you are in position the summit is not the work. It can also be taken from a camp in the Bird Creek drainage on the Devore Creek side, which is the more commonly described base and is covered elsewhere; the Company Creek line is the one that starts from the lower valley road and it suits a party already camped at Harlequin. The views on the way up over Tupshin and Devore are the best part of the walk. July into early October, and the larch colour late in that window is worth planning around.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.water: Company Creek and then Hilgard Creek for most of the climb, which is generous by the standards of these approaches. The pass itself and the ground above it are dry once the snow has gone, so fill in the basin before going up for the summit.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.permit: The trail leaves the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area about two miles up and enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, so the rules change under your feet. A North Cascades backcountry permit covers the recreation area portion and any park camps; the wilderness above is national forest ground with a free self-issued permit and no quota. Work out which side of the line you intend to sleep on before booking anything. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass considerations apply on the forest side. Store food properly throughout; fires are inappropriate at the pass and restrictions are usual lower down by midsummer.
wa_mount_lyall_south_route.capacity: Dispersed. There is workable ground in the upper Hilgard Creek basin and around the pass, room for a party or two, with nothing developed and no facilities. The lower valley has scattered spots along the trail.

wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.name: Rock Lake
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.name: Crescent Lake
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about three hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge and Round Mountain are both fee trailheads on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.name: Merritt Lake
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.name: Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.notes: The lookout itself: you may walk to it and, if it is staffed and the lookout is willing, speak to whoever is on duty, but you may not stay in it or expect shelter from it. Plan the day accordingly and do not treat the building as a bail-out option in bad weather. The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.water: None at all, and none for the last several miles of trail in either direction. There is one seasonal spring close to the Round Mountain trailhead that runs early in the year and cannot be relied on; past it the trail is dry the whole way. From the west, the last water is Merritt Lake, about three miles back. Carry everything.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is required at the Round Mountain trailhead. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery — none of Nason Ridge is designated wilderness. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the surrounding forest is dry enough that fire restrictions are near-permanent through the summer, which is rather the point of the building on the summit.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.capacity: None for the public. This is an active Forest Service fire lookout, staffed through the summer fire season, and it is NOT available to sleep in, not rentable, and not one of the lookouts in this state that take overnight visitors. Treat it as a staffed workplace: the summit is a fine place to stand, and the building is somebody's post. There is no established campsite at the lookout either, and the ground around it is narrow open ridge crest.

wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge and Round Mountain are both fee trailheads on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
wa_mount_mastiff_south_route.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Deer Lake
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Heart Lake
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Cat Basin
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Appleton Pass
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

wa_mount_mathias_scramble.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
wa_mount_mathias_scramble.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_maude_r1.name: Leroy Basin
wa_mount_maude_r1.notes: A flat meadow basin near 6,100 ft, reached by leaving the Phelps Creek trail where it crosses Leroy Creek around 4,100 ft and taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the creek's north side. It is the usual base on this side of the range, and the north side of Maude is gained from here by continuing south-southeast toward the col below the peak and dropping to the Entiat Glacier. Camp on durable ground — the meadows are the reason the basin is worth camping in.
wa_mount_maude_r1.water: Leroy Creek and the meadow springs in the basin
wa_mount_maude_r1.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness: the wilderness permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead register, and no recreation pass is needed to park, since the Forest Service lists the Phelps Creek Trailhead as a no-fee site
wa_mount_maude_r1.capacity: An open flat basin rather than numbered sites — several parties fit, and it is shared with everyone climbing Seven Fingered Jack

wa_mount_maude_r1.name: Upper Ice Lake
wa_mount_maude_r1.notes: The higher of two lakes in a pumice basin directly under the peak, about a mile and 400 ft above Lower Ice Lake, near the 6,900 ft high point of the Ice Creek trail. Parties climbing the north face camp on the snow-free ground at the lake's south end and start around four in the morning, dropping from the lake onto the slopes beside the face and climbing to the glacier; reckon on about four hours from the edge of the Entiat Glacier to the summit. It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.
wa_mount_maude_r1.water: The lake, which can still be partly frozen early in the season
wa_mount_maude_r1.permit: Also in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, with the same free self-issued permit; the standard guidance is to pitch on the pumice and keep off the meadows
wa_mount_maude_r1.capacity: Open pumice flats with room for several parties, at the south end of the lake

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Holden Village
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Holden Lake
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Leroy Basin
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Ice Lakes
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_mount_maude_r2.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_mount_maude_r2.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_mount_maude_r2.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_mount_maude_r2.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_mount_maude_r2.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_mount_maude_r3.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_mount_maude_r3.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_mount_maude_r3.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_mount_maude_r3.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_mount_maude_r3.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_mount_maude_r3.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_mount_maude_r3.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_mount_maude_r3.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_mount_maude_r3.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_mount_maude_r3.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_mount_maude_r3.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_mount_maude_r3.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_mount_maude_r3.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_mount_maude_r3.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_mount_maude_r3.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_mount_maude_r3.name: Leroy Basin
wa_mount_maude_r3.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_mount_maude_r3.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_mount_maude_r3.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_mount_maude_r3.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_mount_maude_r3.name: Ice Lakes
wa_mount_maude_r3.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_mount_maude_r3.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_mount_maude_r3.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_mount_maude_r3.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_mount_maude_r3.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_mount_maude_r3.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_mount_maude_r3.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_mount_maude_r3.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_mount_maude_r3.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.name: Skyline Lake
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_mount_mccausland_n_route.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye.
