From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
wa_mount_olson_standard.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
wa_mount_olson_standard.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
wa_mount_olson_standard.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.name: Glacier Meadows
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.notes: The standard base camp at roughly 17 miles in, shaded and comfortable, with shelters, a bear wire and two working privies — the last toilets before the glacier. It sits about 4,175 to 4,300 ft depending on which part of the meadow you are in. From here the climbers' path runs about 0.8 mile up onto the lateral moraine crest and down onto the Blue Glacier. Camping is explicitly not allowed anywhere between Glacier Meadows and the glacier, so if the day runs long this is where you come back to. About a quarter mile before camp the trail crosses a washout on a roughly 100 ft ladder with a fixed rope, which is the hardest part of the walk in for most parties.
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.water: Streams through the meadows, running all season; this is the last easy water before the glacier
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.permit: An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required and Glacier Meadows is quota'd — reservations are needed for the summer season and go on sale in advance through the federal recreation booking site. A bear canister is required beyond this point, and blue bags are mandatory on the mountain.
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.capacity: An established camp area with individual sites plus a group site; numbers are held down by a quota rather than by ground

wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.name: Snow Dome
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.notes: A high camp rather than an emergency bivy, and the reason parties use it is that it removes the glacier's lower miles from summit day. Reaching it means roped crevasse travel from the glacier toe, so it is not a place you retreat to casually in poor visibility. It is fully exposed on a broad snow dome — wind and weather with nothing to hide behind — and everything you drink has to be melted. The other permitted camp area up here is Caltech Rocks. Nothing between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier may be camped on.
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.permit: One of only two camp areas permitted above Glacier Meadows on this route; blue bags are required for all human waste here, and a bear canister is required beyond Glacier Meadows
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.capacity: Tent sites in the rocks of the lower dome and flatter ground on top near the weather station

wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.name: Elk Lake
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.notes: About 15 miles in, where the Hoh River Trail stops being flat and starts climbing. It is the standard place to break the approach for parties who cannot make Glacier Meadows in a day, and the fallback if the snow slopes above it turn out to need axe and crampons, which they often do in early season. Sheltered forest camp, no alpine exposure — this is a comfort camp, not a mountain bivy.
wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Elk Lake is quota'd like Glacier Meadows, so the site has to be reserved

wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is GLACIER camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Lena Lake designated sites
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Upper Lena Lake
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Lake of the Angels
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

wa_mount_pershing_standard.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_pershing_standard.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
wa_mount_pershing_standard.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
wa_mount_pershing_standard.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
wa_mount_pershing_standard.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: Barclay Lake
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: Read this before planning anything here. wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses

Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: Money Creek Campground
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: Beckler River Campground
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.

wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. It sits about eleven miles up the Index-Galena Road from US 2 at roughly 1,200 ft on the North Fork Skykomish, which put it within twenty minutes of the Lake Serene trailhead and made it the obvious base for Mount Index. Flooding washed out the Index-Galena Road near mileposts 10 and 14, the road is gated closed through that section with permanent repairs estimated in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the county has said environmental review and permitting may take several years. The campground is inaccessible and closed as a result, and the neighbouring campground further up the same road is closed with it. Confirm the road status before counting on it; if the gate is still shut, the working substitutes for an Index-area night are Money Creek down the highway or a dispersed pullout on the Beckler system. Nothing on the Reiter Road side fills the gap — the lower Reiter Foothills road corridor is state land signed day use only with no camping and a Discover Pass required, which is the approach used for Mount Persis, so plan Persis as a day out from the valley.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
wa_mount_persis_the_hexorcist.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.

wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.name: Barclay Lake
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_mount_persis_west_ridge.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses

Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. wa_mount_pilchuck_east_ridge.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
wa_mount_pilchuck_east_ridge.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
wa_mount_pilchuck_east_ridge.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
wa_mount_pilchuck_east_ridge.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
wa_mount_pilchuck_east_ridge.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Middle Fork Campground
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Green Ridge Lake
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.water: The lake is reliable through the summer, and the tarns above hold water into late season most years. Nothing between the road and the lake once the low creeks are behind you, so fill before the steep section.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Rainy Lake
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: Sits directly beneath the exposed south face of Preacher Mountain and is the natural base camp for the Standard Scramble. From the Middle Fork trailhead cross the bridge and follow the Pratt connector west to the junction with the unofficial Rainy Creek path, which the Forest Service abandoned years ago; volunteers keep the brush down in places and much of it is flagged, but it is not maintained tread and route-finding is required, particularly in the lower half. Preacher is around eleven miles and five thousand feet of gain from the road when it goes well, so most parties do it car-to-car. Treat this as the contingency for a slow day, wet brush or a late descent, and as the sensible plan for a winter attempt, when Preacher becomes a real snowshoe objective and the daylight will not stretch. The valley floor here is low enough to be open most of the year, but the lake and the ridge above hold snow into June.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.water: The lake and Rainy Creek are both reliable through the season. Treat.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, group limit twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the Middle Fork trailhead where the approach begins. The lake is just under the 4,000 ft campfire line, but the sites are small and the ground is thin, so use a stove and expect seasonal bans in late summer.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the lake shore. Quiet and rarely busy, since the access path keeps the numbers down.

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: The honest answer for Garfield is that there is no camp, and inventing one would do a party more harm than saying so. It is a low mountain carrying enormous relief straight out of the valley floor, and every documented line begins with steep unmaintained bushwhacking and long rock gullies before any climbing starts. There are no trails, no signs and no established approach; you leave the road at a pull-out and go up. Ascents here are commonly described as needing either a bivouac or the very longest days of the year to finish in daylight, and the bivouacs that actually happen are improvised where a party runs out of light rather than chosen in advance. Plan for that rather than around it: carry a bivy kit on any attempt, expect to sleep on rock or in brush, and treat the multi-summit outing in particular as an opportunistic link-up rather than a route with a known camp on it. Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. Season here is governed by dry rock and daylight rather than snow: the valley is open most of the year, but the brush stays wet late and June through September is when this goes.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.water: Nothing reliable and nothing to plan around. The gullies run in spring and after rain and are dry by late summer, and there is no snow to melt on this mountain in season. Carry water for the whole push and know where the last certain source below you was.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the mountain beyond the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit if your line crosses the boundary, plus a Northwest Forest Pass at whichever pull-out you start from. Note that sleeping at the car is not an option here: the pull-outs at the base of Garfield fall inside the lower-valley dispersed camping closure.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.water: The falls and the creeks crossed low on the trail run most of the year and are the last certain water. There is nothing on the upper mountain and nothing on the Kamikaze line at all. Carry what you need for the day.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.

wa_mount_price_north_route.name: Middle Fork Campground
wa_mount_price_north_route.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.

wa_mount_price_north_route.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
wa_mount_price_north_route.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

wa_mount_price_north_route.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
wa_mount_price_north_route.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
wa_mount_price_north_route.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.
