wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_mount_prophet_east.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_mount_prophet_east.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_mount_prophet_east.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_mount_prophet_east.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_mount_prophet_east.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_mount_pugh_stujack.name: Mount Pugh road end, Forest Road 2095
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.notes: The staging point for MOUNT PUGH, which most parties climb in a single long day from here — around five and a half miles and well over five thousand feet to the summit, with the character changing three times on the way. Forest and stream crossings to the lake at a mile and a half, then a steady climb to the pass, then a rough exposed ridge with a genuine scrambling section around the head of a small remnant glacier before it eases to the top. Sleeping at the car is the honest plan for that day: the spur is short enough that a party staying at any of the valley campgrounds can drive up in the dark, and the trail's first miles are straightforward walking that goes quickly by headtorch. The spur climbs steeply and is rough in places but is normally passable to an ordinary car driven with care. The road in from Darrington is the county-maintained section of the loop and stays open through the year to the seasonal gate further south, which puts this trailhead on the right side of the winter closure — but it is landslide ground and has been blocked outright by a slide within recent memory, so confirm before driving from any distance rather than assuming. Season for the peak is roughly July into October; the ridge above the pass with snow on it is a mountaineering proposition rather than a scramble.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.water: None at the road end and none for the first mile and a half of trail. Everything gets carried up from the valley or drawn at the lake above.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, and the trailhead itself sits OUTSIDE designated wilderness — Glacier Peak Wilderness begins high on the mountain above Stujack Pass, not at the road. Reports differ on whether a fee pass is enforced at this particular trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass costs nothing extra to carry and settles the question. No self-issue permit at the road. Seasonal forest-wide fire restrictions apply and from midsummer normally mean no open flame.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.capacity: Car bivy only, and a thin one. Parking is a few turnouts along the last of the spur rather than a car park, with no sites, no tables and no toilet. Half a dozen vehicles fills it and there is nowhere to overflow to without blocking the road.

wa_mount_pugh_stujack.name: Lake Metan, Mount Pugh trail
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.notes: A mile and a half and about thirteen hundred feet up from the road end, on a short signed spur off the main trail, this is the only established camping on the Pugh approach and it turns a punishing day into a manageable one. Its real value is for a party that wants the ridge above Stujack Pass in the cool of the morning without a two-hour drive and a headtorch start, or for one that arrives too late in the day to sensibly begin. It buys about a third of the climbing but leaves the hardest two thirds — a further two and a half miles to the pass and then the ridge — for the summit day, so treat it as a soft first night rather than a high camp. The setting is wooded and enclosed, mosquito-heavy in early summer and cold in the shade well into the morning. Snow lingers around the lake into June in an ordinary year. Because it is the last water, an efficient party often does not sleep here at all but stops for twenty minutes to load up, and that is a perfectly good use of the place.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.water: The lake, and this is the LAST WATER on the entire route. Nothing above it is dependable, and above the pass there is nothing at all except late-lying snow. Fill everything here going up and note it for the descent.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.permit: National forest outside designated wilderness at this elevation, so no wilderness permit, no quota and no party-size limit for camping here. A Northwest Forest Pass covers the vehicle. Fires are subject to whatever seasonal restrictions are in force and are usually prohibited from midsummer; carry a stove regardless, because this is a small lake basin that takes heavy day-hiker traffic and does not need fire rings.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.capacity: A few primitive spots in the trees on the short spur down to the lake — two or three tents on flat, well-used forest ground, with no built structures of any kind.

wa_mount_pugh_stujack.name: Stujack Pass and the benches just below it
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.notes: This is a high bivouac rather than a camp, and it exists for one purpose — putting a party on the exposed upper ridge of MOUNT PUGH at first light rather than in the afternoon, when the scrambling section around the head of the small glacier is more pleasant and the weather is more predictable. From the saddle the remaining mile and a half of ridge is rough, narrow in places and genuinely exposed, and it is much better done rested and early than at the end of a five-thousand-foot day from the car. The trade is severe and should be weighed honestly: you carry all your water up, you camp on ground with nothing to hide behind, and the pass funnels wind hard enough to make a marginal forecast miserable. Anyone who is not committed to the summit is better off at the lake. Snow holds on the north side of the pass and in the gullies below it long after the trail lower down is clear, and an early-season party will be kicking steps to reach it. In a thunderstorm this is the wrong place to be — the ridge above is the highest ground for some way and there is no descent that is quick. Camp on gravel or bare rock, not on the heather, which is thin and slow to come back.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.water: NONE, and this is the defining constraint. There is no source at or near the pass. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted early in the season and are gone by August, after which every litre comes up from the lake nearly two and a half miles and two and a half thousand feet below.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.permit: The pass itself is the boundary — camping in the saddle sits at the very edge of GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, and the ridge and summit above are inside it. Where wilderness applies, so does the free self-issue permit from the trailhead box and the twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. No fires: this is thin subalpine ground with no wood and nothing that recovers from a scar. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack.capacity: Small and rough — a couple of tents at most on gravel and heather pockets in the saddle and on the shelves a little below it on the approach side. Nothing established, no flat platform, and no shelter of any kind from wind.

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Graves Creek Campground — drive-in staging for the East Fork Quinault
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: This is the only realistic drive-in base on the Quinault side and the natural place to sleep the night before starting up the East Fork toward Anderson Pass and Anderson's Thumb. Vault toilets, fire grates, tables and bear lockers, and nothing else. Reach it from the North Shore Road only — the South Shore Road has a washout roughly eight miles up from the highway, and a phone will still try to route you that way and add several miles of driving for nothing. The last six miles are narrow gravel and RVs and trailers are banned regardless of what the road is doing on the day. Treat the road status as a live question rather than a settled one: this stretch has been closed to vehicles by erosion before, and when it is, both the campground and the trailhead become a two-mile walk or ride. Sleeping here costs you nothing in approach distance, which matters when the first day out is thirteen miles to Enchanted Valley.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.water: None piped — there is no potable water at all, so arrive with everything you need or filter from the Quinault beside the campground
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: No wilderness permit is needed for a night here, and no reservation is possible. The moment you walk past the trailhead you need an Olympic wilderness permit booked on the federal recreation site: eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over, plus a six dollar non-refundable booking fee, or a forty-five dollar annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. A bear canister is required in every wilderness camp area in this park, and they are loaned free to permit holders at the wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: About 30 first-come, first-served sites, open year round and rarely full outside high summer weekends; no reservations are taken

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Dodger Point Camp — the southern gateway to the Bailey Range
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: Dodger Point is 13.5 miles from the old Whiskey Bend trailhead by way of the Long Ridge trail, which leaves the Elwha at Michael's Cabin and crosses the river on a suspension bridge. With the road walk added it is about nineteen miles and well over ten thousand feet of gain to the lookout, so this is a serious approach in its own right. It is the way in to MOUNT DANA and MOUNT WILDER, the southern end of the Bailey Range, and the connecting ridge toward Ludden Peak and on to Ferry Basin, MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER. That connection is not a trail: it involves a faint path off the ridge, a steep gully of loose rock and a section where you climb a tangle of roots and branches to regain the crest. Cream Lake below Ferry Basin is infamous for mosquitoes and for steep alder-choked gullies that swallow time, so budget generously and go in a dry spell if you can. The lookout is the best viewpoint in the valley and the camp is worth a night on its own merits.

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. The camp itself books normally, but any night spent off-trail on the Bailey ridge beyond it is a cross-country zone and must be arranged by telephone with the wilderness information centre. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: A handful of established sites near the old lookout, on an exposed ridge crest; small, and seldom busy

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.name: Enchanted Valley and Anderson Pass — the approach to Anderson's Thumb
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.notes: The East Fork Quinault runs about thirteen miles from Graves Creek to the Enchanted Valley chalet, with staged camps at Pony Bridge around three miles, O'Neil Creek around six and a half and Pyrites Creek around nine, all of which are useful for breaking the walk in. The same pass is reached from the Dosewallips on the east side, which is the shorter approach to the Anderson massif if that road is open — worth checking before committing to the Quinault side.

wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and the EAST FORK QUINAULT RIVER IS A QUOTA AREA — reserve on the federal recreation site rather than turning up hopeful. Summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and reservations for it release on 15 April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for adults, six dollar booking fee. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY AND STRICTLY REQUIRED HERE: this valley was closed to camping over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Canisters are loaned free at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_pulitzer_standard.capacity: A large valley camping area at the chalet meadow that can hold well over a hundred people on a summer weekend, plus a much smaller and quieter camp up near Anderson Pass

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.name: Boundary Camp
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River

The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.

Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
wa_mount_rahm_custer_traverse.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_rahm_standard.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
wa_mount_rahm_standard.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
wa_mount_rahm_standard.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
wa_mount_rahm_standard.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
wa_mount_rahm_standard.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

wa_mount_rahm_standard.name: Boundary Camp
wa_mount_rahm_standard.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
wa_mount_rahm_standard.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late

wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.name: Camp Muir
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.name: Ingraham Flats
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers rather than deciding from a published description. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench

wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.name: Camp Schurman
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.name: Thumb Rock
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.notes: The standard and effectively only bivouac on Liberty Ridge, a notch of snow and rock partway up the ridge on the Carbon Glacier side. It is exposed to rockfall from Thumb Rock itself and from the bands above, and a fatal rockfall struck tents here in 2019, so site selection within the notch and the timing of your arrival matter more than comfort. Warm afternoons that prevent an overnight freeze are the usual trigger, and the park service advises against the route when the freezing level on the mountain is high. The approach from the Carbon River or Mowich side is long and its own seasonal problem, since those roads open on different schedules and can be closed by washouts or fire.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.water: Snow only. There is no water and no shelter, so carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.capacity: Very limited, realistically two to four small tents; parties have ended up stacking tents in a vertical line on the slope when the site is busy, which is not a safe arrangement

wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.name: White River Campground
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft

wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.notes: Between Longmire and Paradise on the southwest side, the practical roadhead camp for anything staging out of Paradise — Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar. Because the Nisqually entrance road is kept open through the year, it is the least season-gated approach on the mountain, though the campground itself runs roughly late May to late September. It sits low and forested at just over 3,000 ft, which makes for comfortable sleeping but no acclimatisation value whatsoever. Book early, since it is one of only two campgrounds in the park taking reservations and fills on summer weekends.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season

Campsites are reservable through Recreation.gov and required during the peak midsummer window. This covers the campground only and is unrelated to the wilderness permit and climbing fee.
wa_mount_rainier_curtis_ridge.capacity: 179 individual sites across six loops, plus separate group sites

wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.name: Camp Muir
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.notes: The planned high camp for the route, on the saddle between the snowfield and the Cowlitz Glacier, with a ranger station and toilets. It is the most sheltered option on this side of the mountain and the public hut is the fallback when a storm makes tents impractical, though the hut is cold and drafty. Rangers here give the forecast before summit attempts. Nothing about it is quiet or private on a summer weekend.
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.water: None running — every drop is melted snow, so plan fuel accordingly
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.permit: A wilderness camping permit is required and the camp is quota'd, plus a climbing permit for anyone travelling on glaciers or above about 10,000 ft. Roughly half the camp's capacity is held back for walk-up registration in summer
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.capacity: 110 people overnight; the public shelter sleeps roughly 25-30 on a first-come basis and the rest is tent ground

wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.name: Ingraham Flats
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.notes: A planned camp that takes a thousand feet off summit day, and the reason parties accept the trade-offs. It has no toilet, so all solid waste is packed out. Large crevasses ring the flat ground — stay roped any time you leave the tent platforms. It also sits directly beneath the seracs of the icefall above; that slope is where an icefall killed eleven climbers in 1981, and parties keep their time in the fall line short.
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.permit: Wilderness camping permit required and quota'd separately from the camp below, plus the climbing permit
wa_mount_rainier_ingraham_direct.capacity: 35 people overnight; tent camping only, no structures

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.name: Curtis Ridge
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.notes: The standard first night, on the broad snow shoulder near the gully used to drop onto the Carbon Glacier, reached over St. Elmo Pass and across the lower Winthrop. Flat ground and comparatively little rockfall exposure. It is not free of hazard: a party camped here watched a large avalanche off the Willis Wall push its debris cloud close to the bivy. Because Thumb Rock is cramped, leaving here early is the difference between a site and no site.
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit for the night plus a climbing permit for the glacier travel above; walk-up registration is at the White River Wilderness Information Center.
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.capacity: Several flat spots — noticeably more room than Thumb Rock, which is why parties expecting company start here.

wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.name: Thumb Rock
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.notes: The one real camp on the ridge itself, in the saddle just above the rock feature, reached by 45-55 degree snow and ice. Published elevations for it disagree — reports place it anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,800 ft. It is exposed to rock and ice coming off the Thumb and off the bands higher up, and that exposure has killed people here, so parties build up or repair the rock walls around the platforms. Strong teams in good conditions skip it entirely, camping at Curtis Ridge and climbing the ridge in a single push to cut the hours spent under the fall line.
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.capacity: Only a few tents. Sites are small and often staggered a few feet apart vertically down the slope rather than side by side.

wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.name: Ptarmigan Ridge bivy above Observation Rock
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.notes: PLANNED camp and the most sheltered ground on this side of the mountain: old stacked rock windbreaks sit here and parties describe it as the best bivy shelter in the area. The catch is position, not comfort — from here you still have to descend loose scree onto the North Mowich Glacier, and parties who camped here have called that descent the inefficient part of their trip. Cross-country zone; permit required.
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.capacity: a couple of tents on hand-built platforms

wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.name: Edmunds/North Mowich glacier divide camp
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.notes: PLANNED alternative used by parties who cross the North Mowich above Needle Rock rather than staying high on Ptarmigan Ridge. Puts you on the correct side of the glacier for the face, at the cost of more elevation to regain in the morning.

wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.name: High camp below the North Mowich headwall
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.notes: PLANNED camp closest to the base of the face, and the most exposed of the three. Parties who have used it wore helmets in camp because of rockfall and icefall shedding off the deteriorating headwall above; there is no fully sheltered ground up here. Worth it only when conditions are cold and you intend to start on the face within a few hours. Search around 9,200 ft first if the higher ground looks loaded — flat sites there are limited but out from under the wall.
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.capacity: one to two tents; flat ground is scarce and has to be dug

wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.name: Liberty Cap saddle
wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.notes: EMERGENCY bivy only, on the broad saddle between Liberty Cap and the summit, used by at least one party benighted after topping out. It is more sheltered than the true summit and less wind-hammered than climbers expect, but it is an unplanned option to know about, not a camp to aim for — going there means you are spending a night above 13,000 ft with whatever you carried up the face.

wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.name: Camp Muir

The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.name: Ingraham Flats

The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it.
