wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench

wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.name: Camp Schurman
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.name: Thumb Rock
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.notes: The standard and effectively only bivouac on Liberty Ridge, a notch of snow and rock partway up the ridge on the Carbon Glacier side. It is exposed to rockfall from Thumb Rock itself and from the bands above, and a fatal rockfall struck tents here in 2019, so site selection within the notch and the timing of your arrival matter more than comfort. Warm afternoons that prevent an overnight freeze are the usual trigger, and the park service advises against the route when the freezing level on the mountain is high. The approach from the Carbon River or Mowich side is long and its own seasonal problem, since those roads open on different schedules and can be closed by washouts or fire.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.water: Snow only. There is no water and no shelter, so carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.capacity: Very limited, realistically two to four small tents; parties have ended up stacking tents in a vertical line on the slope when the site is busy, which is not a safe arrangement

wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.name: White River Campground
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft

wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.notes: Between Longmire and Paradise on the southwest side, the practical roadhead camp for anything staging out of Paradise — Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar. Because the Nisqually entrance road is kept open through the year, it is the least season-gated approach on the mountain, though the campground itself runs roughly late May to late September. It sits low and forested at just over 3,000 ft, which makes for comfortable sleeping but no acclimatisation value whatsoever. Book early, since it is one of only two campgrounds in the park taking reservations and fills on summer weekends.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.permit: Mount Rainier National Park entrance applies, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up on summit morning. Campsites are reservable through Recreation.gov and required during the peak midsummer window. This covers the campground only and is unrelated to the wilderness permit and climbing fee.
wa_mount_rainier_nisqually_icefall.capacity: 179 individual sites across six loops, plus separate group sites

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: Glacier Basin camp
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: PLANNED camp and the last established campground on the White River approach. Composting toilet a short walk away and bear boxes on site. Melts out early and is the last dependable running water before the route goes onto snow and ice for good — most parties fill here rather than carry from the car.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.permit: wilderness camping permit required (reserve or self-register); designated site
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: Curtis Ridge camp
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: PLANNED first-night option when the traverse from White River is split over two days; the park's own route notes list it as the standard intermediate camp before Ptarmigan high camp. Sits on the crest between the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers, which is the point — you hear serac collapse off Willis Wall all night but the crest keeps you out of the runout. Do not drop and camp on the open Carbon below the wall to save an hour.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.capacity: small parties; scattered flat ground on the ridge crest, no established platforms

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: Camp Schurman
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: DESCENT camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.name: Colonnade Ridge
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.notes: PLANNED camp, the first reasonable stopping point once you leave the Wonderland Trail and start up toward the Puyallup Cleaver. It is a snow camp, so it depends entirely on coverage — in a dry year the ground here is bare and the site is much less pleasant. Parties who stop here accept a very long summit day in exchange for an easier first day off the trail.
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay, obtained in person; a separate paid climbing permit is required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.capacity: snow platforms — build what you need

wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.name: Puyallup Cleaver high camp
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.notes: PLANNED camp and the usual high camp for the route, on the cleaver at roughly this height before it is left at about 8,500 ft for the glacier traverse. Mixed snow and rock, wind-exposed on a west-facing rib with nothing upwind of it. Site on the cleaver crest rather than in a runnel, and keep clear of the loose rock edges.
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit also required at this elevation and on the glaciers above
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.capacity: a few tents on cut platforms

wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.name: Open bivouac near 9,600 ft
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.notes: PLANNED but committing — used specifically to cut the summit day down, and on record as an open bivouac rather than a sheltered site. There is nothing here but what you dig. In a dry season the transition from this height onto the face is the part that turns parties around, so the higher camp only pays off if the snow is in.
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft

wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.name: Bergschrund camp in the Sunset Amphitheater
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.notes: PLANNED camp reached by leaving the cleaver near 8,500 ft, traversing the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers and climbing a steep snow gully to a small bergschrund with good ground beside it. The caution is the amphitheater itself: the headwall above sheds ice and rock, so this only makes sense sited where the schrund and the terrain put you out of the fall line, and it is worth reaching it early and cold rather than in afternoon sun.
wa_mount_rainier_sunset_ridge.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft

wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.name: Glacier Basin camp
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.notes: PLANNED camp on the White River approach, which is now the practical way in — the Carbon River side lost public vehicle access when the Fairfax Bridge closed. Composting toilet and bear boxes. Last dependable running water; everything above is melt snow.
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated site
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.name: St Elmo Pass bivy
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.notes: PLANNED staging bivy at the pass where parties change into glacier gear before stepping onto the Winthrop. A short rock wall gives some wind shelter and the site is out of any fall line. Useful when a late trailhead start makes the full traverse to Curtis Ridge too long.
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.capacity: one to two tents on a small flat bench

wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.name: Curtis Ridge camp
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.notes: PLANNED high camp for the wall, on the northeast side of the ridge dividing the Carbon from the Winthrop. This is the camp the route is climbed from — parties leave here before midnight to reach the avalanche cones at the foot of the central rib while everything overhead is still frozen. **Do not camp out on the Carbon Glacier below the wall.** A party that pitched on the Carbon in the fall line watched a large collapse off Willis Wall run close to their tent; the ice cliff at the top of the wall is on the order of 300 ft high and it discharges straight down onto the head of the glacier. The ridge crest is the whole reason this camp exists.
wa_mount_rainier_willis_wall.capacity: small parties; flat ground has to be built by moving rocks or stomping snow

wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.name: Boundary Camp
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
wa_mount_redoubt_south_face.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_mount_roosevelt_standard.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_mount_saul_se_route.name: Airplane Lake
wa_mount_saul_se_route.notes: This is the camp for Mount Saul and effectively the only one, and camping here is what turns a brutal outing into a reasonable two days. Done in a single push from the road the standard route runs about sixteen miles round trip with five thousand three hundred feet of gain, which is a long day by any measure and a very long one on ground this rough. The lake sits roughly two thousand two hundred feet above Indian Creek, in a large depression under the upper east slopes, with the summit still some two thousand feet above it — so a party sleeping here has the worst of the climbing behind them and a clean morning on the east slope and east face. THE APPROACH PATH IS THE HARD PART. It leaves the Indian Creek trail at about four and a half miles, immediately before a valley campsite, marked only by a sign stating that marking of routes is prohibited; there is no other signage and the track is faint. It climbs steeply through the 2016 burn, which means loose footing, no shade, blowdown that changes with every windstorm and standing dead timber overhead. Recent volunteer work has had the trail in good condition in places, but that is a season-by-season matter rather than a promise. Season is roughly mid-July into early October; the east side melts out reasonably early but the upper slopes hold snow and an axe is worth carrying in the first half of the summer.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the climbing season along with snowmelt into the inlet early on. This is the last certain water on the mountain: the two thousand feet of slope between the lake and the summit carry nothing once the snow has gone. Fill everything here for the climb and for the night, and treat it.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the White River trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at the trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground; the basin is small. Carry a stove — the district runs summer fire restrictions on this dry east side as a matter of course and they are often total bans.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.capacity: Informal ground on benches around the lake for one or two parties. Nothing developed, nothing signed, no toilet — and almost certainly nobody else there. This is a genuinely lightly visited basin and solitude is the main thing it offers.

wa_mount_saul_se_route.name: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
wa_mount_saul_se_route.notes: The junction camp is the useful one and it is the landmark as much as the site: the climbers' path for Airplane Lake turns off immediately before it, so a party that reaches an obvious valley campsite and has seen no turning has just walked past the only one there is. Sleeping here rather than at the lake trades a shorter, easier first day for a much harder second one, and most parties would rather push to the lake. Where it earns its place is on the way out, and for a party that has been slowed by the road or the burn and does not want to start the two-thousand-foot climbers' path in the evening. The valley trail itself runs about ten and a half miles in total to the Pacific Crest Trail at Indian Pass, crossing the White River on a bridge right at the trailhead and then climbing very gently; it is brushy and boggy in places, which is a nuisance rather than an obstacle. Expect burn for long stretches, and treat the dead timber overhead as a real reason not to pitch under it in wind.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.water: Indian Creek runs beside the trail for the whole of this stretch and water is abundant; parts of the valley trail are boggy in early season for the same reason. Every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous half of the approach and it ends the moment you start climbing.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal in existing rings at this elevation outside a burn ban, but bans are usual here from midsummer and much of the surrounding forest is fire-killed, so use a stove.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the Indian Creek trail, one or two tents each, including the established spot immediately past the unsigned turn for Airplane Lake. Nothing developed and no facilities.

wa_mount_saul_se_route.name: White River road end trailhead
wa_mount_saul_se_route.notes: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. THE ROAD IS THE FRAGILE PART, AND IT IS CLOSED RIGHT NOW. Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead. It is not named in the Wenatchee River District storm-damage road order (06-17-07-2026-11, 20 May 2026 through 31 December 2027), which closes seventeen other roads. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.water: The White River is at the trailhead and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill here, and fill again from Indian Creek on the way up, because everything above the valley is dry.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit comes from the register here rather than being arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit. Fire restrictions on this side are near-permanent through summer and commonly ban open flame entirely.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.capacity: A gravel parking area at the road end with room to sleep in a vehicle, and no campground facilities. This is a roadhead recorded because a party arriving from the west side in the evening needs somewhere to be before starting an approach this long.

wa_mount_saul_se_route.name: The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
wa_mount_saul_se_route.notes: The honest answer for this peak is that Airplane Lake is the camp and there is nothing above it worth having. The lake already puts the summit within a straightforward morning on the east slope and east face, so climbing higher with a pack buys almost nothing and costs the water, the shelter and the flat ground all at once. The northwest face is sheer and is not the way anyone goes; the east side is open scrambling terrain and the difficulty of this mountain lies in the approach rather than in the climbing. Where a high bivouac has any argument at all is for a party linking Saul with the ridge country toward Indian Head and the crest, which is a different and much longer trip, and even then the sensible pattern is to sleep at water and move over the tops in the day. Treat anything above the lake as emergency ground.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. From roughly August onward there is nothing at all above the lake, and anyone sleeping here carries every drop up two thousand feet. This is the mistake to avoid rather than a plan to make.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the White River trailhead. No fires at this elevation and nothing to burn. The ground is thin alpine turf and scree that scars for years — camp on rock or gravel if you camp at all.
wa_mount_saul_se_route.capacity: None established. There is broken ground and the occasional flat spot on the slope between the lake and the summit rocks where a small party could put a tent down, but nothing has been built and nobody camps here as a matter of course. Recorded so the absence is stated rather than filled in with an invented site.

wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.name: Graves Creek Campground — drive-in staging for the East Fork Quinault
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.notes: This is the only realistic drive-in base on the Quinault side and the natural place to sleep the night before starting up the East Fork toward Anderson Pass and Anderson's Thumb. Vault toilets, fire grates, tables and bear lockers, and nothing else. Reach it from the North Shore Road only — the South Shore Road has a washout roughly eight miles up from the highway, and a phone will still try to route you that way and add several miles of driving for nothing. The last six miles are narrow gravel and RVs and trailers are banned regardless of what the road is doing on the day. Treat the road status as a live question rather than a settled one: this stretch has been closed to vehicles by erosion before, and when it is, both the campground and the trailhead become a two-mile walk or ride. Sleeping here costs you nothing in approach distance, which matters when the first day out is thirteen miles to Enchanted Valley.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.water: None piped — there is no potable water at all, so arrive with everything you need or filter from the Quinault beside the campground
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.permit: No wilderness permit is needed for a night here, and no reservation is possible. The moment you walk past the trailhead you need an Olympic wilderness permit booked on the federal recreation site: eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over, plus a six dollar non-refundable booking fee, or a forty-five dollar annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. A bear canister is required in every wilderness camp area in this park, and they are loaned free to permit holders at the wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.capacity: About 30 first-come, first-served sites, open year round and rarely full outside high summer weekends; no reservations are taken

wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
wa_mount_seattle_noyes_basin.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. wa_mount_seattle_seattle_creek.capacity: About 30 first-come, first-served sites, open year round and rarely full outside high summer weekends; no reservations are taken

wa_mount_seattle_seattle_creek.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend

wa_mount_seattle_south.name: Dodger Point Camp — the southern gateway to the Bailey Range
wa_mount_seattle_south.notes: Dodger Point is 13.5 miles from the old Whiskey Bend trailhead by way of the Long Ridge trail, which leaves the Elwha at Michael's Cabin and crosses the river on a suspension bridge. With the road walk added it is about nineteen miles and well over ten thousand feet of gain to the lookout, so this is a serious approach in its own right. It is the way in to MOUNT DANA and MOUNT WILDER, the southern end of the Bailey Range, and the connecting ridge toward Ludden Peak and on to Ferry Basin, MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER. That connection is not a trail: it involves a faint path off the ridge, a steep gully of loose rock and a section where you climb a tangle of roots and branches to regain the crest. Cream Lake below Ferry Basin is infamous for mosquitoes and for steep alder-choked gullies that swallow time, so budget generously and go in a dry spell if you can. The lookout is the best viewpoint in the valley and the camp is worth a night on its own merits.
wa_mount_seattle_south.water: THE WEAK POINT. There is no water between the Elwha crossing near Michael's Cabin and the tarns just below Dodger Point — a long climb. Fill everything at the river, and expect the tarns to be low or gone by late season.
wa_mount_seattle_south.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. The camp itself books normally, but any night spent off-trail on the Bailey ridge beyond it is a cross-country zone and must be arranged by telephone with the wilderness information centre. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_seattle_south.capacity: A handful of established sites near the old lookout, on an exposed ridge crest; small, and seldom busy

wa_mount_seattle_south.name: Enchanted Valley and Anderson Pass — the approach to Anderson's Thumb
wa_mount_seattle_south.notes: The East Fork Quinault runs about thirteen miles from Graves Creek to the Enchanted Valley chalet, with staged camps at Pony Bridge around three miles, O'Neil Creek around six and a half and Pyrites Creek around nine, all of which are useful for breaking the walk in. This is the approach to ANDERSON'S THUMB, the pinnacle on the Anderson massif, reached by continuing from the valley up to Anderson Pass at 4,480 ft and then onto the glacier remnant and the rock above. Camping at the pass rather than in the valley saves you several miles and roughly two thousand feet on climbing day and puts you in quiet country; camping in the valley gets you a flatter, warmer night and a spectacular setting at the cost of a very long summit day and a great deal of company. Bears are habituated and confident here, so the canister rule is enforced rather than advisory, and food left out is food lost. The same pass is reached from the Dosewallips on the east side, which is the shorter approach to the Anderson massif if that road is open — worth checking before committing to the Quinault side.
wa_mount_seattle_south.water: Reliable everywhere — the East Fork Quinault runs the length of the valley and small streams cross the trail up toward the pass
wa_mount_seattle_south.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and the EAST FORK QUINAULT RIVER IS A QUOTA AREA — reserve on the federal recreation site rather than turning up hopeful. Summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and reservations for it release on 15 April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for adults, six dollar booking fee. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY AND STRICTLY REQUIRED HERE: this valley was closed to camping over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Canisters are loaned free at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_seattle_south.capacity: A large valley camping area at the chalet meadow that can hold well over a hundred people on a summer weekend, plus a much smaller and quieter camp up near Anderson Pass

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower

The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.

wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.
