The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.water: The river and its tributaries are everywhere and never fail, but the North Fork is heavily glacier-fed and runs opaque with rock flour. Filter from a clear side stream rather than the main channel where you can.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.name: Lake Ann
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.notes: A comfortable planned camp about four miles in, reached by a short spur off the climbers' path at the saddle. It is the easy, low-commitment option and the one most parties use, but it leaves the whole talus traverse and the 4th-class chimneys for summit day, and a returning party has to re-gain roughly a thousand feet over the saddle to get back to the car.
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.water: The lake itself, reliable all season — the last dependable water before the climb
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.permit: No national park backcountry permit needed here; the lake sits outside the park boundary, and the Price zone permit applies only to camps higher on the route
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.capacity: Established sites scattered around the lake and its outlet

wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.name: Top of the Chimneys rock outcrop
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.notes: A planned bivy for parties splitting the route, sitting on dry ground just past the top of the chimney system near the edge of the upper glacier. Everything you sleep in has to be carried up a thousand feet of 4th-class scrambling to get here, and going down in bad weather means reversing that same braided ledge system, which is easy to lose in cloud.
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.water: Meltwater pools at the base of the outcrop; seasonal, and unreliable once the snow above has gone
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.permit: Backcountry permit for the Price cross-country zone (max party 12, six parties per night)
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.capacity: A handful of small bivy spots on and around the outcrop

wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.name: Rock rib above Winnie's Slide
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.notes: The highest and best-positioned planned camp, on dry ground on a narrow spur bordering the Upper Curtis Glacier, with the summit day cut down to the glaciers and the summit pyramid. It is also the most committing: it is above the steep snow and ice of Winnie's Slide, so a party that has to bail in a storm must down-climb or rappel that before touching the chimneys. Exposed to wind, and the flat ground is small enough that a late arrival may find it taken.
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.water: A stream or waterfall running off the rib, seasonal and dependent on snow above
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.permit: Backcountry permit for the Price cross-country zone (max party 12, six parties per night)
wa_mount_shuksan_fisher_chimneys.capacity: Room for about three tents; several more single bivy spots reported along the rib

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: Sulphide Glacier camp
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: The standard high camp for the most straightforward route on Shuksan and the best launching point for the summit pyramid. The plateau is flat, spacious and well positioned, and a privy has been maintained on the ridgeline here in recent seasons, which is unusual at this elevation. The permit is the binding constraint on the whole trip rather than the terrain, so plan the paperwork before the climb. Snow covers the site into early summer, and late in the season the approach turns to loose ground and heather that is harder work than the mileage suggests.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.water: Usually available — running water is often audible and reachable over the rocks near camp — but this is a snowmelt supply that varies with the year and the week. Bring the means to melt snow and treat found water as likely rather than certain.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry (wilderness) permit required — this is a DIFFERENT authority from the Mt Baker side, and a Forest Service pass does not cover it. Permits come through Recreation.gov, with a spring early-access lottery followed by a general on-sale, and a share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Reservation and per-person nightly fees apply — these permits are no longer free. The zone carries a small daily party quota.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.capacity: A broad flat plateau on the ridgeline with room for several parties, though the daily permit quota caps how many can legitimately be there

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: The fallback for parties who could not get a North Cascades backcountry permit, and honestly worse than the camp above — lower, drier, and leaving a much longer summit day. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. FS Road 1152 and its spur are low elevation and generally open early in the season with no need for high clearance, which makes this the most road-reliable approach to either mountain. Check where the boundary actually falls on your map before pitching a tent, because the ridge does not advertise it clearly.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.water: Poor. There is essentially nothing between the trailhead streams and the Sulphide Glacier itself, and what does exist on the ridge is gone by late June in most years. Carry water up from the bottom.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE the national park boundary — no backcountry permit needed here, which is the entire reason parties use these sites. A recreation pass is required at the Shannon Ridge trailhead. The park boundary is roughly half a mile further up the ridge, and everything beyond it needs a National Park Service permit.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.capacity: A few small sites along the open ridge; adequate but cramped compared to the Sulphide camp above

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: Sulphide Glacier high camp
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: Some parties carry above the main plateau to shorten summit day to the pyramid, camping on the glacier around 7,500 ft. It is fully exposed, on snow, and above any water, so it only makes sense for a party comfortable with a glacier bivy and a settled forecast. The gain over the lower camp is modest for most people, which is why the 6,400 ft plateau remains the norm. If weather is uncertain, the lower camp is the better place to be.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.water: None dependable — melt snow. Anything running at this elevation is a hot-afternoon accident rather than a supply.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: Lake Ann basin
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: The usual first night for both the Fisher Chimneys and the North Face, and the jurisdictional line running just past it is the single most useful thing to understand about camping on this side of Shuksan — one night at the lake is a Forest Service matter, the next night up on the route is a national park one. The trailhead sits near 4,700 ft and the trail drops before climbing back to the basin, so the return is uphill at the end of a long day. Access is entirely gated by SR 542, plowed to Artist Point on a seasonal schedule and closed with the first serious snowfall in autumn. Snow can linger in the basin into August in a heavy year.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams through most of the season. Treat it.

A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required at the Lake Ann trailhead, camping must be at least two miles from the trailhead between mid-May and mid-November, and the standard 12-person wilderness party limit applies. The permit boundary is signed beyond the lake, and every camp past it needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.capacity: Established sites around the lake basin; popular with hikers as well as climbers and busy on summer weekends

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.

Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: North Face parties share the early approach with the White Salmon Glacier route through a brushy section before the two diverge, and the usual bivy sits near 5,500 ft where the rib abuts the face, above Price Lake. It is a working bivy chosen for position on a serious route rather than for comfort, and the point of it is an early start onto sustained steep snow and ice. Objective hazard governs everything here: the face is avalanche-prone, particularly early in the season and further left, so timing and a cold night matter more than the site itself. This is a spring-into-early-summer route in most years.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.water: Seasonal melt only. Late in the year expect nothing and carry or melt.

Through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; fees apply and the zone quota is small. Do not assume the Lake Ann trailhead pass covers this.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.capacity: One party; rough ground with a couple of usable spots, not a camp

wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.name: Lake Ann basin
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.notes: The usual first night for both the Fisher Chimneys and the North Face, and the jurisdictional line running just past it is the single most useful thing to understand about camping on this side of Shuksan — one night at the lake is a Forest Service matter, the next night up on the route is a national park one. The trailhead sits near 4,700 ft and the trail drops before climbing back to the basin, so the return is uphill at the end of a long day. Access is entirely gated by SR 542, plowed to Artist Point on a seasonal schedule and closed with the first serious snowfall in autumn. Snow can linger in the basin into August in a heavy year.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams through most of the season. Treat it.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness — the lake sits roughly a mile outside the national park boundary, so no park permit is needed to camp here. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required at the Lake Ann trailhead, camping must be at least two miles from the trailhead between mid-May and mid-November, and the standard 12-person wilderness party limit applies. The permit boundary is signed beyond the lake, and every camp past it needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.capacity: Established sites around the lake basin; popular with hikers as well as climbers and busy on summer weekends

wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide

wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.name: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.notes: North Face parties share the early approach with the White Salmon Glacier route through a brushy section before the two diverge, and the usual bivy sits near 5,500 ft where the rib abuts the face, above Price Lake. It is a working bivy chosen for position on a serious route rather than for comfort, and the point of it is an early start onto sustained steep snow and ice. Objective hazard governs everything here: the face is avalanche-prone, particularly early in the season and further left, so timing and a cold night matter more than the site itself. This is a spring-into-early-summer route in most years.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.water: Seasonal melt only. Late in the year expect nothing and carry or melt.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the approach leaves Forest Service ground shortly past Lake Ann and the bivy is inside the park. Through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; fees apply and the zone quota is small. Do not assume the Lake Ann trailhead pass covers this.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.capacity: One party; rough ground with a couple of usable spots, not a camp

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Lena Lake designated sites
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Upper Lena Lake
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Lake of the Angels
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Boundary Camp
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: Lower Depot Creek bench
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes: Where the valley flattens and opens out above the Depot Creek Falls headwall. Parties use it two ways: as a shorter first day when the falls have taken longer than expected, and on the way out to put an hour of walking behind them. From here a scramble up and left onto the big buttress is a shortcut toward the Redoubt Glacier.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.permit: Inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit; cross-country camping is allowed only on durable surfaces and not in meadows or within 100 ft of water.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.capacity: Not published — informal ground rather than an established site.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: Ouzel Lake
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes: The standard high camp and the one that serves both Spickard and Redoubt, on flat sandy treeless benches and a gravel moraine at the head of the valley below the calving front of the Redoubt Glacier. Six to nine hours and roughly 3,300 ft from the road, and the crux of getting here is the Depot Creek Falls headwall — over 900 ft of wet, slippery ground with a greasy rock step, where parties have found fixed hand lines at the two vertical sections. That headwall, not the distance, is why the lower bench gets used. Despite the route's name, the line turns off well before the pass that leads to Silver Lake and never reaches it; Silver Lake is a camp on the separate Silver Creek approach from Ross Lake.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.water: The lake and Depot Creek at its outlet — glacier-fed and milky, and it is not reported to fail. Some parties pitch a little above the outlet for easy access.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, walk-up only — the cross-country zones covering this approach, Depot and Spickard, cannot be reserved in advance. Both cap a party at six people; Depot issues six permits a night and Spickard three. Ask at the Wilderness Information Center which of the two your intended site falls in, because the boundary is often not stated. Camping is allowed only on durable ground and not within 100 ft of water. The approach begins in British Columbia and crosses the border on foot at the boundary monument, where there is a trail register; carry passports.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.capacity: No published tent count; parties regularly find others already there. The number that actually binds is the permit cap of six people.

wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park
wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.notes: The winter and shoulder-season staging point, and the start of the Worm Flows route when the road to Climbers Bivouac is under snow. It is lower than the summer trailhead, so Worm Flows carries a bigger day at roughly 5,700 feet of gain, which is the main argument for sleeping here rather than driving in the dark. wa_mount_st_helens_monitor_ridge.capacity: Two large plowed lots plus adjacent forest; winter parties routinely pitch tents in and beside the lots, so capacity is generous and informal rather than defined

wa_mount_st_helens_worm_flows.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
wa_mount_st_helens_worm_flows.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

wa_mount_steel_first_divide.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
wa_mount_steel_first_divide.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself
