wa_mount_townsend_standard.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

wa_mount_townsend_standard.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
wa_mount_townsend_standard.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

wa_mount_townsend_standard.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
wa_mount_townsend_standard.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
wa_mount_townsend_standard.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.name: Thornton Lakes camp
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.notes: Where the maintained trail ends, about five and a half miles in, at the outlet of the lower lake. It is the easy, legal, reliable option and the one to take if you arrive late or the col is booked out — but it leaves a very long summit day, since the col is still a thousand-plus feet of steep talus and grass above you. Most parties climbing the ridge push past it.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.water: The outlet of the lower lake, immediately at the sites.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.permit: A National Park Service wilderness permit is required. This is a designated camp rather than the Triumph cross-country zone, so it is a different reservation from the col — book the one you actually intend to sleep in. Bear canisters are required and campfires are not allowed; there is a composting toilet.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.capacity: Three individual sites, each capped at a party of four.

wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.name: The Triumph col
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.notes: The standard high camp, on the col northwest of the middle lake, gained by about 1,200 ft of steep talus and grass above the lakes — roughly seven and a half miles and 4,200 ft from the car. Flat ground, running water and a view straight into the Pickets. Published elevations disagree by about 150 ft, from roughly 5,750 to 5,900 ft, so do not plan an altitude-sensitive turnaround off a single figure. A rockier perch just below the col is also used and is well liked.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.water: Snowmelt — a small stream running off the snowpack, and pools near the sites; parties who want more drop toward the stream at the foot of the nearby snowfield. Every published description is of meltwater, and none says when it fails, so treat it as unreliable once the snow has gone.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, in the Triumph cross-country zone: maximum party of six, and only two permits issued per night, which makes it one of the harder zones to get. It is one of the few zones that can be reserved in advance; roughly 40% of capacity is held back for walk-ups issued the day before or the day of, from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount. Cross-country camping is allowed only on durable ground — snow, rock or bare earth.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.capacity: Several good bivy spots on and just north of the col — nobody has had to drop to the glacier for want of ground. The real limit is the permit: the Triumph zone takes two parties a night, six people each.

wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.name: On-ridge bivy above the notch
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.notes: Small sites on the crest a hundred to two hundred feet above the notch, one or two pitches up the Northeast Ridge. Parties use them to shorten the climbing day, at the cost of carrying a full day's water onto the ridge. Several trip reports pass through them at dawn rather than sleep there, so treat the ground as confirmed and the comfort as unknown.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.water: None. Everything comes up from the col with you.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.capacity: A couple of small platforms — a party of two or three, spread out.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Royal Lake
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: This is the front door to the whole Needles group and the default answer for anyone climbing Deception, Clark, Johnson, Walkinshaw, The Incisor or Sundial. It sits about seven miles and two and a half thousand feet from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, up the Dungeness and then the Royal Creek fork, which is walkable with a heavy pack in an afternoon. The honest trade is this: Royal Lake is comfortable, has real designated tent pads and is where the permit system actually issues sites, but it leaves you an extra mile and roughly five hundred to a thousand feet of loose boot path below the upper basin every single climbing morning. On a Needles day that difference is real, because the rock above the basin is dirty and slow and you want to be off it before the afternoon. Parties that only want one peak, or that have anyone who would rather not sleep at six thousand feet on gravel, are right to stay here. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a normal year and the mosquitoes at the lake are notorious through midsummer, which is another argument for going higher. Book the moment the reservation window opens; this is one of the hardest permits on the peninsula to get on a weekend.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: The lake and the outlet creek run all season. Filter or treat; this is a heavily used basin and the shoreline is fragile.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Royal Basin is one of the park's named quota areas. Essentially the whole quota is reservable in advance through the federal recreation booking system, with the summer block released in a single mid-April drop for the mid-May through mid-October season; there is no same-day walk-up window, so a party that turns up without a permit has no legal camp. Expect a flat per-permit reservation charge plus a per-adult, per-night fee, with under-sixteens free and an annual wilderness pass available if you camp here often. Dates outside the online season are arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, and loaners are sometimes available on a first-come basis when you collect the permit. Every camp along Royal Creek and up through the meadows and the basin sits inside the same reservation, so there is no legal way to sneak a night lower down without one.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: Ten designated sites, and only two of them will take more than a single tent. One separate group site holds roughly seven to twelve people and has to be booked as a group site. That is the entire overnight capacity of the lake basin, which is why permits go so fast.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Upper Royal Basin
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: This is the climbers' camp, three quarters of a mile to a mile above the lake on an unmaintained way trail that gains around five hundred to a thousand feet. It puts you at the foot of the west wall of the basin, which is the east side of The Needles, and it is the difference between a reasonable day and a very long one on Deception, Clark, Johnson, The Incisor and Sundial. It is also the working base for Mystery, which is reached over the divide out of the head of the basin, and for Fricaba, which is a comparatively easy scramble from here and a common warm-up or bad-weather substitute. What you pay for the position: exposed camping on gravel with no trees, weather that arrives with no warning, colder nights, and a fiddly load carry up the boot path in the evening. What you get: fewer people, far fewer mosquitoes, and a start that puts you on the loose ground above the basin while it is still frozen together rather than after the sun has been on it for two hours. Snow covers the upper basin well into July most years, which is often an advantage for the approach gullies and a nuisance for finding bare ground to pitch on. If the basin is still largely snow-covered, camp on a gravel bar that has melted out rather than on snow over vegetation.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: Tarns and snowmelt streams through the basin. Late in a dry summer the upper tarns can drop and go stagnant, so check the inlet streams rather than dipping from still water, and be prepared to carry from lower in the basin in September.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Same Olympic National Park quota permit as Royal Lake, booked as the upper basin rather than the lake. All the same conditions apply: advance reservation only, mid-April release for the summer season, per-permit and per-person-per-night charges, and mandatory hard-sided bear canisters. Because there are no constructed sites, the leave-no-trace rules here are enforced in earnest: no camping on vegetation or meadow, no fires, and the park expects you to be on durable surface only. Anyone found camped on the heather is the reason this basin nearly lost overnight use.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: No numbered sites at all. Camping is permitted only on bare ground, gravel bars and rock, so the practical capacity is a handful of parties spread across the gravel beside the tarns. Two of the larger gravel bars near the upper tarn are the usual choice for a group.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Camp Handy
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: A low, sheltered, permit-free camp about three miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, and the most useful fallback in the whole zone. It does not serve The Needles: Royal Basin branches off well below it and Camp Handy is on the wrong fork. What it does is give you a legal, free, roofed place to sleep when the Royal Basin quota is gone, when you arrive too late to start the Royal Creek climb, or when the weather is bad enough that a night in the trees beats a night on gravel at five and a half thousand feet. It is also the natural first night for anyone approaching Fricaba the long way, by Boulder Shelter and Constance Pass. At barely three thousand feet in old growth it is warm, wet and buggy in early summer, and it commits you to a very big day if you try to use it as a climbing base for anything on the divide. Treat it as staging, not as a base camp.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: The Dungeness river runs right past the camp all year. Reliable.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Outside the national park. This is Olympic National Forest, inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so there is no park wilderness permit, no quota and no nightly fee. You do need a valid recreation parking pass on the vehicle at the Upper Dungeness trailhead. Bear canisters are not legally required on forest land here but food does need protecting, and if any part of your trip crosses into the park you will be carrying one anyway.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: An open three-sided shelter with log benches plus several tent sites scattered through the riverside meadow. Comfortably takes a few parties, and rarely full outside a summer weekend. No privy.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Boulder Shelter
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. This is the crossroads camp for the eastern half of the zone: from here the trail climbs to Home Lake and Constance Pass, which is the alternative and much less crowded way at Fricaba. It is permit-free, which matters a great deal in a zone where the good camps are rationed months in advance. It is not a Needles camp and no amount of enthusiasm makes it one. Also worth knowing before you plan around it: the stretch above here toward Home Lake is far more primitive than the trail below, with brush, blowdown and at least one crossing that will get you wet, so budget more time than the mileage suggests. The shelter is genuinely useful in bad weather, which is not something most of the alpine options in this zone can offer.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary is crossed on the way to Home Lake, and from that point an Olympic National Park wilderness permit and a bear canister are required, so if you intend to sleep beyond here get the permit before you leave the road.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Home Lake
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: Just over nine miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, a little over five thousand three hundred feet, and only a few hundred feet below Constance Pass. This is the second door to Fricaba, and the reason it is in this list at all: if the Royal Basin quota is unobtainable, Fricaba can still be climbed from this side without competing for a rationed permit. It is a genuinely long walk in, with the primitive brushy section above Boulder Shelter to negotiate, so it costs you most of a day. It gives you a quiet alpine lake with real water and real shelter from wind, at a height that leaves a sensible summit day. It does nothing at all for The Needles or the Royal Basin peaks, which sit over a major divide from here. Snow holds around the lake and the pass into July. Parties combining Fricaba with Mount Constance frequently use this camp, which is worth remembering when you are guessing at how busy it will be.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: The lake, immediately at camp. Reliable through the season.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Inside Olympic National Park, so an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required, but Home Lake is NOT one of the quota areas. Reserve through the federal recreation booking system with the usual per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee; because it carries no quota, availability is generally straightforward even in midsummer, which is precisely why it is worth knowing about. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, as they are throughout park wilderness.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Cedar Lake
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. Be clear-eyed about the cost: it is a long, remote walk in, well over ten miles, on a trail with a missing river bridge that pushes everyone onto the Slab Camp approach, and it is a completely different road and trailhead from Royal Basin. Almost nobody climbs Baldy or Gray Wolf Ridge from here, because both are done car to car in a long day from the steep Maynard Burn way trail on the Dungeness side, with no camp involved and no permit needed. Cedar Lake earns its place for the party doing the full ridge traverse, or wanting the Gray Wolf approach to Walkinshaw, or simply wanting solitude in a zone where the popular basin is rationed. If you only want to stand on Baldy and Gray Wolf Ridge, do not come here.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Cameron Basin
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.name: Dose Meadows
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
wa_mount_walkinshaw_scramble.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Lena Lake designated sites
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Upper Lena Lake
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Lake of the Angels
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Lower Anderson Lake
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM AS OF 2026: an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four, well below the road end, and that failure has closed the trailhead and the Sno-Park with no quick fix. When it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. From camp the summit is a short ascent to the southeast, and it is possible to reach the top without crossing glaciers at all, which is what makes this a scramble for a competent party rather than a rope-up. Immediately north the ground falls away past post-glacial moraine to the saddle above the green lake below the glacier, and that is the line onward for anyone continuing east or north across the range. It is a fully exposed shelf with nothing to shelter behind and the weather here comes across from Baker with no warning. The season is roughly mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse is a long snow slope, later and the water is gone.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier melt near camp through most of the season, and tarns in the moraine below. Late in a dry summer expect to be melting snow. Treat anything you find, and do not count on liquid water in early season when the whole shelf is still covered.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: This camp sits on the boundary country between the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness and North Cascades National Park, and which one it falls in decides whether you need a permit at all. Ask specifically when you plan the trip: the Forest Service side needs no overnight permit, while the park side needs a backcountry permit written for the correct cross-country zone. No campfires on either side of the line. Camp on snow, rock or gravel and never on the heather, keep well back from water, and pack out all waste — on snow and glacier that means blue bags carried out.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: Open ground for a couple of small parties on gravel, rock and heather about half a mile northeast of the summit; informal, with nothing built and no toilet

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward Berdeen, or for the long line north over the divide toward Hagan and Blum. What sets it apart from every other high site here is that it has water at six thousand feet, which nothing on the connecting ridges does. It is alpine meadow, so the heather is the thing to protect and the tent goes on rock. Snow covers this basin well into July and the lakes can still be part frozen at the start of the season. There is no shelter, no cell coverage, and no quick way down from here in any direction.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: The lakes, dependable and right at camp — the best water this high anywhere on the massif. Treat it.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required for an overnight, collected in person at the wilderness information center. No campfires. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste in a blue bag from snow and glacier ground. The party limit in a park cross-country zone is small — confirm the number when you collect the permit rather than assuming a Forest Service twelve.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: Room for a small party or two on alpine meadow and heather benches beside the upper pair of lakes; established by use rather than designation, with no facilities

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Berdeen Lake benches
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: The camp for Berdeen Peak and the substance of the Bacon Creek side of this zone. The documented approach starts at the Bacon Creek road end at valley-bottom elevation, scrambles up Porkbelly Ridge, crosses the east side of the peak around 6,400 ft and drops to camp above the lake — a very big first day with four thousand feet of gain, much of it trackless. The lake sits in a deep cirque a little over a mile east of Hagan Mountain and drains east over an enormous waterfall into a tributary of Bacon Creek, which is the geography that settles the argument about which road it belongs to: it faces Bacon Creek, not Baker Lake. It can be reached from the Blum Lakes over the divide to the northwest, but that is a traverse variation for a party already committed to a long trip, not an approach. From camp Berdeen Peak's east ridge is the way up, and the ground south and west continues onto the Bacon massif. Season is roughly mid-July into September, held back at the front by snow on the ridge and at the back by short days on a route with no trail.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: The lake and its inlet streams, fed off the glaciers above and reliable all season. Treat it. This is the first dependable water since the valley bottom, over four thousand feet below.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required for any overnight and written for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp — a different thing to ask for, and it must be collected in person at the wilderness information center, which is a long way round on the far side of the range from the Anderson Creek trailheads. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and never in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste. A bear canister is the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from; they can usually be borrowed at the permit office.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: A handful of tent-sized spots on benches above the lake shore; the basin is large but the flat, durable ground is limited, and this is a cross-country zone with a small party cap rather than an established campground

wa_mount_watson_scramble.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
wa_mount_watson_scramble.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMPING ON THIS APPROACH and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brush with better travel once the ridge crest establishes itself, and no benches, clearings or water worth the name in four thousand feet. THE ROAD IS THE FIRST PROBLEM: it carries very large potholes over long stretches, a bridge on the main road beyond one of the side creeks has been out, and the spurs off it are variously blocked by missing bridges, washouts and downed timber, so how far a vehicle gets is a live question that changes year to year and adds miles at the bottom when it goes against you. A party that runs out of daylight on the ridge flattens a spot among the trees and moves at first light; that is the realistic use of this camp, not a plan. The same road end is the start for the Diobsud Creek side of Bacon Peak, which is climbed on a longer line past Salvation Peak with a glacier saddle camp around 6,250 ft — a spring and early summer objective needing snow travel gear, and a different proposition entirely from the summer scramble off the Anderson Creek road.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.water: The creek near the road end, treated. Above it there is nothing dependable until the lake basin high on the ridge, so fill everything before you start climbing.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.permit: The road end and the lower part of the ridge are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, where a night in a pullout is generally tolerated and no permit is issued. The ground higher up crosses into North Cascades National Park, so if you sleep anywhere above the lower ridge you need a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone. The boundary is not marked on the ground on this ridge, so ask at the permit office where it falls before planning a bivy rather than deciding on the hill. No campfires above the road, and total burn bans are common on this side through a dry August.
wa_mount_watson_scramble.capacity: Rough parking at the road end and whatever flat ground you can find in the timber; one party, found rather than chosen. There is no camp here, and that is worth saying plainly.

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Graves Creek Campground — drive-in staging for the East Fork Quinault
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: This is the only realistic drive-in base on the Quinault side and the natural place to sleep the night before starting up the East Fork toward Anderson Pass and Anderson's Thumb. Vault toilets, fire grates, tables and bear lockers, and nothing else. Reach it from the North Shore Road only — the South Shore Road has a washout roughly eight miles up from the highway, and a phone will still try to route you that way and add several miles of driving for nothing. The last six miles are narrow gravel and RVs and trailers are banned regardless of what the road is doing on the day. Treat the road status as a live question rather than a settled one: this stretch has been closed to vehicles by erosion before, and when it is, both the campground and the trailhead become a two-mile walk or ride. Sleeping here costs you nothing in approach distance, which matters when the first day out is thirteen miles to Enchanted Valley.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: None piped — there is no potable water at all, so arrive with everything you need or filter from the Quinault beside the campground
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed for a night here, and no reservation is possible. The moment you walk past the trailhead you need an Olympic wilderness permit booked on the federal recreation site: eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over, plus a six dollar non-refundable booking fee, or a forty-five dollar annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. A bear canister is required in every wilderness camp area in this park, and they are loaned free to permit holders at the wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: About 30 first-come, first-served sites, open year round and rarely full outside high summer weekends; no reservations are taken

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Dodger Point Camp — the southern gateway to the Bailey Range
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: Dodger Point is 13.5 miles from the old Whiskey Bend trailhead by way of the Long Ridge trail, which leaves the Elwha at Michael's Cabin and crosses the river on a suspension bridge. With the road walk added it is about nineteen miles and well over ten thousand feet of gain to the lookout, so this is a serious approach in its own right. It is the way in to MOUNT DANA and MOUNT WILDER, the southern end of the Bailey Range, and the connecting ridge toward Ludden Peak and on to Ferry Basin, MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER. That connection is not a trail: it involves a faint path off the ridge, a steep gully of loose rock and a section where you climb a tangle of roots and branches to regain the crest. Cream Lake below Ferry Basin is infamous for mosquitoes and for steep alder-choked gullies that swallow time, so budget generously and go in a dry spell if you can. The lookout is the best viewpoint in the valley and the camp is worth a night on its own merits.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: THE WEAK POINT. There is no water between the Elwha crossing near Michael's Cabin and the tarns just below Dodger Point — a long climb. Fill everything at the river, and expect the tarns to be low or gone by late season.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. The camp itself books normally, but any night spent off-trail on the Bailey ridge beyond it is a cross-country zone and must be arranged by telephone with the wilderness information centre. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: A handful of established sites near the old lookout, on an exposed ridge crest; small, and seldom busy

wa_mount_wilder_scramble.name: Enchanted Valley and Anderson Pass — the approach to Anderson's Thumb
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.notes: The East Fork Quinault runs about thirteen miles from Graves Creek to the Enchanted Valley chalet, with staged camps at Pony Bridge around three miles, O'Neil Creek around six and a half and Pyrites Creek around nine, all of which are useful for breaking the walk in. This is the approach to ANDERSON'S THUMB, the pinnacle on the Anderson massif, reached by continuing from the valley up to Anderson Pass at 4,480 ft and then onto the glacier remnant and the rock above. Camping at the pass rather than in the valley saves you several miles and roughly two thousand feet on climbing day and puts you in quiet country; camping in the valley gets you a flatter, warmer night and a spectacular setting at the cost of a very long summit day and a great deal of company. Bears are habituated and confident here, so the canister rule is enforced rather than advisory, and food left out is food lost. The same pass is reached from the Dosewallips on the east side, which is the shorter approach to the Anderson massif if that road is open — worth checking before committing to the Quinault side.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.water: Reliable everywhere — the East Fork Quinault runs the length of the valley and small streams cross the trail up toward the pass
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and the EAST FORK QUINAULT RIVER IS A QUOTA AREA — reserve on the federal recreation site rather than turning up hopeful. Summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and reservations for it release on 15 April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for adults, six dollar booking fee. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY AND STRICTLY REQUIRED HERE: this valley was closed to camping over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Canisters are loaned free at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness information centres.
wa_mount_wilder_scramble.capacity: A large valley camping area at the chalet meadow that can hold well over a hundred people on a summer weekend, plus a much smaller and quieter camp up near Anderson Pass

wa_mount_worthington_standard.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
wa_mount_worthington_standard.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

wa_mount_worthington_standard.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
wa_mount_worthington_standard.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

wa_mount_worthington_standard.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
wa_mount_worthington_standard.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

wa_mount_worthington_standard.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
wa_mount_worthington_standard.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

wa_mount_worthington_standard.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
wa_mount_worthington_standard.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
wa_mount_worthington_standard.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

wa_mount_worthington_standard.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
wa_mount_worthington_standard.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks.
