The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Copper Glance Lake
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.name: Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.notes: The obvious place to sleep before starting up either side of the Gardners, and the only one with running water and a toilet. It sits in ponderosa forest just off the highway about four miles beyond Mazama, and the Cedar Creek trailhead is roughly half a mile further along a short forest road — near enough to walk to if you wanted. Coming from the west over the pass, this is the first campground on the dry side and the change is abrupt: open pine, no undergrowth, hot afternoons and cold clear nights. Use it as staging, not as a destination. The practical value is that it lets you drive out the evening before, sleep at the trailhead, and start the long Wolf Creek or Cedar Creek walk at dawn rather than in the heat of the day, which on these approaches matters more than it sounds. Bear in mind the highway itself opened late in 2026 after repair work, and paving through this corridor has been closing individual sites for stretches of a week or so at a time; ring ahead rather than arriving on spec.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.water: Piped water at Klipchuck when the season's system is turned on, and Early Winters Creek nearby. Do not count on the tap outside the main season or in a drought year — check before you drive out, because the alternative is hauling water from town.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.permit: Nightly campground fee. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for the trailhead lots. No wilderness permit required. Campfires are prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions currently in force, including in established rings, and the county burn ban applies as well. Some highway-corridor sites are closed in rotation for paving work between early August and mid September.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.capacity: Around forty sites at Klipchuck; the smaller campgrounds up and down the highway corridor add a few dozen more between them

wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.name: Cedar Creek meadow camps above the falls
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.notes: The western approach camp, and the reason to use this side at all. Cedar Falls comes at about 1.7 miles from the trailhead and is the day-hike turnaround for most visitors; keep going and roughly two miles beyond the falls the trail opens into meadows with good camping. From here the head of the valley and the west flank of North Gardner are within reach, and this is materially shorter than coming round by Wolf Creek. Its real value is seasonal. The trailhead is low and this is one of the first trails in the area to melt out, so in a late spring when Wolf Creek is still buried and the Gardner Meadows approach is a slog, this side goes. The trade is snow higher up and a steeper, less travelled finish. Damage from the 2021 fire is visible in this drainage too, heavier away from the creek than beside it, and the lower trail to the falls is in good order. The trail continues to Abernathy Pass at about 9.2 miles and over into North Creek, which is a useful escape or through-route if weather closes the tops.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.water: Cedar Creek runs alongside for the whole approach and through the meadows, and it is the most dependable water — a snow-fed creek in a north-facing valley that holds well into autumn. Fill here, because the climb east out of the valley toward the Gardner ridge has nothing.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.permit: The Cedar Creek trail is outside the wilderness until it nears Abernathy Pass, where it enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota either side of that line; party limit of twelve inside. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Campfires prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions and the county burn ban.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.capacity: Good established sites for hikers and stock where the trail enters the meadows; several parties can spread out

wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.name: Upper Cedar Creek head basin
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.notes: A spring and early-summer bivouac rather than a camp, used by parties taking the west side of North Gardner when snow still covers the ground. Getting into the head of the valley involves leaving the maintained trail and working up through brush, and it is not pleasant in dry conditions — the argument for it is precisely that on snow the brush is buried and the travel is fast. From the basin the west and southwest flanks of North Gardner rise directly, and a party can take both Gardner summits and be back at the car the following morning, which is appreciably shorter than the Wolf Creek round trip. Expect avalanche terrain on those slopes into June and treat the timing accordingly: an early start, firm snow, and off the slopes before the afternoon. There is no shelter, the basin is a cold sink, and there is no easy retreat except the way you came. This is a competent-party option in a narrow window, not a general-purpose camp.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.water: Snowmelt and the headwaters of Cedar Creek. Reliable in early season, which is when this camp makes sense; in late summer it thins out and the meadows below the falls become the better choice. Melting snow is the normal answer here in spring.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness at the head of the valley. No permit, no quota, party limit of twelve, proper food storage. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions, and there is no fuel. Leave no trace on unestablished ground and camp on rock or snow rather than fragile meadow.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_nw_couloir.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small parties; no established sites and no flat obvious platform

wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.name: Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.notes: The obvious place to sleep before starting up either side of the Gardners, and the only one with running water and a toilet. It sits in ponderosa forest just off the highway about four miles beyond Mazama, and the Cedar Creek trailhead is roughly half a mile further along a short forest road — near enough to walk to if you wanted. Coming from the west over the pass, this is the first campground on the dry side and the change is abrupt: open pine, no undergrowth, hot afternoons and cold clear nights. Use it as staging, not as a destination. The practical value is that it lets you drive out the evening before, sleep at the trailhead, and start the long Wolf Creek or Cedar Creek walk at dawn rather than in the heat of the day, which on these approaches matters more than it sounds. Bear in mind the highway itself opened late in 2026 after repair work, and paving through this corridor has been closing individual sites for stretches of a week or so at a time; ring ahead rather than arriving on spec.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.water: Piped water at Klipchuck when the season's system is turned on, and Early Winters Creek nearby. Do not count on the tap outside the main season or in a drought year — check before you drive out, because the alternative is hauling water from town.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.permit: Nightly campground fee. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for the trailhead lots. No wilderness permit required. Campfires are prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions currently in force, including in established rings, and the county burn ban applies as well. Some highway-corridor sites are closed in rotation for paving work between early August and mid September.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.capacity: Around forty sites at Klipchuck; the smaller campgrounds up and down the highway corridor add a few dozen more between them

wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.name: Gardner Meadows, Wolf Creek trail
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.notes: This is the basecamp for both peaks and the way the great majority of parties climb them. The Wolf Creek trail runs roughly ten miles up the valley bottom from the trailhead near Winthrop to meadows sitting directly beneath Gardner Mountain, with North Gardner a mile further northwest along the connecting ridge. From here a fit party can take both summits in a single long day and walk out the next morning. Know what the approach is now: the first eight miles or so run through forest burned in the 2021 fire, so there is very little shade, the tread is crossed by blowdown in places, and the second half is brushy. Where the trail turns uphill into the meadows it becomes genuinely hard to follow, buried in downed logs and regrowth, and one of the creek crossings is easy to miss even in daylight — this is not a route to be finding for the first time in the dark. Allow four and a half to five hours to camp with a climbing load. Season is July through September; the aspect is dry and eastern so the snow leaves early, but the same thing that clears the snow makes the walk in punishing in midsummer heat. The climbing above is a scramble on loose scree with pinnacles and short cliff bands on the connecting ridge that force you off the crest rather than along it.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.water: A small stream flows south out of Gardner Mountain through the meadows and there is water at camp through a normal summer. This is the critical fill point: the Wolf Creek trail below is notably short of water for a valley-bottom trail, and everything above the meadows is bone dry. Carry the whole day's supply for the climb, and in a heat wave carry water up the approach as well — parties have turned around on these peaks for want of it.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.permit: The upper Wolf Creek trail enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No wilderness permit or quota to hike or camp; sign the trailhead register. Party size limited to twelve people and eighteen head of stock. Northwest Forest Pass at the Wolf Creek trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions, and in a burned valley with standing snags this is a rule worth taking seriously. Proper food storage required.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.capacity: Numerous comfortable sites through the meadows and in the trees at their edge; this is the one place in the zone that will absorb several parties without crowding

wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.name: High basin camp above Gardner Meadows
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.notes: The higher option for a party that wants to shorten summit day rather than take both peaks in one long push from the meadows. Heading north out of Gardner Meadows the ground rises to a small meadow basin at about 6,200 ft, and an old boot path leaves the main trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream to reach it. Stay between roughly 6,200 and 6,400 ft on the way across — drop lower and you land in groves of silver snags with jack-strawed deadfall that cost far more time than the elevation saves. From a camp here the scree slope to the ridge is about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile, which is the steepest and loosest section of the whole climb and much better done early and on firm ground. It is an exposed spot with no shelter to speak of and it is cold; the compensation is the position and the head start. Use it when the forecast is settled and when you have confirmed water. In a dry August the meadows below are the safer plan.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.water: A seep and small stream in the basin, which is what makes the site usable at all — it is boggy underfoot in early season and can be dry by late August in a poor snow year. Confirm it before carrying up on the strength of it, because there is no second option at this elevation and the retreat is all the way back to the meadows.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota, party limit of twelve, food stored properly. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions apply and there is nothing worth burning up here in any case. Camp on durable ground and off the wet meadow.
wa_north_gardner_mountain_southwest.capacity: A small soggy basin with room for one or two tents; a party of two or three at most

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_north_ridge_2.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_north_ridge_2.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_north_ridge_2.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_north_ridge_2.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_north_ridge_2.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_north_ridge_2.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
wa_north_ridge_3.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
wa_north_ridge_3.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
wa_north_ridge_3.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
wa_north_ridge_3.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
wa_north_ridge_3.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
wa_north_ridge_3.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
wa_north_ridge_3.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_north_ridge_3.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
wa_north_ridge_3.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
wa_north_ridge_3.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
wa_north_ridge_3.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
wa_north_ridge_3.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
wa_north_ridge_3.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
wa_north_ridge_3.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
wa_north_ridge_3.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
wa_north_ridge_3.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_north_ridge_3.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
wa_north_ridge_3.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
wa_north_ridge_3.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
wa_north_ridge_3.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
wa_north_ridge_3.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
wa_north_ridge_3.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
wa_north_ridge_3.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_north_ridge_4.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
wa_north_ridge_4.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
wa_north_ridge_4.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
wa_north_ridge_4.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
wa_north_ridge_4.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

wa_north_ridge_4.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
wa_north_ridge_4.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
wa_north_ridge_4.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
wa_north_ridge_4.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
wa_north_ridge_4.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

wa_north_ridge_4.name: Tricouni Camp, Thunder Creek trail
wa_north_ridge_4.notes: Despite sharing the peak's name this camp is about a mile and a half further up the valley than the point where climbers leave the trail, so it is a fallback rather than a first choice. It is worth knowing about when McAllister is booked out on the night you need, since a short extra walk each way costs less than losing the trip. The forest here is more open than at McAllister. Nothing about it shortens the climb.
wa_north_ridge_4.water: Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek nearby, reliable through the climbing season
wa_north_ridge_4.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit system and fees as McAllister — designated site, part reservable and part held for walk-up at Marblemount.
wa_north_ridge_4.capacity: Small designated hiker camp, a few sites

wa_north_ridge_4.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
wa_north_ridge_4.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
wa_north_ridge_4.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
wa_north_ridge_4.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
wa_north_ridge_4.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

wa_north_ridge_4.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
wa_north_ridge_4.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
wa_north_ridge_4.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
wa_north_ridge_4.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
wa_north_ridge_4.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

wa_north_ridge_4.name: Klawatti Col camp, Eldorado ice-cap traverse approach
wa_north_ridge_4.notes: This is the multi-day route in, from the Eldorado side across the ice, and it is NOT how most parties reach these two peaks — it is recorded so the option is visible, not recommended as a shortcut. It is a genuinely different undertaking: full glacier travel with crevasse rescue capability, several nights on snow, and a committing exit. Camps are on rock islands surrounded by ice, so they are windy and there is no shelter. Choose it because you want the traverse.
wa_north_ridge_4.water: Meltwater and snow across the ice cap; essentially always available in season but usually means melting
wa_north_ridge_4.permit: A DIFFERENT approach means a different permit. Parties coming across the ice cap from Eldorado start in a zone that does accept advance reservations, but the zone boundaries out here are not obvious on the ground and a traverse can cross more than one. Sort the whole itinerary night by night with Marblemount, since a reservation for one zone is not a permit for the next.
wa_north_ridge_4.capacity: Rock islands in the ice with room for a few tents; party size capped by the zone permit

wa_north_ridge_7.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_north_ridge_7.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_north_ridge_7.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_north_ridge_7.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_north_ridge_7.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_north_ridge_7.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_north_ridge_7.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_north_ridge_7.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_north_ridge_7.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_north_ridge_7.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_north_ridge_7.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_north_ridge_7.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_north_ridge_7.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_north_ridge_7.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_north_ridge_7.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_north_ridge_7.name: Pelton Basin
wa_north_ridge_7.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_north_ridge_7.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_north_ridge_7.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_north_ridge_7.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_north_ridge_7.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_north_ridge_7.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
wa_north_ridge_7.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
wa_north_ridge_7.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_north_ridge_7.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

wa_north_ridge_7.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_north_ridge_7.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
wa_north_ridge_7.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
wa_north_ridge_7.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
wa_north_ridge_7.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
wa_north_ridge_west_side.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Holden Village
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Holden Lake
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher.
