It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Leroy Basin
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Ice Lakes
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Leroy Basin
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Ice Lakes
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

wa_north_tower_ridge_route.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.notes: This is the base for the north face and the trailhead in one, which is unusual and is what makes the face approachable at all: the walk to the bottom of the routes is under an hour, so a party can sleep at the car and still be climbing at first light without a bivouac. Trail 373 begins across the road from the campground and runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at around 7,150 ft, from where the face is below you. THE DRIVE IS THE COMMITMENT. Three ways reach it and they are not equivalent: a narrow four-wheel-drive road over Lone Frank Pass from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek, about twenty miles; a longer gravel road over Baldy Pass suited to two-wheel drive, about thirty; and a good two-wheel-drive gravel line from the Methow, north out of Winthrop on the Chewuch River road and then east and north on the 37 and 39, about twenty-six miles. Road 39 itself has not been graded in some time and is not recommended for low-clearance passenger cars. At this elevation the road holds snow late into the spring and can shut with the first serious autumn storm, so the usable window is short and both ends of it are worth checking rather than assuming.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.water: NO POTABLE WATER AND NO TAP — this is the single most important practical fact about the place, and its name is misleading. There is no piped supply, no water service and no rubbish service. Bring everything you need for drinking, cooking and washing, or plan to treat from Tiffany Lake, which is a short walk east on the trail and is the nearest dependable open water. In late summer this whole plateau is dry and what looks like a creek on a map may be nothing at all.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.permit: National forest, outside designated wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery — the opposite of the permit expectation a few miles west in the Pasayten. There is a small nightly fee at the campground and sites are first come, first served. Fire restrictions on this dry high plateau run through most of the summer and are commonly total bans, which given what has burned here recently should be treated as the default rather than the exception. Party size and stay limits are the usual forest ones.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.capacity: A small primitive forest campground with a handful of sites, taking tents and modest vehicles. Trailers are not appropriate given the road. It is rarely full and it is the only organised camping anywhere near this face.

wa_north_tower_ridge_route.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.notes: Under a mile from the campground and directly on the approach, this is the camp for a party who would rather sleep on water than at a car, or who has arrived to find the campground full or closed. It is the last certain water before the face. The trail continues around the shore and climbs about six hundred feet to Honeymoon Pass, which is the gateway to the north side; parties leaving a second vehicle at the Freezeout Ridge roadhead can carry on over Whistler Pass at around 7,600 ft to the summit and descend the Freezeout trail, an open loop of some eleven miles that is the standard way to combine the walk-up with a look at the face. THE BURN IS PART OF THE LANDSCAPE HERE. This trail travels through old fire scars that have opened the views and filled the ground with wildflower meadow, and the 2026 fire has added to that directly on this mountain — expect standing dead timber, no shade, and blowdown that changes with each windstorm. Do not pitch under dead trees in wind.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.water: The lakes, and they are the dependable supply for the whole north side of this mountain — everything above them on the pass and the face runs on snowmelt and is dry once that has gone. Access to the water is easy from the trail. Treat it; these are shallow, warm, well-used lakes rather than cold alpine tarns.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.permit: National forest, non-wilderness. No permit, no quota, no reservation, and no fee to camp at the lakes. A pass is not required to park at the campground trailhead across the road. Fire restrictions apply through the summer and are usually total bans; carry a stove. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground, and note that this trail is open to horses and mountain bikes as well as walkers, so pitch clear of it.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.

wa_north_tower_ridge_route.name: Honeymoon Pass
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.notes: The pass is where the trail crosses onto the north side and the face comes into view, and it is the tactical camp rather than the comfortable one. Its argument is a dawn start: from here the base of the routes is a short drop and a scramble rather than a walk from the road, which matters for the north-east couloir where the snow wants climbing early and matters much less for the rock, since the campground is under an hour away regardless. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WIND, in that order, and on a face this short the trade is rarely worth it — most parties are better off sleeping at the campground or the lake and walking in. Where it does earn its keep is for a party spending two days on the face, or one continuing over Whistler Pass to the summit and out by Freezeout Ridge. Nights are cold at this elevation from late August onward and there is no shelter at all if weather comes across the plateau.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.water: None dependable. Snowmelt early in the season and nothing at all once it has gone. Everything is carried up from Tiffany Lake, six hundred feet and half a mile below, and the party that forgets this ends up walking back down for it in the evening. In the ice season it is a snow camp and you melt.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation, no fee. Fire restrictions run through the summer and there is nothing to burn at this height in any case. The turf here is thin and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.capacity: Open ground at the pass for a small party on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and nothing to shelter behind. Windswept is the word most often used about this crest and it is accurate.

wa_north_tower_ridge_route.name: The talus and benches below the north face
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.notes: The routes start here and, on a face six hundred and fifty feet high forty-five minutes from a campground, essentially nobody sleeps here. It is written down because a party reading a list of camps should not be left to assume there is a bivouac at the base — there is not, and the answer to a late arrival is the campground, not the wall. THE FACE ITSELF is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock. Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.water: Snowmelt off the couloirs early, and nothing whatsoever once that has gone. Given how early the snow leaves here after the roads open, that window is short. Carry water from the lakes; there is no source at the base of the face you should plan on.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.
wa_north_tower_ridge_route.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.name: Orsino Creek Basin
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.name: Elbow Lake hiker camps
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.notes: These are the only established campsites anywhere near this range, reached by a spur off the main trail to the east shore of the lake. They are not on the direct line to any of these five summits, sitting on the divide east of the crest rather than under it, so treat them as a legal and comfortable staging camp on public ground rather than as a climbing basecamp. They are most useful for a party coming in from the south with an awkward road situation, or for anyone who wants a settled night before or after a long day on the ridge. The lake is buggy in early summer and the surrounding ground is boggy in places. Because the road access on both ends of this trail has been unreliable and at least one vehicle closure has been in force recently, check the current status of the forest roads and of the river ford before planning a trip around this camp.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.water: The lake, filtered. Reliable all season, though shallow and warm by late summer
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, within or adjoining the wilderness unit. No overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at the trailhead. Fires may be restricted or banned in late summer. Access is the problem rather than the permit: there is no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at the northern trailhead and has not been for decades, so that side requires a ford that is not safe at high flow, and the southern road approach has been subject to a vehicle closure part way in. Confirm both roads and the crossing before committing.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Two established hiker sites on the east shore

wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.name: Orsino Creek Basin
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.name: Elbow Lake hiker camps
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.notes: These are the only established campsites anywhere near this range, reached by a spur off the main trail to the east shore of the lake. They are not on the direct line to any of these five summits, sitting on the divide east of the crest rather than under it, so treat them as a legal and comfortable staging camp on public ground rather than as a climbing basecamp. They are most useful for a party coming in from the south with an awkward road situation, or for anyone who wants a settled night before or after a long day on the ridge. The lake is buggy in early summer and the surrounding ground is boggy in places. Because the road access on both ends of this trail has been unreliable and at least one vehicle closure has been in force recently, check the current status of the forest roads and of the river ford before planning a trip around this camp.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.water: The lake, filtered. Reliable all season, though shallow and warm by late summer
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, within or adjoining the wilderness unit. No overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at the trailhead. Fires may be restricted or banned in late summer. Access is the problem rather than the permit: there is no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at the northern trailhead and has not been for decades, so that side requires a ford that is not safe at high flow, and the southern road approach has been subject to a vehicle closure part way in. Confirm both roads and the crossing before committing.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge.capacity: Two established hiker sites on the east shore

wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_northeast_buttress_4.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_northeast_buttress_4.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_northeast_buttress_4.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_northeast_buttress_4.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_northeast_buttress_4.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_northeast_buttress_4.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_northeast_buttress_4.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_northeast_buttress_4.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_northeast_buttress_4.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_northeast_buttress_4.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_northeast_buttress_4.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_northeast_buttress_4.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: Spider-Formidable Col
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: Drop Creek high camp
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. It starts at the South Fork Cascade River trailhead, which is little more than a bend in the Cascade River Road around mile 17 to 18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, well below the road end at Cascade Pass. The first mile is maintained, then the trail deteriorates into ups, downs and overgrown nettle sections; past the Middle Fork turnoff you cross Drop Creek on a log and turn up into its valley on a climbers' path. That path fades after a few hundred vertical feet, but the forest above about 4,000 feet is open and the bushwhacking is unusually easy for this part of the range, with one short slide alder thicket below 4,600 feet. The camp is the obvious flat ground at around 7,100 feet with water, and from it the ground steepens to class 3 with a permanent snowfield near 7,400 feet and one narrow chasm crossing that is worth protecting. The whole approach avoids glacier travel entirely, which is why it has become the late-season choice, and recent trail work has made it the most pleasant it has been in years. Reckon on roughly twenty-five miles and eight thousand feet for the round trip.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: Running water beside the camp for most of the season, fed by the snowfield above, and a second reliable source lower down around 5,600 feet before the steep meadow climb. Late in a dry summer take the lower water seriously, because the high source is a snowfield that is shrinking.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is the usual requirement for the vehicle at Forest Service trailheads on this road, unlike the park trailhead at the end of it, so check before leaving the car. No fires at this elevation.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for a party or two, on heather and rock. Unimproved, no toilet, no windbreaks.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: South Fork Cascade River valley camps
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: The fallback first night on the Drop Creek approach to Formidable, for a party that starts late or is not confident of reaching the high camp in one push. It exists because the valley section is slower than its mileage suggests once the maintained tread runs out, with overgrown stretches and repeated small gains and losses. Camping here costs you the high camp's position and its view, and it means carrying the whole climb the next day, so most parties push through; it is recorded because the alternative to knowing it is there is a headlamp bushwhack up Drop Creek. No elevation is given because no confident figure was found for the usual sites.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: The South Fork and Drop Creek itself, running all season. Water is never the problem down here; the log crossing in high water can be.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Forest Service trailhead. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but it is damp valley forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: Rough forest sites along the valley trail and near the Drop Creek crossing, party-sized only. Nothing established.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: Le Conte Pass
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

wa_northeast_face_direct.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
wa_northeast_face_direct.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
wa_northeast_face_direct.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
wa_northeast_face_direct.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
wa_northeast_face_direct.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.name: Pelton Basin
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before.
