wa_nw_ridge_2.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_nw_ridge_2.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_nw_ridge_2.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_nw_ridge_2.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_nw_ridge_2.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_nw_ridge_2.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_nw_ridge_2.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_nw_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_nw_ridge_2.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_nw_ridge_2.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_nw_ridge_2.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_nw_ridge_2.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_nw_ridge_2.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_nw_ridge_2.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_nw_ridge_2.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_nw_ridge_2.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_nw_ridge_2.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_nw_ridge_2.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_nw_ridge_2.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_nw_ridge_2.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_nw_ridge_2.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_nw_ridge_2.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_nw_ridge_2.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_nw_ridge_2.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_nw_ridge_2.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_nw_ridge_2.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_nw_ridge_2.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_nw_ridge_2.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_nw_ridge_2.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_nw_ridge_2.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Cub Lake
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_old_guard_peak_east_side_route.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Cub Lake

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps

Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_old_guard_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.name: Goat Lake basin
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.name: Chambers Lake Campground
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.water: The South Fork Tieton and its tributaries throughout, and the lake itself higher up; abundant by the standards of the range's east side but still to be treated
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites

wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is GLACIER camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
wa_olympus_blue_glacier_east_ramps.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season
