wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Scatter Lake basin
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Libby Lake
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_oval_peak_scramble.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_oval_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_oval_peak_scramble.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_painted_mountain_scramble.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
wa_painted_mountain_scramble.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a DAY OBJECTIVE with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
wa_painted_mountain_scramble.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
wa_painted_mountain_scramble.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_painted_mountain_scramble.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

wa_pernod_spire_standard.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_pernod_spire_standard.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_pernod_spire_standard.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_pernod_spire_standard.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_pernod_spire_standard.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_pernod_spire_standard.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_pernod_spire_standard.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_pernod_spire_standard.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_pernod_spire_standard.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_pernod_spire_standard.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_pernod_spire_standard.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_pernod_spire_standard.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_pernod_spire_standard.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_pernod_spire_standard.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_pernod_spire_standard.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6
