The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Park Lakes basin
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Four Point Lake — the Chewuch-side base for Remmel Mountain
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: The base for REMMEL MOUNTAIN, an 8,685 ft pile of granite carrying an old lookout site and one of the great viewpoints of the wilderness. The line in is the Chewuch trail from the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop — a long, gentle valley walk of easy miles past Chewuch Falls with dispersed camping most of the way, to a signed junction at about thirteen miles for the Four Point Lake and Coleman Ridge trail. That trail FORDS THE CHEWUCH RIVER almost immediately and it is the crux of the approach: early in the season with snowmelt running it is genuinely difficult and there is not always a log. Past the ford the grade steepens sharply and about two miles of climbing reaches the lake at 6,850 ft, with a spur into the basin. From camp the summit goes on open ground by way of the Coleman Ridge side, and it is a scramble rather than a climb. Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Scatter Lake basin
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Libby Lake
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.name: Tumwater Camp, Stehekin valley road
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.notes: The first camp of consequence above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge, and its job on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day and the last shuttle up the valley goes in the late afternoon, so nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on day one — you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way up the old road, and sleep in flat riverside forest with no view and no alpine character at all. It has a history of high-water damage and was closed after a bad flood, though it stands in the park's current camp table; confirm it is genuinely open when you arrange the permit rather than assuming, because there are not many camps up here and losing one reshapes the whole itinerary.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.water: The Stehekin River is right there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river carrying silt and everything else off the drainage.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park. THERE IS NO PERMIT DESK IN STEHEKIN — the visitor centre at the landing does not issue them and is closed. For a trip starting in the valley the permit is arranged by EMAIL with the park's wilderness office, sent early on the morning BEFORE your start date, with a short mandatory video to watch and a signed copy to print and carry. There is no cell service in Stehekin, so all of that has to happen before you get on the boat. Food lockers are provided at these valley camps and no bear canister is required.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.capacity: Two sites, each taking up to six people, so six is the party ceiling. No stock. Assigned by night on the permit.

wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.name: Shady Camp, Stehekin valley road
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.notes: Further up the old road than Tumwater and the only camp on this stretch that is held back from the booking system entirely, which is exactly why it is worth knowing about. A party whose permit request comes back with a hole in the middle of the itinerary can often fill it here. It is another flat forested river camp with nothing to look at, used purely for position. Note that the road above the washout is closed to BICYCLES as well as vehicles — the upper section is decommissioned or maintained as a non-motorized, non-mechanized trail, so the obvious idea of riding the old roadbed to save a day is not permitted. It is walking or stock, and that is what makes this approach as long as it is.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.water: River water beside the camp, dependable through the season and needing treatment.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, arranged the same way as the rest of the valley — by email to the wilderness office the morning before you start, since nothing can be issued in Stehekin itself. Because the site is walk-up rather than reservable, it cannot be locked in months ahead; ask for it in that same email.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.capacity: A single site taking up to eight people. No stock. WALK-UP ONLY — this one takes no reservations at all, which makes it the useful fallback when everything else on the road is booked out.

wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.name: Park Creek Camp, at the valley road
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.notes: THIS IS THE CAMP THE PARK ITSELF POINTS OVERNIGHT PARTIES TO NOW THAT FLAT CREEK IS SHUT, and that closure is the single most important planning fact for this peak. The camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, which would otherwise be the obvious base, has its access trail closed for hazard trees and has dropped out of both the park's camp list and its booking system; no reopening date has been given anywhere. Park Creek sits lower down the same road, so using it lengthens an approach that is already long — you are walking further to the trailhead each morning rather than sleeping at it. Note this is the camp on the VALLEY ROAD where the Park Creek trail leaves it, not the stock camp several miles up that trail toward the pass. The four-person cap is worth checking against your party before you plan around it.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.water: Park Creek at the camp, reliable all season.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, arranged by email before you travel as above. A TOTAL CAMPFIRE BAN has been in force across the entire Stehekin valley since the end of June, covering anything that produces ash including propane fire pits, with no end date announced — so the ring here is out of use regardless of what the camp table says about fires. Gas and propane STOVES are still allowed, with clearance around them and a working shut-off valve. Confirm the ban's status when you get the permit.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.capacity: Two sites, each capped at four people, so this is a small-party camp only. No stock. It has a fire ring, which is not the same as permission to use it right now.

wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.name: Cottonwood Camp, end of the closed road
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.notes: At the very end of the closed road section, something under four miles past the Flat Creek junction, roughly twenty-three miles up from the landing. It is the upper valley's anchor camp and the obvious base for a larger party, at the cost of walking past your turning and back each day. It also marks where the OTHER approaches arrive: parties come down over Park Creek Pass from the Thunder Creek side, and over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road, which reaches the Flat Creek junction in something over thirteen miles. Either is a genuine alternative to the boat and both are long. Worth knowing that the current fire closures in this park are all on the Ross Lake and Big Beaver side and do NOT reach the upper Stehekin valley — the camps up here are constrained by flood damage, hazard trees and the fire ban, not by an active fire.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.water: River and tributary water at the camp, reliable and needing treatment like everything else in the drainage.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. WHICH OFFICE DEPENDS ON WHICH WAY YOU COME IN, and getting this wrong costs a day: a party arriving by boat arranges it by email with the wilderness office before travelling, but anyone approaching over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road must collect the permit IN PERSON at Marblemount, and that includes permits for this camp. The camp table allows campfires here, but the valley-wide ban currently overrides that.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.capacity: Two sites, one taking six and one taking twelve, so up to twelve in a party — the largest allowance anywhere on this approach and the reason groups use it.
