wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail of about four miles that gains only a few hundred feet through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. The trail ends well short of the head of the valley and the summit is beyond where it ends. Budget four days minimum for something that would be an afternoon if a road came near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window; the valley walk is snow-free long before the head of it is.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.permit: THE AGENCY CHANGES ON THIS TRAIL, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the national forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside that wilderness. It takes a free self-issue permit filled in at the trailhead rather than a park permit, with no reservation and no fee, and a party limit of TWELVE counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's limit down in the valley, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. Your park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is NO park cross-country zone for Flat Creek; that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice otherwise: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury, and no fires.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble.capacity: No established camping and no site count. THERE IS NOTHING UP HERE. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.

wa_roan_wall_center_stage.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

wa_roan_wall_center_stage.name: Clear Creek Campground
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft

wa_roan_wall_center_stage.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

wa_roan_wall_center_stage.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

wa_roan_wall_center_stage.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need

wa_roan_wall_center_stage.name: Squire Creek Pass
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass

wa_roan_wall_stage_right.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.

Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.name: Copper Glance Lake
wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
wa_robinson_mountain_southeast_ridge.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Rock Lake
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.

Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Crescent Lake
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about three hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Merritt Lake
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.name: Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The lookout itself: you may walk to it and, if it is staffed and the lookout is willing, speak to whoever is on duty, but you may not stay in it or expect shelter from it. Plan the day accordingly and do not treat the building as a bail-out option in bad weather. The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.water: None at all, and none for the last several miles of trail in either direction. There is one seasonal spring close to the Round Mountain trailhead that runs early in the year and cannot be relied on; past it the trail is dry the whole way. From the west, the last water is Merritt Lake, about three miles back. Carry everything.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is required at the Round Mountain trailhead. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery — none of Nason Ridge is designated wilderness. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the surrounding forest is dry enough that fire restrictions are near-permanent through the summer, which is rather the point of the building on the summit.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: None for the public. This is an active Forest Service fire lookout, staffed through the summer fire season, and it is NOT available to sleep in, not rentable, and not one of the lookouts in this state that take overnight visitors. Treat it as a staffed workplace: the summit is a fine place to stand, and the building is somebody's post. There is no established campsite at the lookout either, and the ground around it is narrow open ridge crest.

Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.

This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
wa_rock_mountain_northeast_ridge.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. wa_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

wa_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.

wa_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

wa_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. wa_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

wa_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

wa_ruth_icy_traverse.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.

wa_ruth_icy_traverse.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

wa_ruth_mountain_south_slopes.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.

wa_ruth_mountain_south_slopes.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
wa_ruth_mountain_south_slopes.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Deer Lake
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Heart Lake
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Cat Basin
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Appleton Pass
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
wa_ruth_peak_olympics_scramble.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_sahale_mountain_r1.name: Boston Basin high camp
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.notes: The upper of the basin's two camps, around 6,400 ft, with a composting toilet. It is the natural base for the Quien Sabe: the glacier starts more or less at the tent door, so summit day is short. Snow lingers here well into July, and the rule to pitch only on hardened ground matters — the meadows recover very slowly.
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.water: Meltwater streams off the Quien Sabe Glacier and the snowfields above the basin; strongest early in the season and thinner by late summer
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required, and camping in the basin is legal only at the two designated sites. Permits are picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount and carry a per-person fee plus a reservation fee; demand outstrips supply on peak weekends
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.capacity: A designated cluster of hardened sites shared with everyone climbing Forbidden, Sharkfin and Boston — it fills on summer weekends

wa_sahale_mountain_r1.name: Boston Basin low camp
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.notes: Around 5,300 ft on the edge of a moraine crest among small trees, below the polished slabs the Quien Sabe has left behind. Melts out earlier and is more sheltered than the high camp, at the cost of an extra thousand feet on summit morning.
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.water: Creeks draining the basin run past the camp through the climbing season
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.permit: Same park backcountry permit and the same designated-sites-only rule as the high camp
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.capacity: The second designated site, with its own composting toilet; a fallback when the upper sites are taken

wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.notes: A planned camp and one of the highest in the park, where the maintained trail ends: flat gravel tent pads built onto rock mounds at the foot of the glacier, each ringed by a primitive dry-stone wall, plus a composting toilet. Those walls are there because the site is completely exposed to wind and weather with nothing above it. About six miles and 3,600 ft from the trailhead, and it puts the glacier and the summit pyramid within a short morning.
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.water: Snowmelt and small tarns at the glacier toe early to mid season; many of these dry up by late summer, so a late-season party should expect to melt snow or carry water up from lower down
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.permit: A national park backcountry permit is required and the camp is strictly quota'd — an early-access lottery runs in March and roughly 40% of permits are held for walk-ups, picked up at the wilderness information centre in Marblemount
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.capacity: Four designated sites, four people to a site, four parties a night

wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.name: Doubtful Lake
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.notes: The lower fallback, roughly a mile and a thousand feet down a signed spur off the arm. It has water when the high camp does not and it is far more sheltered in bad weather, at the cost of re-gaining that thousand feet to rejoin the route. Worth knowing because there is no camping permitted anywhere along Sahale Arm between the pass and the high camp — if you cannot get a high-camp site, this basin is the alternative rather than the next flat spot you find.
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.permit: A national park backcountry permit is required
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.capacity: A designated backcountry camping area in the basin

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Entiat Meadows
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_scramble_route.name: Snow Lake Camp
wa_scramble_route.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
wa_scramble_route.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
wa_scramble_route.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
wa_scramble_route.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

wa_scramble_route.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
wa_scramble_route.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
wa_scramble_route.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
wa_scramble_route.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
wa_scramble_route.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

wa_scramble_route.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
wa_scramble_route.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
wa_scramble_route.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
wa_scramble_route.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
wa_scramble_route.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

wa_scramble_route.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_scramble_route.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
wa_scramble_route.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
wa_scramble_route.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
wa_scramble_route.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

wa_scramble_route.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
wa_scramble_route.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.
wa_scramble_route.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
wa_scramble_route.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter

wa_scramble_route.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
wa_scramble_route.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. It has been closed through 2026 for a rehabilitation project, so confirm its status before planning around it. When running it is low, forested and warm, which makes it a reasonable shoulder-season option when the higher campgrounds are shut.
wa_scramble_route.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
wa_scramble_route.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.

wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.name: Lena Lake designated sites
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.name: Upper Lena Lake
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.name: Lake of the Angels
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day.
