wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Nada Lake
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_sherpa_glacier.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
wa_sherpa_glacier.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
wa_sherpa_glacier.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
wa_sherpa_glacier.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
wa_sherpa_glacier.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

wa_sherpa_glacier.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
wa_sherpa_glacier.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
wa_sherpa_glacier.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
wa_sherpa_glacier.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
wa_sherpa_glacier.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

wa_sherpa_glacier.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
wa_sherpa_glacier.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
wa_sherpa_glacier.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
wa_sherpa_glacier.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
wa_sherpa_glacier.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

wa_sherpa_glacier.name: Lake Stuart
wa_sherpa_glacier.notes: The north-side staging point, used by parties approaching the Complete North Ridge or the Sherpa Glacier from Mountaineer Creek rather than walking around the peak from Ingalls. Road access is seasonal in a way the Teanaway side is not: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road generally closes from November until sometime in May, which shortens the window from this side considerably. Where the Stuart Zone boundary falls relative to the upper Mountaineer Creek basin and the Stuart Glacier moraine is genuinely unclear — some maps place Stuart's north side outside the permit zones — so a party bivying high in that basin should confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District rather than assume, and carry a permit if in doubt.
wa_sherpa_glacier.water: The lake and Mountaineer Creek are reliable all season; treat lake water and camp well back from the shore
wa_sherpa_glacier.permit: Enchantment Permit Area, STUART ZONE, Wenatchee River Ranger District. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through Oct 31, allocated by group through the Recreation.gov advance lottery with a small remainder released otherwise. Outside that window no overnight permit is required, though self-registration at the trailhead is asked for. Day use needs only the free trailhead permit plus a Northwest Forest Pass.
wa_sherpa_glacier.capacity: Several established sites around the lake, but the real limit is the permit quota — the Stuart Zone releases only a small number of group permits per night

wa_sherpa_glacier.name: Goat Pass bivies
wa_sherpa_glacier.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
wa_sherpa_glacier.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
wa_sherpa_glacier.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
wa_sherpa_glacier.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

wa_sherpa_glacier.name: North Ridge notch bivy
wa_sherpa_glacier.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
wa_sherpa_glacier.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
wa_sherpa_glacier.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
wa_sherpa_glacier.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: Nada Lake
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.name: Nada Lake
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_silver_star_glacier.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_silver_star_glacier.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_silver_star_glacier.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_silver_star_glacier.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_silver_star_glacier.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_silver_star_glacier.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_silver_star_glacier.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_silver_star_glacier.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_silver_star_glacier.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_silver_star_glacier.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_silver_star_glacier.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_silver_star_glacier.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_silver_star_glacier.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_silver_star_glacier.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_silver_star_glacier.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_silver_star_glacier.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_silver_star_glacier.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_silver_star_glacier.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Cub Lake
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
