wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Cub Lake
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Glacier Gap
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_sitkum_spire_standard.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_sitkum_spire_standard.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_skeena26.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
wa_skeena26.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
wa_skeena26.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
wa_skeena26.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
wa_skeena26.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

wa_skeena26.name: Clear Creek Campground
wa_skeena26.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.
wa_skeena26.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
wa_skeena26.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
wa_skeena26.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft

wa_skeena26.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
wa_skeena26.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
wa_skeena26.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
wa_skeena26.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
wa_skeena26.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

wa_skeena26.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
wa_skeena26.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
wa_skeena26.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
wa_skeena26.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

wa_skeena26.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
wa_skeena26.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
wa_skeena26.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need

wa_skeena26.name: Squire Creek Pass
wa_skeena26.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
wa_skeena26.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
wa_skeena26.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
wa_skeena26.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass

wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.name: Orsino Creek Basin
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.name: Elbow Lake hiker camps
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.notes: These are the only established campsites anywhere near this range, reached by a spur off the main trail to the east shore of the lake. They are not on the direct line to any of these five summits, sitting on the divide east of the crest rather than under it, so treat them as a legal and comfortable staging camp on public ground rather than as a climbing basecamp. They are most useful for a party coming in from the south with an awkward road situation, or for anyone who wants a settled night before or after a long day on the ridge. The lake is buggy in early summer and the surrounding ground is boggy in places. Because the road access on both ends of this trail has been unreliable and at least one vehicle closure has been in force recently, check the current status of the forest roads and of the river ford before planning a trip around this camp.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.water: The lake, filtered. Reliable all season, though shallow and warm by late summer
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, within or adjoining the wilderness unit. No overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at the trailhead. Fires may be restricted or banned in late summer. Access is the problem rather than the permit: there is no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at the northern trailhead and has not been for decades, so that side requires a ford that is not safe at high flow, and the southern road approach has been subject to a vehicle closure part way in. Confirm both roads and the crossing before committing.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble.capacity: Two established hiker sites on the east shore

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: Skyline Lake
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: Trap Lake
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_sky_mountain_s_route.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_sky_mountain_s_route.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Skyline Lake
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Trap Lake
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. The Corkscrew from Bedal Creek is a reasonable single day of thirteen or fourteen hours for a fit party, and successful ascents in under twelve hours are common, so the usual pattern is to sleep at the trailhead and start around four in the morning rather than carry a camp to the ridge.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.water: Carry it, or take it from Bedal Creek on the way in.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass is usually reported as the required parking permit, though not universally; carry one.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.capacity: Roadside parking, not a designated site.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the account.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.water: A tarn at the saddle, and it is the weak point — it is stagnant, and parties have found frog and mosquito larvae in it. Better water is a short way above, around 5,500 ft, where small streams cascade down; fill there rather than at the pond.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.capacity: Four to six tents, so leave room for another party.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.

wa_sloan_peak_r1.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
wa_sloan_peak_r1.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_sloan_peak_r1.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_sloan_peak_r1.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_sloan_peak_r1.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_sloan_peak_r1.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_sloan_peak_r1.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_sloan_peak_r1.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_sloan_peak_r1.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_sloan_peak_r1.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_sloan_peak_r1.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_sloan_peak_r1.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_sloan_peak_r1.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_sloan_peak_r1.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_sloan_peak_r1.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_sloan_peak_r1.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_sloan_peak_r1.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_sloan_peak_r1.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
