wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.name: Colonial Basin
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.notes: Reached by the steep, narrow climbers' path above Pyramid Lake; you break out of trees near 5,600 ft and the basin opens below Colonial and Pyramid. It is a spectacular spot and a genuinely windy one — parties have needed several people and a pile of rocks to get a tent up. A few sites tucked into alcoves shelter far better than the open ground, so look before you pitch.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.permit: Backcountry permit from the North Cascades complex — parties pick these up at the Marblemount ranger station or reserve through Recreation.gov. Cross-country zone permits cover one party per night, camping is on snow, rock or bare ground only and never in meadow or within 100 ft of water, and fires are prohibited.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.capacity: Five or six sites, most of them ringed with rock wind walls.

wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.name: Colonial-Neve col
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.notes: The high camp, on the col between the Colonial and Neve glaciers, and the one most parties push to if they have the legs. Dry ground, better sheltered than the basin below, and it puts the Neve Glacier and the west ridge within a short morning. Getting here involves glacier travel, so it is a rope-up-before-camp proposition rather than a walk.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.water: A stream and a small waterfall at the col, plus tarns nearby.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.capacity: Two or three sites, with wind walls already built.

wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.name: Lower camp below the basin
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.notes: The bail-out option around 5,400 ft, just below where the climbers' path leaves the trees, used by parties who run out of daylight or energy on the steep section above Pyramid Lake. It leaves a long second day to the summit and back.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff; Pyramid Lake at 2,600 ft is the last certain water low on the approach.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: Slide Lake
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: Enjar Lake and Hamar Lake
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes: The working camps on the western side of Snowking Mountain, reached by continuing past Slide Lake for roughly four hours of increasingly rough going. Either lake serves; parties pick whichever the light allows. From here Snowking is climbed on its west and northwest ground rather than by the east ridge and glacier line used from Cyclone Lake, which is the practical reason the two approaches are worth keeping apart. No elevations are recorded because no confident figures were found for either lake. This side is quieter than the Kindy Ridge side and correspondingly less travelled, so route-finding is on you and the boot path is intermittent to absent. Best from July into September, and expect wet brush on the way through regardless.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.water: Both lakes, dependable through the season. These are the last reliable water on the western approach before the ice.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit taken at the Slide Lake register. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Slide Lake trailhead. Camp back from the water, stoves only, pack out human waste.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.capacity: Unimproved lakeside spots for a party or two at either lake. No toilet, nothing established.

wa_south_arete.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_south_arete.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_south_arete.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_south_arete.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_south_arete.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_south_arete.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_south_arete.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_south_arete.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_south_arete.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_south_arete.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_south_arete.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_south_arete.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_south_arete.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_south_arete.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_south_arete.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_southwest_co.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_south_face.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_south_face.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_south_face.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_south_face.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_south_face.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_south_face.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_south_face.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_south_face.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_south_face.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_south_face.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_south_face.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_south_face.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_south_face.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_south_face.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_south_face.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_south_face.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_south_face.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_south_face.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_south_face.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_south_face.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_south_face.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_south_face.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_south_face.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_south_face.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_south_face.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_south_face.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_south_face.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_south_face.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_south_face.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_south_face.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_south_face_10.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
wa_south_face_10.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
wa_south_face_10.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
wa_south_face_10.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
wa_south_face_10.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_south_face_10.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_south_face_10.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
wa_south_face_10.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
wa_south_face_10.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_south_face_10.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

wa_south_face_10.name: Andrews Pass
wa_south_face_10.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
wa_south_face_10.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
wa_south_face_10.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
wa_south_face_10.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

wa_south_face_10.name: Remmel Lake and the Spanish Camp meadows
wa_south_face_10.notes: This sits a short way off the main line to Cathedral Pass and works well as a base if Remmel Mountain is on the list alongside Cathedral and Amphitheater. The meadow ground is soft and easily damaged, so pull back onto the timber edge rather than pitching in the open grass. There is a signed spur from near the guard station running up toward the Cathedral basin, which makes this a workable alternative if the lakes above are full or posted closed. Being lower and more sheltered, it is a considerably kinder camp in bad weather than anything at the pass.
wa_south_face_10.water: Reliable — the lake plus the creeks draining the meadows. Along with Upper Cathedral, the other place on the approach where you can count on filling.
wa_south_face_10.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit, no quota. The cabin at Spanish Camp is a Forest Service ADMINISTRATIVE structure, not a public shelter, and should not be treated as available lodging.
wa_south_face_10.capacity: Broad grassy meadows with room for multiple parties, but the sites are dispersed rather than developed and horse parties use this area heavily

wa_south_face_10.name: Amphitheater Mountain upper basin
wa_south_face_10.notes: Reached by following the trail southeast around Amphitheater's west ridge from Upper Cathedral Lake and then a boot path up scree and grass into the basin. Worth considering only if you want to be on the ridge at first light, because the water problem is real and it gains you very little over camping at the lake. The ground is loose and sparsely vegetated, which makes it easy to occupy without leaving a mark if you are careful. Treat it as an emergency or tactical bivy rather than a planned camp. No elevation is recorded — none was confidently sourced.
wa_south_face_10.water: Snowmelt only, and only early. Once the last patches go there is nothing up here, so plan on carrying everything up from the lake. This is the driest camp option in the zone.
wa_south_face_10.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit covers it; no quota, no reservation, and no designated-site system in this wilderness.
wa_south_face_10.capacity: One or two parties on scree and grass benches; informal ground, no established sites

wa_south_face_10.name: Tungsten Mine camp
wa_south_face_10.notes: This sits on the LOOP leg between Apex Pass and the Chewuch drainage rather than on the direct Andrews Creek line, so it matters if you are traversing out rather than going in and back the same way — a party going in and out via Andrews Creek will never see it. The old bunkhouse and mine hardware from the early 1900s are still standing and the site survived the recent fires. Whether it is genuinely useful shelter is a judgement call and reports differ; plan to be self-sufficient in a tent. The water situation is the deciding factor for most parties, not the buildings.
wa_south_face_10.water: Poor and getting worse as the season goes on. The trail between Cathedral Pass and the mine is reported dry along its whole length, with one small stream roughly a quarter mile short of the site, so fill lower down before starting the climb.
wa_south_face_10.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota and no reservation. The historic structures are protected cultural resources — leave the machinery and the buildings alone.
wa_south_face_10.capacity: Good camping around the mine site; the standing bunkhouse and cabin are historic structures that some parties shelter in, though their condition is not maintained for that purpose

wa_south_face_12.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
wa_south_face_12.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
wa_south_face_12.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
wa_south_face_12.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

wa_south_face_12.name: Sherpa south basin camp
wa_south_face_12.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
wa_south_face_12.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
wa_south_face_12.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

wa_south_face_12.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
wa_south_face_12.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
wa_south_face_12.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
wa_south_face_12.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

wa_south_face_12.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
wa_south_face_12.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
wa_south_face_12.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
wa_south_face_12.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

wa_south_face_12.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
wa_south_face_12.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
wa_south_face_12.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
wa_south_face_12.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

wa_south_face_12.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_south_face_12.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
wa_south_face_12.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
wa_south_face_12.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_south_face_12.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
wa_south_face_12.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
wa_south_face_12.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
wa_south_face_12.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

wa_south_face_12.name: Nada Lake
wa_south_face_12.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
wa_south_face_12.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
wa_south_face_12.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
wa_south_face_12.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

wa_south_face_2.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_south_face_2.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_south_face_2.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_south_face_2.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_south_face_2.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_south_face_2.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_south_face_2.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_south_face_2.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_south_face_2.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_south_face_2.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_south_face_2.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_south_face_2.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_south_face_2.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_south_face_2.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_south_face_2.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_south_face_2.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_south_face_2.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_south_face_2.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_south_face_2.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_south_face_2.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_south_face_2.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_south_face_2.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_south_face_2.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_south_face_2.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_south_face_2.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_south_face_2.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_south_face_2.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_south_face_2.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_south_face_2.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_south_face_2.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_south_face_3.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_south_face_3.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_south_face_3.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_south_face_3.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_south_face_3.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_south_face_3.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_south_face_3.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_south_face_3.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_south_face_3.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_south_face_3.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_south_face_3.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_south_face_3.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_south_face_3.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_south_face_3.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_south_face_3.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_south_face_4.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_south_face_4.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_south_face_4.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_south_face_4.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_south_face_4.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_south_face_4.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_south_face_4.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_south_face_4.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_south_face_4.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_south_face_4.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_south_face_4.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_south_face_4.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_south_face_4.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_south_face_4.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_south_face_4.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_south_face_4.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_south_face_4.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_south_face_4.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_south_face_4.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_south_face_4.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_south_face_4.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_south_face_4.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_south_face_4.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_south_face_4.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_south_face_4.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_south_face_4.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_south_face_4.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_south_face_4.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_south_face_4.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_south_face_4.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_south_face_5.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_south_face_5.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_south_face_5.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_south_face_5.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_south_face_5.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_south_face_5.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_south_face_5.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_south_face_5.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_south_face_5.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_south_face_5.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_south_face_5.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_south_face_5.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_south_face_5.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_south_face_5.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_south_face_5.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_south_face_5.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_south_face_5.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_south_face_5.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_south_face_5.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_south_face_5.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_south_face_5.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_south_face_5.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_south_face_5.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_south_face_5.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_south_face_5.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_south_face_5.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_south_face_5.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_south_face_5.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_south_face_5.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_south_face_5.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_south_face_7.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
wa_south_face_7.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
wa_south_face_7.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
wa_south_face_7.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
wa_south_face_7.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

wa_south_face_7.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
wa_south_face_7.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
wa_south_face_7.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
wa_south_face_7.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
wa_south_face_7.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

wa_south_face_7.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
wa_south_face_7.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
wa_south_face_7.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
wa_south_face_7.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
wa_south_face_7.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

wa_south_face_7.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
wa_south_face_7.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
wa_south_face_7.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
wa_south_face_7.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
wa_south_face_7.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

wa_south_face_7.name: Rampart Lakes basin
wa_south_face_7.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it.
