wa_south_ridge.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_south_ridge.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_south_ridge.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_south_ridge.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_south_ridge.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_south_ridge.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_south_ridge.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_south_ridge.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_south_ridge.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_south_ridge.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_south_ridge.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_south_ridge.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_south_ridge.name: Cub Lake
wa_south_ridge.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_south_ridge.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_south_ridge.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_south_ridge.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_south_ridge.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_south_ridge.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_south_ridge.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_south_ridge.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_south_ridge.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_south_ridge.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_south_ridge.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_south_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_south_ridge.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_south_ridge_2.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_south_ridge_2.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_south_ridge_2.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_south_ridge_2.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_south_ridge_2.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_south_ridge_2.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_south_ridge_3.name: Wing Lake
wa_south_ridge_3.notes: The standard base camp for Black Peak, roughly 6,900 ft in a basin of scree and boulders directly beneath the peak, with larches around the shore that turn gold in late September. It sits about 1,200 ft above Lewis Lake, reached by a rough boot path over a boulder field with one steep step. Nights are cold — near freezing even in good weather — and from here the South Ridge scramble is a half-day round trip. The better tent spots are in the larch groves just below the lake.
wa_south_ridge_3.water: The lake itself, right at camp, all season
wa_south_ridge_3.permit: No backcountry permit is described for camping here — the approach and the lake are on national forest land — but a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is needed to park at Rainy Pass
wa_south_ridge_3.capacity: A site at the lake outlet plus several more on benches above it; the basin is quiet compared with the Maple Pass loop below, and parties regularly have it to themselves midweek

wa_south_ridge_3.name: Lewis Lake
wa_south_ridge_3.notes: About 5,700 ft, the first lake past Heather Pass and the lower fallback if the light goes or the boulder field above looks unappealing. It is a legitimate base — parties do summit and return from here — but it adds 1,200 ft each way to summit day, and the bugs are worse than higher up.
wa_south_ridge_3.water: The lake, though it runs silty
wa_south_ridge_3.permit: Same as Wing Lake: no overnight permit described, parking pass required at the trailhead
wa_south_ridge_3.capacity: At least one good site just above the lake beside the path, and room for a small party or two

wa_south_ridge_4.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
wa_south_ridge_4.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
wa_south_ridge_4.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
wa_south_ridge_4.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
wa_south_ridge_4.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

wa_south_ridge_4.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
wa_south_ridge_4.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
wa_south_ridge_4.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
wa_south_ridge_4.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
wa_south_ridge_4.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

wa_south_ridge_4.name: Eldorado Basin camp
wa_south_ridge_4.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
wa_south_ridge_4.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
wa_south_ridge_4.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
wa_south_ridge_4.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

wa_south_ridge_4.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
wa_south_ridge_4.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
wa_south_ridge_4.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
wa_south_ridge_4.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
wa_south_ridge_4.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

wa_south_ridge_4.name: Klawatti Col camp
wa_south_ridge_4.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_south_ridge_4.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_south_ridge_4.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_south_ridge_4.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_south_ridge_4.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_south_ridge_4.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_south_ridge_4.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_south_ridge_4.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_south_ridge_4.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

wa_south_ridge_6.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_south_ridge_6.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_south_ridge_6.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_south_ridge_6.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_south_ridge_6.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_south_ridge_6.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_south_ridge_6.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_south_ridge_6.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_south_ridge_6.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_south_ridge_6.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_south_ridge_6.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_south_ridge_6.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_south_ridge_6.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_south_ridge_6.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_south_ridge_6.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_south_ridge_6.name: Pelton Basin
wa_south_ridge_6.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_south_ridge_6.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_south_ridge_6.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_south_ridge_6.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_south_ridge_6.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_south_ridge_6.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
wa_south_ridge_6.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
wa_south_ridge_6.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_south_ridge_6.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

wa_south_ridge_6.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_south_ridge_6.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
wa_south_ridge_6.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
wa_south_ridge_6.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
wa_south_ridge_6.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_south_spur.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_south_spur.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_south_spur.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_south_spur.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_south_spur.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_south_spur.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_south_spur.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_south_spur.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_south_spur.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_south_spur.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_south_spur.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_south_spur.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_south_spur.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_south_spur.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_south_spur.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_south_spur.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_south_spur.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_south_spur.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_south_spur.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_south_spur.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_south_spur.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_south_spur.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_south_spur.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_south_spur.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_south_spur.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_south_spur.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_south_spur.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_south_spur.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_south_spur.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_south_spur.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_south_spur.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_south_spur.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_south_spur.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_south_spur.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_south_spur.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_south_spur.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_south_spur.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_south_spur.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_south_spur.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_south_spur.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_south_spur.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_south_spur.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_south_spur.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_south_spur.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_south_spur.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_south_spur.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_south_spur.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_south_spur.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_south_spur.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_south_spur.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_south_spur.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_south_spur.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_south_spur.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_south_spur.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_south_spur.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_south_spur.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.name: Orsino Creek Basin
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.

wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.permit: Private industrial timberland. wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.name: Orsino Creek Basin

The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin

Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies

wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

wa_southeast_face.name: Boston Basin lower camp
wa_southeast_face.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_southeast_face.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
wa_southeast_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
wa_southeast_face.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

wa_southeast_face.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
wa_southeast_face.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
wa_southeast_face.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
wa_southeast_face.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
wa_southeast_face.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

wa_southeast_face.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_southeast_face.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
wa_southeast_face.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
wa_southeast_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
wa_southeast_face.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

wa_southeast_face.name: Pelton Basin
wa_southeast_face.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
wa_southeast_face.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
wa_southeast_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
wa_southeast_face.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

wa_southeast_face.name: Johannesburg Camp
wa_southeast_face.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
wa_southeast_face.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
wa_southeast_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
wa_southeast_face.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

wa_southeast_face.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_southeast_face.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
