wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_spectre_peak_south_route.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_sperry_peak_standard.name: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
wa_sperry_peak_standard.notes: This is the working start for SPERRY PEAK, and Sperry is honestly a day objective with no camp of its own — parties leave from here in the dark, ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, grind up through the talus of Wirtz Basin under Morning Star, take the switchbacked chute to Headlee Pass and traverse under Sperry's south side before scrambling the summit blocks. The only established camp on that line lies beyond the pass in the upper Vesper Creek basin, which the earlier upper-loop file already carries, so the realistic choice here is a long day from the car or a night in that basin. Sleeping at the road end is what most parties do and it works: the spur is short, and a pre-dawn start gets you through the chute before the day's rockfall gets going. Three things decide whether the trip happens at all. The FORD half a mile in is the real gate and it is not a formality — it runs hard in snowmelt and log crossings that worked one season are gone the next. The CHUTE below Headlee Pass is loose, narrow and known for rock coming down it, so parties should not stack up in it and helmets belong on well before the base. And SNOW holds in that chute and on the pass long after the valley is bare, which regularly turns a June or early-July attempt around. The spur itself is rough with potholes and encroaching brush; a low car can usually manage it slowly but scrapes are common. There is no cell coverage from the moment you leave the main loop road.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.water: None at the road end. The creek crossings begin half a mile in and the first of them is the difficult one, so load every litre down in the valley rather than planning to draw here.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass to leave a vehicle, and nothing else. This is national forest but NOT designated wilderness, so there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no party-size cap. Overnight parking is allowed. Fires at the road end are governed by whatever seasonal forest-wide restrictions are running, which from midsummer usually means no open flame at all.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.capacity: Car bivy only. A small gravel turnaround at the end of the spur with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and no sites, tables or pads. It overflows onto the road shoulder on summer weekends and the last cars in walk a fair way back to the trail start.

wa_sperry_peak_standard.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
wa_sperry_peak_standard.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For GOTHIC PEAK this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for DEL CAMPO it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. TREAT THE PROVENANCE OF THIS WATER SERIOUSLY: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.permit: National forest land OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

wa_sperry_peak_standard.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
wa_sperry_peak_standard.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

wa_sperry_peak_standard.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_sperry_peak_standard.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.permit: A developed fee campground on national forest land — the per-night fee is all that is needed and no pass or permit applies to the site itself. Nothing here is inside wilderness. Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.name: Spider-Formidable Col
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.name: Drop Creek high camp
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. It starts at the South Fork Cascade River trailhead, which is little more than a bend in the Cascade River Road around mile 17 to 18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, well below the road end at Cascade Pass. The first mile is maintained, then the trail deteriorates into ups, downs and overgrown nettle sections; past the Middle Fork turnoff you cross Drop Creek on a log and turn up into its valley on a climbers' path. That path fades after a few hundred vertical feet, but the forest above about 4,000 feet is open and the bushwhacking is unusually easy for this part of the range, with one short slide alder thicket below 4,600 feet. The camp is the obvious flat ground at around 7,100 feet with water, and from it the ground steepens to class 3 with a permanent snowfield near 7,400 feet and one narrow chasm crossing that is worth protecting. The whole approach avoids glacier travel entirely, which is why it has become the late-season choice, and recent trail work has made it the most pleasant it has been in years. Reckon on roughly twenty-five miles and eight thousand feet for the round trip.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.water: Running water beside the camp for most of the season, fed by the snowfield above, and a second reliable source lower down around 5,600 feet before the steep meadow climb. Late in a dry summer take the lower water seriously, because the high source is a snowfield that is shrinking.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is the usual requirement for the vehicle at Forest Service trailheads on this road, unlike the park trailhead at the end of it, so check before leaving the car. No fires at this elevation.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for a party or two, on heather and rock. Unimproved, no toilet, no windbreaks.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.name: South Fork Cascade River valley camps

Camping here costs you the high camp's position and its view, and it means carrying the whole climb the next day, so most parties push through; it is recorded because the alternative to knowing it is there is a headlamp bushwhack up Drop Creek. wa_spider_mountain_north_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Forest Service trailhead. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but it is damp valley forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face.capacity: Rough forest sites along the valley trail and near the Drop Creek crossing, party-sized only. Nothing established.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.name: Le Conte Pass

From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. wa_spider_mountain_north_face.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

wa_spider_mountain_north_face.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: Skyline Lake
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: Trap Lake
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_spinnaker_peak_s_route.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_spire_mountain_scramble.name: Spire Mountain — the saddle northwest of the summit
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.notes: Spire Mountain has no established camping of any kind and most parties climb it in a single very long day, which is the honest answer. The route is entirely off-trail: leave the Index-Galena road at the snowplow turnaround just past the bridge, drop south into old forest, and fight through six hundred feet of steep ground choked with fallen timber before the slope becomes merely steep. Cliffs on the north end of the mountain are turned between about 4,200 and 4,400 feet, then a rising traverse southeast reaches open ground around 5,400 feet below the summit spire. The saddle above that, northwest of the true summit, is the only ground on the route flat enough to lie down on, and a party that has misjudged the day will end up there whether they planned to or not. From it the last three hundred feet are technical enough that most rope up for short exposed sections. ROAD STATUS IS THE LIMITING FACTOR: the Index-Galena road has repeatedly been cut by flood damage and bridge failure on the North Fork Skykomish, and when the bridge is out the road is simply not drivable from the Beckler River road, which adds many miles of walking to an approach that is already brutal. Confirm the road is open before committing to this peak. Best season is late July to early October, once the timber is dry and before the first storms make the traverse slabs greasy.
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.water: None. There is no water anywhere on this route once you leave the North Fork Skykomish at the road, and the saddle holds nothing but lingering snow patches into July. Carry everything, or melt snow early season.
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit required. Parking is a roadside pullout, so no forest pass is needed there.
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.capacity: One or two parties at most, on whatever flat ground the ridge crest offers. There is no established site here and nothing has been built.

wa_spire_mountain_scramble.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its availability as a question to answer before you drive rather than an assumption. When the road is cut at the North Fork bridge it is unreachable from the Beckler River side entirely. Even when it is open it is a low, damp, mosquito-heavy site in early summer, and its value is convenience rather than pleasure — it puts a party within twenty minutes of the start of the Spire approach, which is worth a great deal on a climb that wants a pre-dawn departure. Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground serve the same road system and are covered in the neighbouring zone, so check those first if this one is closed.
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.water: River water only, treated. There is no potable supply.
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.permit: Standard national forest campground fee when it is operating. No wilderness permit is involved at this elevation.
wa_spire_mountain_scramble.capacity: A small forest campground of a dozen or so sites in second-growth beside the North Fork Skykomish, with vault toilets and no water system.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Itswoot Ridge
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Cub Lake
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_spire_point_southwest_face.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_spire_point_southwest_face.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_spontaneity_arete.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_spontaneity_arete.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_spontaneity_arete.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_spontaneity_arete.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_spontaneity_arete.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_spontaneity_arete.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_spontaneity_arete.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_spontaneity_arete.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_spontaneity_arete.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_spontaneity_arete.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_spontaneity_arete.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_spontaneity_arete.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_spontaneity_arete.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_spontaneity_arete.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_spontaneity_arete.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_spontaneity_arete.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_spontaneity_arete.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_spontaneity_arete.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_spontaneity_arete.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_spontaneity_arete.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_spontaneity_arete.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_spontaneity_arete.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_spontaneity_arete.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_spontaneity_arete.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_spontaneity_arete.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_spontaneity_arete.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_spontaneity_arete.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_spontaneity_arete.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_spontaneity_arete.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_spontaneity_arete.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_spontaneous_distraction.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_spontaneous_distraction.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_spontaneous_distraction.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_spontaneous_distraction.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_spontaneous_distraction.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_spontaneous_distraction.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_spontaneous_distraction.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_spontaneous_distraction.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_spontaneous_distraction.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_spontaneous_distraction.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge
