wa_stanley_burgner.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_stanley_burgner.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_stanley_burgner.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_stanley_burgner.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_stanley_burgner.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_stanley_burgner.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_stanley_burgner.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_stanley_burgner.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_stanley_burgner.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_stanley_burgner.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_stanley_burgner.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_stanley_burgner.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_stanley_burgner.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_stanley_burgner.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_stanley_burgner.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_stanley_burgner.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_stanley_burgner.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_stanley_burgner.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_stanley_burgner.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_stanley_burgner.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_stanley_burgner.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_stanley_burgner.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_stanley_burgner.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_stanley_burgner.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_stanley_burgner.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_stanley_burgner.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_stanley_burgner.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_stanley_burgner.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_stanley_burgner.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_stanley_burgner.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Scatter Lake basin
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Libby Lake
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_star_peak_sawtooth_scramble.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_storm_king_north_face.name: Neve Camp
wa_storm_king_north_face.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
wa_storm_king_north_face.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
wa_storm_king_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
wa_storm_king_north_face.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

wa_storm_king_north_face.name: Junction Camp
wa_storm_king_north_face.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
wa_storm_king_north_face.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
wa_storm_king_north_face.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
wa_storm_king_north_face.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

wa_storm_king_north_face.name: Skagit Queen Camp
wa_storm_king_north_face.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
wa_storm_king_north_face.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
wa_storm_king_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
wa_storm_king_north_face.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

wa_storm_king_north_face.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
wa_storm_king_north_face.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
wa_storm_king_north_face.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
wa_storm_king_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
wa_storm_king_north_face.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

wa_storm_king_north_face.name: Fremont Glacier moraine high camp
wa_storm_king_north_face.notes: Reached by leaving the trail in the flat sandy meadows a short distance north of Park Creek Pass and climbing several hundred feet into old moraine, this is the high camp for the Fremont Glacier side of Mount Logan and the only realistic way to get above the pass legally. The ground is flat, sandy and sheltered, which matters on a rib this exposed. Parties also report usable bivy ground higher, near where the climbers' route meets the glacier around eight thousand feet, though water up there is entirely a function of what snow is left. Which option is better is genuinely conditions-dependent and worth asking at the permit desk the morning you pick up.
wa_storm_king_north_face.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff, and it is seasonal. Sources near the first stream crossings north of the pass are more dependable; higher moraine camps can go dry late in a hot summer, so carry capacity to melt or haul.
wa_storm_king_north_face.permit: Requires a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE permit from Marblemount, not a designated-camp permit. Fires prohibited outright. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows or within 100 ft of water. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, and out of sight of both. Waste in a cathole, or carried out in a blue bag above treeline or on glaciers.
wa_storm_king_north_face.capacity: Cross-country zone camping rather than a designated site, so no fixed site count. Most zones cap a party at six. One permit covers the party.

wa_storm_king_north_face.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
wa_storm_king_north_face.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
wa_storm_king_north_face.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
wa_storm_king_north_face.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
wa_storm_king_north_face.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_summertime.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_summertime.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_summertime.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_summertime.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_summertime.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_summertime.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_summertime.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_summertime.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_summertime.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_summertime.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_summertime.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_summertime.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_summertime.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_summertime.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_summertime.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_summertime.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_summertime.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_summertime.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_summertime.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_summertime.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_summertime.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_summertime.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_summertime.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_summertime.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_summertime.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_summertime.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_summertime.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_summertime.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_summertime.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_summertime.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Park Lakes Basin
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Royal Lake
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: This is the front door to the whole Needles group and the default answer for anyone climbing Deception, Clark, Johnson, Walkinshaw, The Incisor or Sundial. It sits about seven miles and two and a half thousand feet from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, up the Dungeness and then the Royal Creek fork, which is walkable with a heavy pack in an afternoon. The honest trade is this: Royal Lake is comfortable, has real designated tent pads and is where the permit system actually issues sites, but it leaves you an extra mile and roughly five hundred to a thousand feet of loose boot path below the upper basin every single climbing morning. On a Needles day that difference is real, because the rock above the basin is dirty and slow and you want to be off it before the afternoon. Parties that only want one peak, or that have anyone who would rather not sleep at six thousand feet on gravel, are right to stay here. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a normal year and the mosquitoes at the lake are notorious through midsummer, which is another argument for going higher. Book the moment the reservation window opens; this is one of the hardest permits on the peninsula to get on a weekend.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: The lake and the outlet creek run all season. Filter or treat; this is a heavily used basin and the shoreline is fragile.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Royal Basin is one of the park's named quota areas. Essentially the whole quota is reservable in advance through the federal recreation booking system, with the summer block released in a single mid-April drop for the mid-May through mid-October season; there is no same-day walk-up window, so a party that turns up without a permit has no legal camp. Expect a flat per-permit reservation charge plus a per-adult, per-night fee, with under-sixteens free and an annual wilderness pass available if you camp here often. Dates outside the online season are arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, and loaners are sometimes available on a first-come basis when you collect the permit. Every camp along Royal Creek and up through the meadows and the basin sits inside the same reservation, so there is no legal way to sneak a night lower down without one.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: Ten designated sites, and only two of them will take more than a single tent. One separate group site holds roughly seven to twelve people and has to be booked as a group site. That is the entire overnight capacity of the lake basin, which is why permits go so fast.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Upper Royal Basin
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: This is the climbers' camp, three quarters of a mile to a mile above the lake on an unmaintained way trail that gains around five hundred to a thousand feet. It puts you at the foot of the west wall of the basin, which is the east side of The Needles, and it is the difference between a reasonable day and a very long one on Deception, Clark, Johnson, The Incisor and Sundial. It is also the working base for Mystery, which is reached over the divide out of the head of the basin, and for Fricaba, which is a comparatively easy scramble from here and a common warm-up or bad-weather substitute. What you pay for the position: exposed camping on gravel with no trees, weather that arrives with no warning, colder nights, and a fiddly load carry up the boot path in the evening. What you get: fewer people, far fewer mosquitoes, and a start that puts you on the loose ground above the basin while it is still frozen together rather than after the sun has been on it for two hours. Snow covers the upper basin well into July most years, which is often an advantage for the approach gullies and a nuisance for finding bare ground to pitch on. If the basin is still largely snow-covered, camp on a gravel bar that has melted out rather than on snow over vegetation.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: Tarns and snowmelt streams through the basin. Late in a dry summer the upper tarns can drop and go stagnant, so check the inlet streams rather than dipping from still water, and be prepared to carry from lower in the basin in September.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Same Olympic National Park quota permit as Royal Lake, booked as the upper basin rather than the lake. All the same conditions apply: advance reservation only, mid-April release for the summer season, per-permit and per-person-per-night charges, and mandatory hard-sided bear canisters. Because there are no constructed sites, the leave-no-trace rules here are enforced in earnest: no camping on vegetation or meadow, no fires, and the park expects you to be on durable surface only. Anyone found camped on the heather is the reason this basin nearly lost overnight use.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: No numbered sites at all. Camping is permitted only on bare ground, gravel bars and rock, so the practical capacity is a handful of parties spread across the gravel beside the tarns. Two of the larger gravel bars near the upper tarn are the usual choice for a group.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Camp Handy
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: A low, sheltered, permit-free camp about three miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, and the most useful fallback in the whole zone. It does not serve The Needles: Royal Basin branches off well below it and Camp Handy is on the wrong fork. What it does is give you a legal, free, roofed place to sleep when the Royal Basin quota is gone, when you arrive too late to start the Royal Creek climb, or when the weather is bad enough that a night in the trees beats a night on gravel at five and a half thousand feet. It is also the natural first night for anyone approaching Fricaba the long way, by Boulder Shelter and Constance Pass. At barely three thousand feet in old growth it is warm, wet and buggy in early summer, and it commits you to a very big day if you try to use it as a climbing base for anything on the divide. Treat it as staging, not as a base camp.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: The Dungeness river runs right past the camp all year. Reliable.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Outside the national park. This is Olympic National Forest, inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so there is no park wilderness permit, no quota and no nightly fee. You do need a valid recreation parking pass on the vehicle at the Upper Dungeness trailhead. Bear canisters are not legally required on forest land here but food does need protecting, and if any part of your trip crosses into the park you will be carrying one anyway.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: An open three-sided shelter with log benches plus several tent sites scattered through the riverside meadow. Comfortably takes a few parties, and rarely full outside a summer weekend. No privy.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Boulder Shelter
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. This is the crossroads camp for the eastern half of the zone: from here the trail climbs to Home Lake and Constance Pass, which is the alternative and much less crowded way at Fricaba. It is permit-free, which matters a great deal in a zone where the good camps are rationed months in advance. It is not a Needles camp and no amount of enthusiasm makes it one. Also worth knowing before you plan around it: the stretch above here toward Home Lake is far more primitive than the trail below, with brush, blowdown and at least one crossing that will get you wet, so budget more time than the mileage suggests. The shelter is genuinely useful in bad weather, which is not something most of the alpine options in this zone can offer.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary is crossed on the way to Home Lake, and from that point an Olympic National Park wilderness permit and a bear canister are required, so if you intend to sleep beyond here get the permit before you leave the road.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Home Lake
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: Just over nine miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, a little over five thousand three hundred feet, and only a few hundred feet below Constance Pass. This is the second door to Fricaba, and the reason it is in this list at all: if the Royal Basin quota is unobtainable, Fricaba can still be climbed from this side without competing for a rationed permit. It is a genuinely long walk in, with the primitive brushy section above Boulder Shelter to negotiate, so it costs you most of a day. It gives you a quiet alpine lake with real water and real shelter from wind, at a height that leaves a sensible summit day. It does nothing at all for The Needles or the Royal Basin peaks, which sit over a major divide from here. Snow holds around the lake and the pass into July. Parties combining Fricaba with Mount Constance frequently use this camp, which is worth remembering when you are guessing at how busy it will be.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: The lake, immediately at camp. Reliable through the season.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Inside Olympic National Park, so an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required, but Home Lake is NOT one of the quota areas. Reserve through the federal recreation booking system with the usual per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee; because it carries no quota, availability is generally straightforward even in midsummer, which is precisely why it is worth knowing about. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, as they are throughout park wilderness.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Cedar Lake
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. Be clear-eyed about the cost: it is a long, remote walk in, well over ten miles, on a trail with a missing river bridge that pushes everyone onto the Slab Camp approach, and it is a completely different road and trailhead from Royal Basin. Almost nobody climbs Baldy or Gray Wolf Ridge from here, because both are done car to car in a long day from the steep Maynard Burn way trail on the Dungeness side, with no camp involved and no permit needed. Cedar Lake earns its place for the party doing the full ridge traverse, or wanting the Gray Wolf approach to Walkinshaw, or simply wanting solitude in a zone where the popular basin is rationed. If you only want to stand on Baldy and Gray Wolf Ridge, do not come here.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Cameron Basin
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_sundial_northeast.name: Dose Meadows
wa_sundial_northeast.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.
wa_sundial_northeast.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
wa_sundial_northeast.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
wa_sundial_northeast.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Kool-Aid Lake
wa_sw_ridge.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
wa_sw_ridge.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Yang Yang Lakes
wa_sw_ridge.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
wa_sw_ridge.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

wa_sw_ridge.name: White Rock Lakes
wa_sw_ridge.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
wa_sw_ridge.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Itswoot Ridge
