wa_sw_ridge.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
wa_sw_ridge.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Cub Lake
wa_sw_ridge.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
wa_sw_ridge.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_sw_ridge.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
wa_sw_ridge.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Spire Col bivouac
wa_sw_ridge.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
wa_sw_ridge.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
wa_sw_ridge.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
wa_sw_ridge.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
wa_sw_ridge.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
wa_sw_ridge.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Beaver Pass Camp
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Challenger Arm camp
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: Luna Cirque floor
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Scatter Lake basin
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Libby Lake
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Artist Point and the Heather Meadows road end
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: The obvious place to sleep is, plainly, the one place you cannot. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Silver Fir Campground
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: The closest developed campground to the Heather Meadows end of the highway, roughly fourteen miles east of Glacier on the west side of the road just after the river crossing, and about eight miles below the Heather Meadows lots. This is the practical answer for a party that drives up the night before a scramble on Table Mountain, Mount Herman or Mount Ann and wants to be at the trailhead early without sleeping in a day-use car park. It is emphatically staging rather than plan: you are three thousand feet below the objectives and the drive up in the morning takes twenty minutes. Because there are no reservations it is a gamble on a Friday evening in July and August, and the fallback is the campground further down the valley. It stays open later into the autumn than the road to Artist Point does, which matters for anyone climbing these peaks in October.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: Piped water at the campground during the operating season, and the river alongside. Confirm the water is turned on if you are arriving at the shoulders of the season.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: A campground fee is charged per night and paid on site; this is a fee campground rather than a pass site, so a recreation pass does not cover the overnight. Fires are allowed in the provided rings unless a county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry August is common. Standard national forest food-storage sense applies — black bears work this valley.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: About twenty sites in forest beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and drinking water in season; first come, first served, and it fills on summer weekends

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Douglas Fir Campground
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. This is a busy, family-friendly circuit and the sites go early on a summer weekend, so arrive with a plan for finding all four taken.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: The lakes, and they are reliable all season. There is no potable water anywhere on the circuit, so treat everything.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit is required or issued. Recreation pass on the vehicle at whichever of the four trailheads you start from. CAMPING IS RESTRICTED TO THE MARKED SITES — the meadows here are heather over thin soil and the designation exists because they were being destroyed. No campfires at all, carry-in stoves only. Party size twelve. Food must go in a bear-resistant canister or be hung at least ten feet up and four feet out from the trunk and branches; there is no hardware provided.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Bearpaw Lake
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: The base for Bearpaw Mountain and the only camping anywhere near its own line. Canyon Creek Road leaves the Mount Baker Highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north for a long, slow fourteen miles or so of alternating tarmac and serious potholes before a signed spur climbs right to the lake trailhead; the last couple of miles are single lane with brush closing in that will mark a car. From the trailhead it is roughly a mile to the lake, short but steep. The peak's easiest line is a class three scramble from the southwest, following the timbered ridge east of the lake, with a direct variation onto the steeper part of the ridge that gives a narrow and locally exposed scramble. ROAD ACCESS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK AND NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: Canyon Creek Road has been closed at around mile four by a landslide carrying large timber and debris, with more downed trees below the block, which cuts off the lake spur and the road end entirely. When that closure is in force there is no alternative approach to this peak, only a very long road walk. Snow lies on this ground into July in most years.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: The lake, at camp. Treat it. This is the only water on the peak's own approach and there is nothing on the ridge above.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE any designated wilderness — this ground sits west of the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary, so there is no self-issue permit and no wilderness party limit here, and the twelve-person rule and blanket fire ban that govern the Heather Meadows half of this zone do not automatically apply. What does apply is a recreation pass at the trailhead, and whatever county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry summer is usually a total one. Pack out everything including human waste; there is no toilet.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: A few rough informal sites at a small lake in the trees; low use, no facilities, no toilet and nothing built

wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.name: Excelsior ridge camps and the high spring, Canyon Creek Road end
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.notes: This is the established high camping on the Canyon Creek road system, at the far end of the same road that serves Bearpaw, and it is listed with the caveat that IT IS NOT ON BEARPAW'S OWN ROUTE. Bearpaw is the prominent summit standing to the west, seen across the drainage from the pass and the ridge, and reaching it from here means dropping and re-climbing rather than walking a connecting line. Its value is as the answer to what a party does when the day goes wrong or when they want two objectives out of one long, slow drive: legal, watered, established camping at the road end of a road most people will only want to drive once. The trail leaves the road end, meets a junction in less than a mile with the Canyon Ridge trail going left, reaches the small lakes just beyond and then climbs through forest and into open meadow towards the pass. The same landslide closure that gates the Bearpaw spur gates this trailhead as well; the alternative is to walk up from the highway instead, which is a far bigger day. Meadows here are at their best in July and August and again for autumn colour in September and October.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.water: A spring about half a mile short of Excelsior Pass is the best and most dependable water in this high country and is the reason the camps are where they are. The lakes lower down at the trailhead end are shallow and warm late in the season. Treat everything, and fill at the spring rather than counting on anything on the crest.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.permit: The ridge camps sit inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, which the High Divide trail enters at the pass — so from there on it is party size twelve, no campfires of any kind, carry-in stoves only, camp on durable ground and pack out all waste including human waste. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead and there is a self-issue register. The ground below the pass around the lakes is outside the wilderness and less strictly governed, but the burn bans still apply.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble.capacity: Scattered informal sites on the ridge running south from Excelsior Peak and along the High Divide, plus a cluster near the spring; a handful of small parties, spread out, with no built sites and no toilet

wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.name: Gunn Basin, below Tailgunner Pass
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.notes: This is the high camp for Tailgunner, and it turns a very long day into a comfortable one. The climbers' path leaves the Barclay Creek road below the Barclay Lake trailhead, crosses the creek, and then climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest on a faint boot track, with dirt-covered slabs, a narrow traverse under cliffs and an exposed crossing above a waterfall before the angle relents into the basin. Reckon on three to four hours to camp with overnight loads. From here Tailgunner itself is an easy hour of slabby scrambling, and Gunn Peak and Wing Peak are both within reach the same morning, which is the usual reason parties carry a camp up at all. The shoulder of Tailgunner holds a shallow tarn perched right on the lip of the drop, and it is the obvious place to put a tent, but it is exposed and there is nothing between it and the weather. Season is roughly July to early October; earlier than that the traverse under the cliffs holds hard snow and the waterfall crossing is genuinely dangerous. The approach path is not maintained, is easy to lose on the descent, and should be tracked on the way up.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.water: Snowmelt tarns in the basin through midsummer, and a small stream draining the pass. Both can dry to nothing by late August in a thin year — carry the day's water up from Barclay Creek if the season has been hot.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit or quota for camping. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at the Barclay Lake trailhead and at the pullouts either side of it. Stoves rather than fires — the basin is at the edge of timberline and the scattered wood there is what holds the heather together.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.capacity: Open heather benches and slabs holding perhaps three or four small tents, scattered rather than clustered. No constructed sites, no toilet, no fire ring worth using.

wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.name: Barclay Creek roadhead pullouts
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.notes: This is a staging camp rather than a destination, and it exists because the Tailgunner and Gunn climbers' path leaves the road here rather than at the lake. Sleeping at the roadhead lets a party start the steep forest climb in the dark and reach the basin before the day heats up, which matters on a south-facing approach. The spur road with the clearing drops off the main road a short distance below the pit toilet at the Barclay Lake trailhead; the path itself heads right before that clearing and is unsigned. Do not confuse this with Barclay Lake, which is a maintained walk-in with established lakeside sites and is covered elsewhere. The road is plowed nowhere and is gated by snow from roughly late November to April, which puts the winter ascent of Tailgunner well out of reach for most parties. Expect log trucks and weekend traffic through the summer, and expect the trailhead lot to be full by mid-morning on any fine Saturday.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.water: Barclay Creek runs beside the road and is the only supply. Treat it.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.permit: National forest, dispersed camping, no permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead parking itself. Campfire restrictions follow the district and are common from July onward — check before assuming a fire is legal.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.capacity: A handful of rough dispersed pullouts and one small clearing on a spur road a short walk below the trailhead. Room for two or three vehicles to sleep beside, not a campground.

wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its availability as a question to answer before you drive rather than an assumption. When the road is cut at the North Fork bridge it is unreachable from the Beckler River side entirely. Even when it is open it is a low, damp, mosquito-heavy site in early summer, and its value is convenience rather than pleasure — it puts a party within twenty minutes of the start of the Spire approach, which is worth a great deal on a climb that wants a pre-dawn departure. Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground serve the same road system and are covered in the neighbouring zone, so check those first if this one is closed.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.water: River water only, treated. There is no potable supply.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.permit: Standard national forest campground fee when it is operating. No wilderness permit is involved at this elevation.
wa_tailgunner_peak_w_route.capacity: A small forest campground of a dozen or so sites in second-growth beside the North Fork Skykomish, with vault toilets and no water system.

wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side

wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps

wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps

wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River

wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

wa_tepeh_towers.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
wa_tepeh_towers.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
wa_tepeh_towers.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
wa_tepeh_towers.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
wa_tepeh_towers.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

wa_tepeh_towers.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
wa_tepeh_towers.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
wa_tepeh_towers.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
wa_tepeh_towers.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
wa_tepeh_towers.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

wa_tepeh_towers.name: Eldorado Basin camp
wa_tepeh_towers.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
wa_tepeh_towers.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
wa_tepeh_towers.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
wa_tepeh_towers.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

wa_tepeh_towers.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
wa_tepeh_towers.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
wa_tepeh_towers.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
wa_tepeh_towers.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
wa_tepeh_towers.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

wa_tepeh_towers.name: Klawatti Col camp
wa_tepeh_towers.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
wa_tepeh_towers.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
wa_tepeh_towers.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
wa_tepeh_towers.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

wa_tepeh_towers.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
wa_tepeh_towers.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
wa_tepeh_towers.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
wa_tepeh_towers.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
wa_tepeh_towers.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.name: Lower Lena Lake
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.notes: Three miles in, and worth knowing about mainly so you do not mistake it for the climb's camp — it is a further three miles and about a thousand feet below the ground climbers actually use. It suits a party arriving late in the day or a first night split, not a summit bid.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.water: The lake. There is no potable water at the trailhead, so this is the first fill.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.permit: Olympic National Forest. No overnight fee and no permit, but a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at the Lena Lake trailhead. Camp in the designated sites only; fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.capacity: Designated sites on both sides of the lake, first come and no reservation.

wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.name: Brothers base camp at Lena Forks
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.notes: The base camp for the route, at the confluence of the forks of the East Fork of Lena Creek, roughly five to six miles in and about three miles beyond the north end of Lena Lake. Deep forest with little sun, and the ground is a lumpy mess of long-decayed fallen trees rather than flat duff. The trail beyond Lena Lake is unmaintained — blowdown, washouts and flagging tape — and parties routinely lose it, especially walking in at night. The reliable cue that you have gone past the forks is sound: the creek suddenly drops away and goes quiet. Snow lies at camp into spring. There is a fire ring, but one party found it burned over a foot down into the root mat, so think before lighting it.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.water: The East Fork of Lena Creek runs beside the flat spots, so filtering is easy and reliable. Do not be alarmed on the way in: lower down the valley the creek sinks into the boulders and runs underground, and the bed can be dry on the surface in late summer. That is normal and says nothing about the water at camp.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.permit: Olympic National Forest, The Brothers Wilderness — and note this is national forest, not the national park, so there is no wilderness permit, reservation or quota, whatever some route pages say. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Party size is capped at twelve, and caching gear for more than twenty-four hours is prohibited. Camp sits just below the wilderness fire line, which makes it the one place on this route where an open fire is legal.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.capacity: Four or five separate sites scattered through the trees. It does fill — parties have arrived to find every one taken and had to walk on to the next.

wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.name: Upper camp above the forks
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.notes: A second camp area further up the basin, reached by following the cairned way trail toward the left fork until a small meadow opens. One trip record names it the East Lena Creek Basin and treats it as a separate place from the forks camp, and it is the only source for the elevation, so treat that figure as unconfirmed. It buys a little height at the cost of losing the legal fire and the known water.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.water: Not published for the camp itself. The last water on the route is at or near treeline, around 4,000 ft; above that everything is carried, and parties fill two or more litres there for the summit and the return.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.permit: This camp is above the 3,500 ft wilderness fire line: stoves only, and gathering wood here is prohibited outright.

wa_the_brothers_traverse.name: Lena Lake designated sites
wa_the_brothers_traverse.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
wa_the_brothers_traverse.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
