Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

wa_the_horn_scramble.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
wa_the_horn_scramble.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

wa_the_horn_scramble.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
wa_the_horn_scramble.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

wa_the_horn_scramble.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_the_horn_scramble.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

wa_the_horn_scramble.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_the_horn_scramble.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_the_horn_scramble.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
wa_the_horn_scramble.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

wa_the_horn_scramble.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
wa_the_horn_scramble.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
wa_the_horn_scramble.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
wa_the_horn_scramble.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
wa_the_horn_scramble.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Royal Lake
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: This is the front door to the whole Needles group and the default answer for anyone climbing Deception, Clark, Johnson, Walkinshaw, The Incisor or Sundial. It sits about seven miles and two and a half thousand feet from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, up the Dungeness and then the Royal Creek fork, which is walkable with a heavy pack in an afternoon. The honest trade is this: Royal Lake is comfortable, has real designated tent pads and is where the permit system actually issues sites, but it leaves you an extra mile and roughly five hundred to a thousand feet of loose boot path below the upper basin every single climbing morning. On a Needles day that difference is real, because the rock above the basin is dirty and slow and you want to be off it before the afternoon. Parties that only want one peak, or that have anyone who would rather not sleep at six thousand feet on gravel, are right to stay here. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a normal year and the mosquitoes at the lake are notorious through midsummer, which is another argument for going higher. Book the moment the reservation window opens; this is one of the hardest permits on the peninsula to get on a weekend.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: The lake and the outlet creek run all season. Filter or treat; this is a heavily used basin and the shoreline is fragile.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Royal Basin is one of the park's named quota areas. Essentially the whole quota is reservable in advance through the federal recreation booking system, with the summer block released in a single mid-April drop for the mid-May through mid-October season; there is no same-day walk-up window, so a party that turns up without a permit has no legal camp. Expect a flat per-permit reservation charge plus a per-adult, per-night fee, with under-sixteens free and an annual wilderness pass available if you camp here often. Dates outside the online season are arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, and loaners are sometimes available on a first-come basis when you collect the permit. Every camp along Royal Creek and up through the meadows and the basin sits inside the same reservation, so there is no legal way to sneak a night lower down without one.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: Ten designated sites, and only two of them will take more than a single tent. One separate group site holds roughly seven to twelve people and has to be booked as a group site. That is the entire overnight capacity of the lake basin, which is why permits go so fast.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Upper Royal Basin
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: This is the climbers' camp, three quarters of a mile to a mile above the lake on an unmaintained way trail that gains around five hundred to a thousand feet. It puts you at the foot of the west wall of the basin, which is the east side of The Needles, and it is the difference between a reasonable day and a very long one on Deception, Clark, Johnson, The Incisor and Sundial. It is also the working base for Mystery, which is reached over the divide out of the head of the basin, and for Fricaba, which is a comparatively easy scramble from here and a common warm-up or bad-weather substitute. What you pay for the position: exposed camping on gravel with no trees, weather that arrives with no warning, colder nights, and a fiddly load carry up the boot path in the evening. What you get: fewer people, far fewer mosquitoes, and a start that puts you on the loose ground above the basin while it is still frozen together rather than after the sun has been on it for two hours. Snow covers the upper basin well into July most years, which is often an advantage for the approach gullies and a nuisance for finding bare ground to pitch on. If the basin is still largely snow-covered, camp on a gravel bar that has melted out rather than on snow over vegetation.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: Tarns and snowmelt streams through the basin. Late in a dry summer the upper tarns can drop and go stagnant, so check the inlet streams rather than dipping from still water, and be prepared to carry from lower in the basin in September.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Same Olympic National Park quota permit as Royal Lake, booked as the upper basin rather than the lake. All the same conditions apply: advance reservation only, mid-April release for the summer season, per-permit and per-person-per-night charges, and mandatory hard-sided bear canisters. Because there are no constructed sites, the leave-no-trace rules here are enforced in earnest: no camping on vegetation or meadow, no fires, and the park expects you to be on durable surface only. Anyone found camped on the heather is the reason this basin nearly lost overnight use.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: No numbered sites at all. Camping is permitted only on bare ground, gravel bars and rock, so the practical capacity is a handful of parties spread across the gravel beside the tarns. Two of the larger gravel bars near the upper tarn are the usual choice for a group.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Camp Handy
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: A low, sheltered, permit-free camp about three miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, and the most useful fallback in the whole zone. It does not serve The Needles: Royal Basin branches off well below it and Camp Handy is on the wrong fork. What it does is give you a legal, free, roofed place to sleep when the Royal Basin quota is gone, when you arrive too late to start the Royal Creek climb, or when the weather is bad enough that a night in the trees beats a night on gravel at five and a half thousand feet. It is also the natural first night for anyone approaching Fricaba the long way, by Boulder Shelter and Constance Pass. At barely three thousand feet in old growth it is warm, wet and buggy in early summer, and it commits you to a very big day if you try to use it as a climbing base for anything on the divide. Treat it as staging, not as a base camp.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: The Dungeness river runs right past the camp all year. Reliable.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Outside the national park. This is Olympic National Forest, inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so there is no park wilderness permit, no quota and no nightly fee. You do need a valid recreation parking pass on the vehicle at the Upper Dungeness trailhead. Bear canisters are not legally required on forest land here but food does need protecting, and if any part of your trip crosses into the park you will be carrying one anyway.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: An open three-sided shelter with log benches plus several tent sites scattered through the riverside meadow. Comfortably takes a few parties, and rarely full outside a summer weekend. No privy.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Boulder Shelter
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. This is the crossroads camp for the eastern half of the zone: from here the trail climbs to Home Lake and Constance Pass, which is the alternative and much less crowded way at Fricaba. It is permit-free, which matters a great deal in a zone where the good camps are rationed months in advance. It is not a Needles camp and no amount of enthusiasm makes it one. Also worth knowing before you plan around it: the stretch above here toward Home Lake is far more primitive than the trail below, with brush, blowdown and at least one crossing that will get you wet, so budget more time than the mileage suggests. The shelter is genuinely useful in bad weather, which is not something most of the alpine options in this zone can offer.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary is crossed on the way to Home Lake, and from that point an Olympic National Park wilderness permit and a bear canister are required, so if you intend to sleep beyond here get the permit before you leave the road.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Home Lake
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: Just over nine miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, a little over five thousand three hundred feet, and only a few hundred feet below Constance Pass. This is the second door to Fricaba, and the reason it is in this list at all: if the Royal Basin quota is unobtainable, Fricaba can still be climbed from this side without competing for a rationed permit. It is a genuinely long walk in, with the primitive brushy section above Boulder Shelter to negotiate, so it costs you most of a day. It gives you a quiet alpine lake with real water and real shelter from wind, at a height that leaves a sensible summit day. It does nothing at all for The Needles or the Royal Basin peaks, which sit over a major divide from here. Snow holds around the lake and the pass into July. Parties combining Fricaba with Mount Constance frequently use this camp, which is worth remembering when you are guessing at how busy it will be.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: The lake, immediately at camp. Reliable through the season.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Inside Olympic National Park, so an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required, but Home Lake is NOT one of the quota areas. Reserve through the federal recreation booking system with the usual per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee; because it carries no quota, availability is generally straightforward even in midsummer, which is precisely why it is worth knowing about. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, as they are throughout park wilderness.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Cedar Lake
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. Be clear-eyed about the cost: it is a long, remote walk in, well over ten miles, on a trail with a missing river bridge that pushes everyone onto the Slab Camp approach, and it is a completely different road and trailhead from Royal Basin. Almost nobody climbs Baldy or Gray Wolf Ridge from here, because both are done car to car in a long day from the steep Maynard Burn way trail on the Dungeness side, with no camp involved and no permit needed. Cedar Lake earns its place for the party doing the full ridge traverse, or wanting the Gray Wolf approach to Walkinshaw, or simply wanting solitude in a zone where the popular basin is rationed. If you only want to stand on Baldy and Gray Wolf Ridge, do not come here.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Cameron Basin
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_the_incisor_scramble.name: Dose Meadows
wa_the_incisor_scramble.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
wa_the_incisor_scramble.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_the_monk_le_gibet.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_the_monk_le_gibet.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

wa_the_monk_le_gibet.name: Andrews Pass
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

wa_the_monk_le_gibet.name: Remmel Lake and the Spanish Camp meadows
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.notes: This sits a short way off the main line to Cathedral Pass and works well as a base if Remmel Mountain is on the list alongside Cathedral and Amphitheater. The meadow ground is soft and easily damaged, so pull back onto the timber edge rather than pitching in the open grass. There is a signed spur from near the guard station running up toward the Cathedral basin, which makes this a workable alternative if the lakes above are full or posted closed. Being lower and more sheltered, it is a considerably kinder camp in bad weather than anything at the pass.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.water: Reliable — the lake plus the creeks draining the meadows. Along with Upper Cathedral, the other place on the approach where you can count on filling.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit, no quota. The cabin at Spanish Camp is a Forest Service ADMINISTRATIVE structure, not a public shelter, and should not be treated as available lodging.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.capacity: Broad grassy meadows with room for multiple parties, but the sites are dispersed rather than developed and horse parties use this area heavily

wa_the_monk_le_gibet.name: Amphitheater Mountain upper basin
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.notes: Reached by following the trail southeast around Amphitheater's west ridge from Upper Cathedral Lake and then a boot path up scree and grass into the basin. Worth considering only if you want to be on the ridge at first light, because the water problem is real and it gains you very little over camping at the lake. The ground is loose and sparsely vegetated, which makes it easy to occupy without leaving a mark if you are careful. Treat it as an emergency or tactical bivy rather than a planned camp. No elevation is recorded — none was confidently sourced.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.water: Snowmelt only, and only early. Once the last patches go there is nothing up here, so plan on carrying everything up from the lake. This is the driest camp option in the zone.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit covers it; no quota, no reservation, and no designated-site system in this wilderness.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.capacity: One or two parties on scree and grass benches; informal ground, no established sites

wa_the_monk_le_gibet.name: Tungsten Mine camp
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.notes: This sits on the LOOP leg between Apex Pass and the Chewuch drainage rather than on the direct Andrews Creek line, so it matters if you are traversing out rather than going in and back the same way — a party going in and out via Andrews Creek will never see it. The old bunkhouse and mine hardware from the early 1900s are still standing and the site survived the recent fires. Whether it is genuinely useful shelter is a judgement call and reports differ; plan to be self-sufficient in a tent. The water situation is the deciding factor for most parties, not the buildings.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.water: Poor and getting worse as the season goes on. The trail between Cathedral Pass and the mine is reported dry along its whole length, with one small stream roughly a quarter mile short of the site, so fill lower down before starting the climb.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota and no reservation. The historic structures are protected cultural resources — leave the machinery and the buildings alone.
wa_the_monk_le_gibet.capacity: Good camping around the mine site; the standing bunkhouse and cabin are historic structures that some parties shelter in, though their condition is not maintained for that purpose
