wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.name: Amphitheater Mountain upper basin
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.notes: Reached by following the trail southeast around Amphitheater's west ridge from Upper Cathedral Lake and then a boot path up scree and grass into the basin. Worth considering only if you want to be on the ridge at first light, because the water problem is real and it gains you very little over camping at the lake. The ground is loose and sparsely vegetated, which makes it easy to occupy without leaving a mark if you are careful. Treat it as an emergency or tactical bivy rather than a planned camp. No elevation is recorded — none was confidently sourced.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.water: Snowmelt only, and only early. Once the last patches go there is nothing up here, so plan on carrying everything up from the lake. This is the driest camp option in the zone.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit covers it; no quota, no reservation, and no designated-site system in this wilderness.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.capacity: One or two parties on scree and grass benches; informal ground, no established sites

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.name: Tungsten Mine camp
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.notes: This sits on the LOOP leg between Apex Pass and the Chewuch drainage rather than on the direct Andrews Creek line, so it matters if you are traversing out rather than going in and back the same way — a party going in and out via Andrews Creek will never see it. The old bunkhouse and mine hardware from the early 1900s are still standing and the site survived the recent fires. Whether it is genuinely useful shelter is a judgement call and reports differ; plan to be self-sufficient in a tent. The water situation is the deciding factor for most parties, not the buildings.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.water: Poor and getting worse as the season goes on. The trail between Cathedral Pass and the mine is reported dry along its whole length, with one small stream roughly a quarter mile short of the site, so fill lower down before starting the climb.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota and no reservation. The historic structures are protected cultural resources — leave the machinery and the buildings alone.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.capacity: Good camping around the mine site; the standing bunkhouse and cabin are historic structures that some parties shelter in, though their condition is not maintained for that purpose

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.name: Andrews Pass
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.name: Remmel Lake and the Spanish Camp meadows
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.notes: This sits a short way off the main line to Cathedral Pass and works well as a base if Remmel Mountain is on the list alongside Cathedral and Amphitheater. The meadow ground is soft and easily damaged, so pull back onto the timber edge rather than pitching in the open grass. There is a signed spur from near the guard station running up toward the Cathedral basin, which makes this a workable alternative if the lakes above are full or posted closed. Being lower and more sheltered, it is a considerably kinder camp in bad weather than anything at the pass.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.water: Reliable — the lake plus the creeks draining the meadows. Along with Upper Cathedral, the other place on the approach where you can count on filling.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit, no quota. The cabin at Spanish Camp is a Forest Service ADMINISTRATIVE structure, not a public shelter, and should not be treated as available lodging.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.capacity: Broad grassy meadows with room for multiple parties, but the sites are dispersed rather than developed and horse parties use this area heavily

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.name: Amphitheater Mountain upper basin
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.notes: Reached by following the trail southeast around Amphitheater's west ridge from Upper Cathedral Lake and then a boot path up scree and grass into the basin. Worth considering only if you want to be on the ridge at first light, because the water problem is real and it gains you very little over camping at the lake. The ground is loose and sparsely vegetated, which makes it easy to occupy without leaving a mark if you are careful. Treat it as an emergency or tactical bivy rather than a planned camp. No elevation is recorded — none was confidently sourced.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.water: Snowmelt only, and only early. Once the last patches go there is nothing up here, so plan on carrying everything up from the lake. This is the driest camp option in the zone.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit covers it; no quota, no reservation, and no designated-site system in this wilderness.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.capacity: One or two parties on scree and grass benches; informal ground, no established sites

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.name: Tungsten Mine camp
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.notes: This sits on the LOOP leg between Apex Pass and the Chewuch drainage rather than on the direct Andrews Creek line, so it matters if you are traversing out rather than going in and back the same way — a party going in and out via Andrews Creek will never see it. The old bunkhouse and mine hardware from the early 1900s are still standing and the site survived the recent fires. Whether it is genuinely useful shelter is a judgement call and reports differ; plan to be self-sufficient in a tent. The water situation is the deciding factor for most parties, not the buildings.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.water: Poor and getting worse as the season goes on. The trail between Cathedral Pass and the mine is reported dry along its whole length, with one small stream roughly a quarter mile short of the site, so fill lower down before starting the climb.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota and no reservation. The historic structures are protected cultural resources — leave the machinery and the buildings alone.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.capacity: Good camping around the mine site; the standing bunkhouse and cabin are historic structures that some parties shelter in, though their condition is not maintained for that purpose

wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.name: Neve Camp
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.name: Junction Camp
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.name: Skagit Queen Camp
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.name: Fremont Glacier moraine high camp
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.notes: Reached by leaving the trail in the flat sandy meadows a short distance north of Park Creek Pass and climbing several hundred feet into old moraine, this is the high camp for the Fremont Glacier side of Mount Logan and the only realistic way to get above the pass legally. The ground is flat, sandy and sheltered, which matters on a rib this exposed. Parties also report usable bivy ground higher, near where the climbers' route meets the glacier around eight thousand feet, though water up there is entirely a function of what snow is left. Which option is better is genuinely conditions-dependent and worth asking at the permit desk the morning you pick up.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff, and it is seasonal. Sources near the first stream crossings north of the pass are more dependable; higher moraine camps can go dry late in a hot summer, so carry capacity to melt or haul.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.permit: Requires a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE permit from Marblemount, not a designated-camp permit. Fires prohibited outright. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows or within 100 ft of water. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, and out of sight of both. Waste in a cathole, or carried out in a blue bag above treeline or on glaciers.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.capacity: Cross-country zone camping rather than a designated site, so no fixed site count. Most zones cap a party at six. One permit covers the party.

wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
wa_the_perfect_crime_with_variations.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. The final two miles to Twin Lakes are narrow, unmaintained for passenger cars, short of pullouts, and genuinely want high clearance. Parties turned back at the lower lot are looking at an extra two miles and roughly 1,500 ft of road walking each way before the climb even starts, which turns a comfortable day on Winchester or a two-day Larrabee trip into something much longer, and is a good reason to plan on sleeping out. The road is snowbound well into the season most years and is often not drivable to the upper end until July. Call the ranger station before committing, and if you park low, camping in a pullout the night before is a common and reasonable way to save the morning.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.water: Creeks cross the road in places but there is nothing reliable at the lot itself; carry water up from the valley or plan to filter higher
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and the state parks pass is not accepted here. Fill in the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register where one is provided. Dispersed roadside camping on national forest land outside the wilderness boundary is generally allowed, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a pullout.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: A dozen or so vehicles in the trailhead lot, plus scattered pullouts along the road; it fills on summer weekends and there is nowhere to turn around if you keep going and change your mind

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pack costs you nothing, so most parties on Winchester, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak sleep here and start from the isthmus between the lakes. The Winchester Mountain trail and the High Pass trail both begin there. It does not melt out completely until July in most years, and late-season parties should expect a busy, social camp rather than a quiet one. Everything the lakes hold is heavily used; pick an established site rather than making a new one in the meadow.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.water: The two lakes, right at camp. No treated water; filter or boil.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: A 1935 lookout on the 6,521 ft summit, kept standing by volunteers from a local hiking club rather than by the agency, and genuinely open for anyone to sleep in on a first-come basis. It is 1.7 miles and about 1,300 ft above the Twin Lakes trailhead, which makes it one of the easiest real summits in the range to reach and a fine advance camp for a light party heading on to Mount Larrabee, though it sits off the direct High Pass line and most climbers heading for American Border Peak carry on past the junction rather than up. Treat the building as borrowed. It survives on people sweeping it out, closing the shutters properly, packing out their rubbish and leaving it drier than they found it; a run of poor behaviour is exactly why the winter season was closed. Always carry a tent or bivy, because it may well be occupied when you arrive and there is only room for two on the bunks. There are patches of ground outside the building flat enough to sleep on. The trail crosses steep, exposed snow slopes that linger into July and sometimes August, and an ice axe is the right call before the traverse is bare.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.water: None at the summit. Carry everything up from Twin Lakes, or melt snow early in the season.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: Free, no reservations, no fee, and no way to book it. Locked from November through May, reopening when conditions allow, and off limits as a shelter in winter beyond stepping inside with the shutters left as they are. Wilderness rules apply on the trail and at the summit: no fires at all, party size twelve, no toilet, so pack out everything including human waste.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: Two bunks inside and floor space for a couple more at a squeeze; twelve is the legal party limit but the building comfortably holds far fewer

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: High Pass camp
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: The standard camp for the southeast ridge of Tomyhoi Peak, and the reason Tomyhoi is a comfortable overnight rather than a very long day. From the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft the trail climbs towards Gold Run Pass, forks left onto the meadows trail and reaches the scatter of tarns at roughly 5,580 ft in about four miles. From camp the route drops northwest over a hump to a col near 6,266 ft and follows the ridge over benches and a small glacier remnant to the false summit and the class 3 summit block. This is one of the most heavily impacted alpine basins in the district and the rules exist because the meadow was being destroyed; a single careless night on heather leaves a scar that lasts years. Mountain goats frequent the basin, are habituated, and will come to camp for the salt in urine, so pee on rock well away from the tents. Snow covers the basin into July and the tarns can still be part frozen at the start of the season.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.water: The tarns themselves. They are shallow, warm late in the season and shared with a great many campers, so filter and draw well away from where people wash.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail EXCEPT at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: Perhaps eight to ten small sites among the tarns, all of them well used; expect company, and expect to take whichever pad is left rather than the one you wanted

wa_the_pleiades_scramble.name: Tomyhoi Lake
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.notes: Worth knowing about mostly so you do not plan a climb around it. Despite the name, Tomyhoi Lake is not the camp for Tomyhoi Peak: the trail from the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead climbs to Gold Run Pass and then loses roughly 1,500 ft over two miles down the far side to the lake at about 3,727 ft, while the peak's southeast ridge starts from the tarns high above. Camping here and climbing the peak means regaining everything you gave away. It is a good option for a party that wants a low, sheltered, uncrowded night in the trees when the meadows are snowed under or the tarns are full, and it is the natural bail if weather closes the high ground. The last stretch of trail down to the lake is brushy and easy to lose, and the north side of Gold Run Pass is steep, exposed and holds snow into late summer, so carry an axe and traction if you are dropping in early in the season.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.permit: No camping within one mile of Gold Run Pass, which rules out the whole upper part of the descent; the lake itself is far enough down to be legal. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, recreation pass on the vehicle, no fires, party size twelve, pack out waste.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble.capacity: A handful of rough forested sites at the lake; quiet, and rarely full

wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.name: Stump Hollow bench
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.name: Terror Basin camp
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

wa_the_roof.name: Snow Lake Camp
wa_the_roof.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
wa_the_roof.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
wa_the_roof.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
wa_the_roof.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

wa_the_roof.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
wa_the_roof.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
wa_the_roof.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
wa_the_roof.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
wa_the_roof.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

wa_the_roof.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
wa_the_roof.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
wa_the_roof.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
wa_the_roof.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
wa_the_roof.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

wa_the_roof.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_the_roof.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
wa_the_roof.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
wa_the_roof.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
wa_the_roof.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

wa_the_roof.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
wa_the_roof.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.
wa_the_roof.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
wa_the_roof.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter

wa_the_roof.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
wa_the_roof.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. It has been closed through 2026 for a rehabilitation project, so confirm its status before planning around it. When running it is low, forested and warm, which makes it a reasonable shoulder-season option when the higher campgrounds are shut.
wa_the_roof.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
wa_the_roof.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.

wa_the_temple_south_ridge.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_the_temple_south_ridge.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_the_temple_south_ridge.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_the_temple_south_ridge.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_the_temple_south_ridge.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_the_temple_south_ridge.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_the_temple_south_ridge.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_the_tiger.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
wa_the_tiger.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
wa_the_tiger.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
wa_the_tiger.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
wa_the_tiger.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

wa_the_tiger.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
wa_the_tiger.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
wa_the_tiger.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
wa_the_tiger.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
wa_the_tiger.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

wa_the_tiger.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
wa_the_tiger.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
wa_the_tiger.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
wa_the_tiger.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
wa_the_tiger.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

wa_the_tiger.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
wa_the_tiger.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
wa_the_tiger.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
wa_the_tiger.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
wa_the_tiger.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_the_tiger.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
wa_the_tiger.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
wa_the_tiger.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
wa_the_tiger.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
wa_the_tiger.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

wa_the_tiger.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
wa_the_tiger.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
wa_the_tiger.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
wa_the_tiger.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
wa_the_tiger.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

wa_the_tooth_fairy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
wa_the_tooth_fairy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

wa_the_tooth_fairy.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
wa_the_tooth_fairy.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends

wa_the_tooth_fairy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
wa_the_tooth_fairy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack

wa_the_tooth_fairy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
wa_the_tooth_fairy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

wa_the_tooth_fairy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
wa_the_tooth_fairy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
wa_the_tooth_fairy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites
