Always carry a tent or bivy, because it may well be occupied when you arrive and there is only room for two on the bunks. There are patches of ground outside the building flat enough to sleep on. The trail crosses steep, exposed snow slopes that linger into July and sometimes August, and an ice axe is the right call before the traverse is bare.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.water: None at the summit. Carry everything up from Twin Lakes, or melt snow early in the season.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.permit: Free, no reservations, no fee, and no way to book it. Locked from November through May, reopening when conditions allow, and off limits as a shelter in winter beyond stepping inside with the shutters left as they are. Wilderness rules apply on the trail and at the summit: no fires at all, party size twelve, no toilet, so pack out everything including human waste.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.capacity: Two bunks inside and floor space for a couple more at a squeeze; twelve is the legal party limit but the building comfortably holds far fewer

wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.name: High Pass camp
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower

wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.notes: The standard camp for the southeast ridge of Tomyhoi Peak, and the reason Tomyhoi is a comfortable overnight rather than a very long day. From the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft the trail climbs towards Gold Run Pass, forks left onto the meadows trail and reaches the scatter of tarns at roughly 5,580 ft in about four miles. From camp the route drops northwest over a hump to a col near 6,266 ft and follows the ridge over benches and a small glacier remnant to the false summit and the class 3 summit block. This is one of the most heavily impacted alpine basins in the district and the rules exist because the meadow was being destroyed; a single careless night on heather leaves a scar that lasts years. Mountain goats frequent the basin, are habituated, and will come to camp for the salt in urine, so pee on rock well away from the tents. Snow covers the basin into July and the tarns can still be part frozen at the start of the season.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.water: The tarns themselves. They are shallow, warm late in the season and shared with a great many campers, so filter and draw well away from where people wash.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.permit: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail EXCEPT at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.capacity: Perhaps eight to ten small sites among the tarns, all of them well used; expect company, and expect to take whichever pad is left rather than the one you wanted

wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.name: Tomyhoi Lake
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.notes: Worth knowing about mostly so you do not plan a climb around it. Despite the name, Tomyhoi Lake is not the camp for Tomyhoi Peak: the trail from the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead climbs to Gold Run Pass and then loses roughly 1,500 ft over two miles down the far side to the lake at about 3,727 ft, while the peak's southeast ridge starts from the tarns high above. Camping here and climbing the peak means regaining everything you gave away. It is a good option for a party that wants a low, sheltered, uncrowded night in the trees when the meadows are snowed under or the tarns are full, and it is the natural bail if weather closes the high ground. The last stretch of trail down to the lake is brushy and easy to lose, and the north side of Gold Run Pass is steep, exposed and holds snow into late summer, so carry an axe and traction if you are dropping in early in the season.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.permit: No camping within one mile of Gold Run Pass, which rules out the whole upper part of the descent; the lake itself is far enough down to be legal. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, recreation pass on the vehicle, no fires, party size twelve, pack out waste.
wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.capacity: A handful of rough forested sites at the lake; quiet, and rarely full

wa_tooth_and_claw.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
wa_tooth_and_claw.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
wa_tooth_and_claw.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
wa_tooth_and_claw.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
wa_tooth_and_claw.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

wa_tooth_and_claw.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
wa_tooth_and_claw.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
wa_tooth_and_claw.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
wa_tooth_and_claw.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_tooth_and_claw.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_tooth_and_claw.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
wa_tooth_and_claw.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

wa_tooth_and_claw.name: Klipchuck Campground
wa_tooth_and_claw.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
wa_tooth_and_claw.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

wa_tooth_chair_traverse.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

wa_tooth_chair_traverse.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends

wa_tooth_chair_traverse.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack

wa_tooth_chair_traverse.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

wa_tooth_chair_traverse.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
wa_tooth_chair_traverse.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

wa_tower_arete.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
wa_tower_arete.notes: This is the base for the north face and the trailhead in one, which is unusual and is what makes the face approachable at all: the walk to the bottom of the routes is under an hour, so a party can sleep at the car and still be climbing at first light without a bivouac. Trail 373 begins across the road from the campground and runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at around 7,150 ft, from where the face is below you. THE DRIVE IS THE COMMITMENT. Three ways reach it and they are not equivalent: a narrow four-wheel-drive road over Lone Frank Pass from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek, about twenty miles; a longer gravel road over Baldy Pass suited to two-wheel drive, about thirty; and a good two-wheel-drive gravel line from the Methow, north out of Winthrop on the Chewuch River road and then east and north on the 37 and 39, about twenty-six miles. Road 39 itself has not been graded in some time and is not recommended for low-clearance passenger cars. At this elevation the road holds snow late into the spring and can shut with the first serious autumn storm, so the usable window is short and both ends of it are worth checking rather than assuming.
wa_tower_arete.water: NO POTABLE WATER AND NO TAP — this is the single most important practical fact about the place, and its name is misleading. There is no piped supply, no water service and no rubbish service. Bring everything you need for drinking, cooking and washing, or plan to treat from Tiffany Lake, which is a short walk east on the trail and is the nearest dependable open water. In late summer this whole plateau is dry and what looks like a creek on a map may be nothing at all.
wa_tower_arete.permit: National forest, outside designated wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery — the opposite of the permit expectation a few miles west in the Pasayten. There is a small nightly fee at the campground and sites are first come, first served. Fire restrictions on this dry high plateau run through most of the summer and are commonly total bans, which given what has burned here recently should be treated as the default rather than the exception. Party size and stay limits are the usual forest ones.
wa_tower_arete.capacity: A small primitive forest campground with a handful of sites, taking tents and modest vehicles. Trailers are not appropriate given the road. It is rarely full and it is the only organised camping anywhere near this face.

wa_tower_arete.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
wa_tower_arete.notes: Under a mile from the campground and directly on the approach, this is the camp for a party who would rather sleep on water than at a car, or who has arrived to find the campground full or closed. It is the last certain water before the face. The trail continues around the shore and climbs about six hundred feet to Honeymoon Pass, which is the gateway to the north side; parties leaving a second vehicle at the Freezeout Ridge roadhead can carry on over Whistler Pass at around 7,600 ft to the summit and descend the Freezeout trail, an open loop of some eleven miles that is the standard way to combine the walk-up with a look at the face. THE BURN IS PART OF THE LANDSCAPE HERE. This trail travels through old fire scars that have opened the views and filled the ground with wildflower meadow, and the 2026 fire has added to that directly on this mountain — expect standing dead timber, no shade, and blowdown that changes with each windstorm. Do not pitch under dead trees in wind.
wa_tower_arete.water: The lakes, and they are the dependable supply for the whole north side of this mountain — everything above them on the pass and the face runs on snowmelt and is dry once that has gone. Access to the water is easy from the trail. Treat it; these are shallow, warm, well-used lakes rather than cold alpine tarns.
wa_tower_arete.permit: National forest, non-wilderness. No permit, no quota, no reservation, and no fee to camp at the lakes. A pass is not required to park at the campground trailhead across the road. Fire restrictions apply through the summer and are usually total bans; carry a stove. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground, and note that this trail is open to horses and mountain bikes as well as walkers, so pitch clear of it.
wa_tower_arete.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.

wa_tower_arete.name: Honeymoon Pass
wa_tower_arete.notes: The pass is where the trail crosses onto the north side and the face comes into view, and it is the tactical camp rather than the comfortable one. Its argument is a dawn start: from here the base of the routes is a short drop and a scramble rather than a walk from the road, which matters for the north-east couloir where the snow wants climbing early and matters much less for the rock, since the campground is under an hour away regardless. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WIND, in that order, and on a face this short the trade is rarely worth it — most parties are better off sleeping at the campground or the lake and walking in. Where it does earn its keep is for a party spending two days on the face, or one continuing over Whistler Pass to the summit and out by Freezeout Ridge. Nights are cold at this elevation from late August onward and there is no shelter at all if weather comes across the plateau.
wa_tower_arete.water: None dependable. Snowmelt early in the season and nothing at all once it has gone. Everything is carried up from Tiffany Lake, six hundred feet and half a mile below, and the party that forgets this ends up walking back down for it in the evening. In the ice season it is a snow camp and you melt.
wa_tower_arete.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation, no fee. Fire restrictions run through the summer and there is nothing to burn at this height in any case. The turf here is thin and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
wa_tower_arete.capacity: Open ground at the pass for a small party on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and nothing to shelter behind. Windswept is the word most often used about this crest and it is accurate.

wa_tower_arete.name: The talus and benches below the north face
wa_tower_arete.notes: The routes start here and, on a face six hundred and fifty feet high forty-five minutes from a campground, essentially nobody sleeps here. It is written down because a party reading a list of camps should not be left to assume there is a bivouac at the base — there is not, and the answer to a late arrival is the campground, not the wall. THE FACE ITSELF is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock. Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.
wa_tower_arete.water: Snowmelt off the couloirs early, and nothing whatsoever once that has gone. Given how early the snow leaves here after the roads open, that window is short. Carry water from the lakes; there is no source at the base of the face you should plan on.
wa_tower_arete.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.
wa_tower_arete.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.

wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.name: Granite Pass
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.name: Snowy Lakes basin
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.

wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
wa_tower_mountain_southwest_route.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Basin Creek Camp
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes: The closest designated camp to the Horseshoe Basin trail junction, which sits at about 3,600 ft on the valley trail, so it is the practical base for anything up in the cirque. It has a separate cooking area, a bear box and its own privy. Capacity is tiny — three sites — so a party of four fills most of it and a weekend permit is not something to count on. From here the basin trail climbs roughly 1,300 ft in about 1.5 miles to the Black Warrior Mine and the waterfall headwall below Ripsaw Ridge and Buckner's north side.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.water: Reliable — Basin Creek runs beside the camp all season
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.permit: NPS backcountry permit required (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA); designated camp reserved by site on Recreation.gov, with roughly 40% of inventory held for walk-up the day before at Marblemount or Golden West in Stehekin. Per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Cottonwood Camp
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes: The eastern gateway to the basin, at the end of what used to be the upper Stehekin Valley road. It has a privy, fire rings, picnic table and bear boxes, though the boxes are set well back from the cooking area. ACCESS IS THE THING TO PLAN AROUND: the road washed out for the last time in 2003 and the Stehekin shuttle now turns around at High Bridge, so reaching Cottonwood from the boat means an extra day of walking the old roadbed rather than the bus ride older descriptions assume. Check the current shuttle schedule before committing — upper-valley service has varied year to year.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.water: Reliable — creek water a short walk below the camp
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp, same Recreation.gov reservation and walk-up system as the rest of the complex.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.capacity: Several sites, including one that takes a larger group and a few small secluded ones

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Pelton Basin Camp
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes: A set of hand-built rock-walled tent platforms at the toe of the glacier, at the top of Sahale Arm. It is high, exposed and above the last dependable water, so late-season parties should plan to melt snow or carry up from lower on the arm. For the Horseshoe Basin peaks it is a high camp rather than a basin camp — it serves approaches that cross Sahale Arm and drop toward Doubtful Lake and the head of the basin, and it puts you on the right side of the divide for Buckner's north aspect. Reported elevation varies slightly between sources.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.water: Unreliable — snowmelt and glacier runoff only, and the seasonal trickles commonly dry up by late summer
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; one of the most contested designated camps in the park. Realistically needs the early-access lottery or the general on-sale window in late April.

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Doubtful Lake Camp
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes: Doubtful Lake lies in a cirque below Sahale Arm, reached by a spur that drops off the arm trail. It is the natural middle camp on the Sahale Arm variation of the approach, breaking up a long crossing between Cascade Pass and the head of Horseshoe Basin. Water is the one thing never in question here, which matters if the alternative is Sahale Glacier Camp late in the season. The spur loses meaningful elevation off the arm, so factor the reclimb into the next day.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus its inlet and outlet streams
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camping at the lake, reserved or walked up like the other Cascade Pass-area sites.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.capacity: A small designated camp at the lake, site count not published. Treat it as a handful of spots rather than a place a large party can count on.

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Buckner cross-country zone bivy
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes: The option for climbers who want to sleep on the route rather than at a valley camp — high bivies on moraine, slab or snow under Buckner's north side and the Ripsaw Ridge peaks. Zone rules are strict and worth reading before you go: camp at least a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight, and only on snow, rock or bare ground. No meadow camping, nothing within 100 ft of water, no fires. Because the permit is walk-up only, a trip built around a zone bivy is one you cannot lock in ahead of time — carry a fallback.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.water: Conditions-dependent — snowmelt and seasonal streams in the upper basin, dependable early, thin or gone by late season
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.permit: NPS cross-country zone permit required, WALK-UP ONLY. Buckner is not among the zones that take advance reservations, so it cannot be booked on Recreation.gov and must be picked up in person, generally no more than a day ahead.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.capacity: 6 people per party, 6 parties per night in the zone

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Barclay Lake
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: The traverse of Mount Index's three peaks is the one objective in this zone that is genuinely an overnight rather than a long day, and this is where parties sleep. The line links South, Middle and North Peaks along a crest of loose ridges and gullies with rappels between them, and the recorded practice is a flat spot right on the crest between the two Middle Peak summits with snow nearby, which solves the water problem in early season. Parties who have done it in a push describe going light and treating the bivouac as an emergency plan that they were glad to have and glad not to need — take minimal gear rather than a full camp, because everything you carry has to come over some genuinely poor rock. Approach is the Lake Serene trail as for everything else on the mountain. The rock on Index is famously rotten and the descent options off the ridge are limited, so committing to a bivouac here means committing to finishing the traverse; do not plan it as a place to sit out bad weather.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: Snow on the crest into early summer, and nothing at all once it goes. On a dry traverse you carry water for the whole ridge or you drop off it.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: One small party. A flat patch on the ridge crest between the two Middle Peak summits — a stance, not a site.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Money Creek Campground
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Beckler River Campground
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.

wa_traverse_of_mount_index.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. It sits about eleven miles up the Index-Galena Road from US 2 at roughly 1,200 ft on the North Fork Skykomish, which put it within twenty minutes of the Lake Serene trailhead and made it the obvious base for Mount Index. Flooding washed out the Index-Galena Road near mileposts 10 and 14, the road is gated closed through that section with permanent repairs estimated in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the county has said environmental review and permitting may take several years. The campground is inaccessible and closed as a result, and the neighbouring campground further up the same road is closed with it. Confirm the road status before counting on it; if the gate is still shut, the working substitutes for an Index-area night are Money Creek down the highway or a dispersed pullout on the Beckler system. Nothing on the Reiter Road side fills the gap — the lower Reiter Foothills road corridor is state land signed day use only with no camping and a Discover Pass required, which is the approach used for Mount Persis, so plan Persis as a day out from the valley.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
wa_traverse_of_mount_index.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Middle Fork Campground
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Green Ridge Lake
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Access is a faint unmaintained miners' and fishermen's path leaving the upper road at about 1,350 ft, roughly a mile below the Dingford Creek trailhead, climbing steeply northeast through timber; it is easy to lose in the first thousand feet and the brush is heavy when wet. Above the ridge crest at about 4,700 ft the ground opens into heather and scattered tarns and travel becomes pleasant. For most parties this is a contingency rather than the plan, since Treen goes in a long day when the road is open, but the road washout and the sheer gain from 1,350 ft make an overnight the sensible choice at present, and the ridge camp splits a brutal day into two reasonable ones. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: The lake is reliable through the summer, and the tarns above hold water into late season most years. Nothing between the road and the lake once the low creeks are behind you, so fill before the steep section.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Rainy Lake
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: Sits directly beneath the exposed south face of Preacher Mountain and is the natural base camp for the Standard Scramble. From the Middle Fork trailhead cross the bridge and follow the Pratt connector west to the junction with the unofficial Rainy Creek path, which the Forest Service abandoned years ago; volunteers keep the brush down in places and much of it is flagged, but it is not maintained tread and route-finding is required, particularly in the lower half. Preacher is around eleven miles and five thousand feet of gain from the road when it goes well, so most parties do it car-to-car. Treat this as the contingency for a slow day, wet brush or a late descent, and as the sensible plan for a winter attempt, when Preacher becomes a real snowshoe objective and the daylight will not stretch. The valley floor here is low enough to be open most of the year, but the lake and the ridge above hold snow into June.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: The lake and Rainy Creek are both reliable through the season. Treat.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, group limit twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the Middle Fork trailhead where the approach begins. The lake is just under the 4,000 ft campfire line, but the sites are small and the ground is thin, so use a stove and expect seasonal bans in late summer.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the lake shore. Quiet and rarely busy, since the access path keeps the numbers down.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: The honest answer for Garfield is that there is no camp, and inventing one would do a party more harm than saying so. It is a low mountain carrying enormous relief straight out of the valley floor, and every documented line begins with steep unmaintained bushwhacking and long rock gullies before any climbing starts. There are no trails, no signs and no established approach; you leave the road at a pull-out and go up. Ascents here are commonly described as needing either a bivouac or the very longest days of the year to finish in daylight, and the bivouacs that actually happen are improvised where a party runs out of light rather than chosen in advance. Plan for that rather than around it: carry a bivy kit on any attempt, expect to sleep on rock or in brush, and treat the multi-summit outing in particular as an opportunistic link-up rather than a route with a known camp on it. Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. Season here is governed by dry rock and daylight rather than snow: the valley is open most of the year, but the brush stays wet late and June through September is when this goes.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: Nothing reliable and nothing to plan around. The gullies run in spring and after rain and are dry by late summer, and there is no snow to melt on this mountain in season. Carry water for the whole push and know where the last certain source below you was.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the mountain beyond the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit if your line crosses the boundary, plus a Northwest Forest Pass at whichever pull-out you start from. Note that sleeping at the car is not an option here: the pull-outs at the base of Garfield fall inside the lower-valley dispersed camping closure.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.

wa_treen_peak_scramble.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
wa_treen_peak_scramble.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.water: The falls and the creeks crossed low on the trail run most of the year and are the last certain water. There is nothing on the upper mountain and nothing on the Kamikaze line at all. Carry what you need for the day.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
wa_treen_peak_scramble.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.

wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Tricouni Camp, Thunder Creek trail
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: Despite sharing the peak's name this camp is about a mile and a half further up the valley than the point where climbers leave the trail, so it is a fallback rather than a first choice. It is worth knowing about when McAllister is booked out on the night you need, since a short extra walk each way costs less than losing the trip. The forest here is more open than at McAllister. Nothing about it shortens the climb.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek nearby, reliable through the climbing season
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit system and fees as McAllister — designated site, part reservable and part held for walk-up at Marblemount.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Small designated hiker camp, a few sites

wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Klawatti Col camp, Eldorado ice-cap traverse approach
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: This is the multi-day route in, from the Eldorado side across the ice, and it is NOT how most parties reach these two peaks — it is recorded so the option is visible, not recommended as a shortcut. It is a genuinely different undertaking: full glacier travel with crevasse rescue capability, several nights on snow, and a committing exit. Camps are on rock islands surrounded by ice, so they are windy and there is no shelter. Choose it because you want the traverse.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.water: Meltwater and snow across the ice cap; essentially always available in season but usually means melting
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.permit: A DIFFERENT approach means a different permit. Parties coming across the ice cap from Eldorado start in a zone that does accept advance reservations, but the zone boundaries out here are not obvious on the ground and a traverse can cross more than one. Sort the whole itinerary night by night with Marblemount, since a reservation for one zone is not a permit for the next.
wa_tricouni_peak_southwest_slopes.capacity: Rock islands in the ice with room for a few tents; party size capped by the zone permit

wa_true_grit_2.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
