wa_true_grit_2.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
wa_true_grit_2.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
wa_true_grit_2.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
wa_true_grit_2.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

wa_true_grit_2.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
wa_true_grit_2.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
wa_true_grit_2.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
wa_true_grit_2.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
wa_true_grit_2.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

wa_true_grit_2.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
wa_true_grit_2.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
wa_true_grit_2.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
wa_true_grit_2.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
wa_true_grit_2.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

wa_true_grit_2.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
wa_true_grit_2.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
wa_true_grit_2.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
wa_true_grit_2.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
wa_true_grit_2.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

wa_true_grit_2.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
wa_true_grit_2.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
wa_true_grit_2.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
wa_true_grit_2.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
wa_true_grit_2.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

wa_true_grit_2.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
wa_true_grit_2.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
wa_true_grit_2.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
wa_true_grit_2.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
wa_true_grit_2.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Scatter Lake basin
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Libby Lake
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Boiling Lake basin
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
wa_tupshin_peak_scramble.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: Skyline Lake
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: Trap Lake
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_tye_peak_e_route.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_tye_peak_e_route.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_tye_peak_e_route.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_ultramega_ok.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
wa_ultramega_ok.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
wa_ultramega_ok.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
wa_ultramega_ok.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_ultramega_ok.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

wa_ultramega_ok.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
wa_ultramega_ok.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
wa_ultramega_ok.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
wa_ultramega_ok.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
wa_ultramega_ok.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

wa_ultramega_ok.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
wa_ultramega_ok.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
wa_ultramega_ok.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
wa_ultramega_ok.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
wa_ultramega_ok.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

wa_ultramega_ok.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_ultramega_ok.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
wa_ultramega_ok.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
wa_ultramega_ok.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
wa_ultramega_ok.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

wa_ultramega_ok.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
wa_ultramega_ok.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
wa_ultramega_ok.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
wa_ultramega_ok.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
wa_ultramega_ok.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

wa_ultramega_ok.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
wa_ultramega_ok.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
wa_ultramega_ok.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
wa_ultramega_ok.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
wa_ultramega_ok.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_unicorn_peak_r1.name: Snow Lake Camp
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

wa_unicorn_peak_r1.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

wa_unicorn_peak_r1.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

wa_unicorn_peak_r1.name: Cougar Rock Campground
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

wa_unicorn_peak_r1.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter

wa_unicorn_peak_r1.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. It has been closed through 2026 for a rehabilitation project, so confirm its status before planning around it. When running it is low, forested and warm, which makes it a reasonable shoulder-season option when the higher campgrounds are shut.
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
wa_unicorn_peak_r1.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: Lake Valhalla
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: Skyline Lake
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: Trap Lake
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

wa_union_peak_se_route.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
wa_union_peak_se_route.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
wa_union_peak_se_route.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
wa_union_peak_se_route.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
wa_union_peak_se_route.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Lake Stuart
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: The north-side staging point, used by parties approaching the Complete North Ridge or the Sherpa Glacier from Mountaineer Creek rather than walking around the peak from Ingalls. Road access is seasonal in a way the Teanaway side is not: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road generally closes from November until sometime in May, which shortens the window from this side considerably. Where the Stuart Zone boundary falls relative to the upper Mountaineer Creek basin and the Stuart Glacier moraine is genuinely unclear — some maps place Stuart's north side outside the permit zones — so a party bivying high in that basin should confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District rather than assume, and carry a permit if in doubt.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.water: The lake and Mountaineer Creek are reliable all season; treat lake water and camp well back from the shore
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.permit: Enchantment Permit Area, STUART ZONE, Wenatchee River Ranger District. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through Oct 31, allocated by group through the Recreation.gov advance lottery with a small remainder released otherwise. Outside that window no overnight permit is required, though self-registration at the trailhead is asked for. Day use needs only the free trailhead permit plus a Northwest Forest Pass.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.capacity: Several established sites around the lake, but the real limit is the permit quota — the Stuart Zone releases only a small number of group permits per night

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Goat Pass bivies
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: North Ridge notch bivy
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

wa_vanishing_point.name: Barclay Lake
wa_vanishing_point.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.
wa_vanishing_point.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
wa_vanishing_point.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
wa_vanishing_point.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.

wa_vanishing_point.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
wa_vanishing_point.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.
wa_vanishing_point.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
wa_vanishing_point.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
wa_vanishing_point.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

wa_vanishing_point.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_vanishing_point.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
wa_vanishing_point.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
wa_vanishing_point.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
wa_vanishing_point.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

wa_vanishing_point.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
wa_vanishing_point.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake.
