wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.

wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.permit: COUNTY park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_r1.capacity: A developed county campground with tent and equestrian sites on a large park property; nightly fee

wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
wa_wilmans_peak_scramble.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. The final two miles to Twin Lakes are narrow, unmaintained for passenger cars, short of pullouts, and genuinely want high clearance. Parties turned back at the lower lot are looking at an extra two miles and roughly 1,500 ft of road walking each way before the climb even starts, which turns a comfortable day on Winchester or a two-day Larrabee trip into something much longer, and is a good reason to plan on sleeping out. The road is snowbound well into the season most years and is often not drivable to the upper end until July. Call the ranger station before committing, and if you park low, camping in a pullout the night before is a common and reasonable way to save the morning.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.water: Creeks cross the road in places but there is nothing reliable at the lot itself; carry water up from the valley or plan to filter higher
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and the state parks pass is not accepted here. Fill in the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register where one is provided. Dispersed roadside camping on national forest land outside the wilderness boundary is generally allowed, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a pullout.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: A dozen or so vehicles in the trailhead lot, plus scattered pullouts along the road; it fills on summer weekends and there is nowhere to turn around if you keep going and change your mind

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pack costs you nothing, so most parties on Winchester, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak sleep here and start from the isthmus between the lakes. The Winchester Mountain trail and the High Pass trail both begin there. It does not melt out completely until July in most years, and late-season parties should expect a busy, social camp rather than a quiet one. Everything the lakes hold is heavily used; pick an established site rather than making a new one in the meadow.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.water: The two lakes, right at camp. No treated water; filter or boil.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: A 1935 lookout on the 6,521 ft summit, kept standing by volunteers from a local hiking club rather than by the agency, and genuinely open for anyone to sleep in on a first-come basis. It is 1.7 miles and about 1,300 ft above the Twin Lakes trailhead, which makes it one of the easiest real summits in the range to reach and a fine advance camp for a light party heading on to Mount Larrabee, though it sits off the direct High Pass line and most climbers heading for American Border Peak carry on past the junction rather than up. Treat the building as borrowed. It survives on people sweeping it out, closing the shutters properly, packing out their rubbish and leaving it drier than they found it; a run of poor behaviour is exactly why the winter season was closed. Always carry a tent or bivy, because it may well be occupied when you arrive and there is only room for two on the bunks. There are patches of ground outside the building flat enough to sleep on. The trail crosses steep, exposed snow slopes that linger into July and sometimes August, and an ice axe is the right call before the traverse is bare.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.water: None at the summit. Carry everything up from Twin Lakes, or melt snow early in the season.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: Free, no reservations, no fee, and no way to book it. Locked from November through May, reopening when conditions allow, and off limits as a shelter in winter beyond stepping inside with the shutters left as they are. Wilderness rules apply on the trail and at the summit: no fires at all, party size twelve, no toilet, so pack out everything including human waste.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: Two bunks inside and floor space for a couple more at a squeeze; twelve is the legal party limit but the building comfortably holds far fewer

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: High Pass camp
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: The standard camp for the southeast ridge of Tomyhoi Peak, and the reason Tomyhoi is a comfortable overnight rather than a very long day. From the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft the trail climbs towards Gold Run Pass, forks left onto the meadows trail and reaches the scatter of tarns at roughly 5,580 ft in about four miles. From camp the route drops northwest over a hump to a col near 6,266 ft and follows the ridge over benches and a small glacier remnant to the false summit and the class 3 summit block. This is one of the most heavily impacted alpine basins in the district and the rules exist because the meadow was being destroyed; a single careless night on heather leaves a scar that lasts years. Mountain goats frequent the basin, are habituated, and will come to camp for the salt in urine, so pee on rock well away from the tents. Snow covers the basin into July and the tarns can still be part frozen at the start of the season.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.water: The tarns themselves. They are shallow, warm late in the season and shared with a great many campers, so filter and draw well away from where people wash.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail EXCEPT at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: Perhaps eight to ten small sites among the tarns, all of them well used; expect company, and expect to take whichever pad is left rather than the one you wanted

wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.name: Tomyhoi Lake
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.notes: Worth knowing about mostly so you do not plan a climb around it. Despite the name, Tomyhoi Lake is not the camp for Tomyhoi Peak: the trail from the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead climbs to Gold Run Pass and then loses roughly 1,500 ft over two miles down the far side to the lake at about 3,727 ft, while the peak's southeast ridge starts from the tarns high above. Camping here and climbing the peak means regaining everything you gave away. It is a good option for a party that wants a low, sheltered, uncrowded night in the trees when the meadows are snowed under or the tarns are full, and it is the natural bail if weather closes the high ground. The last stretch of trail down to the lake is brushy and easy to lose, and the north side of Gold Run Pass is steep, exposed and holds snow into late summer, so carry an axe and traction if you are dropping in early in the season.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.permit: No camping within one mile of Gold Run Pass, which rules out the whole upper part of the descent; the lake itself is far enough down to be legal. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, recreation pass on the vehicle, no fires, party size twelve, pack out waste.
wa_winchester_mountain_south_trail.capacity: A handful of rough forested sites at the lake; quiet, and rarely full

wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.name: Four Point Lake — the Chewuch-side base for Remmel Mountain
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.notes: The base for REMMEL MOUNTAIN, an 8,685 ft pile of granite carrying an old lookout site and one of the great viewpoints of the wilderness. The line in is the Chewuch trail from the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop — a long, gentle valley walk of easy miles past Chewuch Falls with dispersed camping most of the way, to a signed junction at about thirteen miles for the Four Point Lake and Coleman Ridge trail. That trail FORDS THE CHEWUCH RIVER almost immediately and it is the crux of the approach: early in the season with snowmelt running it is genuinely difficult and there is not always a log. Past the ford the grade steepens sharply and about two miles of climbing reaches the lake at 6,850 ft, with a spur into the basin. From camp the summit goes on open ground by way of the Coleman Ridge side, and it is a scramble rather than a climb. Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.

wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
wa_windy_peak_iron_gate_trail.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.

Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
wa_windy_peak_windy_creek_trail.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
wa_windy_peak_windy_creek_trail.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
wa_windy_peak_windy_creek_trail.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

wa_witches_tower_south_face.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
wa_witches_tower_south_face.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

wa_witches_tower_south_face.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
wa_witches_tower_south_face.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
wa_witches_tower_south_face.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

wa_witches_tower_south_face.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_witches_tower_south_face.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
wa_witches_tower_south_face.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
wa_witches_tower_south_face.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

wa_witches_tower_south_face.name: Gnome Tarn
wa_witches_tower_south_face.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
wa_witches_tower_south_face.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_witches_tower_south_face.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
wa_witches_tower_south_face.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
wa_witches_tower_south_face.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

wa_witches_tower_south_face.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
wa_witches_tower_south_face.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
wa_witches_tower_south_face.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
wa_witches_tower_south_face.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.name: The Tungsten Creek trail camps below the Boundary Trail junction
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.notes: This is where a party climbing Wolframite from the Chewuch actually sleeps on the second night, and it matters because the arithmetic of the approach is punishing without it. The Tungsten Creek trail breaks off the Chewuch trail a little past eight miles and climbs steadily for about six more, with the creek on the left and the bulk of Wolframite ahead — so a party that has walked in from Thirtymile is looking at a long day before the climbing even begins. Breaking the climb here rather than pushing to the Boundary Trail junction puts you on running water, in shelter, and with the steep work done in the cool of the morning. It is also the sensible fallback when the ground at the junction is occupied by a horse party, which happens more often than the remoteness suggests. Expect burned forest in stretches, little shade, and blowdown that changes with every windstorm. Late July through September is the working season; snow holds on the north sides of the passes above into July.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.water: Tungsten Creek runs alongside for the whole climb and is the dependable supply on this approach, holding into the autumn. THIS IS WHERE YOU FILL FOR THE SUMMIT, because the Boundary Trail crest above the junction runs on tarns and snowmelt and is unreliable by August, and the peak itself carries nothing. Old iron pipe from the mining days is scattered along the trail, which tells you where the workings took their water and not that any of it is usable now. Treat everything.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the easy one: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation and nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Thirtymile. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight — this is heavily used horse country. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer in this dry drainage and the wood is scarce enough that most parties do without.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the climb beside the creek, most taking one or two tents, with the better ground in the lower half where the timber is still standing. Nothing developed and no facilities, and you are unlikely to meet anyone.

wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.name: The Boundary Trail horse camp east of the Tungsten junction
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.notes: The obvious camp for a party climbing Wolframite and then continuing east along the Boundary Trail toward Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Basin, which is the classic way to use this corridor — the summits along it are all short detours off the trail with very little gain, and Wolframite is the first of them. Being a mile east of the junction it sits below the peak's south-east side rather than directly under the west approach, so a party going in and straight back out is better served staying at the mine junction ground or lower on Tungsten Creek. Its real value is that it is prepared, level and used, on a crest where most of the camping is improvised. THE WEST SIDE IS THE ROUTE. From the junction the Boundary Trail is followed roughly a mile west to where it turns south for Apex Pass, and the peak is climbed off-trail to the north-east up gentle open slopes; taken well this is easy scrambling, and taken badly it puts you on short steps of harder rock for no reason. Pick the line from below in good light rather than committing to the first gully you meet.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.water: Seasonal and worth checking rather than assuming. There is water at the site early in the year and it becomes unreliable as the summer goes on, in common with everything on this crest — parties have found streams dry and pools with cracked bottoms along this trail in September. Carry up from Tungsten Creek if you are arriving late in the season.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Camp on the existing bare ground. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are the norm here by midsummer.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.capacity: An established site roughly a mile east of the junction with the Tungsten Creek trail, laid out with horse feed in mind, so it takes a stock party comfortably and a walking party easily. One of very few genuinely prepared camps along this stretch of the Boundary Trail.

wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.name: Apex Pass and the high ground west of Wolframite
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.notes: The pass is where the Boundary Trail bends south a mile west of the Wolframite approach, and it is the link between this peak and the Cathedral country — Apex Mountain stands immediately above it, Amphitheater and Cathedral Peak are further west, and a party collecting summits along this crest will pass through here whichever direction they are travelling. As a camp it is bought and paid for in water and wind: the position is superb and the ground gives no protection at all. Its argument is position rather than comfort, since from here Wolframite is a short morning to the east and Apex is a short morning above. WHAT IT IS NOT is a substitute for a lower camp on a first night — a party arriving here tired and dry has made the trip harder, not easier. Snow lies on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much longer after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when the crest is worth traversing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights up here are properly cold by then.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.water: Snowmelt and the odd tarn early in the season, and frequently nothing at all by late summer. This is a place you carry water to, not one you collect at. The last dependable source coming up is Tungsten Creek; coming from the Cathedral side it is the lake basins, which are a long way west. A party that has not carried enough will be walking a long way down for it.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota, no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at whichever trailhead you used. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this height and the alpine turf is fragile enough that a footprint lasts years, so pitch on gravel or rock.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.capacity: Open alpine ground at and around the pass with room for a small party or two on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind from wind.

wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.name: Teapot Lake and the Boundary Trail benches toward Bauerman Ridge
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.notes: The eastern half of the Wolframite corridor, and the camp for a party crossing between this peak and the Horseshoe Basin country rather than going in and out from the Chewuch. It is roughly fourteen miles of mild, high walking from the Tungsten junction east to Horseshoe Basin, staying largely above seven thousand feet, with Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Mountain all coming off the trail as short detours in the same way Wolframite does. THIS TRAVERSE IS DECIDED BY WATER AND NOT BY DISTANCE. In a dry September the crest carries almost nothing, and parties have walked it past empty pools and dry streambeds with this lake and the occasional trickle as the only supply — which turns a gentle high walk into a rationing exercise. Plan the days around the sources rather than around the miles, fill at every one, and treat any pool as suspect. The far end of this line is the Iron Gate trailhead above Toats Coulee, whose last six miles of road want high clearance, and whose Horseshoe Basin camps are recorded in the eastern Pasayten file rather than here.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.water: Teapot Lake is the dependable one on this stretch and that is precisely why parties camp at it rather than on the ridge — but it is a small standing body and has been found stagnant in a dry year, so treat it properly and take it from an inlet if there is one running. The streams and pools between here and the Wolframite junction go dry through the season and cannot be counted on.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from whichever trailhead kiosk you started at, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, but there is little to burn and the ground is thin.
wa_wolframite_mountain_scramble.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and on the benches either side of the trail, room for a party or two at each. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and long odds against meeting anyone.

wa_wright_pond.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
wa_wright_pond.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
wa_wright_pond.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
wa_wright_pond.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
wa_wright_pond.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

wa_wright_pond.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
wa_wright_pond.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
wa_wright_pond.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
wa_wright_pond.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
wa_wright_pond.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_wright_pond.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
wa_wright_pond.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
wa_wright_pond.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
wa_wright_pond.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
wa_wright_pond.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_wright_pond.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
wa_wright_pond.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
wa_wright_pond.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
wa_wright_pond.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
wa_wright_pond.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

wa_wright_pond.name: Lone Fir Campground
wa_wright_pond.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
wa_wright_pond.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
wa_wright_pond.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

wa_wright_pond.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
wa_wright_pond.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
wa_wright_pond.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
wa_wright_pond.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
wa_wright_pond.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway
